note: Raw leads from the 2026-09-09 prior-art sweep: 28 angles, 385 of 408 leads opened by the searching agent. NOT hand-verified except where cited in PRIOR_ART_2026-09-09.md.

leads.title: WWDC19 Session 422 — Designing for Adverse Network and Temperature Conditions
leads.claim: Apple states verbatim that at thermalState .serious "Some measures we take on the system include lowering the frame rate of ARKit apps and Facetime so that they're less intensive," and at .critical "your app should stop using peripherals such as the camera." At .fair iOS "pause[s] discretionary background work like photos analysis."
leads.why: This is the single most load-bearing fact for P1 and P2 together. Your ARKit baseline hit 59.9 poses/s while spending 0 s in serious; your build spent 173/300 s in serious. Under YOUR thermal condition iOS would have throttled ARKit's frame rate too — so the 28.4 vs 59.9 gap is partly a consequence of P2, not an independent problem. It also means the pose-rate target must be defined at a stated thermal state, and that any A/B against ARKit must report the thermal state both arms ran at, or it is not the same condition.

leads.title: ARKit Capture Frame Rate Throttling — Apple App Analytics report definition
leads.claim: Apple ships a production analytics report whose abstract is "Analyze how long it takes for ARKit to throttle the camera frame rate," with the field "Time Until Frame Rate Throttling: Time in seconds until ARKit starts to throttle the capture frame rate" (float), bucketed 0-10 s, 10-30, 30-60, 60-120, 120-180, 180-240, 240-300, 300-600, 600-900, 900-1200, 1200-inf seconds.
leads.why: Direct proof that camera-capture-rate throttling under sustained AR load is normal and expected even for ARKit itself, and that Apple considers the interesting range to run from under 10 s to over 1200 s. It hands you a ready-made KPI for your own engine: 'time until we have to throttle', measured in seconds, with Apple's own bucket boundaries — a better P1/P2 metric than mean poses/s over a fixed 300 s window, which hides when the collapse happened.

leads.title: Unity ARKit XR Plugin CHANGELOG 3.0.0-preview.3 — matchFrameRate did not account for thermal throttling
leads.claim: Verbatim from the 2019-09-26 entry: "The 'match frame rate' option did not account for thermal throttling, which can put ARKit into a 30 frames per second update mode while Unity would keep trying to update at 60 frames per second. This could lead to visual artifacts like judder. The calculated frame rate now takes the thermal state into account and will do a better job matching ARKit's update rate."
leads.why: A shipping product's bug report that quantifies the ARKit thermal behaviour: ARKit falls to a 30 fps update mode under thermal throttling. That is almost exactly your 28.4 poses/s. It also shows the shipping fix is not 'go faster' but 'let the consumer follow the producer's actual rate' — i.e. the back-pressure/latency collapse you describe in P1 is what happens when the consumer keeps assuming 60 while the producer has been throttled to 30. Reading the thermal state and re-deriving the target rate is the cheap, already-proven mitigation.
leads.license: Unity Companion License (the changelog text is the usable part; do not copy the code)

leads.title: Kimera: an Open-Source Library for Real-Time Metric-Semantic Localization and Mapping (Kimera-VIO)
leads.claim: Verbatim: "Feature detection, stereo matching, and geometric verification are executed at each keyframe, while we only track features at intermediate frames." Measured front-end cost: ~4.5 ms average on intermediate (tracking-only) frames vs ~45 ms combined average on keyframes — a 10x difference.
leads.why: This is the authoritative, permissively licensed (Kimera-VIO is BSD-2, MIT-SPARK) counter-example to 'detection runs on EVERY frame because that is what the upstream tracker does'. It is a whole-source replication candidate for the front-end scheduling policy: KLT on every frame, detect/match/verify only on keyframes. If your CLAHE+corner-detection is the ~19-22 ms item that misses the 16.7 ms budget at 60 fps, running it on keyframes only is the structural fix for P1 and removes most of the per-frame GPU energy behind P2. Their 4.5 vs 45 ms split is the number to size your own budget against.

leads.title: AOSP Performance management — sustained performance mode
leads.claim: Verbatim: "a device using normal max clocks might be able to render at 60 FPS for a few minutes, but after the device heats up, it may throttle to 30 FPS by the end of 30 minutes. When using sustained mode, the device can, for example, render consistently at 45 FPS for the entire 30 minutes." Implementation: POWER_HINT_SUSTAINED_PERFORMANCE in the power HAL, isSustainedPerformanceModeSupported(), Window.setSustainedPerformanceMode(); "the power hint caps the maximum frequencies of the CPU and GPU at the highest sustainable levels." CTS runs ~30 minutes and requires <5% change in frame rate over time.
leads.why: This is the canonical statement of the exact failure you describe in P1 — nominal clocks give 5 ms, then downclocking gives 19-22 ms and the engine falls behind — and the canonical shipping mitigation: never run at boost clocks at all, run at the sustainable clock from t=0 so the frame budget is constant. It is a one-call API on Android and gives you a defensible target: a <5% drift in pose rate over 30 minutes rather than a high mean over 300 s. There is no iOS equivalent API, so on iOS the same idea has to be implemented by self-limiting work (see the ADPF and Unity leads).

leads.title: Android Thermal API (ADPF) — getThermalHeadroom and mitigation ordering
leads.claim: getThermalHeadroom(forecastSeconds) returns 0.0-1.0; documented action thresholds: >0.95 or >1.0 reduce workload immediately, >0.85 keep watch and reduce if possible, <=0.85 safe to increase quality. Maximum polling frequency is once every 10 seconds — calling more often returns NaN. Recommended mitigation order: (1) shift to smaller cores, (2) reduce frame rate, (3) lower graphics fidelity/resolution, (4) reduce network work. NDK: AThermal_acquireManager / AThermal_getThermalHeadroom / AThermal_registerThermalStatusListener. Java API 30+, headroom thresholds API added in Android 15.
leads.why: Gives you a forecast, not just a current state — you can start shedding work ~30 s before throttling instead of after back-pressure has already collapsed latency. The documented mitigation ORDER is itself the answer to 'what do we drop first' for P1/P2: frame rate before fidelity. Note the 10 s / NaN trap, which is exactly the kind of silent-exit failure your project keeps hitting. iOS has only the coarse 4-level ProcessInfo.thermalState with no headroom or forecast, so the Android arm can act earlier than the iOS arm — plan the policy for the weaker signal.

leads.title: android/games-samples — agdk/adpf reference implementation
leads.claim: Apache-2.0 licensed native C/C++ sample that displays thermal status via the Thermal API, "Reduces the target framerate when the device thermal state changes," and drives the render thread with PerformanceHintManager. Requires API 24 minimum, API 30+ for Thermal, API 31+ for Performance Hints.
leads.why: An authoritative implementation under a license you can copy from in full, which is your stated requirement — you do not have to invent the thermal control loop. It is the Android half of a thermal governor for your front end; the iOS half has to be written against ProcessInfo.thermalState because no Apple sample equivalent exists. Also note PerformanceHintManager: telling the OS your target frame duration lets the scheduler pick a lower, steadier clock instead of boosting and then collapsing — the software analogue of sustained performance mode.

leads.title: Apple DTS answer: avoiding frame-rate drop when ThermalState is serious (forum thread 696078)
leads.claim: iPhone 12 Pro / iOS 15.0.1: TrueDepth capture through ARKit drops from ~15 fps to 5 fps once ThermalState.serious is reached. Apple DTS engineer's accepted answer: iterate ARConfiguration.supportedVideoFormats and pick the lowest resolution and frame rate; "dropping from 60 fps to 30 fps should have significant thermal improvement"; profile with Time Profiler; accept that some throttling is outside developer control (e.g. outdoor sunlight).
leads.why: Apple's own support position on exactly your P2, and it is not 'optimise the kernels' — it is 'capture less'. Two things follow. First, the reduction is on the CAPTURE configuration, not on your compute: at 1920x1440 you are paying camera+ISP+bandwidth for pixels your tracker does not need. Second, it warns that ambient conditions (sun, charging) move the result, which matters because your 300 s baseline was measured while charging — a condition your own memory already flags as a 1.7x thermal penalty on Android bench runs.

leads.title: Configuring the camera — ARCore CameraConfig (separate CPU image and GPU texture streams)
leads.claim: Verified on the page: "Selecting a lower resolution GPU texture may help improve app performance by reducing GPU load and lowering memory bandwidth requirements, although is not guaranteed to improve performance in all cases." ARCore exposes CameraConfig.getImageSize() ("image frames for processing that are sent on CPU stream") separately from getTextureSize() ("image frames for texture that are sent on GPU stream"). NOT VERIFIED — appeared only in search snippets and I could not find it on the camera-configs page, the CameraConfig reference, or issues #547/#667: the frequently repeated claim that the CPU stream defaults to VGA 640x480, that ARCore uses that stream for world comprehension, and that imageSize 640x480 + textureSize 1920x1080 uses ~43% less DRAM bandwidth than 1920x1080 + 1920x1080.
leads.why: The architectural point stands even without the unverified 43%: the only shipping mobile AR platform with a public API here deliberately splits a low-resolution CPU/tracking stream from a high-resolution display/texture stream. You run tracking at 1920x1440 — roughly 9x the pixel area of VGA — through CLAHE, pyramid, Scharr and Harris every frame. Decoupling 'resolution the tracker sees' from 'resolution the user sees' is the biggest single lever on P1 and P2, and it is a product decision (it changes results), so it needs flagging as such rather than being treated as a lossless speed-up.

leads.title: LLM Inference at the Edge: Mobile, NPU, and GPU Performance Efficiency Trade-offs Under Sustained Load
leads.claim: iPhone 16 Pro (A18 Pro, 6-core GPU): peak 40.49 tok/s for iterations 1-2, Warm state from iteration 3 (~96 s in) averaging 24.96 tok/s (-38.4%), Hot state from iteration 17 plateauing at 23.67 +/- 0.28 tok/s (-41.5% from peak). Galaxy S24 Ultra (Adreno 750): GPU clock falls from a brief 1000 MHz boost to a 720-770 MHz plateau by iteration 8, throughput -15.0%. A 1-second inter-iteration gap was not enough for either phone to recover thermally. Raspberry Pi 5 + Hailo-10H NPU showed 0.04% CV with no throttling at 52.7 +/- 0.8 C (CPU) / 58.5 +/- 1.1 C (NPU).
leads.why: Independent measurement of the exact curve shape you are fighting on a device one generation newer than yours: the sustained plateau on a modern iPhone GPU is ~58-60% of peak, and it arrives within ~100 seconds. That calibrates your 5 ms nominal vs 19-22 ms throttled figure (a 3.8-4.4x gap, considerably worse than their 1.7x, which suggests part of your slowdown is contention with the camera pipeline rather than pure DVFS). It also says the plateau is flat and predictable — so designing for the plateau (sustained mode thinking) is sound, and that a 1 s idle gap buys nothing, which kills naive duty cycling at that granularity.

leads.title: Vector-Processing for Mobile Devices: Benchmark and Analysis (Swan)
leads.claim: On Snapdragon 855 (1x Cortex-A76 @2.8 GHz + 3x @2.4 GHz + 4x A55 @1.8 GHz, Adreno 640 GPU, Hexagon 690 DSP): "GPU and DSP kernel launch overhead alone is 1.9x and 19% of the average execution time" of nine CPU-accelerated libraries — GPU launch overhead 230 us, DSP 20 us. "vector processing outperforms GPU in matrix multiplication with less than 4M FP32 operations despite 96x less throughput." Library speedups from NEON: libjpeg-turbo 3.3x (3.6x energy), libpng 3.3x (3.2x), libwebp 4.2x (4.4x).
leads.why: The negative result you asked for, with a number: on a mobile GPU each dispatch costs ~230 us of launch overhead, so a front end built from many small dispatches per frame pays a fixed tax that NEON does not. Your own segment accounting already found the cost is in per-dispatch sub-range binding rather than in the layout, which is the same phenomenon from the other side. It argues for fewer, larger dispatches (which you have already started) and for honestly benchmarking a NEON arm on the small stages — and note the energy column: NEON gave 3.2-4.4x energy improvement, i.e. CPU SIMD is not automatically the hot option for P2.

leads.title: Unity Adaptive Performance 5.0 — the scaler menu and thermal-driven targets
leads.claim: Concrete shipping scaler set driven by thermal warning level and thermal trend: Framerate (Application.targetFrameRate), Variable Refresh Rate, Resolution (dynamic resolution / render scale), LOD Bias, MSAA/SMAA, Shadows (distance, cascades, resolution), Transparency, View Distance, Physics fixedDeltaTime, Batching, LUT size, Decals, Layer Culling. Three states: Nominal, Throttling Imminent, Throttling. Default target 60 FPS, reduced to 45 FPS under thermal stress; a physics sample went from 28 ms to 21 ms average frame time with scaling on.
leads.why: The most complete published taxonomy of what a shipping engine actually turns down, and in what order, when a phone heats up — plus the key structural idea of acting at 'Throttling Imminent' rather than at 'Throttling'. Translate the list to your front end: pyramid levels, detection cadence, CLAHE tile count, tracking resolution, max features. The 60 to 45 FPS default is also a useful precedent for P1: shipping products deliberately choose a lower constant rate over a high rate that collapses. Unity's own code is not permissively licensed, so treat this as the design menu and take the implementation from the Apache-2.0 ADPF sample.
leads.license: Unity Companion License — do not copy the code

leads.title: Power and Thermal Analysis of Commercial Mobile Platforms
leads.claim: Nexus 6P (Snapdragon 810: 4x A53, 4x A57, Adreno 430) and Odroid-XU3 (Exynos 5422, Mali T628). Measured throttling-induced frame-rate drops on real apps: Paper.io 35 -> 23 FPS (-34%), Stickman Hook 59 -> 40 FPS (-32%), Facebook 35 -> 24 FPS (-31%), Amazon 35 -> 28 FPS (-20%), Hangouts 42 -> 38 FPS (-10%). Package temperature reached 50 C without throttling on one workload; with the thermal governor enabled another was held below 40 C. Critical power threshold for system stability on Exynos 5422: 5.5 W; 3DMark + a background load drew 3.65 W total.
leads.why: Gives the order of magnitude of the whole-phone sustained power envelope — single-digit watts, ~3.5-5.5 W total for the entire device — which is the budget your camera at full resolution plus full-resolution GPU work every frame has to fit inside alongside everything else. For P2, where you know CPU load matches ARKit (0.80 core-equivalents) and the extra energy is elsewhere, this frames the search: at a ~4 W budget, a full-res camera stream plus per-frame full-res GPU passes is a large fraction, not a rounding error. Also useful as an independent measurement of what 30% throttling looks like on real apps.

leads.title: UNISOC leverages ADPF for enhanced Android gaming performance (case study)
leads.claim: LineageW (NCSOFT) on UNISOC SoCs with ADPF (PerformanceHintManager + getThermalHeadroom + Game Mode): frame rate +11.5% at Low graphics, +28.1% at Medium, +50.1% at High; power change +9.9% (Low), -3.7% (Medium), +3.1% (High). No temperature delta in degrees C is published.
leads.why: Evidence with numbers that the hint-plus-headroom loop is worth large sustained frame-rate gains on real hardware, not a rounding error — +50% at the heaviest setting is the same regime as your P1 gap. The power column is the honest caveat: ADPF bought frame rate roughly at constant energy, so it fixes 'the engine falls behind' but does not by itself fix '173 s in serious'. For P2 you still need to remove work, not just schedule it better.

leads.title: WWDC25 Session 226 — Profile and optimize power usage in your app (Power Profiler)
leads.claim: Power Profiler runs either connected to Xcode or on-device without Xcode, and attributes energy per subsystem: "There are a number of metrics I can inspect, related to different subsystems: the CPU, GPU, display, and networking power impact," plus a system power usage lane. Worked example: CPU power impact score 21 during a spike, 4.3 after optimisation, 1 at baseline; a selected trace region reported 10.5%/hr system power usage. The transcript gives no camera-subsystem metric and no thermal thresholds.
leads.why: Your P2 statement is 'CPU load is 0.80 core-equivalents, same as ARKit, so the extra energy is going somewhere else' — this is the Apple-supported instrument for actually attributing that energy to CPU vs GPU vs display vs network on device, in the field, over a 300 s run, instead of inferring it. Note the gap it will not close: there is no camera lane, so isolating camera/ISP cost still has to be done by differential measurement (same session with the tracker's compute disabled but the camera running at the same format).

leads.title: Zero-Copy GPU Compute on Camera Frames in React Native — What Actually Worked
leads.claim: Someone else is running WGSL compute shaders on live phone camera frames through Dawn, with zero pixel copies: AVCaptureSession → CVPixelBuffer (IOSurface) → Dawn SharedTextureMemory::ImportSharedTextureMemory(ioSurface) → wgpu::Texture → compute → output texture. Measured on iPhone 16 Pro at 4K: GPU frame time 2.88 ms single compute pass, 4.0 ms with two passes, sustained 120 fps camera + 120 fps display, thermalState 'nominal', no drops. Negative results recorded in the same post: copying raw pixels to JS (8 MB/frame at 30 fps) 'overwhelms the garbage collector' and crashes from memory pressure within seconds; device.queue.writeTexture() 'returns zeros through JSI'; copyBufferToTexture() 'completely stubbed out'; ImportSharedTextureMemory() is C++ only. Android path uses AHardwareBuffer through the same SharedTextureMemory API. Multi-pass uses ping-pong texA/texB alternation.
leads.why: This is the closest thing found to our exact architecture (Dawn/WebGPU compute on phone camera frames) and it says the two things we most need to know: (a) the import path that makes the camera frame cost 0 MB of extra footprint and 0 bytes of copy traffic on both iOS and Android, which attacks P3 (276 MB) and P2 (DRAM traffic = heat); (b) at 4K a two-pass compute chain is 4 ms on an A18 while sustaining thermalState nominal — so a compute chain alone is not what puts us 173 s into 'serious'; the suspects are the extra copies, the full-res camera channel, and the number of passes, not compute per se. It also names the ping-pong texture pattern we need for pyramid reuse.
leads.license: article on DEV; companion repo github.com/kbrandwijk/react-native-webgpu-camera, license not stated in the post

leads.title: Dawn feature docs: SharedTextureMemory
leads.claim: Dawn's own feature doc lists the import handle types as wgpu::FeatureName::SharedTextureMemoryIOSurface (Apple), SharedTextureMemoryAHardwareBuffer (Android), SharedTextureMemoryDmaBuf / OpaqueFD (Linux), SharedTextureMemoryDXGISharedHandle / D3D11Texture2D (Windows), SharedTextureMemoryZirconHandle (Fuchsia). Textures created from shared memory 'are not valid to use inside a queue operation until access to the memory is explicitly started using BeginAccess'; 'Access is ended using EndAccess'. Shared fences are passed in on BeginAccess (GPU waits on them) and exported on EndAccess.
leads.why: Authoritative primary source for the one API that lets our Dawn front end consume the camera frame without a copy on all three of our targets — IOSurface on iOS, AHardwareBuffer on Mali and Adreno — so it satisfies the 'no platform-specific knife' rule. Every full-res frame we currently stage through a WebGPU buffer/texture write is both a duplicate allocation (P3) and DRAM write+read traffic (P2). The BeginAccess/EndAccess fence contract is the thing that has to be replicated exactly; it is also where a wrong lifetime silently stalls the camera producer.

leads.title: WWDC21 Session 10153 — Create image processing apps powered by Apple silicon
leads.claim: Apple, verbatim: 'Both CVPixelBuffer and the Metal textures -- which we just rendered into -- are backed by the same underlying IOSurface copy in the system memory'; 'due to the Unified Memory Architecture, we can seamlessly move data between GPU and media engine block with no memory copies'. Restructuring one pipeline to fuse passes and drop intermediates: 'Bandwidth goes down from 2.16 gigabytes to just load and store worth 810 megabytes, and that's 62 percent reduction in memory traffic to the device memory' and 'We don't need two intermediate device buffers saving 270 megabytes of memory per frame.'
leads.why: Apple's own numbers for the exact lever we have not pulled: fusing passes so intermediates never round-trip to device memory. 62% less memory traffic and 270 MB/frame of intermediates removed is the shape of the P2 fix, and it is a lossless restructuring (same output, fewer stores). Our chain CLAHE → pyramid → Scharr → Harris → LK writes a full-res intermediate at nearly every step; each one is a store plus a load at 1920x1440. This is also the citable authority for treating the camera CVPixelBuffer as already-GPU memory rather than uploading it.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums — 'AVCaptureVideoDataOutput consumes three times more memory than AVCaptureMovieFileOutput'
leads.claim: Same app, same session: AVCaptureMovieFileOutput sits at 56 MB idle and 56 MB while recording. Swapping to AVCaptureVideoDataOutput with setSampleBufferDelegate and alwaysDiscardsLateVideoFrames = true, and delegate methods that do nothing at all, takes idle footprint to 151–187 MB, and 260 MB while writing with AVAssetWriter. Community diagnosis (not an Apple engineer): 'I suspect your memory increase is caused by CVPixelBufferPool ... I believe it maintains 10 (or 12 or 15) buffer references (unable to find definitive documentation), and I've not found a way to configure or change the pool size.' Device and resolution are not stated in the thread.
leads.why: Directly sizes a chunk of our P3 gap that we may be blaming on the tracker. Just attaching a video-data-output delegate costs ~100–130 MB of pool in someone else's empty app. At 1920x1440 the pool unit is ~4.1 MB (420 biplanar) or ~11 MB (BGRA); 12 buffers is ~50 MB or ~132 MB. So the first P3 experiment is not in our code at all: measure the pool, and drop the tracking channel's resolution and/or pixel format. Note ARKit also runs a capture session, so the honest comparison is our pool vs its pool.

leads.title: Arm — How low can you go? Building low-power, low-bandwidth Arm Mali GPUs
leads.claim: Arm's own figure: 'Every time the GPU reads or writes one byte of memory, it consumes about 150 picojoules (pJ)' (2x32 LPDDR2, ballpark). At 4–8 GB/s that is 0.6–1.2 W, i.e. 'memory bandwidth can eat up our entire power budget' against a mobile GPU budget of roughly one watt. Concrete win from cutting traffic: on Mali-T604 running Angry Birds, transaction elimination took total GPU bandwidth from 6.5 MB/frame to 3.4 MB/frame (~50%) and removed ~75% of tile writebacks.
leads.why: Gives P2 a unit. Our front end at 1920x1440 grayscale is 2.76 MB per full-res pass; CLAHE + pyramid + Scharr + Harris + LK is easily 8–12 full-res touches, i.e. ~25–35 MB/frame of DRAM traffic, ~1 GB/s at 30 fps and ~2 GB/s at the 60 fps we want. On Arm's number that is a meaningful fraction of the GPU's whole power budget spent on moving pixels, not computing them — which matches 'CPU load equal to ARKit, energy going somewhere else'. It also says the fix is fewer/larger passes and less traffic, the same direction as the WWDC21 62% number.

leads.title: Comparison of modern open-source Visual SLAM approaches (arXiv 2108.01654)
leads.claim: Measured RAM (avg / max MB) on an Intel Core i7-8565U with 16 GB: VINS-Mono 87.0 / 92.1 and Basalt 107.8 / 109.2 on TUM VI corridor; OpenVINS 1686.2 / 3329.1 on the same sequence and 6490.8 / 12819.5 on TUM VI outdoors; ORB-SLAM2 705.9 / 869.9 on EuRoC MH_05; Kimera 250.5 / 273.6 on EuRoC MH_05; DRE-SLAM 5010.7 / 6288.1. CPU load in the same table: Basalt 418.3% avg, ORB-SLAM2 187.2%, Kimera 80.5%, VINS-Mono 68.5%. The paper attributes the blow-ups to sequence length — long trajectories accumulate 'a huge amount of visual features'.
leads.why: Calibrates P3. A bounded-window VIO in the same family as XRSLAM lands at 87–110 MB of algorithm state; systems that let the map grow land at 0.7–12 GB. Our whole process is 276 MB, so the tracker's own state is almost certainly not the problem — the buffers around it are (camera pool, GPU textures, pyramids). It also flags the failure mode to guard against on a 300 s live run: unbounded feature/keyframe accumulation, which is what a map size cap fixes.
leads.license: paper (evidence); systems measured have mixed licenses, VINS/ORB-SLAM2 are GPL

leads.title: FastTrack: GPU-Accelerated Tracking for Visual SLAM (arXiv 2509.10757)
leads.claim: GPU port of the ORB-SLAM3 tracking front end. Desktop RTX 3090 stereo-inertial: overall tracking 14.08 → 5.47 ms (2.57x), ORB extraction 5.38 → 1.88 ms (2.85x), stereo matching 1.10 → 0.42 ms (2.60x), track-local-map 6.35 → 2.11 ms (3.00x); ~71 → ~182 FPS. Embedded Jetson Xavier NX (384-core Volta): 29.39 ms average tracking, 34 FPS, 2.63x. Two memory-specific results: keeping the image pyramid in GPU memory and reusing it for the next stage cut pyramid data transfer from 0.80 ms to 0.08 ms, and they 'eliminate redundant GPU memory allocations' by pre-allocating at startup. ATE essentially unchanged.
leads.why: Independent confirmation of two things we should do regardless of algorithm: (1) the pyramid must be produced and consumed entirely in GPU memory with no round trip — 10x on the transfer line alone; (2) all GPU buffers pre-allocated once at startup, never per frame — that is both a latency win and the thing that keeps peak footprint flat over a 300 s run (P3). Code exists at github.com/sfu-rsl/FastTrack, but it derives from ORB-SLAM3, so the code is GPL and unusable to us — read it for the pattern, cite the paper, do not copy.
leads.license: derives from ORB-SLAM3 → GPLv3, code NOT copyable; paper usable as evidence

leads.title: OpenCV wiki — OE 15. Bit Exactness
leads.claim: OpenCV's own design note on bit-exactness. Bit-exact functions avoid floating point inside the processing loop; 'we are using a variation of softfloat package embedded to OpenCV, i.e. we emulate those operations using integer arithmetics and therefore we guarantee absolutely the same results on each single platform.' resize has separate bit-exact variants; GaussianBlur on 8-bit was converted to bit-exact (tests updated rather than a new API); morphology was 'already de-facto bit-exact'. On the GPU side, verbatim: 'Unfortunately, on GPUs floating-point is usually a faster type than integers, and so the performance may drop a bit' when making OpenCL kernels bit-exact. Platform FMA availability is named as a source of float divergence. Status marked WIP as of Feb 2019.
leads.why: This is the authoritative source for the constraint we chose, and it warns about the exact tax we are paying. Our bit-exact WGSL replicas of OpenCV 4.0.1 must reproduce the fixed-point/softfloat integer paths, and OpenCV's maintainers say plainly that integer emulation is the slow type on GPUs. That is a first-principles explanation for why our 5 ms nominal becomes 19–22 ms when clocks drop, and it frames the P1 tradeoff honestly: a float GPU path would likely be much faster but would no longer be bit-identical, so it is a product decision, not a free speed-up.

leads.title: Resolution and Frequency Effects on UAVs Semi-Direct Visual-Inertial Odometry (SVO) for Warehouse Logistics
leads.claim: Systematic sweep of input resolution x frame rate for a VIO front end on a Jetson Nano (Maxwell 128-core, ARM A57 quad @1.43 GHz, LPDDR4 4 GB, 25.6 GB/s), stereo fisheye 848x800 native + BNO055 IMU. CPU usage table: 424x400 = 14 / 16.6 / 18.1 / 19.1 % at 15 / 20 / 25 / 30 Hz; 636x600 = 24.5 / 35 / 37.3 / 45.3 %; 848x800 = 40.7 / 48 / 49.5 / 49.6 %. Best accuracy came at the MIDDLE resolution 636x600 (all axes under 0.25 m error), with error rising at both 848x800 and 424x400; 25–30 Hz gave lower X/Y error than 15–20 Hz. Conclusion: 636x600 at 25 Hz was the best balance.
leads.why: Measured evidence for the P1/P2 product decision of shrinking the tracking channel: dropping from 848x800 to 636x600 (a 0.56x pixel count) roughly halved CPU cost with BETTER accuracy, and going further to 424x400 cost accuracy. It also cuts against a naive 'just go 60 fps': in this study rate mattered less than resolution, and the accuracy gain from 25 → 30 Hz was small. If the same curve holds for us, the answer to 'we deliver 28.4 poses/s at 1920x1440' may be 'run tracking at ~720x540 and 60 fps' rather than making the full-res GPU pass faster.

leads.title: opencv/opencv issue #8144 — the performance is not improved when using GPU on android
leads.claim: Snapdragon 820 Android device, GaussianBlur applied 4x to a 2560x1920 image: 'the running time for GaussianBlur is not changed when I use UMat or Mat' — i.e. the OpenCL/T-API GPU path gave no speed-up over the NEON CPU path. Maintainers closed it as invalid without a technical explanation. Related search evidence in the same area: mobile GPU kernel-launch and transfer overheads can exceed the compute for fine-grained kernels, and OpenCV's own OpenCL guidance is to avoid host/device transfers.
leads.why: A negative result worth having on record before we spend another week on the GPU front end: on a flagship Android SoC, a full-res separable blur on the GPU was not faster than the CPU. It is weak evidence (no profiling, closed as invalid), but it is the recurring shape of the failure — on a phone, a per-frame chain of medium-sized full-res kernels is bandwidth- and launch-bound, not ALU-bound, which is exactly what our own 5 ms → 19–22 ms downclock behaviour looks like. It argues for measuring an NEON reference arm for CLAHE + Harris at our target resolution before optimizing WGSL further.

leads.title: Faster than Fast: Accelerating Oriented FAST Feature Detection on Low-end Embedded GPUs (arXiv 2506.07164)
leads.claim: Abstract, verbatim in part: 'the time-consuming Oriented FAST calculations accounting for approximately half of the entire SLAM system'. Two methods — 'a binary-level encoding strategy to determine candidate points quickly' and 'a separable Harris detection strategy with efficient low-level GPU hardware-specific instructions'. 'Extensive experiments on a Jetson TX2 embedded GPU demonstrate an average speedup of over 7.3 times compared to widely used OpenCV with GPU support.'
leads.why: Aimed squarely at P1's hot spot: corner detection every frame. Two ideas are directly portable to WGSL and are candidate-reduction/separability tricks rather than algorithm changes — a binary-encoded early reject for FAST candidates (most pixels fail; we currently pay full cost for all of them) and a separable Harris. 7.3x over OpenCV-CUDA on a low-end embedded GPU is the right order to turn a 19–22 ms downclocked pass into something that fits 16.7 ms. Caveat before adopting: 'hardware-specific instructions' may not survive the three-platform rule, and a candidate-reject changes nothing numerically only if the reject is provably exact — verify that or treat it as a product decision.
leads.license: arXiv CC-BY 4.0 for the paper; code availability not stated

leads.title: MS-SLAM: Memory-Efficient Visual SLAM With Sliding Window Map Sparsification
leads.claim: Sliding-window map sparsification that keeps only useful non-local map points while retaining all local points for tracking; runs concurrently with tracking and preserves loop closure. README claims memory consumption reduced 'by over 70%' in large-scale scenes, with one example keeping 'only 10.9% of original map points'. Published in Journal of Field Robotics (2024/2025). Crucially: 'This project is built on ORB-SLAM3' and the repo README carries no license statement.
leads.why: The right idea for a map-size cap on a long session (our 300 s run is short; a real user session is not), and the numbers show how far a point cap can go — 10.9% of points retained, >70% memory saved, comparable accuracy. But it is a derivative of ORB-SLAM3, so the code is GPLv3 and unusable to us under our own rules, and the repo does not even state a license. Treat as a published method to be re-derived from a clean source (or from the paper's description with our own implementation), never as code to copy. Flagging it so nobody re-discovers it and starts reading the source.
leads.license: UNSTATED in repo; derives from ORB-SLAM3 → GPLv3, code NOT copyable

leads.title: LiDAR Depth Maps on the GPU in React Native — And a Dawn Upstream Contribution
leads.claim: Names the exact Dawn source location that decides whether a CVPixelBuffer can be imported zero-copy: GetFormatEquivalentToIOSurfaceFormat() in SharedTextureMemoryMTL.mm. The author added kCVPixelFormatType_DepthFloat16/32 and DisparityFloat16/32 → R16Float/R32Float (CL: dawn-review.googlesource.com/c/dawn/+/297995). Failure mode when a format is missing: 'Bind group mismatch, silent black output' — textureLoad returned zeros because Dawn did not recognise the IOSurface format code; the fallback was a CPU readback via CVPixelBufferLockBaseAddress + queue.WriteTexture(). Also: 320x180 depth at 60 fps = 115 KB/frame = 6.9 MB/s of CPU→GPU transfer, 'on a device that does 25GB/sec bandwidth, this is invisible'. 1920x1080 camera input at 60 fps throughout.
leads.why: Operational detail we would otherwise learn the hard way. We only need the luma plane, so the import we want is the 420 biplanar Y plane as R8Unorm; if Dawn's format table does not carry our exact camera format code the page comes back silently black — the same class of silent-exit bug that is already our number-one recurring defect. It also shows the escape hatch (upstream a few case statements to Dawn, which is permissively licensed) and gives a bandwidth yardstick: small transfers are free, full-res ones are not.
leads.license: Dawn is BSD-3-Clause/Apache-2.0; article on DEV

leads.title: OKVIS2 (BSD-3) and Basalt (BSD-3) — permissively licensed bounded-memory VIO back ends
leads.claim: OKVIS2 is released under the 3-clause BSD license and keeps the problem tractable 'by limiting the optimization to a bounded window of keyframes through marginalization', turning marginalized observations into pose-graph edges that can be converted back into landmarks on loop closure. Basalt (gitlab.com/VladyslavUsenko/basalt, TUM) is BSD-3-clause, uses KLT optical flow in the front end and fixed-lag smoothing in the back end. Independently measured RAM for Basalt in the comparison study above: 107.8 MB avg / 109.2 MB max on TUM VI corridor, and 136.5 / 161.5 MB on TUM VI outdoors — i.e. it stays bounded where OpenVINS grew to 12.8 GB on the same outdoor sequence.
leads.why: These are the two clean-licensed sources for 'how do you bound memory over a long session' — marginalization with a fixed keyframe window, with an implementation we are actually allowed to replicate line-for-line, unlike VINS/ORB-SLAM/OKVIS-adjacent GPL work. Basalt's measured 107→136 MB across a short and a long sequence is the proof that the bound holds. Relevant to P3 as the durable answer once the buffer-side savings are taken, and Basalt's KLT front end is the same family as ours so its window management maps onto XRSLAM directly.

leads.title: Dawn ShaderModule.h / ShaderModuleMTL.mm — GetStrictMath(), #pragma METAL fp math_mode(safe), and the dawn:2503 TODO
leads.claim: Dawn's Metal backend emits `(*compileOptions).fastMathEnabled = !GetStrictMath().value_or(false);` and, on macOS 15 / iOS 18+, prepends `#pragma METAL fp math_mode(safe)` or `(relaxed)` to the translated MSL (the pragma "takes precedence over global flags provided to the compiler"). ShaderModule.h declares `std::optional<bool> GetStrictMath() const;` / `std::optional<bool> mStrictMath;` with the comment: "TODO(dawn:2503): Remove the optional when Dawn can has a consistent default across backends. Right now D3D uses strictness by default, and Vulkan/Metal use fast math by default."
leads.why: This is the single most load-bearing fact for your bit-exactness claim. Your WGSL front end is compiled by Dawn on Metal, and Dawn's DEFAULT on Metal is fast math ON (-ffast-math / math_mode(relaxed)) — which legally permits reassociation, x/y -> x*(1/y), FMA contraction and -0/NaN/Inf assumptions. Your measured CPU==GPU identity on the A16 is therefore an artifact of one Apple compiler version, not a contract. The lever exists and is one line: set strict math on the shader module. Equally important, the same comment says Vulkan also defaults to fast math, and Dawn does not implement the strict path there — so the Mali/Adreno arm of your "three platforms together" rule has no equivalent switch today. Verify GetStrictMath is reachable from your native Dawn version before relying on it.

leads.title: WebGPU developer features — strictMath on GPUShaderModuleDescriptor (Chrome)
leads.claim: "A boolean `strictMath` developer option has been added to GPUShaderModuleDescriptor to let you enable or disable strict math during shader module compilation." Usage: `device.createShaderModule({ code, strictMath: true })`. It is "supported on Metal and Direct3D" (Vulkan not mentioned), gated behind chrome://flags/#enable-webgpu-developer-features. Introduced in Chrome 131 (released 2024-11-06). With strict math OFF the compiler may: ignore NaN/Infinity, treat -0 as +0, replace division with reciprocal multiplication, and rearrange operations by associativity/distributivity.
leads.why: Names the exact API surface for the Dawn lever above and confirms in vendor documentation that the strict path is Metal + D3D only. That means: on iOS you can make bit-exactness a compiler contract instead of a lucky observation, but on Android (Vulkan) you cannot — so a bit-exact-on-all-three-platforms guarantee is currently unobtainable through this mechanism, and your no-platform-specific-knives rule collides with it head-on. Worth deciding explicitly whether bit-exactness is an iOS-only property.

leads.title: gpuweb issue #2076 — "Add method to disable fast-math on a per-shader basis"
leads.claim: Filed against the WebGPU spec because fast-math "caused severe numerical inconsistencies across platforms"; one reported case was results "8 orders of magnitude off on Mac OS (Metal backend)" versus Windows and Linux. The issue records the backend asymmetry: D3D12 does not expose fast-math controls and follows IEEE-754 closely except denorms; Vulkan/SPIR-V exposes a granular FP Fast Math Mode bitfield; Metal enables fast-math by default, disableable with -fno-fast-math. PR #2080 is open; the issue is still not a standardized guarantee.
leads.why: Primary-source confirmation that the WebGPU working group itself treats cross-backend numerical divergence as an open, unsolved problem, and that the divergence is large enough to be catastrophic (8 orders of magnitude), not a last-ULP curiosity. If you ever want to say "our WGSL front end is bit-exact", this issue is the reason the claim must be pinned to a specific Dawn revision, a specific backend, and an explicit strictMath setting, and re-verified on every Dawn roll.
leads.venue: W3C GPU for the Web CG

leads.title: luma.gl — GPU Floating-Point Precision Techniques (WGSL evaluation rules)
leads.claim: "The WGSL floating-point evaluation rules permit reassociation and fusion, and do not specify a single rounding direction for all floating-point evaluation." And: WGSL's `fma` "also does not provide the portable, correctly rounded fused-operation contract" needed by Dekker-style TwoProd. Source-level tricks "may affect a particular compiler version, but they cannot turn an optimization-sensitive transform into a WebGPU guarantee."
leads.why: States, with direct links to the normative WGSL sections (§15.7 Floating Point Evaluation, §15.7.5 Reassociation and Fusion), that the language spec itself permits the two transforms that break bit-exactness — reassociation and contraction. Even with strictMath set, the *language* does not promise you a rounding mode. Practical consequence: any WGSL kernel of yours whose parity depends on evaluation order (Scharr accumulation, Harris M-matrix sums, LK 2x2 solve, CLAHE histogram-to-LUT) is parity-fragile by specification, and your parity test must be a gate on every toolchain bump, not a one-time result.

leads.title: tomoaki_teshima (OpenCV contributor) — "OpenCVの丸め誤差bit-exactnessについて"
leads.claim: "基本的にOpenCVのAPIはbit-exactnessを保証しない" (OpenCV APIs generally do not guarantee bit-exactness). Always bit-exact: transpose, split/merge, flip, reshape (pure data rearrangement). Sometimes: cvtColor (e.g. RGB2GRAY), resize with INTER_LINEAR_EXACT / INTER_NEAREST_EXACT, GaussianBlur, imwrite (PNG/BMP only, not JPEG). Everything else: no guarantee. Crucially, validating bit-exactness with tolerance=0 on one platform is insufficient — "別アーキテクチャが必要" (a different architecture is required), e.g. PC vs Raspberry Pi.
leads.why: Two things you can act on. (1) An explicit, function-by-function list from an OpenCV committer of what is and is not bit-exact upstream — note that goodFeaturesToTrack/Harris, Scharr, pyrDown and calcOpticalFlowPyrLK are all in the 'no guarantee' bucket, so 'bit-exact replica of OpenCV 4.0.1' means bit-exact to one build of OpenCV on one CPU, not to OpenCV as a portable definition. (2) The validation rule you are currently missing: a zero-tolerance match on a single device proves nothing about portability; the parity gate must run on a second architecture. You have Mali (Mate 10) and Adreno 660 (P50 Pocket) benches already — running the parity fixture there is the cheap experiment this source prescribes.

leads.title: OpenCV issue #10871 — OpenCL tests too strict; PyrLK is not bit-exact where FMA exists
leads.claim: On a TinkerBoard (ARM/Mali), OCL_Video/PyrLKOpticalFlow.Mat/4 fails, plus 32 opencv_test_core failures (Mul, AddWeighted) and 110 opencv_test_imgproc failures. Reporter (tomoaki0705, an OpenCV maintainer) diagnoses: the LK eigenvalue computation in lkpyramid.cpp involves a square root, and "if the platform hires FMA, the result won't be 'bit-exact'". The failing comparison is an ABSOLUTE threshold: `eq = std::abs(cpuErr[i] - err[i]) < 0.01`. He advocates relative rather than absolute tolerances.
leads.why: The closest published precedent to exactly what you are doing: someone tried to hold a GPU pyramidal-LK implementation to a bit-exact/tight-tolerance CPU reference on an ARM mobile GPU, and it failed specifically because of FMA. It names the exact function (lkpyramid.cpp eigenvalue + sqrt) that is most likely to break your Mali/Adreno parity, and the OpenCV maintainers' response was to loosen the tolerance rather than to make the GPU path exact — i.e. upstream judged bit-exact GPU LK not worth pursuing. Treat that as a cost signal for your Android arm.

leads.title: OpenCV issue #6532 — cuda::SparsePyrLKOpticalFlow error differs from CPU by ~534x (the missing factor of 32)
leads.claim: Same input, same parameters: CUDA mean flow error 0.053374, CPU mean flow error 28.514989. Cause traced to the CPU using fixed-point descaling that the GPU port dropped — CUDA: `err(y,x) = static_cast<float>(errval) / (c_winSize_x * c_winSize_y);` vs CPU: `err[ptidx] = errval * 1.f/(32*winSize.width*cn*winSize.height);`, with the CPU also applying `CV_DESCALE(..., W_BITS1-5)` during interpolation. Reporter: "the factor of 32 is missing - but it might be as well be related to the fixed point computation". Closed via PR #6769.
leads.why: Direct evidence that OpenCV's CPU pyrLK is internally a FIXED-POINT algorithm (W_BITS1, CV_DESCALE, the /32), and that OpenCV's own GPU port silently diverged by a factor of ~534 because the porter reimplemented in float instead of replicating the fixed-point path. This is both a warning (a divergence this large hid in a shipping library for years, because no test checked err) and an opportunity: because the CPU inner loop is integer, a WGSL replica using i32 arithmetic can be bit-exact on Metal AND Mali AND Adreno regardless of fast-math, which is the only route to your three-platform parity.

leads.title: OpenCV issue #6923 — HOGDescriptor: CPU finds a detection, OpenCL finds none
leads.claim: On the same rescaled image (downsample factor 1.199009) with the default people detector, the CPU path returns 1 detection at (x=349, y=148) and the OpenCL path returns 0 detections. The reporter notes it is an edge case with the default SVM but reproduces far more readily with a custom SVM. No maintainer explanation; issue left open.
leads.why: The strongest short argument for why bit-exactness is not pedantry in a SLAM front end: sub-ULP numerical divergence does not stay numerical, it flips discrete decisions. Your pipeline has three such cliffs — Harris/Shi-Tomasi score vs quality threshold in goodFeaturesToTrack, the non-max-suppression comparison, and the LK convergence/eigenvalue rejection test. A one-bit difference on either side of any of those changes the keypoint SET, which changes tracks, which changes pose. This gives you a citable precedent when justifying the parity gate to anyone who calls it overkill.

leads.title: OpenCV issue #26361 — remap: CPU and OpenCL share a 5-bit interpolation LUT, CUDA does not
leads.claim: cv::remap on CPU and OpenCL uses an interpolation lookup table with INTER_BITS = 5 (table size 32), so bilinear weight precision is only ~1/32 = 3.125% ≈ 8/255; CUDA's remap uses raw interpolation. Measured against PyTorch grid_sample: CPU max error 4.54, OpenCL max error 4.54, CUDA max error 0.014. Marked duplicate, milestone 5.0-alpha, no substantive maintainer reply.
leads.why: Useful in two directions. First, it shows OpenCV's OpenCL backend was written to match the CPU's fixed-point LUT exactly (both 4.54) — i.e. bit-exact-by-construction GPU ports of OpenCV DO exist upstream, and the technique is 'copy the integer LUT, do not re-derive in float'. Second, it quantifies the accuracy you inherit by being faithful: your bit-exact replica of OpenCV 4.0.1 also inherits the 3.125% weight quantization in any remap/warp-shaped step. If you ever consider a 'more accurate' GPU variant, this is the explicit product decision to flag.

leads.title: SPV_KHR_float_controls2 — FPFastMathDefault / AllowContract / AllowReassoc, deprecating NoContraction
leads.claim: Defines FPFastMathMode bits AllowContract (0x10000) "Allows a floating-point operation to be contracted with any operation(s) producing its operands", AllowReassoc (0x20000) "…reordered…according to real-number associativity rules", AllowTransform (0x40000). Deprecates the NoContraction decoration in favour of FPFastMathMode. Default: if an instruction has no FPFastMathMode decoration and the entry point sets no FPFastMathDefault execution mode, "the flags to be applied are determined by the client API". AllowTransform must also include AllowContract and AllowReassoc.
leads.why: This is the Android-side lever that corresponds to Metal's math_mode(safe), and it is the mechanism a strict-math implementation on Dawn's Vulkan backend would have to use (per-entry-point FPFastMathDefault with all bits clear). Two operational consequences: (a) the default is delegated to the client API, so Vulkan drivers on Mali and Adreno may legally contract and reassociate your Scharr/Harris/LK arithmetic differently from each other; (b) if you want the Android arm of parity, this extension — plus whether Tint emits it — is the exact thing to check, and if Tint does not, the fixed-point route from OE-15 is your only remaining option.

leads.title: SPIRV-Tools issue #5658 — spirv-opt FMA folding costs 20–30% throughput on Adreno (negative result)
leads.claim: Reporter (castano) measured that suppressing spirv-opt's mul+add -> FMA folding gives "20% to 30% increased throughput" for Spark codecs on Adreno. Adreno offline compiler output: with the fix, 868 total instructions (52x 32-bit ALU, 466x 16-bit ALU); without, 1077 total instructions (200x 32-bit ALU, 335x 16-bit ALU). Root cause: the Adreno compiler has "poor handling of explicit FMA operations", particularly limited fp32 support — fp16 args get promoted to fp32, computed, demoted. Affects "all the Adreno devices"; no impact on ARM, minor gain on PowerVR, slight regression on AMD/Samsung. On NoContraction: "we could overload it to mean that an FMA needs to be evaluated as if it was part of a precise statement, however this is not specified anywhere."
leads.why: A measured, per-vendor cost for the thing you would have to do to make parity portable. It says that on Adreno, forcing or forbidding contraction is worth 20–30% of a shader's throughput and that Adreno's fp32 FMA path is weak — so if you ever add FPFastMathDefault-strict on the Vulkan arm to chase bit-exactness, budget a double-digit percentage regression on the Adreno 660 you already bench on. It also confirms in a Khronos thread that no portable per-instruction 'evaluate precisely' contract exists, which corroborates the WGSL finding above.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums #131733 — Metal fast math is ON by default; use metal::precise for fine-grained control
leads.claim: A developer saw "drastically different behaviour on different iPad's" from a Metal shader, fixed by passing -fno-fast-math. Apple Graphics and Games engineer: "By default Xcode sets Enable Fast Math flags to YES which should correspond to passing the -ffast-math flag to the Metal compiler. If you change the option to NO this will correspond to the -fno-fast-math option being passed to the compiler." Recommended alternative: "The namespace metal::precise provides developers with a mechanism to use the more precise version of Metal standard library functions in a more fine grained way." And: "Fast math allows for compiler optimizations like reassociation over common operations like addition/subtraction/etc. which are not valid under precise math rules… For best performance, in general it is better to try and keep as much of the shader using Fast Math."
leads.why: Vendor confirmation of the two facts that bracket your iOS parity: fast math is the default (so your current bit-exactness is unguaranteed), and Apple's own engineers say results can differ ACROSS APPLE DEVICES with it on — which is a same-vendor portability hazard, not just a cross-vendor one. It also gives a cheaper middle path than global strict math: mark only the parity-critical expressions (the Harris/Shi-Tomasi score, the LK 2x2 solve, the CLAHE clip/redistribute accumulation) as precise rather than de-optimizing every kernel — relevant to P1, since blanket strict math would slow the 5 ms detection budget you are already short on.

leads.title: Accelerated Feature Detectors for Visual SLAM: A Comparative Study of FPGA vs GPU
leads.claim: Ruiqi Ye, Mikel Lujan. Compares FAST, Harris and SuperPoint feature detection on an Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin (OpenCV 4.5.4 / CUDA 11.4 / TensorRT 8.4, VPI Harris) against an AMD Versal VCK190 (Vitis Vision 2022.1), with an Intel Xeon + OpenCV 4.5.5 software baseline, profiling the ICE-BA localization thread on EuRoC-style sequences. Reports the FPGA reaching "up to 3.1x and 1.4x improvements" in run-time and energy efficiency respectively over the GPU implementation, "without sacrificing the accuracy". Power is broken out per implementation into processor watts and accelerator watts (e.g. FAST: FTFast on Orin-VersalSimilar 0.8 W processor + 5.6 W accelerator; FTFast on Orin-max 4.4 + 8.8 W; Vitis FAST 4.9 + 10.8 W). ICE-BA localization thread run-time with 2 Arm cores at 600 MHz: 14.9 ms on A78 vs 31 ms on A72.
leads.why: Relevant to P2 in a way little else is: it measures the ENERGY, not just the latency, of running feature detection on an embedded GPU versus alternatives, and separates processor watts from accelerator watts. Your P2 puzzle is that CPU load matches ARKit (0.80 core-equivalents) yet you sit 173/300 s in thermalState serious — this paper's accelerator-watt column is the shape of the missing measurement, and its headline is that the GPU is the energy-expensive way to do detection even when it is the fast way. It is Jetson/Versal, not a phone, so treat the absolute watts as indicative only; the usable part is the methodology and the direction of the result.

leads.title: ARM Compute Library v20.02 — optical_flow_pyramid_lk.cl (OpenCL pyramidal LK, MIT)
leads.claim: Verbatim from the kernel: `#define W_BITS (14)`, `#define FLT_SCALE (1.0f / (float)(1 << 20))`, `#define D0 ((float)(1 << W_BITS))`, `#define DETERMINANT_THR 1.0e-07f`, `#define EIGENVALUE_THR 1.0e-04f` — i.e. the SAME fixed-point constants as OpenCV's CPU lkpyramid.cpp. Mapping is ONE WORK-ITEM PER KEYPOINT (`idx = get_global_id(0)`), with the window accumulated by a serial nested loop inside that single work-item: `for(int ky = 0; ky < window_dimension; ++ky) { for(int kx = 0; kx < window_dimension; ++kx)`. Bilinear weights are integerised explicitly (`w.s3 = ab.x*ab.y; w.s0 = w.s3 + 1.0f - ab.x - ab.y; w.s12 = ab - w.s3; w = round(w * D0)`) — there are NO `read_imagef`/sampler calls at all; pixels come from `vload2(0, offset(&new_image, ...))`. Convergence test `all(fabs(delta + prev_delta) < 0.01f)`. Removed from ACL in v21.05 ("Remove computer vision support from CL backend"), so v20.02 or earlier must be pinned.
leads.why: This is the only permissively-licensed (MIT) mobile-GPU pyramidal LK we found that keeps OpenCV's exact fixed-point arithmetic instead of falling back on a hardware bilinear sampler — i.e. the only existing GPU LK that is even structurally capable of being bit-exact against the OpenCV CPU path. It is also the OPPOSITE workgroup mapping from OpenCV's OCL kernel: 1 lane per point + serial window, which eliminates the barrier/reduction/divergence machinery entirely. It was written by Arm for Mali, so it is the natural single authoritative source to replicate for the LK stage of a Mali/Adreno/Metal port. Caveat: it was deleted from ACL upstream, so cite the v20.02 tree.

leads.title: OpenCV OCL kernel modules/video/src/opencl/pyrlk.cl — hardware-sampler bilinear, 64 work-items per feature
leads.claim: The kernel declares `__constant sampler_t sampler = CLK_NORMALIZED_COORDS_FALSE | CLK_ADDRESS_CLAMP_TO_EDGE | CLK_FILTER_LINEAR;` and contains NO `W_BITS` / `CV_DESCALE` fixed-point code (only an unused `#define SCALE (1.0f / (1 << 20))`). Mapping: `#define LSx 8`, `#define LSy 8`, `#define BUFFER (LSx*LSy)` = 64 work-items per feature point, `#define GRIDSIZE 3` so each work-item covers a 3x3 = 9-pixel sub-tile, local patch buffer `LM_W = LSx*GRIDSIZE+2` = 26x26 with a border for Sobel; iteration `for (k = 0; k < c_iters; ++k)` with early exit at `#define THRESHOLD 0.01f`; residuals scaled as `((read_imagef(J,...).x * 16384) + 256) / 512`.
leads.why: Direct evidence that OpenCV's own GPU LK CANNOT be bit-exact against its CPU LK by construction: the CPU path uses 14-bit integer bilinear weights, the OCL path delegates interpolation to the texture unit (`CLK_FILTER_LINEAR`), whose rounding is vendor-defined and differs across Mali/Adreno/Apple. If our WGSL replica uses `textureSampleLevel` with linear filtering anywhere in the LK or pyramid stage, bit-exactness is silently lost on every device. It also gives the canonical alternative workgroup mapping (64 lanes/point, 3x3 sub-tile per lane) to benchmark against ARM's 1-lane/point.

leads.title: OpenCV CPU reference — modules/video/src/lkpyramid.cpp fixed-point constants
leads.claim: `const int W_BITS = 14, W_BITS1 = 14;` and `const float FLT_SCALE = 1.f/(1 << 20);`. Bilinear weights: `iw00 = cvRound((1.f-a)*(1.f-b)*(1 << W_BITS)); iw01 = cvRound(a*(1.f-b)*(1 << W_BITS)); iw10 = cvRound((1.f-a)*b*(1 << W_BITS)); iw11 = (1 << W_BITS) - iw00 - iw01 - iw10;` (note iw11 is a residual, not an independent round). Descale macro `CV_DESCALE(x,n) = (((x) + (1 << ((n)-1))) >> (n))`. Derivatives via `calcScharrDeriv()` which dispatches `cv_hal_ScharrDeriv` then a parallel `ScharrDerivInvoker`; SSE path uses `v_dotprod`/`v_muladd`/`v_zip` accumulating into qA11/qA12/qA22, NEON path uses `vmull_s16`/`vaddq_s32`/`vcvtq_f32_s32` into nA11/nA12/nA22.
leads.why: This is the exact arithmetic a bit-exact WGSL replica must reproduce, and it names the two traps: iw11 is derived by subtraction (so a GPU that recomputes it by rounding will diverge on ~half the sub-pixel positions), and the SSE and NEON accumulators are different code paths — so 'the CPU path' itself is only bit-exact if you fix which SIMD arm is the reference. Worth checking which arm our reference used when we validated the port.

leads.title: OpenCV CUDA sparse PyrLK kernel — dual path because "the texture path keeps failing accuracy tests"
leads.claim: One CUDA block per feature point, `const int BLOCK_SIZE = 128;` (__CUDA_ARCH__ <= 110) else `256`; `tid = threadIdx.y * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`; shared-memory reduction of the 2x2 structure tensor via `reduce<BLOCK_SIZE>(smem_tuple(smem1, smem2, smem3), thrust::tie(A11, A12, A22), tid, ...)`. Two kernels exist: `sparseKernel` using `TextureLinear<cn,T>` with `cudaFilterModeLinear`, and `sparseKernel_` using explicit `BorderReader`+`LinearFilter`, used for `unsigned short`/`int` because, per the source, the texture path keeps failing accuracy tests. Residuals scaled by a hard-coded 32 (`work_type diff = (J_val - I_val) * 32.0f;`), early exit at `fabs(delta.x) < 0.01f && fabs(delta.y) < 0.01f`.
leads.why: OpenCV's own maintainers document that hardware bilinear filtering breaks their accuracy tests badly enough that they shipped a second, sampler-free kernel. That is independent confirmation (from a second GPU backend) of the pyrlk.cl finding above: for a bit-exact port, manual integer interpolation is not a purist choice, it is the only choice. The block-per-point + shared-memory reduction mapping here is the third data point on workgroup mapping (128/256 lanes per point).

leads.title: opencv#12828 — race condition in the OpenCL pyrlk reduction from WAVE_SIZE-guarded barriers
leads.claim: In `modules/video/src/opencl/pyrlk.cl` (around lines 198-210) the `barrier()` calls after the reduction stages were compiled out by `#if WAVE_SIZE >= 32` / `#if WAVE_SIZE >= 16`, letting multiple work-items read/modify `smem1` without synchronisation. Reported on Windows 10 x64 / NVIDIA GTX 1060 / CUDA 10.0 / VS2015. Proposed fix: drop the WAVE_SIZE conditionals and always execute the barriers.
leads.why: Our WGSL port has the same temptation: WebGPU exposes subgroups only behind an extension and Dawn's iOS branch has already burned us once with a bogus subgroup size (memory: vendorId hard-wired to 0 => subgroup reported [4,64]). Any wave-size-implied-synchronisation shortcut in a per-feature reduction is a silent, device-dependent correctness bug, not a performance question. If our LK reduction has WAVE_SIZE-style assumptions, this is a ready-made bug report to check against.

leads.title: A Hacker's Craic — "OpenCL Kanade Lucas Tomasi feature tracking" (N-threads-per-feature design + barrier/early-exit trap)
leads.claim: Design: for an NxM feature window, N threads are assigned per feature, each working a column of M rows, with the first thread of the sub-group tallying results and making the keep/drop decision; local memory holds partial sums; the flat work size is independent of the local workgroup size so it can be tuned. Measured on a GeForce GTX 480 at 640x480 with 3 pyramid levels (1/4 area per level): ~500 us for image preprocessing (pyramid + gradients), and ~1 ms to track 3300 16x16 features, i.e. ~1.5 ms total; incremental cost quoted as ~0.3 us per additional 16x16 feature. Break-even vs CPU quoted at around 500 features. Update note records that early exit of some sub-workgroups broke barrier usage (upsetting at least the AMD CPU driver), and the fix was to keep all threads executing to the end and mask the result.
leads.why: This is the clearest public statement of the serial-per-point iteration problem and its resolution: you cannot let converged points exit early when a barrier-synchronised reduction spans the sub-group — you must run every point to the max iteration count and mask. That converts LK cost from data-dependent to worst-case, which is exactly the kind of thing that turns a 5 ms nominal kernel into a 19-22 ms downclocked one (P1). The ~500-feature break-even is also a useful sanity threshold for whether GPU LK is worth doing at our point counts at all.

leads.title: Hwangbo, Kim & Kanade — "Realtime Affine-photometric KLT Feature Tracker on GPU in CUDA Framework" (CMU RI)
leads.venue: ICCV Workshop on Embedded Computer Vision 2009 (extended in IJRR 2011)
leads.claim: Two thread types: a "pixel thread" (pyramid, gradients, cornerness) and a "feature thread" where ONE thread owns one feature; the feature table is laid out transposed in global memory so that the n-th thread reads every n-th element of each row, giving coalesced access; max features fixed a priori at 512 or 1024 (must be a multiple of 16). Measured: cornerness computation 1.8 ms on GPU vs 4.2 ms for the equivalent CPU version. Setup: GeForce 8800 GTX + Intel Xeon 3.2 GHz, 640x480, 512 features (re-select when < 400 remain), 5 pyramid levels, 15x15 template per level; tracking step ~10 ms/frame, feature selection step ~30 ms, ~40 ms/frame overall. Explicit negative result: "Processes that have many flow controls tend to run faster on the CPU... the sorting process of cornerness measures and the matrix inversion process of the Hessian fall in this category. They may run faster on the CPU even when accounting for additional data transfer between the CPU and the GPU." They keep the lost-feature index table on the CPU and ship it to the GPU.
leads.why: Two things we can act on. (1) It is the second independent design (with ARM's) that puts one thread per feature rather than a workgroup per feature — two of the three serious implementations reject the OpenCV-OCL mapping. (2) It is a measured, authoritative statement that the branchy per-point steps (cornerness sorting, small-matrix solve, feature bookkeeping) belong on the CPU even paying transfer cost — relevant to P1, where our CPU is only at 0.80 core-equivalents and has headroom while the GPU is the thing that downclocks.

leads.title: Swan: "Vector-Processing for Mobile Devices: Benchmark and Analysis" — Adreno 640 OpenCL kernel-launch overhead vs NEON
leads.claim: Measured on Snapdragon 855. Table 7: launching a dummy kernel costs 230 us on the Adreno 640 GPU (Qualcomm OpenCL driver) and 20 us on the Hexagon 690 DSP (fastRPC), against Neon kernel execution times of min 0.1 us / avg 117 us / max 1209 us — i.e. "GPU and DSP kernel launch overhead alone is 1.9x and 19% of the average execution time" of the nine libraries studied. Figure 6: with memory-copy overhead eliminated (unified memory), Neon beats OpenCL GEMM below ~4M FP32 MAC operations despite the GPU having 96x more throughput; for SpMM the crossover is also ~4M. The paper also states GPU "suffers from high power consumption, which reduces the battery life of mobile devices," and that none of the nine fine-grained Chromium libraries offload to GPU because of transfer + launch cost.
leads.why: Hard numbers for the dispatch-overhead floor on a mobile GPU: 230 us per kernel launch on Adreno. At a 60 fps budget of 16.7 ms, a CLAHE + pyramid + Harris + LK chain of, say, 20 dispatches burns ~4.6 ms in launch overhead alone before any work happens — which reframes P1 as a 'fewer, larger dispatches' problem rather than a 'faster kernels' problem, and lines up with our own finding that the Adreno win came from fewer/bigger bindings. Also the cleanest citation for 'GPU is the power-hungry option' (P2).

leads.title: Arm Community 8516 — Peter Harris (Arm) on when Mali OpenCL compute loses to NEON
leads.venue: Arm Community — Mobile, Graphics and Gaming
leads.claim: Poster measured fp32 matrix multiply and vector compute via OpenCL: Mali-T720 (4 cores @ 500 MHz) came out 2-4x SLOWER than an 8-core Cortex-A53 @ 1.5 GHz with NEON. Arm's Peter Harris explained the system has "12GHz of total CPU performance, but only 2GHz of total GPU performance", that T720 is "designed for casual gaming and efficient UI rendering, not peak arithmetic performance", and that "the GPU will benefit if you can use narrower data inputs such as fp16 inputs, as the GPU supports double throughput for fp16 compared to fp32"; Mali-T760 has ~2x the arithmetic per clock of T720.
leads.why: Vendor-authoritative negative result: on low/mid Mali the GPU can simply lose to NEON for fp32 arithmetic, so 'port everything to the GPU' is not a portable win. The actionable half is the fp16 remark — Mali gives 2x fp32 throughput at fp16, but fp16 is incompatible with bit-exact replication of a 14-bit fixed-point CPU path, so fp16 would have to be an explicit product decision. Note our own three-platform rule ('no platform-specific knives') makes this a cross-device tradeoff, not a Mali-only one.

leads.title: ARM-software/ComputeLibrary#889 — ACL NEON Lucas-Kanade is ~20% slower than OpenCV's LK
leads.claim: On an Ambarella CV25 platform (quad-core Cortex-A53, Linux, ACL v21.02 built with NEON): ACL NEON LK measured 92,144-104,801 us across seven runs vs OpenCV LK 76,556-80,311 us on the same tests — ACL ~20% slower on average. No Arm engineer reply is visible in the thread; no OpenCL comparison is given.
leads.why: Important qualifier on the top lead: adopt Arm's OpenCL LK kernel as the source for the GPU arithmetic, but do NOT assume Arm's CPU LK is a good performance reference — OpenCV's NEON LK beats it. Also warns that any 'ACL is the Arm-blessed fast path' assumption is unearned; the value of the ACL CL kernel is its fixed-point fidelity and its 1-lane-per-point mapping, not measured speed.

leads.title: Basalt (TUM) — inverse-compositional patch optical flow, BSD-3-Clause
leads.claim: LICENSE confirmed BSD 3-Clause (Usenko, Demmel, 2019). The patch uses a sparse sampling `Pattern` (`static constexpr int PATTERN_SIZE = Pattern::PATTERN_SIZE;`, coordinates in `Pattern::pattern2`) rather than a dense NxN window; intensities are mean-normalised (`mean = sum / num_valid_points; data /= mean;`) for photometric invariance; the inverse-compositional Hessian is precomputed ONCE per patch: `H_se2 = J_se2.transpose() * J_se2` then stored as `H_se2_inv_J_se2_T = H_se2_inv * J_se2.transpose();`, and residuals are `residual[i] = num_valid_points * val / sum - data[i];`. Patch invalid unless `mean > epsilon` and all precomputed values are finite.
leads.why: The only permissive (BSD-3) production VIO front end we found whose tracker is deliberately cheaper per iteration than OpenCV LK: a sparse pattern instead of a 21x21 window (roughly an order of magnitude fewer samples per iteration) plus an SE2 inverse-compositional warp whose Hessian is inverted once, not per iteration. That is a real lever on P1/P2 — but it is a DIFFERENT algorithm, so adopting it breaks bit-exactness with the OpenCV/XRSLAM front end and must be flagged as an explicit product decision, replicated whole (one source, cited to lines) rather than mixed into the existing LK.

leads.title: OpenCV OCL PyrLK accuracy test tolerance (modules/video/test/ocl/test_optflowpyrlk.cpp) + known OCL correctness/limit issues
leads.claim: The OCL accuracy test only requires `std::abs(a.x - b.x) < 1 && std::abs(a.y - b.y) < 1` (sub-pixel agreement within 1 px), with `eps = 0.03f` (up to 3% of points may fail the distance/status check) and `erreps = 0.1f` (up to 10% of points may have err differing by more than `0.01 * max(1.0f, cpuErr[i])`). Reported OCL failures at that bar anyway: issue #5915 (OpenCV 3.1, WITH_OPENCL) gives point (14.43814, 29.317863) instead of (231.08749, 469.09006) and err values like -4.3160208e+08, reproducing only on GRAYSCALE input and not on colour; issue #19579 reports the OCL path is silently skipped unless winSize is inside an undocumented range (regression vs 2.4.13, no warning when the CPU fallback is taken).
leads.why: Calibrates the bar: OpenCV's own gate for its GPU LK is '97% of points within 1 pixel', which is many orders of magnitude looser than our bit-exact gate — so no published GPU LK number can be assumed to be a like-for-like comparison with our port. The #19579 pattern (a silent fallback to CPU when a precondition fails, with no warning) is also our own recurring 'silent exit' defect; worth checking our WGSL dispatcher for the equivalent winSize/precondition gate.

leads.title: MediaPipe Box Tracking — Google ships flow-based motion analysis on the CPU while detection runs on the GPU
leads.claim: The MotionAnalysis calculator "extracts features (e.g. high-gradient corners) across the image, tracks those features over time, classifies them into foreground and background features, and estimates both local motion vectors and the global motion model." On the mobile pipeline, "Object detection is using TensorFlow Lite on GPU while tracking is on CPU" (the graph inserts a GpuBufferToImageFrameCalculator to move the frame back to CPU for tracking); desktop GPU versions of tracking are listed as unavailable. No ms/frame numbers are published in this doc.
leads.why: A production counter-example worth weighing before spending more on the GPU LK path: the team that shipped this stack in Motion Stills, YouTube privacy blur and Google Lens deliberately keeps the corner-extraction + flow tracker on the CPU on phones and reserves the GPU for the neural detector — the opposite split from ours. Apache-2.0, so the tracker itself (motion_analysis / flow_packager) is copyable if we ever want a CPU reference. Low confidence because Google publishes no rationale or timings, so this is a signal, not evidence.

leads.title: XR-VIO: High-precision Visual Inertial Odometry with Fast Initialization for XR Applications (Zhai, Wang, Chen, Bao, Zhang — same lab as XRSLAM/RD-VIO)
leads.claim: Initialization from only 4 keyframes uniformly spaced at 0.1 s = a 0.3 s data window; measured submodule cost on their benchmark machine: 2-view reconstruction 24.24 ms + VG-BA 12.12 ms + VA-Align 0.09 ms + VI-BA 14.86 ms = 55.45 ms total. EuRoC 4KF: scale error 26.88%, ATE 0.026 m, gravity error 2.26 deg, success rate 83.98%. Full-sequence ATE 0.107 m avg vs OpenVINS 0.146 m and VINS-Mono 0.190 m. Deployed live on iPhone 13 Pro and Huawei Mate30 Pro at 640x480, 30 Hz images, IMU 100/200 Hz.
leads.why: This is the direct replacement for the initializer you already ship. It comes from the same group that wrote XRSLAM/RD-VIO, so the state representation, preintegrator and Ceres factors it assumes are the ones already in your tree. The pipeline is explicitly staged (VG-SfM tightly couples the gyro into 2-point RANSAC + VG-PnP + VG-BA, then VA-Align solves velocity/scale/gravity loosely with the accelerometer, then VI-BA jointly refines with parallax-adaptive weighting) — that is a full, citable recipe for cutting P4 from 3.6 s toward ~0.3-0.5 s of data. Caveat flagged below: the code is NOT in the public xrslam repo, so this is a paper-to-code replication, not a copy.

leads.title: XRSLAM initializer.cpp + config.cpp defaults (the actual reason your time-to-first-pose is 3.6 s)
leads.claim: Defaults in xrslam/src/xrslam/config.cpp: initializer_keyframe_num()=8, initializer_keyframe_gap()=5, initializer_min_matches()=50, initializer_min_parallax()=10, initializer_min_triangulation()=50, initializer_min_landmarks()=30, initializer_refine_imu()=true; sliding_window_size()=10, sliding_window_subframe_size()=3, solver_iteration_limit()=10. mirror_keyframe_map() picks frames as init_frame_index_first + i*gap for i in [0,8), i.e. 8 keyframes spanning 35 frame intervals = ~1.17 s of history at 30 fps BEFORE a single attempt can succeed. Parallax is measured in PIXELS, not normalized coords — the code is total_parallax += (apply_k(frame_i->get_keypoint(ki), frame_i->K) - apply_k(frame_j->get_keypoint(kj), frame_j->K)).norm(), averaged over common tracks, rejected if < 10. Failure returns nullptr/false and the whole thing retries on the next keyframe. Other hard gates: homography decomposition indicating pure rotation, reprojection prune at a hard-coded 3.0 px, and scale rejected unless 0.001 < scale < 1.0.
leads.why: Before importing anything external, this quantifies P4 from your own source: the floor is ~1.2 s of frame history plus however long the user takes to produce 10 px of mean parallax plus one or more failed retries. Two immediately testable levers, both product decisions (they change results): (a) keyframe_num/gap directly set the window; (b) the 10 px parallax threshold is NOT normalized by focal length or image size — you run 1920x1440 where XRSLAM/RD-VIO were tuned at 640x480, so the same physical motion produces ~3x the pixel parallax and the threshold is effectively 3x looser than upstream intended. Check which resolution you feed the tracker before touching anything else.
leads.venue: github.com/openxrlab/xrslam (tip of main = 4beb1a9, Feb 10 2026 — the exact rev you pinned)

leads.title: Instant Visual Odometry Initialization for Mobile AR (Concha, Burri, Briales, Forster, Oth — Facebook Zurich)
leads.claim: 6-DoF monocular VO that initializes instantly with zero motion parallax, by decoupling the 5-DoF relative rotation+translation-direction from the 1-DoF translation magnitude and transitioning naturally into metric scale once the user starts translating. Verbatim from the paper: standard VO/VIO initialization 'require translational motion to initialize (approx. 10 cm, depending on the scene depth)'. Measured full VO (frame-to-frame tracker + pose estimator) average compute: ~10 ms on Samsung Galaxy S10 and ~25 ms on Huawei P20; the tracker is ~60% and the pose estimator ~40% of that. Shipped as a full odometry OR as a 'pre-SLAM component of any supported SLAM system (ARKit, ARCore)' for world-locked effects on Instagram and Facebook. Relative-pose evaluation dataset released at github.com/facebookresearch/relative_pose_dataset.
leads.why: This is the authoritative answer to 'how do ARKit-like systems yield tracking in under 2 s' and it is a shipping-scale answer, not an academic one: you do not make SfM converge faster, you run a rotation-capable estimator that emits a world-locked pose from frame 1 and hand over to the metric system later. It also gives you the number your P4 is really fighting — ~10 cm of translation. The exact architecture (instant VO in front, full VI-SLAM behind) maps cleanly onto XRSLAM, which already has the pure-rotation machinery (RD-VIO R-frames/subframes) sitting unused during init. Note: the estimator itself is not open-sourced, only the evaluation dataset, so this is an architecture lead plus evidence, not copyable code.
leads.license: paper; dataset repo license not verified; method not open-sourced

leads.title: An Efficient Closed-Form Solution to Full Visual-Inertial State Initialization (Cerezo, Lee, Civera)
leads.claim: Fully analytical (no nonlinear solver) initialization of the complete VI state including gyro AND accel bias, on small-rotation + constant-velocity approximations, with a two-stage observability-driven trigger. EuRoC, 2248 independent init tests (exhaustive init every 0.5 s): total initialization 0.96 ms vs AS-MLE 30.54 ms, VINS-Mono 30.94 ms, DRT-tight 5.18 ms; module breakdown gyro-bias 0.02 ms, velocity+gravity 0.52 ms, point triangulation 0.42 ms (optional, post-init); core-only (bias + vel/grav) 0.54 ms = 56.6x lower than AS-MLE. Initialization WINDOW: 0.48 +/- 0.27 s adaptive, vs Campos et al. 2.16 +/- 0.01 s and He et al. (DRT) 2.50 s — a 4x shorter delay. 10-20% lower init error than optimization-based methods. Approximations hold to 1.5-2 deg of accumulated relative rotation; 85% of consecutive EuRoC pairs are under 2 deg.
leads.why: Directly attacks P4's real cost, which is the data WINDOW, not the compute: 0.48 s vs 2+ s. It skips the SfM stage entirely (30 ms in AS-MLE/VINS-Mono), which is exactly the stage your initializer.cpp spends its time in (homography/essential + triangulation + PnP + BA). The two-stage observability criterion is the citable rule for 'attempt now vs wait'. Caution: I found no code URL in the paper, so this would be a paper replication; and the small-rotation approximation degrades past ~2 deg of inter-frame rotation, which is a real risk for handheld phone scanning.
leads.license: arXiv CC BY 4.0; no code URL found in the paper

leads.title: Kimera-VIO src/initial/InitializationFromImu.cpp — permissive gravity-aligned static initializer
leads.claim: BSD-2-Clause (LICENSE.BSD: 'Copyright 2019 Massachusetts Institute of Technology', two redistribution clauses). Three functions: getInitialStateEstimate(), guessPoseFromImuMeasurements() and guessImuBias(). It averages the IMU samples, negates the mean acceleration to get measured gravity ('We measure the negative of gravity. Assumes static vehicle.'), and calls UtilsOpenCV::AlignGravityVectors() to rotate measured gravity onto true gravity; position is set to zero because absolute translation is unobservable; accel bias = mean acceleration + local gravity, gyro bias = mean angular velocity. The header explicitly warns it assumes the vehicle is stationary and upright. Sibling files in the same directory: OnlineGravityAlignment.cpp, InitializationBackend.cpp, CrossCorrTimeAligner.cpp, TimeAlignerBase.cpp.
leads.why: This is the permissively-licensed static/gravity-aligned initializer you can actually copy under your rules — small, self-contained, one authoritative source, replicable in full and citable to function names. It buys the 'phone is sitting still in the user's hand for a moment before the scan' case: gravity + both biases with zero visual work and zero parallax, which is the cheapest possible first pose. It does not solve scale, so it is a bootstrap for a 3-DoF/attitude-first pose (see the Concha lead) rather than a full replacement.

leads.title: OpenVINS ov_init StaticInitializer.cpp is GPL-3.0 — the brief's premise is wrong
leads.claim: Verbatim license header on the file: 'OpenVINS: An Open Platform for Visual-Inertial Research / Copyright (C) 2018-2023 Patrick Geneva ... This program is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms of the GNU General Public License as published by the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later version.'
