Algorithm (readable, but not copyable): two adjacent IMU windows each of params.init_window_time (window_2to1 older, window_1to0 newer); requires accel variance a_var_1to0 > params.init_imu_thresh while a_var_2to1 < params.init_imu_thresh, i.e. a stationary period followed by a jerk; z-axis = a_avg_2to1 / a_avg_2to1.norm(), Gram-Schmidt to build Ro, rot_2_quat() to q_GtoI; bg and ba from the stationary means; fixed initial covariances 0.02^2 (orientation), 0.05^2 (position), 0.01^2 (velocity).
leads.why: Negative result that saves a week: the whole OpenVINS family — ov_init StaticInitializer AND DynamicInitializer (Dong-Si & Mourikis) AND the learned-depth extension below — is GPLv3, in the same bucket as ORB-SLAM/VINS/DSO/SVO. You cannot copy any of it. The METHOD above is described in enough detail to re-derive, but if you want a line-citable implementation for a static initializer, use Kimera-VIO (BSD-2) or Basalt (BSD-3) instead. Note the shape of the OpenVINS criterion is 'still, then a jerk' — it needs a deliberate motion trigger, which is a UX assumption you may not want.

leads.title: Basalt sqrt_keypoint_vio.cpp — BSD-3 one-line gravity bootstrap
leads.claim: BSD 3-Clause License, 'Copyright (c) 2019, Vladyslav Usenko and Nikolaus Demmel' (header verbatim in src/vi_estimator/vio_estimator.cpp). Initialization is literally: T_w_i_init.setQuaternion(Eigen::Quaternion<Scalar>::FromTwoVectors(data->accel, Vec3::UnitZ())); with vel_w_i_init.setZero() and biases taken from the caller. Priors are injected through the marginalization prior: marg_data.H.diagonal().head<3>().setConstant(sqrt(config.vio_init_pose_weight)), marg_data.H(5,5) = sqrt(config.vio_init_pose_weight), and segments 9-11 / 12-14 set from sqrt(config.vio_init_ba_weight) / sqrt(config.vio_init_bg_weight).
leads.why: The minimum viable permissive gravity-aligned bootstrap: a single accelerometer sample defines attitude, and the unobservable yaw/position are pinned by an explicit prior weight in the marginalization block rather than by a special case. That prior trick is the part worth copying into XRSLAM — it lets you START the sliding-window solver immediately with a weakly-constrained state instead of blocking until SfM converges. BSD-3, one authoritative source, citable to line.

leads.title: RD-VIO: Robust Visual-Inertial Odometry for Mobile AR in Dynamic Environments — the algorithm your XRSLAM build actually is
leads.claim: Measured on iPhone X at 640x480, 30 Hz: average frame processing 18.38 ms vs VINS-Mono 44.72 ms. Pure-rotation frames (R-frames) are detected by comparing observation angles; their landmark triangulation is POSTPONED and the frames are attached to keyframes as 'subframes', constrained by bearing-vector orientation terms plus a ZUPT-like regularizer instead of depth. Code released as github.com/openxrlab/xrslam.
leads.why: Two things for you. (1) P1/P2 calibration: the authors' own real-time claim is at 640x480/30 Hz on an iPhone X — you are running 1920x1440 on an iPhone 14 Pro and chasing 60 Hz, i.e. ~9x the pixels per frame at 2x the rate against a design point that was never that. That is the single strongest piece of evidence that full-resolution every-frame work (not the GPU port) is the thermal problem in P2. (2) P4: the R-frame/subframe machinery for pose-during-pure-rotation already exists in your codebase — it is used AFTER init but the initializer explicitly rejects pure rotation (homography degeneracy check). Reusing it to emit poses during the init window is the cheapest path to an ARKit-like instant pose.

leads.title: Fast Monocular Visual-Inertial Initialization Leveraging Learned Single-View Depth (Merrill, Geneva, Katragadda, Chen, Huang)
leads.claim: Replaces per-feature 3D states in the closed-form linear init with just a scale+offset on a learned depth map, enabling RANSAC on a small minimal problem. TUM-VI, 5 keyframes over a 0.3 s window — 'to the best of our knowledge, this is the shortest initialization window ever reported for monocular VIO with unknown initial conditions'. Success rate on TUM-VI at 5KF/0.3 s: 100.00% (60 feats), 95.00% (45), 96.25% (30), 47.50% (15) vs baseline DS 3D at 81.25/17.50/33.75/2.50. Timing (seconds, TUM-VI Room 2): MiDaS v2.1 small depth prediction 0.2166 +/- 0.0070 run on CPU, linear system build 0.0027, solve 0.0024, MLE build 0.0005, MLE solve 0.0127. Robust to 40-45% outlier features. Authors explicitly say: if a longer window is acceptable, use a traditional method instead.
leads.why: Evidence that 0.3 s is achievable, and a clean statement of the trade: monocular depth priors buy you the low-parallax case at the cost of a 0.21 s CPU network run per init (once, on the first frame only — and MiDaS v2.1 small is a mobile-class model, so it could plausibly ride your existing WGSL/Dawn compute path). Blocker: it is implemented on top of OpenVINS ov_init, which is GPL-3.0, so the implementation is unusable to you; only the formulation and numbers transfer.
leads.license: paper open; implementation sits on GPL-3.0 ov_init

leads.title: Efficient Feature-Free Initialization for Monocular Visual-Inertial Systems Using a Feed-Forward 3D Model
leads.claim: Initializes from up-to-scale point clouds predicted by a feed-forward 3D model with no visual feature tracking at all; reports 'the highest success rate, exceeding 90%' and initialization time 'typically under 1.2 s', against 'the traditional 3-4 seconds required by existing approaches'. Paper released CC BY 4.0; the code/dataset link in the submission is a placeholder.
leads.why: Two uses. First, it is a third independent source stating that classical SfM-based VI initialization takes 3-4 s — your measured 3.6 s is not a bug in your port, it is the published behaviour of the class of method XRSLAM uses, which reframes P4 as an architecture choice rather than a defect. Second, the direction (feed-forward 3D prior instead of triangulated features) is the 2026 version of the Merrill lead, but the model class is far too heavy for a phone today and no usable code URL exists yet — record it, do not chase it.
leads.license: CC BY 4.0 (paper); code link is a placeholder

leads.title: ARCore Instant Placement — vendor doc for the product-level answer to time-to-first-pose
leads.claim: Verbatim: 'The Instant Placement API allows the user to place AR objects instantly, without having to first move their device to allow ARCore to establish full tracking and detect surface geometry.' 'After the user has placed an object, its pose is refined in real time as the user moves through the environment.' 'Once ARCore is able to determine the correct pose in the region where the AR object has been placed, it updates the object's pose and tracking method.' The point starts at tracking method SCREENSPACE_WITH_APPROXIMATE_DISTANCE and transitions to FULL_TRACKING; Google's recommended UX is rendering the object in grayscale until the pose is corrected, and the docs warn the pose jump 'also affects the apparent size or perceived scale of the object'.
leads.why: Both shipping AR SDKs solve time-to-first-pose the same way and it is not by making initialization converge faster: they emit an approximate, explicitly-labelled pose immediately and upgrade it, with UI that admits the uncertainty. If your product can tolerate a labelled approximate pose for the first second (grayscale, 'hold steady', no world-locked geometry committed), P4 becomes a UX task rather than an estimator task — which is far cheaper than replacing the initializer. Flagging this as a product decision, since it changes what a 'pose' means to your callers.
leads.license: documentation only (ARCore itself is off-limits per your constraints)

leads.title: A Benchmark Comparison of Four Off-the-Shelf Proprietary Visual-Inertial Odometry Systems (Sensors 2022)
leads.claim: Compared Apple ARKit (iPhone 12 Pro Max, iOS 14.7.1), Google ARCore (LG V60 ThinQ, Android 10, ARCore 1.29), Intel RealSense T265, Stereolabs ZED 2 against OptiTrack ground truth. Pose output rates: ARKit ~60 Hz, ARCore ~30 Hz, T265 200 Hz, ZED 2 30 Hz. ARKit drift ~0.02 m per second; final drift error ARKit 0.19-2.68 m across sequences vs ARCore 0.07-140.08 m. The paper contains NO data on initialization time, CPU load, thermal behaviour or power for any system.
leads.why: Independent corroboration that ARKit's ~60 Hz pose output is a platform constant (your measured 59.9/s on an iPhone 14 Pro matches an iPhone 12 Pro Max measurement from 2022), so P1's target of 60 Hz is the right bar and not an artefact of your instrumentation. Equally important as a negative: the most-cited proprietary-VIO benchmark publishes nothing on power, thermal or time-to-first-pose, so there is no third-party number to compare your 173 s in thermalState serious or your 1.5 s ARKit TTFP against — you will have to keep measuring those yourself.

leads.title: drt-vio-init (A Rotation-Translation-Decoupled Solution for Robust and Efficient Visual-Inertial Initialization, CVPR 2023) — GPLv3, unusable
leads.claim: Repository states GPLv3. Dependencies Eigen 3.3.7, OpenCV 3.4.9, Boost 1.58.0, Ceres 1.14.0; no runtime numbers in the README. Paper claim: rotation-only solve for gyro bias tightly coupling gyro + camera observations, then velocity and gravity from linear translation constraints solved globally-optimally WITHOUT reconstructing a 3D point cloud, '8~72 times faster (with respect to a 10-frame set) than state-of-the-art methods'. Independently measured by the Cerezo/Civera RA-L paper as DRT-tight total 5.18 ms with a fixed 2.50 s initialization window.
leads.why: Negative result on licensing for the most-cited fast-init repo, plus one useful design fact: DRT gets its speed by never triangulating during init. Note also the measurement that DRT's advantage is compute, not latency — its window is still 2.50 s, which would not fix your P4 even if you could copy it. Do not spend time on this repo.

leads.title: DRT-PNEC: Robust and Efficient Visual-Inertial Initialization with Probabilistic Normal Epipolar Constraint — CC BY-NC-SA, unusable
leads.claim: Extends the rotation-translation-decoupled framework with a gyroscope-bias estimator using probabilistic normal epipolar constraints, plus a gravity/scale refinement module; reports on EuRoC a 16% reduction in gyro bias error, 4% in rotation error and 29% in gravity error. Code at https://github.com/MUCS714/DRT-PNEC.git under Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0.
leads.why: Second licensing dead end in the same family, recorded so nobody re-opens it: CC BY-NC-SA is non-commercial AND share-alike, which is worse than GPL for a shipped product. The gyro-bias-from-epipolar-geometry idea survives as a method reference only, and XR-VIO's VG-SfM covers the same ground from a source you can at least re-implement cleanly.

leads.title: AROrientationTrackingConfiguration — Apple's own 3-DoF fallback (search-snippet only, not fetched)
leads.claim: Per Apple's documentation as reported in search results: AROrientationTrackingConfiguration tracks the device with three degrees of freedom (roll, pitch, yaw) only; it cannot track device movement and does not support plane detection or hit testing; Apple's guidance is to 'use 3DOF tracking only as a fallback in situations where 6DOF tracking is temporarily unavailable'. I could NOT fetch the Apple page itself (developer.apple.com documentation is JS-rendered and returns no content to WebFetch), so treat the wording as second-hand.
leads.why: Relevant to P4 only as confirmation that Apple ships an explicit attitude-only tracking mode and treats it as a legitimate degraded state. Combined with the Concha paper and ARCore Instant Placement, three independent shipping systems converge on the same pattern: emit an attitude-only or approximate pose immediately, upgrade to metric 6-DoF later. Low confidence on the exact wording because the primary source could not be opened.

leads.title: Kimera-VIO MonoVisionImuFrontend.cpp — feature detection gated on keyframes, KLT tracking on every frame
leads.claim: In processFrame(), tracker_->featureTracking(...) runs on EVERY frame (~lines 205-209); shouldBeKeyframe(*mono_frame_k_, *mono_frame_lkf_) at ~line 214 gates the expensive half; feature_detector_->featureDetection(mono_frame_k_.get()) plus undistortKeypoints run only inside the keyframe branch (~lines 227-232); RANSAC outlier rejection also keyframe-only (~lines 219-226); the non-keyframe path just sets mono_frame_k_->isKeyframe_ = false (~line 249) and extracts no measurements. Same structure exists in StereoVisionImuFrontend.
leads.why: This is the authoritative, permissively-licensed, copy-in-full answer to P1's root cause ('detection currently runs on EVERY frame because that is what the upstream tracker does'). A mature BSD-2 VIO front end that is architecturally the same as yours (Shi-Tomasi/goodFeaturesToTrack + pyramidal LK) explicitly does NOT detect every frame. If you replicate this gate, your 60 fps channel only has to fit CLAHE+LK inside 16.7 ms; the ~19-22 ms downclocked detection cost moves to keyframe rate. It is a single source, cited to source lines, with no algorithm invention. Note: it changes results (fewer detections), so it is a product decision, not a lossless speed-up.

leads.title: Apple Technical Note TN2445: Handling Frame Drops with AVCaptureVideoDataOutput
leads.claim: Authoritative iOS statement of the drop-stale policy: with alwaysDiscardsLateVideoFrames = YES (the default) AVFoundation 'enforces a buffer queue size of 1 at the end of the video processing pipeline... if you don't pull a frame on time because you were late, it will never get further behind than the current frame — it will throw out the current frame, and append the new one.' Three documented kCMSampleBufferDroppedFrameReason values: FrameWasLate (client slower than real time, only when discarding is on), OutOfBuffers (client holding buffers too long, only when discarding is off), Discontinuity (system too busy / capture reset, unknown number of frames lost). The delegate 'must be able to process a sample buffer within the amount of time allotted to a frame.'
leads.why: Directly usable on your platform today, two ways. (1) It is the vendor's own statement that a depth-1 newest-frame queue is correct practice for exactly your case, so your back-pressure collapse in P1 is a design bug, not a physics limit. (2) captureOutput:didDropSampleBuffer: with the droppedFrameReason attachment is a free, zero-cost instrument that tells you, per drop, whether you are late (FrameWasLate) or holding buffers (OutOfBuffers) or the system reset you (Discontinuity) — that would let you prove whether your 28.4 poses/s is your engine being late or the camera channel never delivering 60.

leads.title: Android CameraX ImageAnalysis — backpressure strategies (STRATEGY_KEEP_ONLY_LATEST vs STRATEGY_BLOCK_PRODUCER)
leads.claim: KEEP_ONLY_LATEST is the default non-blocking strategy with a buffer of fixed depth one that is always overwritten (setImageQueueDepth() has no effect in this mode); if a new image arrives while the analyzer is still working, it overwrites the previous buffered image and intermediate frames are silently dropped. BLOCK_PRODUCER queues up to imageQueueDepth images and only starts dropping when the queue is full, and it 'blocks across the entire camera device scope' — e.g. preview is blocked too while analysis runs. Documented guidance: analyzers whose total time is under one frame duration (<16 ms at 60 fps) work with either; high-latency-but-fast-enough analyzers should use blocking mode with a longer queue; analyzers that cannot keep up should use non-blocking so frames drop without blocking other use cases.
leads.why: The Android half of the same policy, so adopting newest-frame-only is consistent across the three platforms you must ship on. The 16 ms / 60 fps threshold in the doc is literally your P1 budget. The BLOCK_PRODUCER warning ('preview would also be blocked') is the documented mechanism behind your 'back-pressure kicks in and latency collapses' — if your Android path ever uses a blocking queue, camera preview and the whole camera device stall with it.

leads.title: MediaPipe FlowLimiterCalculator (Apache-2.0) — drop input frames to keep pace, keep only the latest queued frame
leads.claim: Header comment (~lines 33-42): 'FlowLimiterCalculator is used to limit the number of frames in flight by dropping input frames when necessary,' and verbatim: 'The combination of max_in_flight: 1 and max_in_queue: 1 generally gives best throughput/latency balance' — throughput near optimal because the graph is never idle, latency near optimal because the queue always stores the latest available frame. Implementation: frames drop off the FRONT of the per-stream deque when input_queue.size() > options_.max_in_queue() (~lines 147-151); a new frame is released only while frames_in_flight_.size() < options_.max_in_flight() (~line 190); a FINISHED stream signals completion. Proto defaults are max_in_flight=1, max_in_queue=0. The MediaPipe FAQ (https://developers.google.com/edge/mediapipe/framework/getting_started/faq) states: 'For online processing, it is often necessary to drop input packets in order to keep pace with the arrival of input data frames. The recommended technique for dropping packets is to use the MediaPipe calculators designed specifically for this purpose such as FlowLimiterCalculator and PacketClonerCalculator.'
leads.why: This is the one source you can replicate whole for the queue policy itself: a small, Apache-2.0, cross-platform (iOS/Android/desktop) implementation of exactly 'one frame in flight, one newest frame queued, drop the rest', with an explicit rationale for why 1/1 beats both 0 (idle gaps) and larger (stale). It is the closed-loop version of drop-stale — it drops based on a FINISHED signal from the consumer, which is what your engine needs so that back-pressure never accumulates. Pair it with PacketClonerCalculator if you need the last result re-emitted at output rate.

leads.title: Towards Streaming Perception (ECCV 2020) — always-latest vs shrinking-tail idle scheduling, and streaming AP
leads.license: paper: arXiv; code repo mtli/sAP is MIT
leads.claim: Formalizes the two policies you are choosing between. Idle-free baseline = process the latest available frame the instant the previous one finishes. Proposed shrinking-tail policy = sometimes WAIT (sit idle) for a fresher frame, with the rule return [tau(s+r) < tau(s)] where tau(t)=t-floor(t) is the fractional part of the frame-interval clock and r is the runtime. Measured on GTX 1080 Ti, 30 FPS Argoverse-HD, Mask R-CNN R50 @ scale 0.5 = 56.7 ms runtime: scheduling raises detection-only streaming AP 12.0 -> 13.0 sAP, and detection+forecasting 16.7 -> 17.8 sAP (+2.3 AP_L). The paper explicitly attacks the folk rule: 'Common folk wisdom for real-time applications like online detection requires that detectors run within the sensor frame rate' — they argue that is 'too myopic' and get better streaming accuracy while exceeding the frame interval. Dropped frames carry no direct accuracy penalty in this formulation; a zero-order hold re-serves the most recent output.
leads.why: Answers your P1 framing question directly and with a counterintuitive result: you do NOT have to fit detection inside 16.7 ms to serve a 60 fps channel, and 'process the newest frame immediately' is not the optimum — a policy that deliberately idles when the frame it would grab is about to go stale beats it. MIT-licensed reference implementation (Streamer meta-detector + the scheduling policy) means it is copyable under your rules. The sAP metric is also the honest yardstick for comparing your pose stream against ARKit's: it scores what the consumer had available at each instant, not what you eventually computed.

leads.title: GTSAM PreintegrationBase::predict (BSD) — emit poses at IMU rate by propagating the last optimized state
leads.license: BSD (GTSAM Copyright 2010, Georgia Tech Research Corporation; see LICENSE)
leads.claim: PreintegrationBase declares predict (~lines 148-160): 'Predict state at time j, for a given gravity vector in the nav frame' and an overload 'Predict state at time j, using the gravity vector from params' — i.e. a NavState at time i plus preintegrated IMU measurements yields a NavState at time j without any new image. GTSAM is the back-end Kimera-VIO uses, so this composes with lead 1.
leads.why: Attacks P1 from the output side rather than the GPU side: your metric is poses/s (28.4 vs ARKit 59.9), not images/s. ARKit is documented as emitting 60 Hz poses (see the four-VIO benchmark lead) while its camera channel and vision update rate need not be 60 Hz. If you propagate the last optimized state forward with preintegrated IMU, you can serve 60+ poses/s off a 30 fps vision channel and off keyframe-rate detection — which is exactly what makes leads 1 and 5 affordable. Same trick shortens P4's visible gap: you can publish an IMU/gravity-propagated pose while SfM bootstrap is still converging (flag it as a product decision — those early poses have no metric scale).

leads.title: ROS 2 Quality of Service policies (design.ros2.org) — sensor-data profile: timeliness over completeness, drop the older sample
leads.claim: Primary statement of the policy as robotics middleware doctrine: 'For sensor data, in most cases it's more important to receive readings in a timely fashion, rather than ensuring that all of them arrive,' hence the sensor-data profile 'uses best effort reliability and a smaller queue depth.' History 'Keep last' is defined as 'only store up to N samples, configurable via the queue depth option', and the article states 'A best effort connection should drop an older message if a subscriber has taken a newer one.' rclcpp::SensorDataQoS is KEEP_LAST, depth 5, BEST_EFFORT, VOLATILE; image_pipeline follows REP-2003 and subscribes with Sensor Data QoS.
leads.why: The 'who documents this as correct practice' citation for your angle, from middleware rather than a vendor SDK, and it is the same policy as Apple's and Google's — three independent authorities agreeing gives you a defensible design rule rather than a hunch. One practitioner caveat worth knowing before you trust a depth-1 queue: in ROS 1 the classic failure is that queue_size=1 does NOT drop image messages unless the transport buff_size is raised above the image size (default 65536 bytes), so the queue silently behaves as if it were unbounded — the analogous trap in your stack is a depth-1 queue sitting behind a deeper buffer somewhere else in the camera path.

leads.title: RD-VIO: Robust Visual-Inertial Odometry for Mobile AR in Dynamic Environments (the algorithm XRSLAM implements)
leads.license: paper: arXiv perpetual non-exclusive; code: github.com/openxrlab/xrslam
leads.claim: The upstream design point is 30 Hz images at 640x480 with 100 Hz IMU — not 60 Hz at 1920x1440. Runtime 18.38 ms average per frame on an Intel i7-7700 @3.6 GHz vs VINS-Mono 44.72 ms. Pure-rotation frames (R-frames) are detected when all keypoint motion is explained by a common rotation; they are kept as 'subframes' in the sliding window with delayed triangulation (depth postponed until enough translation is seen) plus ZUPT-like regularizers. The paper contains no statement about dropping or skipping frames when the system falls behind real time. Initialization is a visual-only SfM over a sequence of initial frames; the paper does not quantify a minimum translation, but does cite OpenVINS needing 40 s / 35 s to initialize on EuRoC MH_01/MH_02 as the comparison it beats.
leads.why: Two things for your budget arguments. (1) Your operating point is far outside the source's: 1920x1440 at 60 fps is ~9x the pixels per frame and 2x the rate of the 640x480@30 the method was designed and timed at — a large part of P1 and P2 is that you are running the upstream tracker outside its documented envelope, and no frame-drop or degradation policy exists upstream to protect it. (2) The R-frame/subframe machinery is the upstream's own answer to the pure-rotation case, which is adjacent to P4: it does not remove the need for translation to bootstrap, so 3.6 s to first pose is structural to this method, not a bug in your port.

leads.title: Real-Time Camera Tracking: When is High Frame-Rate Best? (Handa, Newcombe, Angeli, Davison)
leads.venue: ECCV 2012 (Imperial Robot Vision Group project page)
leads.license: n/a (paywalled at Springer; project page open)
leads.claim: Systematic study of accuracy, robustness and computational cost as a function of frame-rate for a whole-image-alignment tracker, on a purpose-built photorealistic multi-frame-rate / multi-resolution / multi-light-level ray-traced dataset ('tens of thousands of hours of CPU rendering time'), with measured photometric response and noise models. Central finding as stated on the project page: 'increasing frame-rate is mitigated by reduced computational cost per frame in trackers which take advantage of prediction' — i.e. per-frame cost falls as frame-rate rises because inter-frame motion shrinks and prediction is better. Second finding: higher frame-rate shortens the shutter, so less motion blur but more sensor noise, making the optimum a trade rather than 'faster is always better'. Could not open the Springer full text, so no Hz/ms table here.
leads.why: It falsifies the arithmetic assumption behind P1. You are budgeting 60 fps as '30 fps work, twice as often'. This paper's result is that the per-frame cost of a prediction-based tracker (your pyramidal LK is one) drops as the frame interval shrinks — smaller displacements mean fewer pyramid levels and fewer iterations to converge. Before you accept that 60 fps needs a 16.7 ms detection budget, measure your LK cost at 60 fps rather than assuming the 30 fps number. It also gives you a citable reason to consider that 60 fps may be worse for accuracy at fixed light level (more noise per frame), which is a real argument for staying at 30 fps and fixing poses/s with IMU propagation instead.

leads.title: NVIDIA DeepStream Gst-nvinfer 'interval' — vendor-documented inference-cadence reduction with tracker in between
leads.claim: The nvinfer plugin documents an 'interval' property: 'Specifies the number of consecutive batches to be skipped for inference' (Integer, primary mode only, e.g. interval=1). NVIDIA forum guidance on the same knob reports that going from interval=0 (infer every frame) to interval=1 (every other frame) can roughly double channel throughput, and that enabling tracker prediction between inferences keeps accuracy loss small; the SDK doc page itself does not state the tracker recommendation or the accuracy claim.
leads.why: A third independent vendor documenting the same structural answer as Kimera for P1 — expensive detector at reduced cadence, cheap tracker filling the gaps — and pricing it at roughly 2x throughput. Useful as corroboration that the detection-cadence knob is standard industry practice rather than a hack, when you are arguing that dropping to keyframe-rate detection is an acceptable product decision. Not implementable code for you (it is CUDA/GStreamer), evidence only.

leads.title: Predictive Visual Tracking: A New Benchmark and Baseline Approach (latency-aware evaluation on Jetson)
leads.claim: Latency-aware evaluation pairs ground truth at each timestamp with 'the latest output result' available then, because 'the output will be at least one frame behind the ground-truth'. Measured on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier at a 30 FPS world rate across DTB70/UAVDT/UAV123: SiamRPN++_res loses 76.7% distance precision on DTB70 under latency-aware evaluation vs offline; the lighter SiamRPN++_alex loses about 22.9%. Slower trackers lose more. The baseline explicitly processes 'the latest available frame number' and skips the rest, so 'the processed frame id could be nonconsecutive'.
leads.why: This is the price tag on the policy you are considering, measured on an embedded device rather than a workstation: newest-frame-only does not cost you accuracy directly, but the LATENCY it hides costs a lot, and the penalty scales with how slow your per-frame path is. That reframes P1 for you: getting from 19-22 ms downclocked to ~5 ms matters more than getting from 28.4 to 59.9 poses/s, because the accuracy loss tracks per-frame latency, not frame count. It also supplies the evaluation protocol you would need to compare fairly against ARKit under thermal downclocking.

leads.title: GStreamer queue element — 'leaky' property (drop old buffers downstream) as the live-pipeline idiom
leads.license: GStreamer core is LGPL (documentation only; no code copied)
leads.claim: Official enum for the queue's leak policy: no (0) 'Not Leaky', upstream (1) 'Leaky on upstream (new buffers)', downstream (2) 'Leaky on downstream (old buffers)'; default max-size-buffers is 200. The widely used live-pipeline recipe is a one-buffer-deep queue with leaky=downstream, which keeps the consumer on the most recent frame instead of working through a backlog.
leads.why: Rounds out the 'who documents this' answer with a fourth independent framework, and gives you precise vocabulary for a design review: leak-downstream (drop oldest, keep newest) is what you want; leak-upstream (drop newest) is the policy that quietly ruins real-time perception. Also a warning for your instrumentation: the default is 200 buffers deep and NOT leaky, so any generic queue you inherit is a latency accumulator by default. LGPL, so treat as documentation of practice, not code to copy.

leads.title: Basalt frame_to_frame_optical_flow.h (BSD-3) — a permissive counter-example: detect every frame, but only in empty grid cells
leads.claim: addPoints() (~lines 215-238) is called unconditionally from processFrame() after tracking, i.e. Basalt DOES run detection on every frame — but it calls detectKeypoints(pyramid->at(0).lvl(0), kd, config.optical_flow_detection_grid_size, 1, pts0) (~line 225), a grid-cell detector that excludes cells already occupied by tracked points, so in a well-tracked scene almost no cells are searched and cost collapses. Related tuning knob vio_new_kf_keypoints_thresh gates keyframing on the ratio of tracked landmarks to tracked keypoints.
leads.why: A second permissive design that reaches the same place as Kimera by a different route, and it may be the cheaper one for you because it is lossless-ish rather than a cadence change: instead of skipping detection on non-keyframes (which changes results), mask the cells that already hold tracked features so the per-frame detection work is proportional to feature attrition, not to image area. That is directly compatible with a bit-exact GPU port — you keep detecting every frame but dispatch over far fewer tiles. Worth a measurement before you accept the keyframe-gate product decision.

leads.title: XRSLAM already has a built-in detection gate you are not using: sliding_window_tracker_frequent (default 1)
leads.claim: In FeatureTracker::work(), lines 47-49 compute `bool slidind_window_frame_tag = !is_initialized || frame->id() % config->sliding_window_tracker_frequent() == 0;` Line 128-129: `if (slidind_window_frame_tag) frame->detect_keypoints(config.get());` Line 92 `last_frame->track_keypoints(frame.get(), config.get());` is UNCONDITIONAL. Line 151 also gates `detail->frontend->issue_frame(...)`. Default in xrslam/src/xrslam/config.cpp line 78: `size_t Config::sliding_window_tracker_frequent() const { return 1; }` -- i.e. every frame, which is exactly why you observe detection on every frame. Other defaults (config.cpp): feature_tracker_max_keypoint_detection = 150, feature_tracker_min_keypoint_distance = 20.0, feature_tracker_clahe_clip_limit = 6.0, clahe 8x8, feature_tracker_max_frames = 200, max_init_frames = 60, feature_tracker_predict_keypoints = true, sliding_window_force_keyframe_landmarks = 35. Frame::detect_keypoints (map/frame.cpp:55-72) is a TOP-UP: it passes the currently tracked pkeypoints into image->detect_keypoints(pkeypoints, 150, 20.0) and appends only the new ones. License: Apache-2.0 (`Copyright 2022 XRSLAM Authors`).
leads.why: This is a zero-code-change, in-tree knob in the exact rev you ship: setting sliding_window_tracker_frequent()=2 halves detection (and CLAHE-gated work only if you also move CLAHE) and directly attacks P1/P2. Two caveats that must be measured: (a) it ALSO halves the rate at which frames are issued to the sliding-window tracker (line 151), so it is not a pure front-end change -- it changes SWT input rate and therefore results, i.e. an explicit product decision, not a lossless speed-up; (b) `frame->image->preprocess(clahe...)` at line 39 is UNCONDITIONAL, so gating detection alone does NOT save your CLAHE pass -- and CLAHE cannot simply be gated because KLT tracks on the preprocessed image and would break photometric consistency between gated/ungated frames. See the vilib lead for the clean way out (per-patch gain+offset estimation instead of CLAHE).

leads.title: Kimera-VIO: feature detection ONLY on keyframes, KLT tracking on every frame -- 45 ms vs 4.5 ms measured
leads.claim: Kimera paper (Section III-D, Timing), verbatim: "The vision front-end module shows a bi-modal distribution since, for every frame, we just perform feature tracking (which takes an average of 4.5ms), while, at keyframe rate, we perform feature detection, stereo matching, and geometric verification, which, combined, take an average of 45ms." (CPU model is NOT stated in the paper.) Code: MonoVisionImuFrontend.cpp processFrame() -> `const bool new_keyframe = shouldBeKeyframe(*mono_frame_k_, *mono_frame_lkf_); if (new_keyframe) { feature_detector_->featureDetection(mono_frame_k_.get()); ... } else { mono_frame_k_->isKeyframe_ = false; }`. shouldBeKeyframe() is VisionImuFrontend.cpp:175-209 and the trigger is an OR of five terms: `need_new_keyframe = max_time_elapsed || max_disparity_reached || disparity_flipped || nr_features_low || frame.isKeyframe_`, where nr_features_low = `nr_valid_features <= min_number_features_`, disparity_flipped = `(enough_disparity || disparity_low_first_time) && min_time_elapsed`. EuRoC defaults (params/Euroc/FrontendParams.yaml): min_intra_keyframe_time 0.2 s, max_intra_keyframe_time 5.0 s, minNumberFeatures 0, max_disparity_since_lkf 1000, maxFeaturesPerFrame 300, quality_level 0.001, min_distance 20, klt_win_size 24, klt_max_level 4, klt_max_iter 30, maxFeatureAge 25. License: LICENSE.BSD is BSD-2-Clause.
leads.why: This is the canonical permissive implementation of your exact assignment, and it is the ONLY one I found whose authors published the cost split (10x between a tracking-only frame and a detection frame). min_intra_keyframe_time = 0.2 s at a 20 Hz camera means detection runs at most once every 4 frames. The trigger is not a bare count -- it is median disparity with a min-time floor, which is what you want on a phone where a user can hold still (no disparity -> no detection -> no cost, exactly your P2 case). Note the detection trigger is a superset of yours: it also fires on nr_features_low, so it degrades gracefully.

leads.title: ICE-BA (Baidu, Apache-2.0): re-detect only when grid occupancy < 40% OR tracked count < per-grid minimum
leads.claim: FeatureTrackDetector::optical_flow_and_detect() (feature_utils_feature_track.cc, function at line 802). Line 863, verbatim: `bool re_detect = grid_occ_ratio < 0.4 || propagated_feat_num < feat_min_num_thres;`. compute_grid_mask() (lines 111-156) sets `const int grid_pixel = 80;  // 640 x 480 = 8 x 6 grid_pixel`, `grid_occ_threshold = request_feat_num / xbins / ybins;  // 70 / (8 * 6)`, `*grid_occ_ratio = grid_occ_num / (xbins * ybins)`, `*feat_min_num_thres = grid_occ_threshold * xbins * ybins`. When it fires (line 896-906): `int request_new_feat_num = (request_feat_num > propagated_feat_num) ? request_feat_num - propagated_feat_num : 10;` then `this->detect(img_in_smooth, mask_with_of_out_, request_new_feat_num, pyra_level_det, fast_thresh, ...)` -- detection is masked to the cells that are NOT already occupied. In-code comment states the two criteria: "1) Features are too concentrated: the grid occupancy ratio is too low" and "2) Features are too few". License header: `Copyright 2017 Baidu Robotic Vision Authors. All Rights Reserved. Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0`.
leads.why: Apache-2.0, self-contained (~990-line file, OpenCV-only), and it is a strictly better trigger than a bare count: it fires on SPATIAL collapse as well as numeric collapse, which is the failure mode a pure count misses (100 tracks all bunched in one corner). This is the one source I would replicate whole for the trigger if you want a count-based gate rather than Kimera's disparity-based keyframe gate. It is also the exact frontend that RPG benchmarked at 11.64-12.90 ms/frame on Tegra TX2 (see the Faster-than-FAST lead), so there is a published absolute cost for it.

leads.title: Faster than FAST (RPG/UZH): re-detection at 30% of target, AND a hard negative result -- OpenCV CUDA tracker is 2.1x SLOWER than OpenCV CPU on an embedded GPU
leads.claim: Table VI, captioned "FEATURE TRACKER AVERAGE EXECUTION TIME COMPARISON, TRACKING 100 FEATURES, RE-DETECTION AT 30 FEATURES", on Tegra X2 / Jetson TX2: OpenCV CPU 1.88 ms, OpenCV CUDA 3.96 ms, theirs (translation only) 0.96 ms, theirs (trans+gain+offset) 1.01 ms. On i7-6700HQ+960M: OpenCV CPU 1.38 ms, OpenCV CUDA 0.74 ms. Text: "we... triggered feature re-detection whenever the feature track count falls below 30% of the actual target." Table V, FAST detector at 640x480 / 752x480 (GPU timings INCLUDE image upload + feature download): OpenCV CPU with MT 4.78 / 2.23 ms; OpenCV CUDA with MT 2.73 / 1.09 ms; ArrayFire CPU 60.83 / 36.42 ms; ArrayFire CUDA 1.47 / 0.51 ms; ArrayFire OpenCL - / 0.91 ms; KFAST CPU (x86 SIMD) - / 0.63 ms; ours 1.11 / 0.28 ms. Table VII, their GPU frontend + ICE-BA backend vs ICE-BA's own CPU frontend on EuRoC MH01-05, Tegra X2: 4.67-6.41 ms vs 11.64-12.91 ms per frame; relative translation RMSE 0.86/0.90/1.40/1.85/1.19 % vs 0.40/0.50/0.71/0.81/1.08 %. Whole VIO ~200 fps on TX2. Code: github.com/uzh-rpg/vilib, LICENSE.txt is BSD 3-Clause (Balazs Nagy, RPG UZH, 2019-2020).
leads.why: Three things you can use. (1) A published, credible re-detection threshold: 30% of target. (2) The negative result you asked for: on an EMBEDDED GPU (TX2), OpenCV's CUDA KLT tracker is 2.1x slower than the CPU one, while on a desktop GPU it is 1.9x faster -- i.e. naive GPU offload of the tracking half loses on mobile-class GPUs, and only a hand-written kernel wins. Same table shows a good CPU SIMD detector (KFAST, 0.63 ms) is within 2.25x of a hand-written CUDA detector (0.28 ms) at 752x480, which bounds what your bit-exact GPU port can be worth on the DETECTION half. (3) The accuracy price of a lower-quality/faster frontend: RTE roughly 0.6-1.0 pp worse on 4 of 5 EuRoC sequences. Caveat for your license audit: vilib's repo LICENSE.txt is BSD-3-Clause, but individual files (e.g. visual_lib/include/vilib/feature_tracker/feature_tracker_options.h) carry a second header "This file is part of SVO - Semi-direct Visual Odometry... subject to the terms and conditions defined in the file 'LICENSE'" with a 2014 Christian Forster copyright. SVO is GPL. Do a file-by-file provenance check before copying anything from vilib.
leads.license: BSD-3-Clause (repo) with SVO-derived file headers -- verify per file

leads.title: vilib feature tracker: the exact threshold knob, and per-patch gain+offset estimation that would let you delete CLAHE
leads.claim: FeatureTrackerOptions, verbatim: `/// If number of tracks falls below this threshold, detect new features.` `size_t min_tracks_to_detect_new_features = 100;` and `/// Reset tracker before detecting new features. This means that all active tracks are always the same age, and the reference frame is the same for all feature tracks. This can be good for VO initialization.` `bool reset_before_detection = true;`. Also `bool affine_est_offset = false; bool affine_est_gain = false;` with `/// Add illumination compensation  /// Note: only applicable to the GPU version`, `bool klt_template_is_first_observation = true` ("if the klt template is the first observation, the reference patch and the Hessian's inverse only needs to be computed once"), klt_max_level = 4, klt_patch_sizes = {16,16,16,8,8}. Usage site, feature_tracker_gpu.cpp: `if(tracked_features_num_[c] < options_.min_tracks_to_detect_new_features)`. Measured cost of the illumination compensation on Tegra X2 (Table VI of the paper): translation-only 0.96 ms vs trans+gain+offset 1.01 ms, i.e. ~5% for full affine photometric estimation.
leads.why: Two distinct uses. First, the literal implementation of your assignment with a named default (100). Second and more valuable for P2: vilib estimates illumination GAIN and OFFSET per patch inside the KLT solve for ~5% extra time, which is the principled alternative to running CLAHE on every full-resolution frame. If the tracker is photometrically invariant you can (a) drop CLAHE from the tracking path entirely and (b) then legitimately gate CLAHE to detection frames only -- which is what unblocks the XRSLAM lead above, where CLAHE is currently unconditional at line 39 and eats the savings. Note the cost of reset_before_detection=true: every re-detection throws away ALL existing tracks, so track length is capped by the re-detection interval -- a real accuracy price you should not copy blindly given your SfM bootstrap depends on long tracks (P4).
leads.license: BSD-3-Clause (repo) -- file carries an SVO/GPL provenance header, audit before copying

leads.title: Basalt: the other strategy -- detect EVERY frame but only inside grid cells that contain no tracked point
leads.claim: src/utils/keypoints.cpp, `void detectKeypoints(const basalt::Image<const uint16_t>& img_raw, KeypointsData& kd, int PATCH_SIZE, int num_points_cell, const Eigen::aligned_vector<Eigen::Vector2d>& current_points)` at line 161. It bins current_points into cells, then for each cell: `if (cells((y - y_start) / PATCH_SIZE, (x - x_start) / PATCH_SIZE) > 0) continue;` (lines 193-194) -- occupied cells are skipped entirely. Only for empty cells does it take a SubImage of PATCH_SIZE x PATCH_SIZE and run `cv::FAST(subImg, points, threshold)` with a threshold ladder `int threshold = 40; while (points_added < num_points_cell && threshold >= 5)` stepping 40 -> 20 -> 10 -> 5. Call site frame_to_frame_optical_flow.h:320: `detectKeypoints(pyramid->at(0).lvl(0), kd, config.optical_flow_detection_grid_size, 1, pts0);` and addPoints() is called unconditionally in BOTH branches of processFrame (lines 137 and 170). data/euroc_config.json: `optical_flow_detection_grid_size: 50`, `optical_flow_levels: 3`, `optical_flow_max_iterations: 5`, `optical_flow_skip_frames: 1`. Note optical_flow_skip_frames only throttles pushing to output_queue (`if (output_queue && frame_counter % config.optical_flow_skip_frames == 0)`), it does NOT skip tracking or detection. License: BSD 3-Clause (2019, Vladyslav Usenko and Nikolaus Demmel).
leads.why: This is the alternative that is compatible with a bit-exact GPU port and does NOT change the pose stream: instead of skipping detection on some frames, you make detection nearly free on every frame by restricting it to unoccupied cells. At your 1920x1440 with a 50 px grid that is ~1100 cells; in steady state with ~150 tracks the vast majority are occupied but empty cells still dominate area, so the real win depends on your track density -- measure it. Two GPU-relevant consequences: the work becomes data-dependent (a sparse, per-cell dispatch, which is exactly the "fewer, larger bindings" problem you already fought), and the FAST threshold ladder means a variable number of passes per cell. Basalt is BSD-3 so you may copy the cell-skip logic verbatim.

leads.title: OpenVINS TrackKLT: early-return from detection at 50% of target, plus an in-code statement that whole-image re-extraction is the slow way
leads.claim: perform_detection_monocular() begins at line 395. Lines 468-470: `double min_feat_percent = 0.50; int num_featsneeded = num_features - (int)pts0.size(); if (num_featsneeded < std::min(20, (int)(min_feat_percent * num_features))) return;`. Immediately after (line ~473) the authors left the old code commented out with the reason: "This is old extraction code that would extract from the whole image / This can be slow as this will recompute extractions for grid areas that we have max features already". When it does run, lines 483-488: `num_features_grid = num_features/(grid_x*grid_y) + 1; num_features_grid_req = max(1, (int)(min_feat_percent * num_features_grid)); ... if ((int)grid_2d_grid.at<uint8_t>(y,x) < num_features_grid_req && (int)mask0_grid.at<uint8_t>(y,x) != 255)`. Stereo variants at lines 603-626 and 784-802. Defaults (ov_msckf/src/core/VioManagerOptions.h): num_pts = 150 ("The number of points we should extract and track in *each* image frame"), fast_threshold = 20, grid_x = 5, grid_y = 5, min_px_dist = 10, downsample_cameras = false, use_klt = true, histogram_method = HISTOGRAM. feed_new_camera builds the pyramid once per message with cv::buildOpticalFlowPyramid (line 71) and applies CLAHE only when histogram_method == CLAHE (lines 58-60). LICENSE: GNU General Public License v3+.
leads.why: EVIDENCE ONLY -- GPLv3, do not copy. But it pins a second published threshold value (50% of target, floored at 20 features) that agrees in spirit with vilib's 30% and ICE-BA's grid rule, and the authors' own comment is the clearest authoritative statement that recomputing detection over the whole image when cells are already full is the thing to stop doing. With num_pts=150 the gate is min(20, 75) = 20, so OpenVINS skips detection entirely whenever >= 131 of 150 tracks survived -- on a slow-moving handheld phone that is most frames. Also note grid_x=grid_y=5 at ANY resolution, i.e. they never scale the grid with image size.
leads.license: GPL-3.0 -- code UNUSABLE to you, evidence only

leads.title: XR-VIO: detection is 4.2 ms of a 14.0 ms tracking budget at 640x480, measured, with iPhone 13 Pro deployment
leads.claim: Table 3, "Time Statistics of Each Submodule in VIO". Tracking, KLT column vs Hybrid column: Feature Detection 4.2 / 3.9 ms; Feature Matching 4.1 / 7.9 ms; Others 5.7 / 4.4 ms; Total 14.0 / 16.2 ms. Initialization submodules: 2-View Reconstruction 24.24 ms, VG-BA 12.12 ms, VA-Align 0.09 ms, VI-BA 14.86 ms, Total 55.45 ms; "On average, each frame takes about 13 ms to initialize". Deployment: "We deployed our VIO system on mobile platforms (Android & iOS)... Using 30 Hz image data at a resolution of 640x480 and IMU data... captured at 100/200Hz by the iPhone 13 Pro and Huawei Mate30 Pro, our system operates in real-time." Text also notes "leveraging the prior knowledge of KLT eliminates the need to extract an excessive number of ORB points (in our case, only 150 points are extracted)".
leads.why: A same-class measurement (mobile AR VIO, iPhone, 640x480) that puts detection at 30% of the per-frame tracking budget. That bounds what perfect detection scheduling can buy you in the CPU-equivalent case: gating detection to every 4th frame removes ~22% of front-end time, not 60%. Useful as a sanity check before you spend a week on scheduling: if your GPU CLAHE + detection is 19-22 ms of a 16.7 ms budget when downclocked, gating detection alone will not get you to 60 fps -- CLAHE and pyramid, which must run every frame for tracking, are the residual. The initialization table (55.45 ms total, 13 ms/frame) is also the closest published breakdown to your P4.

leads.title: VINS-Mono decouples tracking rate from detection rate via FREQ / PUB_THIS_FRAME (GPL code, method documented in Chinese)
leads.claim: In VINS-Mono's FeatureTracker::readImage, KLT tracking runs on every incoming camera frame, but goodFeaturesToTrack (with a setMask() that blanks a MIN_DIST radius around every surviving track) is called only when PUB_THIS_FRAME is true. PUB_THIS_FRAME is set by comparing the running average publish rate against the config parameter FREQ: if the current average is above FREQ the frame is tracked but not published and no new corners are extracted. Typical config: FREQ = 10 Hz against a 20 Hz camera, MAX_CNT = 150, MIN_DIST = 30 px. goodFeaturesToTrack is asked for exactly (MAX_CNT - forw_pts.size()) new corners inside the non-zero mask region.
leads.why: A third distinct trigger design and the one closest to what your camera-channel problem needs: it is a RATE gate, not a count gate, so detection cost is bounded by a wall-clock budget regardless of scene. That maps cleanly onto your 60 fps channel -- track at 60, detect at 15-20 Hz. Also the direct precedent for XRSLAM's `frame->id() % N` gate, but rate-based rather than index-based, which is more robust when frames are dropped. IMPORTANT: VINS-Mono/VINS-Fusion are GPLv3, so the code is unusable to you; use this only as evidence that the design exists and is shipped, and replicate the mechanism from Kimera (BSD-2) or ICE-BA (Apache-2.0) instead. I could not open the primary source guyuehome.com/38871 (page body not returned); the Zhihu and CSDN write-ups agree on the mechanism and the constants.
leads.license: described method; VINS-Mono code is GPL-3.0 and UNUSABLE

leads.title: maplab / ROVIOLI VO pipeline is a counter-example: it detects and extracts on EVERY frame (Apache-2.0)
leads.claim: VOFeatureTrackingPipeline::trackFeaturesSingleCamera() calls `detectors_extractors_[camera_idx]->detectAndExtractFeatures(frame_kp1);` (line 125) unconditionally, BEFORE `trackers_[camera_idx]->track(q_Ckp1_Ck, *frame_k, frame_kp1, &matches_kp1_k);` (line 154) -- there is no count threshold and no keyframe gate on detection. The spatial control is instead a gridded detector: feature-detection-extraction.cc lines 77-90 call detectKeypointsGridded(...) with detector_settings_.gridded_detector_cell_num_features, gridded_detector_num_grid_cols, gridded_detector_num_grid_rows, gridded_detector_num_threads_per_image, max_feature_count, plus localNonMaximumSuppression with detector_nonmaxsuppression_radius / ratio_threshold. LICENSE at repo root is Apache License 2.0.
leads.why: Negative result that saves you a search: despite the widely repeated claim that ROVIOLI 'detects when tracks drop below a threshold', maplab's VO feature-tracking pipeline is descriptor-matching-based (BRISK) and detects on every frame; the threshold behaviour people cite belongs to ROVIO's internal patch tracker, not to this pipeline. So maplab is NOT a source for this angle. It IS a permissive (Apache-2.0) source for a gridded detector with tunable per-cell feature counts and local NMS, if you want that instead.

leads.title: HybVIO (Spectacular AI) is GPLv3 -- ruled out despite being the closest iPhone-targeted open VIO
leads.claim: The LICENSE file at the root of SpectacularAI/HybVIO is verbatim the GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 29 June 2007.
leads.why: Dead end recorded so nobody re-checks it. HybVIO is the most obvious candidate for 'someone already tuned a hybrid KLT VIO for phones', and its detection scheduling would have been directly relevant, but GPLv3 puts its code out of reach under your rules. Same category as ORB-SLAM2/3, VINS, DSO, SVO and (as confirmed above) OpenVINS.

leads.title: ARCore's 60 Hz pose feature request has sat open since 2018 with no vendor answer
leads.claim: Issue #604, 'Textures and device pose at 60Hz', opened by TrackBallPower on 12 October 2018, labelled 'feature request', still Open. The requester notes 60 fps-capable phone cameras have existed since the Samsung S6 and that the 30 Hz cap blocks 6DoF positional tracking use cases. There is no response from the ARCore team in the thread.
leads.why: Directly relevant context for P1 and for your 'is our approach one anyone else has taken' question: the pose-rate-vs-camera-rate tradeoff you are fighting is the same one Google has left unresolved on Android for 7+ years, which is weak evidence that decoupling pose rate from a 60 fps camera channel is genuinely hard rather than something you are getting wrong. It also reinforces that ARKit's 59.9 poses/s is almost certainly NOT achieved by running your pipeline at 60 Hz -- it is IMU-rate pose output with vision fused at a lower rate. Before spending on detection scheduling, measure whether ARKit's vision stage actually runs at 60 Hz; if it does not, matching its pose rate is an output-interpolation problem, not a front-end throughput problem.

leads.title: Basalt / OpenVINS / Kimera all cap detection spatially rather than temporally -- and none of them ever scales the grid with resolution
leads.claim: Cross-source comparison of the spatial caps, all read from source: OpenVINS grid_x = 5, grid_y = 5, num_pts = 150, min_px_dist = 10 (fixed regardless of image size, downsample_cameras = false by default). Basalt optical_flow_detection_grid_size = 50 px with num_points_cell = 1. ICE-BA grid_pixel = 80 px with the comment `// 640 x 480 = 8 x 6 grid_pixel` and grid_occ_threshold = request_feat_num / xbins / ybins (comment `// 70 / (8 * 6)`). Kimera maxFeaturesPerFrame = 300, min_distance = 20 px. XRSLAM feature_tracker_max_keypoint_detection = 150, feature_tracker_min_keypoint_distance = 20.0 px.
leads.why: Every one of these systems was tuned at VGA-to-WVGA and expresses its spacing constraint in absolute pixels. You are running 1920x1440. At that size XRSLAM's min_keypoint_distance = 20 px is ~3x tighter in relative terms than the designers intended, which means goodFeaturesToTrack has far more surviving candidates to sort and suppress, and the 150-point cap is being applied to a candidate set an order of magnitude larger. Before (or alongside) detection scheduling, the cheapest lossless-in-spirit experiment is to run detection on a downsampled level of the pyramid you already build -- OpenVINS ships exactly this switch (downsample_cameras) and Kimera/ICE-BA both detect on a pyramid level (pyra_level_det). This attacks P1, P2 and P3 at once and does not touch the pose stream's structure the way frame gating does.
leads.license: mixed -- Basalt BSD-3, ICE-BA Apache-2.0, Kimera BSD-2 usable; OpenVINS GPL evidence only

leads.title: Kimera EuRoC front-end defaults: what a shipped keyframe-gated tracker actually uses
leads.claim: params/Euroc/FrontendParams.yaml: klt_win_size 24, klt_max_iter 30, klt_max_level 4, klt_eps 0.1, maxFeatureAge 25, feature_detector_type 3, maxFeaturesPerFrame 300, quality_level 0.001, min_distance 20, min_intra_keyframe_time 0.2, max_intra_keyframe_time 5.0, minNumberFeatures 0, max_disparity_since_lkf 1000, max_nr_keypoints_before_anms 2000, ransac_threshold_mono 1e-06, ransac_threshold_stereo 1.
leads.why: Concrete numbers for the keyframe-gated design if you replicate Kimera. Two are load-bearing for you: min_intra_keyframe_time = 0.2 s is a hard floor on detection frequency (at 60 fps that is at most 1 detection per 12 frames -- exactly the duty cycle that would fit your 16.7 ms budget at downclocked GPU rates), and maxFeatureAge = 25 caps how long a track survives without re-detection, which is the accuracy-side counterweight you must tune together with the gate. Note minNumberFeatures = 0 on EuRoC means the count-based trigger is DISABLED there and the gate is purely disparity + time; on a handheld phone where the user can stand still you would want it nonzero.

leads.title: Faster than FAST: GPU-Accelerated Frontend for High-Speed VIO (IROS 2020) + vilib
leads.venue: IEEE/RSJ IROS 2020 (Nagy, Foehn, Scaramuzza, UZH RPG)
leads.claim: Their Table VI ("FEATURE TRACKER AVERAGE EXECUTION TIME COMPARISON, TRACKING 100 FEATURES, RE-DETECTION AT 30 FEATURES") measures, on a Tegra X2 (Jetson TX2, max-N clocks, 640x480 and 752x480): OpenCV CPU pyramidal tracker 1.88 ms vs OpenCV CUDA 3.96 ms -- the GPU library is 2.1x SLOWER than the CPU on the ARM/embedded platform -- while on a laptop (i7-6700HQ + GTX 960M) the same comparison flips to CPU 1.38 ms vs CUDA 0.74 ms. Their own CUDA tracker is 0.90-1.01 ms on TX2. Table V (detection only): OpenCV CPU multi-threaded 4.78 ms, OpenCV CUDA 2.73 ms, ArrayFire CUDA 1.47 ms, ArrayFire OpenCL 0.91 ms (desktop only), theirs 1.11 ms. Table III NMS on Tegra X2: Foerstner spiral 294.03 us vs theirs 141.36 us at 3x3, 1772 us vs 929.82 us at 9x9. Table IV: FAST CRF kernel on Tegra X2 298.7-784.3 us depending on score function, with L1 cache-hit 83.9-91.8%. Full pyramidal detection breakdown (upload + pyramid + CRF + NMS + download) is ~1000-2250 us at 640x480/752x480 on Tegra X2.
leads.why: Two things we can act on. (1) It is the cleanest published proof that the SAME GPU code that wins on a desktop LOSES to the CPU on an ARM embedded SoC -- exactly the regime our iPhone 14 Pro sits in when it downclocks, and exactly the P1 failure mode. (2) The table title itself states the policy: they track 100 features and RE-DETECT AT 30 FEATURES, i.e. detection is NOT run every frame. That is a permissive (BSD-3) authoritative source for the 'do not detect every frame' change that P1 needs, from a group whose front end is FAST + pyramid + KLT-style tracking, the same shape as ours. The code is CUDA, but BSD-3 lets us copy the algorithm and constants line-for-line into WGSL.

leads.title: OpenCV for High-Performance, Low-Power Vision Applications on Snapdragon (Qualcomm, Embedded Vision Summit 2024)
leads.venue: Embedded Vision Summit 2024, Xin Zhong, Director of Product Management, Qualcomm Technologies
leads.claim: Qualcomm's own acceleration plan for OpenCV 4.9.0 on Snapdragon. Slide 6 lists the exact functions we ported -- "Corner detector", "Good feature to track", "Pyramid", "Image filters", "LK optical flow" -- and assigns them to CPU/DSP/EVA. Slide 11 ("all performance numbers measured on Snapdragon 8 Gen1") gives, relative to native OpenCV = 1x: Neon-optimized min 0.5x, median 2.3x, average 24x, max 79x; DSP-optimized min 0.2x, median 1.2x, average 11x, max 53x. Slide 12 selected functions: Remap bilinear = 1.0x Arm-compatible, 1.1x Neon, 0.4x DSP, 11.8x EVA; Bilinear downscale = 1.7x Neon, 0.6x DSP, 5.5x EVA. Slide 13: "Performance of EVA-based OF is about 5x faster than LK optical flow in OpenCV". Slide 16: EVA gives "up to 4x power saving and up to 25x performance". Critically, although the HW stack slide names EVA/DSP/GPU/CPU, NEITHER performance table has a GPU column -- Qualcomm's shipped acceleration path for OpenCV corner detection, GFTT, pyramids and LK is CPU/Neon + DSP + fixed-function EVA, not the Adreno GPU.
leads.why: This is the strongest vendor-level signal that we should question the premise of the whole port. The silicon vendor with the best possible OpenCL driver access, given the exact function list we ported, chose not to put any of it on the GPU. It also shows the min columns (0.5x Neon, 0.2x DSP) -- vendors ship acceleration paths that are 2-5x SLOWER than baseline for some functions, so 'the accelerator lost' is normal, not a bug in our port. EVA is Qualcomm-only so it violates our no-vendor-specific rule, but the 4x power saving number bounds what P2 could ever be worth.

leads.title: OpenCV 4.0.1's own OpenCL front end: clahe.cl, covardata.cl, corner.cl, gftt.cl, pyr_down.cl, pyrlk.cl, fast.cl + ocl_goodFeaturesToTrack
leads.claim: The exact source we already replicate ships a GPU implementation of the exact front end we ported. Confirmed present at tag 4.0.1: modules/imgproc/src/opencl/{clahe.cl 6905 B, covardata.cl 10783 B, corner.cl 8997 B, gftt.cl 5939 B, pyr_down.cl 11341 B, precornerdetect.cl}, modules/video/src/opencl/pyrlk.cl (16754 B), modules/features2d/src/opencl/{fast.cl, orb.cl}. ocl_goodFeaturesToTrack (featureselect.cpp) splits the work as: GPU runs cornerHarris/cornerMinEigenVal, then a maxEigenVal reduction kernel, then a maxEigenValTask kernel that turns qualityLevel into an absolute threshold, then a findCorners kernel that atomically compacts surviving candidates into a small buffer sized possibleCornersCount = max(1024, image_area * 0.1); ONLY that candidate list is read back (corners_buffer.getMat(ACCESS_RW)), and the CPU then does std::sort and the cell_size = round(minDistance) grid min-distance suppression. Both the CPU and OpenCL paths carry explicit comparators commented "Ensure a fully deterministic result of the sort".
leads.why: Directly usable under our own rules: it is one authoritative source, permissively licensed, and it is the SAME source we already replicate bit-exactly, so we can cite it to source lines without adding a second upstream debt. Two concrete P1 levers fall out: (a) never read back a full response image -- read back only an atomically compacted candidate list capped at max(1024, 0.1*area), which for 1920x1440 caps at 276480 entries but in practice is tiny; (b) the deterministic-sort comparators are the exact tie-break rules a bit-exact GPU port has to reproduce, and OpenCV already wrote them down.

leads.title: Fire in Your Hands: Understanding Thermal Behavior of Smartphones (KAIST)
leads.claim: FLIR ONE thermographic measurement of 10 phones (Nexus 5/5X/6, Pixel, Pixel 2, iPhone 7/7+/8, Galaxy S7, Huawei P20 lite). Key results: a pure CPU-intensive workload at 90% utilisation on a Nexus 5X "did not cause significant overheating. The surface temperature did not exceed 46 C due to frequency scaling and core disabling", but high-quality VIDEO RECORDING on the same phone "continued to rise and reached 60 C in 20 minutes, despite frequency scaling and core disabling", attributed to the multimedia/codec block in the AP which "typically does not have its own thermal management capability". Pokemon Go with AR mode ON: 53 C surface hot-spot, over half the surface above 45 C, and above 51 C they observed "unnatural and discontinuous rendering of 3D graphics due to thermal throttling"; with AR mode OFF the surface was ~46 C. GPU deep learning (DeepMon/YOLO on Galaxy S7, ~1 s inference every 3 s, so roughly 33% GPU duty cycle) reached 54 C, "9 C higher than simply capturing images from the rear camera (45 C)", taking 21 minutes. Charging vs non-charging AP/PMIC curves looked similar until the battery hit 0%, when both leapt to nearly 100 C.
leads.why: P2's puzzle is that our CPU load matches ARKit (0.80 cores) yet we spend 173/300 s in 'serious'. This paper measured exactly that decomposition on real phones: CPU load alone is thermally self-limiting because DVFS caps it, while the CAMERA/codec path and a duty-cycled GPU are what actually push a phone past the throttle point -- +9 C from a GPU running only ~33% of the time on top of camera capture. It also gives us the right experiment shape (surface hot-spot vs component, AR-on vs AR-off as the single variable) and the charging caveat for our own charging-run methodology.

leads.title: Characterizing WebGPU Dispatch Overhead for LLM Inference Across Four GPU Vendors, Three Backends, and Three Browsers
leads.claim: Measures per-dispatch cost of the WebGPU stack itself across NVIDIA/AMD/Apple/Intel on Linux/Windows/macOS, comparing Dawn and wgpu-native under Chrome, Safari and Firefox. WebGPU API overhead alone is 24-36 us per dispatch on the Vulkan backend and 32-71 us on the Metal backend; total per-operation overhead including the host language is ~95 us. Implementation choice matters: 2.2x variation between Dawn and wgpu-native on Metal. Conclusion: "at batch=1 with the current dispatch-heavy pipeline, per-operation overhead dominates regardless of kernel quality", and "naive single-operation benchmarks overestimate dispatch cost by ~20x". Kernel fusion gave +53% throughput on Vulkan. No mobile/phone device was measured.
leads.why: The only quantitative measurement we found of the Dawn layer itself, which is the layer our whole front end sits on. 32-71 us per dispatch on Metal is small against 16.7 ms individually but not against a chain of tens of dispatches per frame, and it is the desktop floor -- a downclocked phone will be worse. The 2.2x Dawn-vs-wgpu spread on Metal also warns that our numbers are Dawn-version-sensitive. The warning about single-dispatch microbenchmarks over-reporting overhead by ~20x is a direct methodology correction for how we time our WGSL arms.

leads.title: Vulkan Documentation Project - Mobile and Embedded Compute: mobile optimization
leads.claim: Explicit mobile-compute guidance with a worked bandwidth example: two separate passes over a 12-megapixel FP16 image generate ~384 MB of DRAM traffic; fusing blur and tone-map into one kernel by "keeping the blurred pixel in a register" halves it to ~192 MB. States that mobile limits are much tighter than desktop -- maxComputeWorkGroupInvocations "can be 128" and maxComputeSharedMemorySize "can be 16 KB" -- so the desktop convention of 256-1024 invocations is wrong on phones, and workgroup size should align to subgroupSize. FP16 runs at "twice the rate of FP32 and, critically, move[s] half as many bytes". On thermals: "Measure sustained, not peak. Benchmark over tens of seconds, not a single dispatch, to see the throttled steady state", and amortising work across frames at a lower clock yields more work per joule than bursting. Summary principle: "the fastest kernel is frequently the one that touches DRAM the least."
leads.why: This is the vendor-doc statement of exactly the failure we are living: our kernel is ~5 ms at nominal clocks and 19-22 ms once the phone downclocks, i.e. we benchmarked peak and shipped against sustained. It also names the specific lossless lever for both P1 and P2 -- fuse the CLAHE/pyramid/derivative/response chain into fewer passes so the 1920x1440 intermediate images never round-trip to DRAM. Bandwidth, not arithmetic, is the power budget, which is the missing energy in P2's accounting.

leads.title: Jetson-ORB-SLAM3: Accuracy-Preserving GPU Implementation for Edge Computing Devices
leads.license: not stated in abstract; no repo found
leads.claim: A GPU port of the ORB-SLAM3 visual front end onto an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (7 W), sustaining "32FPS mean over the eleven EuRoC sequences" in monocular-inertial mode. Their definition of accuracy-preserving is explicitly statistical, not exact: "94.7% exact keypoint agreement and 99.9% descriptor bit agreement" against the reference CPU detector, with trajectories agreeing "to within 0.10cm in mean absolute trajectory error". Mapping and optimisation stay on the CPU; front end and loop closure go to the GPU. Loop-closure inference via native TensorRT drops to 2.2 ms per query, a claimed 180x over generic ONNX Runtime.
leads.why: Answers the cross-cutting question about how unusual our approach is. The state of the art in 'accuracy-preserving GPU SLAM front ends', published in 2026, accepts 94.7% keypoint agreement -- one keypoint in twenty differs -- and validates on downstream ATE rather than on the detector output. Our bit-identical CPU/GPU WGSL front end is therefore strictly stronger than anything published, which means (a) nobody has a bit-exact reference we can borrow test vectors from, and (b) our exactness constraint is a self-imposed cost no competitor pays, so it should be priced explicitly when we decide whether a lossy speed-up is worth it.

leads.title: FastTrack: GPU-Accelerated Tracking for Visual SLAM
leads.claim: Measured on NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX (384-core Volta, 6-core ARM Carmel) and on desktop (RTX 3090 + i7-12700K). Jetson: overall tracking 77.49 ms -> 29.39 ms (2.63x). Desktop: overall tracking 14.08 -> 5.47 ms (2.57x), ORB extraction 5.38 -> 1.88 ms (2.85x), stereo matching 1.10 -> 0.42 ms (2.60x), track-local-map 6.35 -> 2.11 ms (3.00x). They deliberately left 'Update Local Map' on the CPU: although it involves "large loops, the execution cost per iteration is low, while GPU offloading causes a large amount of data transfer", so it is "not well-suited for GPU optimization". Pose optimisation was disabled rather than ported, with "negligible impact on ATE performance".
leads.why: A recent, code-released worked example of the CPU/GPU split decision inside a SLAM tracker, with the negative half stated explicitly: the stage they refused to move is the one with many cheap iterations and heavy data movement. That is the same test we should apply to our corner-list post-processing (sort, min-distance suppression) -- OpenCV already keeps it on the CPU for the same reason. The Xavier NX numbers also show what a competent CUDA tracker costs on an ARM SoC: ~29 ms per frame, i.e. still nowhere near a 16.7 ms budget.

leads.title: Phase Matters: Characterizing Heterogeneous Vision-Language Inference on a Mobile SoC
leads.claim: Measured on a Qualcomm SM8750 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) with a 100-run thermal-stability protocol. Moving the vision encoder off the CPU onto an accelerator gives "20-45x speedups over CPU" for encoder operations, and a heterogeneous CPU/NPU configuration yields "10.47 degrees C lower steady-state temperature" and "2.52x lower energy" than CPU-only execution, avoiding thermal throttling in always-on settings. Phase matters: NPU gives 1.64x on prefill but only 1.18x on decode.
leads.why: Two P2 calibrations. First, the magnitude: moving continuous vision work to the right engine is worth ~10 C of steady-state surface temperature on a current Snapdragon -- which is the right order to explain 173 s in 'serious' vs ARKit's 0 s. Second, the method: a 100-run steady-state protocol rather than a single 300 s pass, which is what we would need to attribute our own thermal gap to the GPU rather than to the camera. Caveat: it is VLM inference, not corner detection, so the mechanism transfers but the numbers do not.

leads.title: llama.cpp issue #5965: "Using OpenCL on Adreno & Mali GPUs is slower than CPU"
leads.claim: Reporter measured that on both Qualcomm Adreno and ARM Mali, "the more GPUs are used, the slower the speed becomes", and traced the cause to the backend copying data between host and GPU memory when "in most embedded SoCs, the host and GPU share memory", citing ARM's own guidance (developer.arm.com/documentation/100614/0314 .../Do-not-create-buffers-with-CL-MEM-USE-HOST-PTR-if-possible) and demonstrating the fix with CL_MEM_ALLOC_HOST_PTR plus clEnqueueMapBuffer. Commenter akingoverlook adds that even after Qualcomm's heavy optimisation of the MLC/TVM OpenCL path (textures instead of buffers, changed weight layouts, Android-specific kernels), the mobile GPU path ends up "just faster than CPU on the master branch, but is already slower than the ARM matmul Int8 PR", and that "memory bandwidth with mobile GPUs is still low, especially in the GPU-to-host direction"; Vulkan on Adreno was called unusable at the time "due to some driver/shader compatibility problems and small max allocation size".
leads.why: Forum-level but first-hand and specific: it names the two mechanisms that would make our WGSL front end lose on Android (host/device copies on a unified-memory SoC, and asymmetric GPU-to-host bandwidth) and it is the GPU-to-host direction that our corner readback lives in. The Adreno max-allocation warning also rhymes with the 256 MB Mali binding wall we already hit, suggesting the limit class is a recurring Android-driver hazard rather than a Mali quirk.

leads.title: Adaptive Monocular Visual-Inertial SLAM for Real-Time Augmented Reality Applications in Mobile Devices
leads.claim: Runs on a Nexus 6 (Android 7.0) at 640x480, 15 fps images, 100 Hz IMU, with the authors stating explicitly "Our system only runs on a CPU and does not use any hardware acceleration methods." They switch between a cheap optical-flow-only visual odometry and full VIO based on IMU preintegration values, reporting the optical-flow VO is "3.85 times faster than the VIO method", and four adaptive levels that cut average tracking time by 7.8%, 12.9% and 18.8% at levels 1-3.
leads.why: Evidence for the P1 alternative we have not costed: instead of making detection fast enough to run every frame at 60 fps, run the expensive path only when the motion state demands it. It also frames P4 -- their bootstrap/motion-state machine is the same class of mechanism ARKit uses to hand back a pose in 1.5 s. Weak on our terms (no code, CPU-only, 2017 hardware) so it is evidence rather than a source to replicate, but it shows the adaptive lever is worth roughly 8-19% of tracking time, not 2x -- useful for not over-expecting.

leads.title: GPUImage / GPUImage2 - HarrisCornerDetector, NobleCornerDetector, ShiTomasiFeatureDetector on iOS GPU
leads.claim: A BSD-licensed iOS framework shipping GPU corner detectors: "Runs the Harris corner detection algorithm on an input image, and produces an image with those corner points as white pixels and everything else black", plus Noble and Shi-Tomasi variants with adjustable blur radius, sensitivity and threshold, and a cornersDetectedCallback returning corners in normalised 0..1 coordinates. README performance claims are for filters, not corners: "On an iPhone 4, a simple image filter can be over 100 times faster to perform on the GPU than an equivalent CPU-based filter", and 2.5 ms on an iPhone 4 to upload a camera frame, apply a gamma filter and display versus 106 ms for Core Image. The README contains no discussion of the cost of reading corner positions back off the GPU.
leads.why: The only widely used permissively licensed mobile-GPU Harris/Shi-Tomasi implementation we found for iOS, and it is worth reading for one specific reason: it produces a corner IMAGE and then needs a readback + CPU scan to turn it into a corner list, which is precisely the step OpenCV's OpenCL path avoids with atomic compaction. Comparing the two designs on device would settle how much of our per-frame time is detection versus extraction. Ranked last because the published numbers are for trivial filters on a 2010 phone and prove nothing about corner detection.

leads.title: Energy Characterization and Optimization of Image Sensing Toward Continuous Mobile Vision (LiKamWa, Priyantha, Philipose, Zhong, Bahl)
leads.claim: Five commercial CMOS image sensors measured on separate voltage rails at a 24 MHz clock: P_active = 163.5 / 189.5 / 338.6 / 225.1 / 137.1 mW and P_idle = 161.9 / 141.8 / 225.4 / 218.6 / 105.9 mW (sensors A1, A2, B1, B2, B3; B1 and B2 are the two 'Mobile' market parts, max res 3264x2448 and 2592x1944). Energy per megapixel is 6-8 mJ/MP for four of the five sensors (3 mJ/MP for B3 with column-parallel readout). Standby mode is 0.5-1.5 mW. Headline finding, verbatim: 'modern image sensors are not energy-proportional: energy per pixel is in fact inversely proportional to frame rate and resolution of image capture'. Their model for streaming capture is P_seq = (P_active - P_idle)*N*R/f + P_idle. Optimal external clock scaling cuts sensor power up to 50% (photo) / 30% (video); aggressive standby between frames adds ~40% for low frame rates; in their registration case study (0.1 MP, 3 fps) clock scaling gave 36% and aggressive standby 95% power reduction.
leads.why: This is the quantitative handle for P2. Because P_idle is 62-97% of P_active in every sensor they measured, halving the camera frame rate saves far less sensor energy than intuition says (plugging their model into sensor B1: 338.6 mW at full rate vs 282 mW at half rate, i.e. only ~17%), while resolution scales the (P_active - P_idle)*N term almost linearly. So for P1 the marginal sensor cost of going 30 -> 60 fps is modest, and for P2 the big camera-side lever is pixels per frame, not frames per second. At 1920x1440 = 2.76 MP and 6-8 mJ/MP, the raw sensor alone is ~17-22 mJ/frame, ~0.5-0.66 W at 30 fps, before any ISP or GPU work.

leads.title: Energy Drain of the Object Detection Processing Pipeline for Mobile Devices: Analysis and Implications
leads.claim: Nexus 6 (Snapdragon 805), Monsoon Power Monitor wired to a custom circuit soldered to the battery connector, 200 detections per data point, 150-frame cooling-off period. Per-frame energy for local execution: 5.037 J (performance governor) vs 17.926 J (powersave). Stage breakdown for the 300x300 local case with the interactive governor: image generation + preview 2.622 J (47.8%), inference 1.153 J (21.0%), image conversion 0.992 J (18.1%), base/OS 0.621 J (11.3%). Across all configurations 'image generation and preview ... contributes the highest energy consumption (i.e., approximately 45.3% - 70.0%)'. Disabling the 3A algorithms (AF/AE/AWB) plus noise reduction, colour correction and edge enhancement cut image-generation power by 14.8% with no measured loss of detection performance. Dropping camera FPS 30 -> 5 cut per-frame energy ~27%. At 30 fps camera FPS, 'less than 2% of the power is consumed for sampling the detectable image frames'.
leads.why: Direct evidence for P2 that the camera + ISP path, not the compute, is usually the largest single energy line in a continuous mobile vision pipeline - and that the ISP post-processing our SLAM front end does not need (3A, NR, CC, EE) is measurably ~15% of that line and can be switched off without hurting the vision task. Also directly relevant to P1: if the engine only consumes a fraction of the frames the camera produces, the unused frames are almost pure waste (their 'reactive energy'). Same group's TMC extension measures a 3000 mAh battery exhausted in ~2.3 hours running a continuous camera->detect AR loop.

leads.title: Comparing Energy Efficiency of CPU, GPU and FPGA Implementations for Vision Kernels
leads.claim: ARM57 CPU (OpenCV) vs Jetson TX2 GPU (VisionWorks/OpenVX) vs ZCU102 FPGA (xfOpenCV), 1080p, 1000 frames per platform, measured with each board's on-board power ICs (TX2 sampled by shell scripts on its own CPU; ZCU102 via the Xilinx system controller talking to an MSP430 over UART). Table II, energy/frame reduction vs the CPU reference: input processing GPU 1.79x / FPGA 1.41x; image arithmetic 3.19x / 2.93x; image filters 3.17x / 3.89x; image analysis 2.34x / 5.67x; geometric transform 10.3x / 16.6x; image features + optical flow + stereo BM 7.44x / 22.3x. Concrete kernel example: full 1080p image copy costs CPU 6.945 ms / 0.41 mJ per frame vs GPU 1.298 ms / 0.19 mJ per frame. The GPU does badly on morphological ops (dilate/erode, hit-and-miss branching), median filters, and image-analysis kernels (integral image, min/max, histogram) with complex memory access.
leads.why: The single best answer to 'which processor is most energy efficient for sparse feature tracking, and by how much', in kernel categories that map exactly onto our ported front end. Corner detection + optical flow is their best GPU category (7.44x energy/frame better than an ARM CPU running OpenCV), while the pointwise stages we also ported (CLAHE-ish arithmetic, bit-depth conversion) only earn 1.8-3.2x. It also names the kernel shapes where a GPU port is energy-negative (sorting, histogram/integral-image style reductions) - relevant because CLAHE's histogram stage is exactly one of those.

leads.title: Accelerated Feature Detectors for Visual SLAM: A Comparative Study of FPGA vs GPU (Ye and Lujan, Manchester)
leads.claim: FAST, Harris and SuperPoint on Nvidia Jetson Orin (embedded GPU) vs AMD Versal VCK190 FPGA, EuRoC 752x480. Measured power: FAST 12.6 W (Orin at the VS config) / 20.4 W (Orin max) vs 16.7 W FPGA; Harris 17.5 W / 21.5 W vs 16.5 W; SuperPoint 18.5 W / 22 W vs 30 W (Intel Xeon quoted as 120 W TDP, not measured). FAST GPU latency 0.25-0.26 ms/frame vs FPGA 0.23-0.30 ms/frame; FAST GPU energy ~2.2-2.3 mJ/frame. For Harris the GPU reaches 136x-146x energy-efficiency improvement over the CPU baseline and the FPGA only gets 1.02-1.1x over the GPU. Only for the learned detector (SuperPoint) does the FPGA clearly win: 3.1x speedup and 1.4x energy efficiency, 28 FPS vs ~14 FPS on Orin.
