leads.why: The cleanest published statement that, for classical (non-learned) corner detection, the GPU is the energy-optimal processor and even a modern FPGA barely beats it - i.e. our decision to put goodFeaturesToTrack/Harris on the GPU is the right one on energy grounds, and the P1/P2 problem is not 'wrong processor', it is duty cycle and clock/thermal behaviour. The 2.2-2.3 mJ/frame FAST figure at 752x480 gives us a sanity yardstick to compare our own measured GPU energy against.

leads.title: Qualcomm, 'Digital Signal Processing Applications for Mobile Computing Devices' (ESPA 2012 keynote) - Augmented Reality Feature Detector slide
leads.claim: Vendor-measured, on real silicon: an 'Augmented Reality Feature Detector' run on MSM8660 (Fluid 8660, Gingerbread build), comparing 'Scorpion 1.2G with Neon-Optimized' against 'Q6V3L 400 MHz Multithreaded'. Result: 1.7x faster on the DSP and 4.2x lower energy on the DSP (charge axis in mAs, execution time axis in ms). Footnote: 'Power measured with QEPM'. Elsewhere the same deck notes FastCV kernels running at roughly one third of CPU power on Hexagon.
leads.why: This is the only first-party, on-phone measurement I found that compares a feature detector's energy across processors on the same SoC, and the answer is that a DSP at 400 MHz beats NEON at 1.2 GHz by 4.2x on energy while also being faster. It is evidence, not a path: Hexagon is Qualcomm-only, so adopting it would violate the 'no platform-specific knives' rule (iOS/Mali have no equivalent). Useful mainly as an upper bound on how much energy is being lost to running the detector on general-purpose engines, and as ammunition that 'the same work has a 4x energy spread depending on where it runs'.

leads.title: LLM Inference at the Edge: Mobile, NPU, and GPU Performance Efficiency Trade-offs Under Sustained Load
leads.claim: Sustained-load thermal characterisation including iPhone 16 Pro (A18 Pro) and Galaxy S24 Ultra (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 / Adreno 750). iPhone 16 Pro 'loses nearly half its throughput within two iterations', falling from 40.35 tok/s peak to 22.56 tok/s by iteration 8; it enters Warm thermal state by iteration 3 and stays in the Hot state for 65% of all iterations. S24 Ultra suffers a hard OS-enforced thermal cut at iteration 6: GPU frequency floored to 231 MHz from 629-680 MHz, GPU 78.3 C, CPU 73.8 C. Measurement methodology table states iPhone power is only available via UIDevice.batteryLevel ('coarse energy proxy; no per-component power exposed') and that the Android Battery Manager API is 'unreliable under active GPU load and is excluded'. Contrast case: Hailo-10H NPU held 0.04% throughput CV with no throttling at 1.87 W, 270.5 mJ/token.
leads.why: Independent, same-generation confirmation of exactly the P1 failure mode we observe: a sustained mobile-GPU compute load downclocks within seconds and roughly halves effective throughput, on both an iPhone and an Adreno phone. It also tells us our measurement plan for P2: on iOS there is no per-subsystem power API, so a phone-side joules number is not obtainable from app code - we must use Instruments Power Profiler (see the Apple lead) or an external monitor, and on Android we must read the PMIC rails, not BatteryManager.

leads.title: Efficient Deployment of Vision-Language Models on Mobile Devices: A Case Study on OnePlus 13R
leads.claim: OnePlus 13R, Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 (Adreno 740), Android 15. Methodology: utilisation, power and thermals logged at 100 ms intervals from root-readable /proc, /sys, /sys/class/power_supply/ and thermal zones, in parallel with the workload. CPU-only stacks: battery current rises from 0.2 A idle to ~3.1 A (approx 10 W), die temperature climbs from ~40 C to an 88-90 C plateau within 15 s; peak package power 10-12 W at 90-95 C. GPU-offloaded stacks: MobileVLM-3B 3.5 W and 72 C; Imp-v1.5-3B ~0.33 A (approx 1.3 W) at 60 C peak, about 30 C cooler than the CPU-only run. One framework left the Adreno 740 at 0% busy the entire run and reported a flat ~57 mA rail current for the phase where the GPU should have been used.
leads.why: A concrete, reproducible Android measurement recipe we can copy for the Mali and Adreno legs of P2 (sysfs power_supply current + thermal zones at 100 ms, no external hardware), plus a hard number for how much thermal headroom moving work onto a mobile GPU actually buys on an Adreno phone: an order of magnitude in package power and ~30 C in die temperature. If our GPU port is not showing that kind of separation, the energy is going somewhere other than the shaders.

leads.title: Introducing SLAMBench, a performance and accuracy benchmarking methodology for SLAM (PAMELA project)
leads.claim: ODROID-XU3 (Exynos 5422: 4x Cortex-A15, 4x Cortex-A7, Mali-T628) has 'on-board voltage/current sensors and split power rails, which allows the power consumption of the big Cortex-A15 cores, the LITTLE Cortex-A7 cores, GPU and DRAM to be measured individually', read directly by the benchmark at instrumented points. Fig. 6 plots energy per frame per resource combination for KinectFusion (C++ single-core, OpenMP, OpenCL) with mean frame time annotated (1.23 s and 2.33 s for C++ on A15/A7, 0.50 s and 0.86 s for OpenMP, 0.18 s for both OpenCL configs). 'The OpenCL/GPU implementation uses significantly less energy than approaches that rely solely on the conventional CPU cores.' For OpenCL, using the A15 as host instead of the A7 gives negligible performance benefit but 'the energy consumed is 50% higher (507.28 compared with 337 Joules)'. Reported 5.5 FPS at 2.1 W average dissipation on this board.
leads.why: Two things. (1) It is the only open-source SLAM benchmark harness that instruments energy per frame per processing element - the shape of the experiment we should be running for P2, including the split-rail idea (on Android we can approximate this with per-rail sysfs). (2) The 50% finding is directly actionable: which CPU cluster hosts the GPU submission/wait thread changed total energy by 50% for zero speed gain. Our engine's Dawn submit thread and its wait behaviour (busy-wait vs block) is exactly this knob, and it is invisible in a wall-clock measurement.
leads.license: benchmark code is open source (SLAMBench, github.com/pamela-project)

leads.title: Reconfiguring the Imaging Pipeline for Computer Vision (Buckler, Jayasuriya, Sampson)
leads.claim: Proposes a sensor/ISP 'vision mode' and reports it 'can save approximately 75% of the average energy of a baseline photography mode' with negligible vision-task accuracy loss. Their analysis finds only two ISP stages matter for downstream vision - demosaicing and gamma compression - and that the sensor should be configured for subsampled, lower-precision output with tunable ADCs. (Abstract-level; the per-stage absolute energies are in the full paper, which I did not open.)
leads.why: Independent second source for the P2 claim that most of the camera-side energy in a CV pipeline is spent producing image quality the vision algorithm does not use. Combined with the Nexus 6 measurement (3A/NR/CC/EE off = -14.8% with no accuracy loss), this argues for asking AVFoundation for the cheapest format that still feeds our front end - binned/subsampled, minimal post-processing - rather than a full-resolution photographic stream. Also a warning: bit-exactness against OpenCV is preserved by our shaders, but changing the sensor/ISP configuration changes the input pixels, so this is a product decision, not a lossless speed-up.
leads.license: paper; the authors released a configurable-pipeline simulator separately

leads.title: DeepEn2023: Energy Datasets for Edge Artificial Intelligence
leads.claim: Energy measurement platform built on the Monsoon Power Monitor (chosen for millisecond-level granularity; power sampled while the Monsoon also supplies the device), covering eight modern edge devices with eight different mobile SoCs from Qualcomm, HiSilicon and MediaTek, at least one high-end and one mid-range per vendor. Three released datasets: kernel-level, model-level and application-level, with per-kernel energy in mJ (tables give ranges such as 0.001-132.861 mJ per kernel). Stated observation: 'the kernels, GPU exhibit better energy efficiency under same configurations' (16 kernel types measured on CPU, 10 on GPU). Dataset and code at https://amai-gsu.github.io/DeepEn2023.
leads.why: A ready-made, published methodology and open dataset for exactly the measurement we lack: per-kernel joules on real phone SoCs, CPU versus GPU, with an external monitor rather than OS estimates. Even though the kernels are DNN ops rather than CLAHE/Scharr/LK, the harness design (Monsoon supplying the phone, sync between app logs and the power trace) is directly transferable to our Mali and Adreno legs, and their cross-SoC GPU-beats-CPU result is a second independent data point for the core question in this assignment.
leads.license: dataset and code publicly released (site does not state a license in what I read)

leads.title: Measuring Power Usage on iOS Devices (GameBench engineering blog)
leads.claim: Uses Apple's Energy Diagnostics instrument in Wireless Mode; reports battery drain percentage and average current drain in mA; no jailbreak or Xcode project needed; sessions must run at least 15 minutes for usable numbers. Critical limitation stated: on iPhone 8 and newer, only battery-drain percentage is available because of a documented Apple Instruments bug that prevents current-drain measurement; the mA metric works only on iPhone 7 and earlier with iOS 10.3+. They describe it as 'not the engineering grade measurement'.
leads.why: Saves a wasted day on P2. The obvious path - Energy Diagnostics / mA drain - is broken on every iPhone we own, so on an iPhone 14 Pro the only in-OS options are the WWDC25 Power Profiler subsystem scores and %/hr, and anything in real joules has to come from an external monitor or from battery-percentage deltas over long, controlled runs. It also sets the minimum run length (15 min) for a stable phone-level power figure, which is longer than our current 300 s protocol.

leads.title: LEVIO: Lightweight Embedded Visual Inertial Odometry for Resource-Constrained Devices (ETH PBL)
leads.claim: A full 6-DoF VIO pipeline written in plain C, deployed on the GreenWaves GAP9 RISC-V SoC (8-core cluster + fabric controller, max 370 MHz): under 100 mW total, approximately 5 mJ per frame at 20 FPS on QQVGA (160x120), with WVGA used for benchmark comparisons against VINS-Mono and ORB-SLAM3 on EuRoC (0.9-3.5 m ATE vs sub-0.5 m for the heavyweight baselines), and a projected 15x efficiency gain over VINS-Mono on a Jetson Nano. Code at https://github.com/ETH-PBL/levio.
leads.why: An energy floor for the whole problem, from a permissively-published C implementation rather than a GPL SLAM stack. 5 mJ/frame for a complete VIO front end plus back end at low resolution says the algorithm class is not intrinsically expensive - our 173 s in 'serious' thermal is coming from resolution, duty cycle and platform overhead, not from VIO being hard. (The MIT Navion ASIC makes the same point harder: 752x480 stereo VIO at 20 fps for 2 mW average, 24 mW at 171 fps, arXiv 1809.05780 - unimplementable for us, but it bounds how much of our energy is essential.) Caveat: I did not verify the GitHub repo's actual software licence, only that the code is public.
leads.license: code public on GitHub; software licence not verified

leads.title: XRSLAM upstream iOS reference app: VGA 640x480 @ 30 fps, detection gated to every 3rd frame (slam_params.yaml + Camera.swift + ViewController.swift @ rev 4beb1a9)
leads.claim: At the exact revision you ported (4beb1a9): xrslam-ios/visualizer/configs/slam_params.yaml sets `sliding_window: tracker_frequent: 3`, `feature_tracker: max_keypoint_detection: 300`, `min_keypoint_distance: 25.0`, `solver: time_limit: 0.1 / iteration_limit: 10`. xrslam-ios/visualizer/src/Camera.swift:28 defaults `preset: AVCaptureSession.Preset = .vga640x480`; ViewController.swift:255 calls `camera.setFps(30)`. configs/iPhone 14 Pro.yaml (the config for YOUR device) declares `resolution: [640, 480]`.
leads.why: P1 premise correction with source lines. You are running 1920x1440 (9x the pixels) at 30 fps aiming for 60, i.e. ~27x the front-end pixel throughput of upstream's own shipped iOS reference configuration. Every published XRSLAM/RD-VIO on-device result is at VGA/30. Your 60 fps target has never been an upstream operating point; the 16.7 ms budget you are trying to hit is being spent on 9x more pixels than the algorithm was tuned for.

leads.title: XRSLAM feature_tracker.cpp: detect_keypoints() is gated by `frame->id() % sliding_window_tracker_frequent() == 0` — upstream does NOT detect every frame; the C++ default of 1 does
leads.claim: At rev 4beb1a9, feature_tracker.cpp:47-49 computes `bool slidind_window_frame_tag = !is_initialized || frame->id() % config->sliding_window_tracker_frequent() == 0;`. Line 128-129: `if (slidind_window_frame_tag) frame->detect_keypoints(config.get());`. Line 151-152: `if (slidind_window_frame_tag) detail->frontend->issue_frame(...)`. Meanwhile xrslam/src/xrslam/config.cpp:78 has `size_t Config::sliding_window_tracker_frequent() const { return 1; }` — the hard-coded fallback is 1 (every frame), but the shipped iOS yaml overrides it to 3. CLAHE preprocess (line 39-41) is unconditional, every frame.
leads.why: Directly falsifies your stated P1 premise ('Detection currently runs on EVERY frame because that is what the upstream tracker does'). Upstream's iOS app detects on 1 frame in 3 and also hands only every 3rd frame to the backend. If your port reads the C++ default instead of the yaml you are paying 3x the detection AND 3x the backend work upstream pays. Setting tracker_frequent=3 is an upstream-authoritative change (cite these lines), not self-invention — but it is NOT bit-lossless, so flag it as a product decision. Note the tension with P4 below. Also note CLAHE stays per-frame in upstream, so your CLAHE cost is legitimate — the corner detection is the part upstream throttles.

leads.title: XRSLAM initializer.cpp + config.cpp: structural floor for time-to-first-pose is keyframe_num(8) x keyframe_gap(5) = 35 frames of history, plus 10 px parallax
leads.claim: initializer.cpp:26-38 computes `init_frame_index_gap = initializer_keyframe_gap()` and `init_frame_index_distance = gap * (initializer_keyframe_num() - 1)`, and returns early (`map.reset(); return;`) until that many frames of history exist. config.cpp defaults: initializer_keyframe_num()=8, initializer_keyframe_gap()=5, initializer_min_matches()=50, initializer_min_parallax()=10, initializer_min_triangulation()=50, initializer_min_landmarks()=30, feature_tracker_max_init_frames()=60. So 5*(8-1)=35 frames must be buffered before the first bootstrap attempt: 1.17 s at 30 fps, 0.58 s at 60 fps.
leads.why: P4 root cause, quantified with source lines. Of your 3.6 s, ~1.2 s is a hard frame-count floor at 30 fps and the rest is waiting for 10 px of accumulated parallax across 8 spaced keyframes. Two consequences: (a) doubling the camera to 60 fps halves the frame-count floor but does nothing to the parallax term; (b) if you adopt tracker_frequent=3 the frontend sees only 1 in 3 frames, so the 35-frame history becomes 105 camera frames = 3.5 s at 30 fps — you would trade P1/P2 directly against P4. Any change to keyframe_num/gap/min_parallax is a result-altering product decision.

leads.title: Faster than FAST: GPU-Accelerated Frontend for High-Speed VIO (Nagy, Foehn, Scaramuzza, IROS 2020) — NEGATIVE RESULT: OpenCV's own CUDA KLT is 2.1x SLOWER than OpenCV CPU on embedded ARM+GPU
leads.claim: Table VI (tracking 100 features, re-detection at 30, EuRoC 752x480), Tegra X2 column: OpenCV CPU 1.88 ms, OpenCV CUDA 3.96 ms, their custom GPU tracker 0.90-1.01 ms. On the laptop (i7-6700HQ + GTX 960M): OpenCV CPU 1.38 ms, OpenCV CUDA 0.74 ms. Table V (FAST detection + NMS), Tegra X2: OpenCV CPU multithreaded 4.78 ms, OpenCV CUDA 2.73 ms, ArrayFire CPU 60.83 ms, ArrayFire CUDA 1.47 ms, theirs 1.11 ms. Full frontend+ICE-BA backend: 4.67-6.41 ms/frame on Tegra X2 (vs 11.64-12.91 ms for ICE-BA's own frontend), ~200 fps VIO, 2.25x speedup, 0.47% mean accuracy loss. Released as vilib.
leads.why: This is the negative result you asked for, and the closest published analogue of what you built. A straight GPU port of the OpenCV pyramidal LK tracker LOSES to the OpenCV CPU tracker on an embedded ARM+GPU part; only a purpose-rewritten GPU kernel (fused detection+NMS, cell-grid, no round-trips) wins, and only by ~2x. It says the win is not in porting OpenCV faithfully but in restructuring the kernels — which is exactly the tension with your bit-exact constraint. Their vilib is BSD-3-Clause (verified: LICENSE.txt says 'BSD 3-Clause License, Copyright (c) 2020, Balazs Nagy, Robotics and Perception Group, University of Zurich'), so it IS a copyable authoritative source for the fused FAST+NMS and the affine LK with gain/offset.

leads.title: RD-VIO (the XRSLAM algorithm paper, TVCG 2024): module timings, iPhone X deployment at 640x480/30 Hz, head-to-head vs ARKit and ARCore with VICON ground truth
leads.claim: Table 2, running time per module on an Intel i7-7700 @3.6 GHz / 16 GB (V1_01_easy), VINS-Mono front-end vs RD-VIO: Keypoint Tracking 8.34 / 7.47 ms; Pre-Integration 0.44 / 0.04; Non-Keyframe PnP 17.78 / 1.27; IMU-PARSAC - / 1.07; Keyframe BA 19.18 / 30.9; Keyframe Marg 32.91 / 3.99; Keyframe Average 60.87 / 42.4 ms; All-frame Average 44.72 / 18.38 ms. Sec 4.4.4: 'We use 30 Hz images data with resolution 640 x 480 and IMU data ... 100 Hz captured by the iPhone X.' Table 4 (VICON ground truth, three phones strapped together, ARKit on iPhone X, ARCore on Xiaomi Mi 8, RD-VIO on a second iPhone X), APE in mm: A0 ARKit 15.643 / ARCore 16.625 / RD-VIO 22.385; A1 28.361 / 23.973 / 28.902; A2 22.576 / 31.576 / 20.931; A3 33.339 / 40.387 / 19.583; A4 42.615 / 34.492 / 23.049. Also, Sec 4.4.1: 'OpenVINS requires 40 seconds for initialization on MH_01_easy and 35 seconds on MH_02_easy.'
leads.why: Authoritative upstream numbers. All-frame average 18.38 ms on a DESKTOP i7-7700 (keyframe frames 42.4 ms) means the algorithm you ported was never a 60 Hz design even on x86 — 60 fps would need 16.7 ms end-to-end for a pipeline whose own authors measure 18.38 ms on a 3.6 GHz desktop core. That reframes P1: the ceiling may not be your GPU front end at all. The ARKit/ARCore APE table is the only published same-scene comparison of this exact algorithm against your baseline. The OpenVINS 35-40 s init figure is the strongest published evidence that slow bootstrap (P4) is endemic to academic VIO, not a bug in your port.

leads.title: HybVIO (Seiskari et al., WACV 2022): 8.3 ms/frame on one desktop core, 49 ms/frame on a Raspberry Pi 4 ARM Cortex-A72 — and Basalt goes 5 ms -> 36 ms when limited to 2 cores
leads.claim: Table 3 (stereo, per-frame processing time): 'Fast VIO' config (FAST features, 70 stereo / 100 mono max features, LK window 13, 8 iterations) = 8.3 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X single core and 49 ms on a Raspberry Pi 4 (ARM Cortex-A72); 'Normal VIO' (GFTT, 200 features, window 31, 20 iterations) = 32 ms on Ryzen. Max RAM on EuRoC < 500 MB. Table B1 (stereo SLAM, Ryzen frame time): HybVIO 32 ms on all 12 CPUs vs 47 ms on 2 CPUs; ORB-SLAM3 56 -> 78 ms; BASALT 5 ms on all 12 CPUs vs 36 ms on 2 CPUs. Conclusion: 'real-time performance was demonstrated on a Raspberry Pi without the use of GPU, VPU or ISP resources, which could further improve the speed and energy consumption of visual processing.' Sec 4.3 records ARKit on an iPhone 11 Pro (iOS 14.3) and ARCore 1.21 on a Huawei Mate 20 Pro side by side with their own method on the same input data.
leads.why: Two things for P1/P2. (1) A complete VIO front+back end runs at 49 ms/frame on a Cortex-A72 with NO GPU at all — the A16 P-cores are several times faster than an A72, which says the CPU path was never obviously the bottleneck at VGA and that your 19-22 ms downclocked GPU pass is not automatically a win over NEON at the feature counts VIO actually uses (70-200 features). (2) Basalt's 5 ms becomes 36 ms (7.2x) when squeezed to 2 cores while HybVIO only degrades 1.5x — mobile VIO speed is dominated by how well work is spread across cores, not by raw kernel speed. Your CPU load is 0.80 core-equivalents (same as ARKit) while you are 2x behind on pose rate: that ratio suggests serialization/back-pressure, matching the HybVIO/Basalt core-count result. Code is GPLv3 so it is EVIDENCE ONLY, not copyable.
leads.license: GPL-3.0 (code unusable to you); paper usable as evidence

leads.title: Faster than Fast (Chang et al. 2025), Jetson TX2/AGX power table: a FASTER GPU detector draws MORE instantaneous watts (4.16 -> 6.07 W) while using LESS energy per frame (0.133 -> 0.037 J)
leads.claim: Table 5, Jetson TX2 (Pascal, 256 CUDA cores, 7.5/15 W board), Oriented-FAST on the Echeveria image with 4-layer pyramid: Baseline SYS_GPU 4.157 W, runtime 18.12 ms, 0.133 J/frame, 7.52 FPS/W. Semi-Sep_ORB (their fastest): SYS_GPU 6.069 W, runtime 3.83 ms, 0.037 J/frame, 26.78 FPS/W. SYS_DDR also rises 1.492 -> 1.683 W because of shared-memory tiling. On AGX Xavier: 10.61 -> 15.49 W, 7.64 -> 1.21 ms, 0.109 -> 0.024 J/frame, 6.31x speedup. Text: 'with continuous kernel optimization, SYS_GPU increases significantly, indicating that our approach effectively enhances thread parallelism, thereby improving GPU utilization.' Video processing: 768x432 at ~144 FPS on TX2; 1280x720 at ~55 FPS on TX2. Note 'Oriented FAST calculations account for approximately half of the entire SLAM system.'
leads.why: Directly reframes P2. Your instinct is probably 'make the GPU kernel faster so it fits in 16.7 ms', but this is the only measurement I found that separates the two: optimizing a mobile-class GPU detector RAISES peak power (+46% on TX2, +46% on AGX) even as it cuts energy per frame by 3.6x. If iOS thermalState is driven by sustained package power rather than joules-per-frame, a faster kernel can make thermals WORSE at a fixed frame rate — the only reliable lever is doing less work (fewer pixels, fewer detected frames, smaller bindings), not the same work faster. That is a testable prediction you can check on your own bench in an afternoon, and it argues against spending more effort on kernel micro-optimization for P2.

leads.title: License audit of the mobile VIO field: OpenVINS is GPL-3.0 (unusable), but Kimera-VIO is BSD-2, Basalt BSD-3, vilib BSD-3, maplab Apache-2.0, ICE-BA Apache-2.0
leads.claim: Verified via the GitHub API license field: rpng/open_vins = GPL-3.0 (3086 stars); MIT-SPARK/Kimera-VIO = BSD-2-Clause (1912 stars); VladyslavUsenko/basalt-mirror = BSD-3-Clause; uzh-rpg/vilib = LICENSE.txt is 'BSD 3-Clause License, Copyright (c) 2020, 2019-2020 Balazs Nagy, Robotics and Perception Group, University of Zurich' (GitHub misreports it as NOASSERTION); ethz-asl/maplab = Apache-2.0 (2870 stars); baidu/ICE-BA = Apache-2.0 (762 stars); openxrlab/xrslam = Apache-2.0; SpectacularAI/HybVIO = GPL-3.0; HKUST-Aerial-Robotics/VINS-Mobile README states 'The source code is released under GPLv3 licence' and lists supported devices 'iPhone7 Plus, iPhone7, iPhone6s Plus, iPhone6s, iPad Pro' on 'iOS 10.2.1 and above'.
leads.why: Your brief lists OpenVINS as a system to look at — its CODE is GPL-3.0 and therefore unusable to you under your own rule, same bucket as ORB-SLAM/VINS/DSO/SVO. Worth correcting before anyone reads its source. The usable half of the field is bigger than your brief assumes: Kimera-VIO (BSD-2), Basalt (BSD-3), vilib (BSD-3, GPU frontend), maplab (Apache-2.0), ICE-BA (Apache-2.0, the fastest published VI local BA and the backend the vilib paper pairs with). GitHub's own license badge on vilib says NOASSERTION and is wrong — check LICENSE.txt, not the badge, before you rule it out.

leads.title: ADVIO (Cortes et al., ECCV 2018): ARKit emits 60 Hz poses on an iPhone 6s from 1280x720@60 video; ARCore emits 30 Hz on a Pixel
leads.claim: Table of raw iPhone capture: 'iPhone / ARKit pose / Position/orientation / Metric position / 60 Hz'; 'Video / RGB video / Resolution 1280x720 / 60 Hz'; Gyroscope, Accelerometer, Magnetometer 100 Hz; 'Pixel / ARCore pose / 30 Hz'; 'Tango / Raw pose / 60 Hz', Tango fisheye video 640x480 60 Hz. Captured on an iPhone 6s running iOS 11.0.3, chosen because 'the iPhone 6s (published 2015) is hardware-wise closer to an average smartphone than most recent flagship iPhones'.
leads.why: Independent confirmation of your P1 ARKit baseline (59.9 poses/s), and it establishes that ARKit was already delivering 60 Hz poses on an A9 in 2017 — so the 60 Hz target is not an A16-era luxury, it is what ARKit does on hardware five generations older than yours. It also documents the resolution at which the AR-VIO community actually records: 1280x720, not 1920x1440. Corroborated independently by 'An Empirical Evaluation of Four Off-the-Shelf Proprietary VIO Systems' (arXiv 2207.06780), which logs ARKit on an iPhone 12 Pro Max (iOS 14.7.1) 'as a translation vector and a unit quaternion at 60 Hz' via github.com/PyojinKim/ios_logger.
leads.license: dataset: see paper; ios_logger tool separate

leads.title: A Smartphone Thermal Temperature Analysis for VR and AR (Zhang, Vadodaria, Li, Kang, Liu — AIVR 2020): a shipped AR app exceeds the Snapdragon 855's 5 W TDP by 20-80% and temperatures rise monotonically for the full 20 minutes
leads.claim: Abstract and Sec VI: measuring Minecraft Earth (AR) on rooted Google Pixel 4 and Samsung Galaxy S10 (Snapdragon 855, 5 W TDP per their Table I): 'the battery power consumption frequently exceeds the thermal design power by 20-80%, while the peak battery, CPU, GPU, and WiFi module temperature exceeds 45, 70, 70, and 65 C, respectively.' GPU utilization is 'higher than 60%' and the phone performs continuous CPU frequency scaling between 0.6-1.8 GHz; battery temperature 'keeps increasing' through the 20-minute run despite that scaling. For the 360-degree VR video case the surface reaches near 39 C and power stays 'well below the 5 W TDP'.
leads.why: The best published grounding I found for P2: a mainstream, heavily-optimized AR app on flagship silicon still runs 20-80% over TDP with the GPU >60% busy, and thermal control never reaches steady state inside 20 minutes. That says your 173 s-of-300 s in 'serious' is in the normal range for a full-res camera+GPU AR workload, and that closing the gap to ARKit's 0 s is not a matter of shaving milliseconds — ARKit must be running a structurally smaller workload (lower internal resolution and/or fixed-function ISP/AMX paths). Combine with the XRSLAM 640x480 finding above: the most likely single explanation for P2 is that you are doing full-res GPU work on 9x the pixels ARKit's tracker sees.

leads.title: XRSLAM issue #44 'WebAssembly build for mobile browsers' — open and unanswered since Feb 2024; GitHub repo search for 'webgpu slam' returns zero repositories
leads.claim: Issue #44, opened 2024-02-22 by user DNRN, state OPEN, zero comments: 'Would it be possible to build the project as WebAssembly, so it's possible to run from a browser on Android and iOS?'. `gh search repos "webgpu slam"` returns an empty result set. Across the full XRSLAM issue list (40 issues) there is no thread about GPU acceleration, frame rate, thermals or memory; the only device-specific thread is #10 'No new supported iPhone14pro/pro max.yaml found', answered by a maintainer with 'We will add parameters of iphone14 series soon.'
leads.why: Answers your cross-cutting question directly, in the negative: I found no published system, paper, or repository that drives an OpenCV-replica SLAM front end through WebGPU/Dawn on a phone. The one person who asked upstream about a browser build got no reply in over two years. You are first here, which means (a) no prior art to copy for the port itself, and (b) no prior art warning you off it either — the closest analogue is vilib (CUDA), whose measurements say a faithful OpenCV-to-GPU port loses and a restructured one wins ~2x. Weigh that against the fact that XRSLAM's own maintainers did not have an iPhone 14 Pro config until users asked.

leads.title: Official OpenXRLab XRSLAM announcement (Chinese, Zhihu): the design target is 30 fps on an ordinary phone
leads.claim: The authors' own announcement states the system '支持普通手机终端30fps的实时处理帧率' (supports a 30 fps real-time processing frame rate on ordinary mobile terminals) and that the algorithm '处理效率可以支持30Fps以上的数据处理帧率'. It also states the codebase '支持Linux、Mac、Android、iOS等多个平台的编译运行'. No resolution, per-frame latency, CPU load, memory, power, or initialization-time figures are given, and there is no ARKit/ARCore comparison. (Fetched through r.jina.ai; zhuanlan.zhihu.com returns 403 to direct fetches.)
leads.why: The authors' own stated operating point is 30 fps, in the community's native language, matching the 640x480/30 config and the RD-VIO paper. Nothing upstream — paper, repo, config, or announcement — has ever claimed or measured 60 fps. That means P1 is not 'we regressed against upstream'; it is 'we are attempting an operating point upstream never targeted, at 9x the resolution'. Worth saying explicitly before more GPU effort is spent on the 16.7 ms budget.

leads.title: WWDC19 Session 249 — Introducing Multi-Camera Capture for iOS (hardware cost, system pressure cost, binned formats)
leads.claim: Apple states verbatim: "Bin formats are super low power. Whenever you use ARKit with a camera, you are using a binned format, because ARKit uses binned formats exclusively to save power." 2x2 binning = 4x reduction in bandwidth (and 4x noise reduction, 4x intensity/pixel) through the single ISP. Apple gives a quantified system-pressure-cost model on iPhone XS-class hardware: cost <1.0 = runnable indefinitely; 1.0–2.0 = up to 15 minutes; 2.0–3.0 = up to 10 minutes; >3.0 = short duration only before the session is interrupted. 'Serious' system pressure is described as: "System throttles; fewer GPU cycles; quality may be compromised." Contributors to cost are resolution, frame rate, binning, OIS/EIS stabilization and Smart HDR. Critically: "Lowering frame rate alone doesn't help because AVCaptureDevice allows runtime frame rate changes — the system must assume worst case", so Apple added AVCaptureDeviceInput.videoMinFrameDurationOverride (CMTime(value:1,timescale:30)) so you "only pay hardware cost for 30 FPS, not 60". Fastest in-flight relief from system pressure is: "Lower frame rate — immediately, that will relieve system pressure."
leads.why: This is the single most decision-relevant Apple statement for P2. It says ARKit's own energy advantage comes partly from running the camera in a binned, low-power format exclusively — so the fair comparison for our 300 s run is not 'ARKit does magic', it is 'ARKit pays 1/4 the ISP bandwidth'. It also gives us (a) an actual budget arithmetic to predict how long a given capture config can run before interruption, (b) videoMinFrameDurationOverride as a lever if we ever open a 60 fps channel but only need 30 fps of it, and (c) confirmation that at 'serious' the system itself gives us fewer GPU cycles — which is exactly the 5 ms -> 19–22 ms collapse in P1. Directly attacks P1 and P2.
leads.license: Apple proprietary session content — evidence + API recipe, no code to copy

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums — "Metal Compute Never beats 2.5ms?" (mobile GPU loses to NEON below a threshold; GPU sleep-clock penalty)
leads.claim: On iPhone 6s Plus (A9) an EMPTY Metal compute encoder could not go below ~2.5 ms per iteration, while the equivalent NEON code ran in ~0.04 ms. The thread attributes this to fixed CPU–GPU coordination cost (wired MTLResource setup, command encoding, JIT compile, GPU wake-up, readback, thread scheduling), and states: "The GPU clock slows way down when it is asleep and takes a long time to come back up again. 2-4x performance loss can occur due to this on even extremely large workloads." Guidance: use NEON when data starts and ends on the CPU, the workload is small, or ultra-low latency is needed; use the GPU when data is already on the GPU, when processing millions of pixels, or when you can batch (e.g. 16 frames at once); keep the GPU busy by queueing the next command buffer before the current one completes.
leads.why: This is exactly the credible negative result the brief asked for, and it names the mechanism behind P1. Our GPU stage is ~5 ms at nominal clocks and 19–22 ms once the phone downclocks — a 4x swing that matches the quoted 2–4x sleep-clock penalty. It also warns that a per-frame burst-then-idle pattern (ours) is the worst case for Apple's GPU power management, and that on this class of workload a NEON/CPU path can win outright. Before we chase 60 fps on the GPU we should measure the same CLAHE+Harris stage on NEON, and try keeping the GPU continuously fed rather than one dispatch per frame.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums — "OS choosing performance state poorly for GPU use case" (clock heuristic is per-command-buffer saturation, not GPU load)
leads.claim: A real-time Metal-compute audio app (Anukari, ~3 ms work chunks, alternating non-overlapping CPU and GPU phases, few threadgroups) runs ~2x slower standalone than when Instruments forces the GPU performance state to 'Maximum'. The developer's analysis, echoed in the thread: the OS clock-scaling heuristic keys off GPU saturation per command buffer, not overall GPU load — while the CPU works the GPU is idle and vice versa, which signals to the OS that higher clocks are not needed. Perverse consequence stated: more efficient kernels using fewer threadgroups trigger the heuristic even less, so optimizing the shader makes the clock problem worse. Their workaround was to spin a GPU threadgroup in a busy loop 100% of the time ('waste makes haste') — effective but power-wasteful and not future-proof. An Apple DTS engineer redirected to Audio Workgroups rather than endorsing the busy-spin; Apple confirmed the issue under investigation (May 2025).
leads.why: Our pipeline has the identical shape: a short GPU burst per camera frame with idle gaps, on a device whose OS decides clocks from command-buffer saturation. That predicts precisely the P1 symptom — nominal-clock 5 ms that becomes 19–22 ms — and it means our downclock may be as much a scheduling-heuristic artefact as a thermal one. Two testable implications: (1) measure our stage under a locked 'Maximum' performance state to separate 'thermally throttled' from 'never ramped up'; (2) fusing CLAHE + pyramid + Scharr + Harris into fewer, larger, better-saturated command buffers may raise the clock rather than just reduce work. Also a documented warning that our lossless-optimization work could make the clock problem worse.

leads.title: WWDC22 Session 10126 — Discover ARKit 6 (ARKit's HD stream is a 2x2-binned 1920x1440; 60 fps HD is Apple's recommendation for high-refresh apps)
leads.claim: ARKit's standard HD mode bins 2x2 pixel regions from 3840x2880 down to 1920x1440 "to reduce memory consumption and processing power"; 4K mode (3840x2160) skips that binning step and runs at 30 fps only. Apple's guidance: "Dealing with higher resolution images takes up additional system resources, so for games and other apps that rely on a high refresh rate, we still suggest using full HD video at 60 frames per second." HDR is only available on non-binned formats and "turning on HDR will have a performance impact, so make sure to only use it when there is a need for it." Frame-retention warning: "Do not hold on to an ARFrame for too long. This might prevent the system from freeing up memory, which might further stop ARKit from surfacing newer frames to you. This will become visible through frame drops in your rendering. Ultimately, the ARCamera's tracking state might fall back to limited."
leads.why: Establishes the baseline our 1920x1440 measurement sits on: that resolution IS the binned low-power format, and 60 fps at that resolution is what Apple explicitly recommends — so P1's 60 fps target is sanctioned by the vendor and the camera channel is not the thing that has to give. It also implies the energy delta in P2 is not the camera format but what we do with each frame (full-res GPU work every frame). The ARFrame-retention warning is a concrete P3/P1 checklist item: buffer retention shows up as frame drops and tracking degradation, which is the same signature as our back-pressure collapse.
leads.license: Apple proprietary session content — evidence, no code to copy

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums — "ARKit FPS drop when device gets hot?" (Apple engineer: expected; FPS halves and persists across app restart)
leads.claim: An Apple Graphics and Games engineer confirms that ARKit/RealityKit apps having their FPS drop when the device gets hot is expected behaviour: iOS devices have no active cooling, so the system reduces processing power. Reported symptom (iOS 15 beta 19A5340a, RealityKit): frame rate drops by approximately half and stays down until the device cools — it persists even after killing and relaunching the app, and returns to 60 fps only after the device rests. The engineer's answer at the time also stated there is no official API to detect the thermal/power state from the application, and recommended monitoring ARView.showStatistics and optimizing rendering instead.
leads.why: Direct counter-evidence to the framing in P2 that 'ARKit spends 0 s in serious'. ARKit sessions demonstrably do drive devices into throttling, and when they do the penalty is ~2x frame rate and it is sticky across process restarts. That matters for our benchmark hygiene: a 300 s ARKit run that reported 59.9 poses/s and 0 s serious was probably started from a cold device, and our run may have inherited residual heat — the two arms need identical thermal starting conditions and a cool-down between them, or the 173 s figure is partly a measurement artefact.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums — "How can I profile iOS GPU clock speed?" (Apple: no API for GPU clock or performance state; ~10% loss after 30 s)
leads.claim: Reported on iOS: measurably better GPU performance during roughly the first 30 seconds after app start, then about 10% degradation, suspected clock throttling. An Apple Graphics and Games engineer replies that there is no way to query the GPU clock speed or the device performance state programmatically, and that the supported approach is to lock the performance state (maximum / medium / minimum) from Xcode for apples-to-apples comparisons, pointing at WWDC 2021 session 10157 (Discover Metal debugging, profiling, and asset creation tools) at t=476 s. Recommended loop: GPU capture -> profile with the stopwatch at a locked performance state -> edit shaders in the Xcode GPU debugger -> re-profile at the same locked state.
leads.why: Methodological requirement for every number in P1. We report '~5 ms at nominal GPU clocks' and '19–22 ms once downclocked' — but there is no API to read the clock, so those two regimes can only be separated by locking the performance state in Xcode. Until we do that we cannot tell how much of our 60 fps shortfall is thermal throttling, how much is the ramp-up heuristic, and how much is genuinely too much work. It also gives a hard 30 s warning: any GPU benchmark shorter than ~30 s on iOS measures the boosted clock, not the sustained one.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums — "Ensuring peak GPU performance for short running kernels" (Apple: no way to hint the GPU to ramp up)
leads.claim: Apple GPUs ramp frequency slowly and do not reach peak performance for kernels that run less than a few seconds, which causes short single-image workloads (and benchmarks such as Geekbench 5) to under-report Apple GPU throughput. An Apple Graphics and Games engineer states verbatim: "There is currently no way to hint the GPU to ramp up before executing work." The only offered path is the GPU Performance State inducer in Apple's profiling tooling (WWDC 2021 session 10157).
leads.why: A hard negative result that closes a design avenue for P1: there is no supported pre-warm/ramp-hint API, so any plan of the form 'ask the GPU to be at high clock before the frame arrives' is dead. What is left is (a) making dispatches large and continuous enough that the OS heuristic raises the clock on its own, (b) moving work to the CPU/NEON side where clocks respond faster, or (c) doing less work per frame. Combined with the previous two leads, this says our 16.7 ms budget must be met at the LOW clock, not the nominal one.

leads.title: WWDC22 Session 110429 — Discover advancements in iOS camera capture: Depth, focus, and multitasking (reduce footprint via binned/low-res/non-HDR)
leads.claim: Apple's stated reason camera access was previously blocked while multitasking: "Resource-intensive apps like games running alongside an app using the camera can induce frame drops and other latency, resulting in a poor camera feed." Guidance to developers: "Make your app resilient to increasing system pressure by monitoring for its notifications, and take action to reduce the impact, like lowering the frame rate" and "You can reduce your app's footprint on the system by requesting lower-resolution, binned, or non-HDR formats."
leads.why: Apple naming camera+compute contention as a real, quality-degrading effect is the vendor-side answer to the cross-cutting camera/GPU-contention question: heavy GPU work running next to a live capture session is expected to cause capture frame drops and latency — which is precisely our back-pressure collapse in P1. The prescribed responses (monitor system pressure notifications, lower frame rate, request binned/lower-res/non-HDR formats) form a concrete, citable adaptation policy we can implement instead of inventing a thermal controller.
leads.license: Apple proprietary session content — evidence, no code to copy

leads.title: Apple Docs — AVCaptureDevice.SystemPressureState (the API that reports capture-system thermal/power pressure)
leads.claim: Apple documents that camera capture performance and availability on iOS is subject to external factors including power usage and device temperature: "When system pressure reaches excessive levels during a capture session, the capture system automatically shuts down, causing a session interruption. Under less heavy pressure, the system may automatically reduce capture quality." The state exposes an overall `level` plus a `factors` set giving the underlying causes; it is monitored by key-value observing the capture device's `systemPressureState`. Apple's recommended response to rising pressure is to reduce the capture frame rate, lower resolution, decrease quality parameters, and listen for AVCaptureSessionWasInterrupted. Available iOS 11.1+. (Reachable only via the docs JSON API — the HTML page is JS-rendered.)
leads.why: This is a second, camera-specific pressure signal distinct from ProcessInfo.thermalState, and it is the one that will silently degrade or interrupt our capture channel before thermalState ever says 'serious'. If our 300 s run only instrumented ProcessInfo.thermalState, we are blind to the channel that actually governs P1's 30 fps camera stream — and the documented fact that the system 'may automatically reduce capture quality' under pressure means some of our 28.4 poses/s may already be the OS quietly derating the capture, not our engine falling behind. Cheap to add, and it gives per-factor attribution.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums — "Recording Constant Frame Rate at 4K 60 fps mode" (autoVideoFrameRateEnabled silently halves capture rate)
leads.claim: A developer's 4K60 capture intermittently ran at a constant 20 fps. An Apple Media engineer gave two causes: (1) only the maximum frame duration had been set — to hold a constant 60 fps you must set BOTH videoMinFrameDuration and videoMaxFrameDuration to CMTime(1, 60); (2) AVCaptureDevice.autoVideoFrameRateEnabled was left true, which automatically reduces the frame rate in low light to improve exposure — it must be set false to hold 60.
leads.why: Before we conclude the GPU is what caps P1, we have to rule out the capture channel capping itself. Our camera channel runs at 30 fps and the plan is to raise it to 60; this thread documents two ways iOS will silently refuse to deliver 60 — an unset min frame duration and auto frame rate in anything less than bright light. Both are one-line checks, and either would invalidate a 60 fps experiment. Also a caution for indoor SLAM benchmarking generally: auto frame rate makes the effective sensor rate a function of scene luminance, which would confound any pose-rate comparison against ARKit.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums — "Metal and low performance with parallel execution of kernels" (Apple: concurrent dispatches rarely help on Apple GPUs)
leads.claim: A developer trying CUDA-stream-style concurrency on Apple silicon found kernels serialized with MTLResourceStorageModeShared, at most ~2-way parallelism with hazard tracking untracked, and worse performance with multiple command buffers than with one. Apple's reply: "In my experience on Apple GPUs, the case where concurrent dispatches improve overall compute performance is rare" — it only helps when one dispatch's latency (e.g. waiting on memory reads) can be hidden by another's work, occasionally useful when bandwidth-bound but not typical. Apple's recommendation is to analyse bottlenecks at the shader level instead, pointing to WWDC 2020 session 10603 (Optimize Metal apps and games with GPU counters).
leads.why: A negative result that saves us an experiment on P1. The obvious idea for hitting 16.7 ms — overlap independent dispatches (e.g. pyramid levels, or CLAHE of frame N+1 with Harris of frame N) — is stated by Apple to rarely pay off on their GPU architecture. It redirects the effort to per-shader limiter analysis, and it interacts badly with the performance-state finding above: more command buffers with lower saturation each can also depress the clock. Worth knowing before we spend a week building a concurrent scheduler.

leads.title: WWDC25 Session 236 — Unlock GPU computing with WebGPU (Apple's own position on WebGPU compute on iPhone)
leads.claim: Apple states WebGPU is "supported on all platforms where Metal is supported, specifically: Mac, iPhone, iPad, and Vision Pro" and gives "safe access to GPU devices for graphics and general-purpose computation", with compute shaders presented as the main reason to choose WebGPU over WebGL. Platform-specific warning: "On iOS and visionOS specifically, storing data in f16 or compressed formats can really help you avoid getting your program terminated due to memory pressure." Optimization advice includes render bundles to cut validation overhead ("closer to native performance"), one command buffer per update loop, and consolidating bind groups — e.g. one 640-byte buffer with dynamic offsets rather than ten 64-byte bind groups. Apple publishes no latency, throughput or FLOPs comparison between WebGPU and native Metal on any device, and says nothing about subgroup size or workgroup tuning.
leads.why: The closest thing to prior art on the cross-cutting question from the Apple side, and mostly a null answer: Apple confirms WebGPU compute is a supported first-class path on iPhone, but publishes zero WebGPU-vs-Metal performance numbers, no subgroup guidance, and treats it as a web-content API rather than a vision-pipeline substrate. Two usable specifics: WebGPU's per-call validation overhead is real enough that Apple recommends render bundles and buffer consolidation — the same 'fewer, larger bindings' direction our Adreno/Mali work already landed on — and Apple explicitly flags iOS memory-pressure termination as a WebGPU-on-iPhone failure mode, which is the risk attached to P3 and to any plan to keep large persistent buffers resident.
leads.license: Apple proprietary session content — evidence, no code to copy

leads.title: Characterizing WebGPU Dispatch Overhead for LLM Inference Across Vendors
leads.claim: Per-dispatch CPU overhead, measured with an amortized sequential-dispatch method: Metal — Safari on Apple M2 31.7 us/dispatch, wgpu-native on Apple M2 71.1 us/dispatch (a 2.2x implementation gap inside the same backend); Vulkan — Dawn on RTX 5090 23.8 us, wgpu-native 35.8 us, wgpu on AMD iGPU 24.5 us; D3D12 — Chrome on RTX PRO 2000 58.7 us, Chrome on Intel iGPU 66.5 us; Firefox ~1038.7 us on all platforms (rate-limiting). Breakdown on Vulkan: of 32.5 us total per dispatch, Submit is 12.9 us (~40%) and encoder create+finish 12.2 us. Naive single-dispatch benchmarks overestimate dispatch cost by ~20x because they fold in a ~450 us GPU sync. No smartphones tested (Apple M2, AMD/Intel iGPU are the closest to mobile).
leads.why: This is the only quantitative account of WebGPU/Dawn fixed per-dispatch cost, and it is CPU-side, so it lands on the same core budget as your camera thread. A CLAHE + 4-6 level pyramid + Scharr + Harris + pyramidal LK front end is tens of dispatches per frame; at 32-71 us each on Metal that is 1.3-3.5 ms of pure CPU dispatch cost inside a 16.7 ms budget, before any GPU work. It also hands you a correct measurement protocol (N dispatches, one sync at the end, divide) so your '5 ms nominal / 19-22 ms throttled' number is not silently a sync artifact. Directly P1; the CPU energy of that overhead also feeds P2.

leads.title: Dawn source: src/dawn/native/Toggles.cpp (exact toggle strings + crbug refs)
leads.claim: Verbatim toggle strings and descriptions read from the file: "skip_validation" — "Skip expensive validation of Dawn commands." (crbug dawn/271); "disable_robustness" — "Disable robust buffer access" (dawn/480); "enable_integer_range_analysis_in_robustness" — "Compute the range of the index with Integer Range Analysis in the robustness transform and skip doing index clamping when the out of bound access cannot happen."; "lazy_clear_resource_on_first_use" — "Clears resource to zero on first usage..." (dawn/145); "disable_lazy_clear_for_mapped_at_creation_buffer" — "Disable clearing buffers to zero for buffers which are mapped at creation." (dawn/145); "disable_workgroup_init" — "Disables the workgroup memory zero-initialization for compute shaders." (tint/1003); "timestamp_quantization" — "Enable timestamp queries quantization to reduce the precision of timers..." (dawn/1800); "disable_timestamp_query_conversion" — "Resolve timestamp queries into ticks instead of nanoseconds." (dawn/1305); "spontaneous_queue_events" — "Queue events spontaneously complete, either via a dedicated Dawn owned thread, or backend specific implementations."
leads.why: These are the levers on your already-ported path, in one authoritative file you can cite to source lines, under a permissive license, and every one of them is host-side (no algorithm change). skip_validation attacks exactly the 32-71 us/dispatch CPU cost from lead 1. disable_robustness / integer-range-analysis removes the bounds-clamp code Tint injects into your generated MSL/SPIR-V — bit-identical output if your kernels never read out of bounds, so it is a lossless candidate you can prove with your existing byte-for-byte gate. lazy_clear_resource_on_first_use and disable_lazy_clear_for_mapped_at_creation_buffer are the named Dawn mechanism behind the per-frame zeroing of your 372 MB packed buffer that you already measured as -6.3% on A16 (PYR_PERSIST) — this is the upstream knob, so you can replicate one source instead of keeping a bespoke workaround. disable_workgroup_init removes per-dispatch workgroup-memory zeroing, which is real cost for CLAHE histogram / Harris tiles (flag as a product decision only if any kernel reads workgroup memory before writing it). timestamp_quantization explains why timings are quantized to 100 us unless you turn it off.

leads.title: Dawn source: src/dawn/native/metal/PhysicalDeviceMTL.mm — timestamp-query is not enabled on iOS
leads.claim: The timestamp-query feature is gated to macOS; the file carries the comment "TODO(dawn:2249): Enable on iOS. Some XCode or SDK versions seem to not match the docs." GPU counter availability is further gated by "GPU counters are only available if sampling at least one of the command or stage boundaries is supported" (IsGPUCounterSupported checks SupportCounterSamplingAtCommandBoundary / SupportCounterSamplingAtStageBoundary).
leads.why: Negative result that changes your instrumentation plan: on the iPhone 14 Pro you cannot get GPU-side timestamps out of Dawn at all, so any per-pass GPU attribution you have is wall-clock around submit+wait — which conflates queue latency, CPU dispatch overhead and actual GPU time. That is precisely the ambiguity in P1's '~5 ms at nominal clocks but 19-22 ms once the phone downclocks': you cannot currently tell downclocking from back-pressure. Either patch this gate locally (it is BSD-3, one file) or accept that on-device GPU timing must come from Metal directly, outside Dawn.

leads.title: Measuring and Reducing WebGPU Dispatch Overhead for LLM Inference
leads.claim: Vulkan 24-36 us and Metal 32-71 us per dispatch, independent of data type (fp32 == fp16). Command-buffer Submit is the single dominant term at ~40% of CPU time (12.9 us/dispatch). Cutting dispatch count from 876 to 564 (-36%) raised throughput 53% on the test model. Defines dispatch amortization: submit N identical dispatches with one sync at the end and divide; the naive single-op measurement is ~20x too high because it includes a ~450 us sync.
leads.why: It is the direct evidence for 'fuse passes' as the P1 fix: a 36% cut in dispatch count bought 53% throughput on a workload with the same shape as yours (many small dependent kernels, batch of one). Your pyramid + Scharr + Harris chain is exactly a long sequence of tiny dependent dispatches. It also warns that the win is in the number of dispatches, not the kernel, which matches your own finding that WGSL-level kernel tuning is at its ceiling on all three GPUs.

leads.title: Dawn source: src/dawn/native/vulkan/PhysicalDeviceVk.cpp — per-vendor Android workarounds (Adreno, Mali, Kirin, PowerVR)
leads.claim: Qualcomm/Adreno: "VulkanSplitCommandBufferOnComputePassAfterRenderPass" — "Recording compute pass after render pass in same buffer frequently causes crash"; also AlwaysResolveIntoZeroLevelAndLayer, VulkanAddWorkToEmptyResolvePass, ScalarizeMaxMinClamp ("Extended op NClamp modifies other vector components when one is NaN"), VulkanSampleCompare2DWorkaround. ARM/Mali: ResolveMultipleAttachmentInSeparatePasses, PolyFillPackUnpack4x8Norm (pack4x8snorm/unorm and unpack4x8snorm are broken), VulkanDirectVariableAccessTransformHandle (texture handles as function parameters fail for textureLoad), VulkanCooperativeMatrixStrideIsMatrixElements, VulkanSleepAfterLostDeviceWait. Huawei/Kirin: VulkanSplitBufferTextureForArrayLayers — "Mis-stride multi-layer buffer-texture copies; only first layer lands correctly". ImgTec/PowerVR: VulkanPolyFillSwitchWithIf, VulkanDisallowNPOTDepthStencilMipmaps.
leads.why: Two things you need. (a) On Adreno, Dawn splits the command buffer whenever a compute pass follows a render pass — an extra submit per frame, i.e. an extra dose of the 24-36 us Vulkan submit cost, so your Adreno 660 numbers may carry a structural penalty your Metal numbers do not. (b) The Kirin workaround is about multi-layer buffer-to-texture copies landing only the first layer — you run a Mate 10 (Kirin) and a P50 Pocket, and your pyramid is exactly a multi-layer texture. Also: on Mali, pack/unpack 4x8 norm ops are driver-broken and polyfilled, which matters if any of your OpenCV-replica kernels pack pixels. These are all authoritative, cite-to-line, permissive.

leads.title: WebGPU on Android + 100 us timestamp quantization (Chrome 121)
leads.claim: "WebGPU is now enabled by default in Chrome 121 on devices running Android 12 and greater powered by Qualcomm and ARM GPUs." Timestamp queries shipped in the same release and are "quantized at 100-microsecond resolution" for security.
leads.why: Confirms the 100 us quantization figure that Dawn's "timestamp_quantization" toggle controls — if you ever measure through a browser or leave the toggle at its default, every GPU pass under 100 us is unresolvable, which is most of your kernels. Also fixes the Android support envelope for the shipping product: Qualcomm + ARM on Android 12+, which matches your Adreno 660 / Mali G72 targets but leaves everything else uncertified.

leads.title: Dawn feature doc: timestamp_query_inside_passes — timestamps are unreliable on tiler GPUs
leads.claim: Adds ComputePassEncoder::writeTimestamp and RenderPassEncoder::writeTimestamp, but warns: "This method might not always make a lot of sense on tiler GPUs (so basically any modern GPU) where the ordering of operations inside render passes is not strictly like the order of commands recorded" (each tile executes independently).
leads.why: Every device you ship on is a tiler — Apple A16, Mali G72, Adreno 660. Combined with the iOS gate in lead 3, this says your on-device GPU segment accounting cannot come from intra-pass timestamps and must be pass-boundary or wall-clock. Worth knowing before you build another probe generation; your own memory notes record repeated cases of probes that were themselves dead.

leads.title: WebSplatter: Enabling Cross-Device Efficient Gaussian Splatting (real WebGPU-on-phone numbers)
leads.claim: Measured WebGPU frame times on actual phones for the bicycle-c scene: iPhone 15 Pro Max (Safari) 38.5 ms/frame; Redmi K70 Pro (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3) 33.6 ms; Oppo Find X2 (Snapdragon 865) 105.2 ms. WebSplatter renders all scenes on all test devices while competing web viewers crashed on mobile from memory constraints; overall 36-57% memory reduction versus baselines and 1.2-4.5x speedup over state-of-the-art web viewers. No thermal-throttling analysis and no discussion of mobile WebGPU limits; testing was primarily on Chrome, with a note that WebGPU landed in Safari on iOS 26 in September 2025.
leads.why: One of the very few published measurements of a real WebGPU compute+render workload on named phones, including an iPhone. Two takeaways for you: (a) 33-38 ms/frame on current flagships for a heavy per-pixel workload sets a realistic expectation that 16.7 ms end-to-end on a phone is tight, supporting the case that P1 needs a work-reduction decision rather than only host-side tuning; (b) mobile WebGPU dies on memory before it dies on speed — the baselines crashed on phones — which is a direct warning for P3 and for your plan to keep a 372 MB packed buffer resident.

leads.title: motion-microscope — real-time WebGPU compute pipeline on a live camera feed (MIT)
leads.claim: Phase-based Eulerian video magnification (Riesz-pyramid variant, Wadhwa et al. SIGGRAPH 2014) plus rPPG heart rate and optical-flow breathing, entirely in WebGPU compute shaders with no external dependencies: "ten compute passes per pyramid level"; "At 640x480 the frame costs ~40 small compute dispatches across a 4-level pyramid (~0.55 Mpx of rgba16float work) — well under a millisecond on any recent GPU, so the pipeline idles at the camera's 30 fps." Browser support listed as Chrome/Edge 113+, Safari 26+, Firefox 141+; no mobile devices measured.
leads.why: The closest public analogue to your front end: a multi-level image pyramid driven from a live camera, entirely in WGSL compute, running at camera rate. Its dispatch budget is the useful number — ~40 dispatches per frame for a 4-level pyramid at 640x480. Multiply by the Metal 32-71 us/dispatch from leads 1 and 4 and you get 1.3-2.8 ms of CPU overhead per frame from dispatch alone, and this project is at 1/9 of your pixel count. It is also evidence that nobody in this space is doing a bit-exact OpenCV replica — they implement the paper directly, MIT-licensed.

leads.title: Dawn source: src/dawn/native/metal/DeviceMTL.mm — submit model and Kalman-filtered timestamp period
leads.claim: Commands accumulate and are flushed as one MTLCommandBuffer per submit via Queue::SubmitPendingCommandBuffer(), driven from Device::TickImpl() — i.e. a polling model, not interrupt-driven completion; MTLSharedEvent backs SharedFence. Timestamp period is estimated with a Kalman filter (UpdateTimestampPeriod) correlating mach_absolute_time and GPU timestamps via sampleTimestamps:gpuTimestamp:, converging when "the kalman gain is less than 0.01" (initial guess 83.333 ns on Intel, 1.0 ns elsewhere). The companion toggle "metal_disable_timestamp_period_estimation" exists because "Calling samplerTimestamps:gpuTimestamp: from MTLDevice to estimate timestamp period leads to GPU overheating on specific Intel GPUs due to driver issue".
leads.why: Two P1/P2 facts. (a) Completion and map callbacks are driven by your Tick/ProcessEvents cadence — if you tick once per frame, readback of e.g. a corner count is a frame late by construction, which looks exactly like the 'engine falls behind, back-pressure kicks in, latency collapses' failure you describe. (b) Dawn itself has a known case where its timing path overheats a GPU; it is Intel-only, but it establishes that Dawn-internal instrumentation is not free, worth checking before you attribute 173 s of thermalState serious purely to your kernels.

leads.title: Dawn docs/building.md — Dawn documents no iOS platform and calls Android cross-compiles untested
leads.claim: Documented platforms are Linux, macOS and Windows. On Android: "Cross-compilation for Android as described above works to compile targets, but the resulting binaries have not been tested. If you want to run them you may need to set up an Android Chromium build." iOS is not mentioned anywhere in the build documentation.
leads.why: Cross-cutting risk statement in Dawn's own words: your production configuration (Dawn on an iPhone, Dawn on Mali and Adreno) is not a documented Dawn platform. That is consistent with lead 3 (timestamp-query still gated off on iOS with a TODO) and with the Adreno/Mali workaround density in lead 5. It does not say do not do it — Chrome ships Dawn on Android and AndroidX now ships it as a library — but it does mean you should expect to be the first to hit iOS-side Dawn bugs and should budget for carrying local patches.

leads.title: AndroidX WebGPU — Dawn shipped as an official Android Jetpack library
leads.claim: androidx.webgpu:webgpu 1.0.0-alpha05 released 2026-04-22; minSdk raised to API 24 in alpha02; the AAR ships a dawn_build_metadata.json in assets recording the exact Dawn git SHA used for the build (dc741dd as of alpha04). alpha05 adds GPUCompatibilityModeLimits and texture binding view dimensions. Still alpha, API expected to change; no published benchmarks. Documentation is noted as Gemini-generated and possibly containing errors.
leads.why: Answers 'is anyone else running Dawn natively on a phone': Google is, on Android, as a supported Jetpack artifact with a pinned Dawn SHA — which is a cleaner Android delivery path than your own Dawn build and a place to compare toggle defaults. The compatibility-mode limits matter for your Mali/Adreno coverage. It also implies iOS remains the unsupported half of your pair, reinforcing lead 12.

leads.title: Dawn feature docs: BufferMapExtendedUsages and HostMappedPointer (copy elimination on UMA)
leads.claim: BufferMapExtendedUsages lets a buffer carry MapRead/MapWrite together with other usages (e.g. Storage), so a buffer can be CPU-mapped and GPU-used without a separate staging buffer; it is a superset of BufferMapWriteExtendedUsages. The doc does not enumerate backend support. The companion HostMappedPointer feature (wrapping existing host memory as a GPU buffer) is documented only for Mac/Linux (4 KB alignment) and Windows (64 KB, must be the start of the mapping) — iOS and Android are not listed, and mapping APIs cannot be called on such buffers.
leads.why: iPhone and both Android SoCs are unified-memory, so every staging buffer you keep is pure waste in both bandwidth (P2) and footprint (P3, you are 10 MB over ARKit). BufferMapExtendedUsages is the supported way to delete the staging hop for uploads and for small readbacks like corner counts, which also shortens the round trip that back-pressure is currently forming around (P1). The negative half matters too: HostMappedPointer, the more aggressive zero-copy route, is not available to you on either mobile platform — do not plan around it.

leads.title: HN: WebGPU-on-Android launch thread and WebGPU CPU-overhead commentary
leads.claim: In the Chrome-121 Android launch thread, a Chrome team member (Tojiro) says of untested Android GPUs: "our team hasn't been able to sufficiently test on them yet...it's a question of spending the time to ensure they're performing as expected", and notes "devices get blacklisted and telling common users to access browser flags is not an option for most products"; pjmlp contrasts native APIs where "we can work around them" with browser APIs where "the device gets blacklisted end of story"; fidotron on Mali: "I look forward to the day I never have to think about the Mali GLSL compiler ever again." Separately, on the WebGPU-ecosystem thread (HN 38235266) flohofwoe states that high-frequency WebGPU calls have "even higher CPU overhead than similar WebGL2 calls", and on HN 37767220 that "WebGPU is still in the 'make it work' phase, and not yet in the 'make it fast' phase."
leads.why: Weak evidence but on-point for two of your open questions. It independently corroborates the CPU-overhead-per-call finding that leads 1 and 4 quantify, from practitioners rather than a paper. And the blocklist point is a real advantage for you specifically: because you embed Dawn natively rather than going through a browser, you are not subject to Chrome's device blocklist and can patch driver workarounds yourself — which is the one structural argument in favour of your current architecture on Android.

leads.title: OpenXRLab XRSLAM — upstream's own iPhone 14 Pro config: 640x480 camera and keypoint detection only every 3rd frame
leads.claim: The shipped iOS visualizer config sets `sliding_window: tracker_frequent: 3`, `feature_tracker: max_keypoint_detection: 300, min_keypoint_distance: 25.0, max_frames: 100`, `sliding_window: size: 5`, `solver: time_limit: 0.1, iteration_limit: 10`. The companion device file `xrslam-ios/visualizer/configs/iPhone 14 Pro.yaml` declares `resolution: [640, 480]` with intrinsics fu=448.97, fv=449.14, cu=321.35, cv=240.72. In `xrslam/src/xrslam/core/feature_tracker.cpp` the flag is computed as `bool slidind_window_frame_tag = !is_initialized || frame->id() % config->sliding_window_tracker_frequent() == 0;` and BOTH `if (slidind_window_frame_tag) frame->detect_keypoints(config.get());` and `if (slidind_window_frame_tag) detail->frontend->issue_frame(...)` are gated by it, while `last_frame->track_keypoints(frame.get(), config.get())` (the LK stage) runs unconditionally every frame. The library default is `size_t Config::sliding_window_tracker_frequent() const { return 1; }` (xrslam/src/xrslam/config.cpp:78). docs/en/config_parse.md documents it as "`tracker_frequent`: use one frame for every n frames".
leads.why: This directly contradicts the premise behind P1. 'Detection runs on EVERY frame because that is what the upstream tracker does' is true only of the compiled-in default (1); upstream's own reference application for this exact device (iPhone 14 Pro) ships tracker_frequent=3 and a 640x480 tracking stream. You are running 1920x1440 = 9x the pixels and 3x the detections that the source you replicated specifies for the same phone. Changing it is a one-value change inside the authoritative source you already replicate — no self-invention, no license question, and it is upstream's own configuration rather than a threshold you picked. It cuts CLAHE+detection work to 1/3 of frames (P1's 16.7 ms budget), cuts GPU energy and camera bandwidth (P2), and cuts frame-buffer residency (P3). It changes results, so it is a product decision, but the bit-exactness of your ported kernels is untouched — you run the same kernels, fewer times, on fewer pixels.

leads.title: Navion: A 2mW Fully Integrated Real-Time Visual-Inertial Odometry Accelerator (IEEE JSSC 2019)
leads.venue: IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, vol. 54
leads.claim: Purpose-built 65nm VIO ASIC implementing exactly your front end: "Feature Tracking (FT) uses the Pyramidal Lucas-Kanade optical flow [24] to track features ... across all frames, including non KFs" and "Feature Detection (FD) extracts features in the left stereo frame using the lightweight Shi-Tomasi corners [25]. Features are detected on a grid to keep the number of features in different regions of a KF constant." Fig. 2 caption: "VFE is KF based, i.e., it tracks features in all frames, but removes outliers, adds new features to compensate lost ones, and performs stereo matching only at KFs." Power breakdown: "FT consumes the largest amount of power in VFE because it is always active regardless of the frame type"; "The average power consumption of BE is 40% of the total power since it is active only at KFs"; "the large on-chip SRAM power is only 21% of the total power consumption, although it accounts for 77% of the chip area". Table III (EuRoC, 752x480 stereo): Xeon 27.9 W / 3638.6 mJ per KF; ARM 2.4 W / 1573.2 mJ per KF, 19 fps tracking and 2 fps total KF throughput; Navion 0.024 W / 2.3 mJ per KF, 71 fps tracking, 0.28% trajectory error. Table V configurations: max rate 62.5 MHz VFE / 83.3 MHz BE / 71 fps tracking / 24 mW; fixed rate 20 fps / 6 mW; with per-sequence adaptation 2 mW. Adaptation (per-sequence feature count and horizon) gives "an average of 2.5x" energy reduction. One throughput mode is "Fixed distance ... a constant distance between KFs (5 cm/KF)".
leads.why: The most authoritative answer to 'what does an efficient tracker actually run on, and what does it run every frame'. A team that spent a whole ASIC on this ran LK every frame and Shi-Tomasi detection only at keyframes — the same split your upstream config already exposes. It also gives you the reference point for P2: the identical algorithm on an embedded ARM CPU costs 2.4 W. Your 0.80 core-equivalents plus full-res GPU work every frame is in the same order of magnitude as that 2.4 W software baseline, which is exactly why you sit in thermalState 'serious' while ARKit does not. And its 5 cm/KF distance mode is the same lever your capture pipeline already uses.

leads.title: Navion VLSI 2018 digest — full comparison table (Xeon / ARM / FPGA / prior ASIC / Navion) and keyframe clock gating
leads.venue: 2018 Symposium on VLSI Circuits, Digest of Technical Papers, pp. 133-134
leads.claim: Chip specs (Fig. 6): 65nm CMOS, chip area 4.0 x 5.0 mm, core 3.54 x 4.54 mm2, 2043 kgates, 854 kB SRAM, 1 V supply, VFE 62.5 MHz, BE 83.3 MHz, camera rate 28-171 fps, keyframe rate 16-90 fps, average power 24 mW, resolution 752x480. Comparison table (Fig. 7) Power (W): Xeon 26.10 | ARM 2.33 | FPGA 1.46 | prior ASIC 0.027 | Navion 0.024; Memory (MB): 16 | 2.5 | 2.1 | 0.09 | 0.83; VFE max fps: 21 | 5 | 20 | NA | 171. Text: "Most of the VFE, except FT, is active only at KFs; clock gating reduces the power consumption by over 10%." "The IFE ... accounts for only 2.4% area and 1.2% power." On-chip lossy image compression: "compression reduces the frame memory size by 4.4x and power by 4.9x" using 4x4 block quantization storing 26 bits per block, "increases the average error by only 0.06%", and "Compressed frames are not used in FD due to blocking and quantization noise". Feature-track memory: two-stage sparse/dense layout cuts 962 kB to 177 kB (5.4x). Linear-solver sparsity: 5.2x memory and 7.2x speed-up.
leads.why: P2 gets its headline number: an ARM CPU running this exact VIO is 2.33 W and only reaches 5 fps on the vision front end. P3 gets a memory playbook: the frame buffers, not the code, are the footprint, and lossy 4x4 block compression buys 4.4x frame memory for +0.06% trajectory error — but note they explicitly refused to feed compressed frames to the detector, only to the tracker. The clock-gating line is the hardware restatement of the tracker_frequent lever: everything except LK is idle on non-keyframes.

leads.title: Kimera-VIO (MIT SPARK) — BSD-2 C++ implementation that calls featureDetection() only inside the keyframe branch
leads.claim: Per-frame flow: `tracker_->featureTracking(...)` (pyramidal LK) runs unconditionally; then `const bool new_keyframe = shouldBeKeyframe(stereoFrame_k_->left_frame_, stereoFrame_lkf_->left_frame_);` and only inside `if (new_keyframe) { ... }` does it run, with the comment "// Perform feature detection (note: this must be after RANSAC, since if we discard more features, we need to extract more)", `feature_detector_->featureDetection(left_frame_k, stereo_camera_->getR1());` followed by `stereo_matcher_.sparseStereoReconstruction(...)`. Identical structure in MonoVisionImuFrontend.cpp. The keyframe predicate in VisionImuFrontend.cpp is `const bool need_new_keyframe = max_time_elapsed || max_disparity_reached || disparity_flipped || nr_features_low || frame.isKeyframe_;` where `disparity_flipped = ((enough_disparity || disparity_low_first_time) && min_time_elapsed)`, disparity is the median disparity of matched keypoints against the last keyframe, and nr_features_low is `nr_valid_features <= min_number_features_`. The detector itself is `cv::GFTTDetector::create(...)` (goodFeaturesToTrack) with FAST/ORB alternatives and ANMS non-maximum suppression.
leads.why: This is the copyable half of Navion. Same authors' lab, permissive BSD-2, C++, and it uses cv::GFTTDetector — the exact OpenCV entry point you already replicated bit-exactly. If you want a keyframe policy richer than XRSLAM's modulo-N (which is blind to motion), this is one authoritative source you can replicate whole, with the predicate citable to source lines. It is also the natural place to look for P4: the same file governs how many frames the bootstrap needs before it emits a pose.

leads.title: HiSilicon IVE vendor header — fixed-function Shi-Tomasi + LK optical flow silicon, hard-capped at 720x576 input
leads.venue: HiSilicon MPP SDK header (Hi3516AV100), mirrored in OpenIPC/openhisilicon
leads.license: proprietary vendor header — EVIDENCE ONLY, do not copy
leads.claim: The IVE (Intelligent Video Engine) hardware block exposes exactly your front end as fixed-function calls: `HI_MPI_IVE_STCandiCorner` ("The first part of corners detection using Shi-Tomasi-like method: calculate candidate corners"), `HI_MPI_IVE_STCorner` ("select corners by certain rules"), `HI_MPI_IVE_LKOpticalFlow` (takes pre/cur U8C1 frames, a point list, and accumulated per-layer movements, i.e. pyramidal LK driven from the host), plus `HI_MPI_IVE_Sobel`, `HI_MPI_IVE_NormGrad`, `HI_MPI_IVE_EqualizeHist`, `HI_MPI_IVE_Filter`, `HI_MPI_IVE_CannyHysEdge`, `HI_MPI_IVE_Map`, `HI_MPI_IVE_NCC`, `HI_MPI_IVE_SAD`. Every one of the three carries the identical hardware spec line: "The size of the input data ranges from 64x64 pixels to 720x576 pixels. The physical addresses of the input data and output data must be 16-byte-aligned. The stride must be 16-pixel-aligned."
leads.why: This is the answer to your ISP-side question, and it is a resolution argument, not an API argument. The one mass-produced piece of silicon that implements CLAHE-equivalent, Sobel, Shi-Tomasi and pyramidal LK as fixed-function blocks refuses inputs above 720x576. Navion is 752x480. Kimera/EuRoC is 752x480. GAP9 VIO is QQVGA. XRSLAM's own iPhone config is 640x480. Nobody who cares about energy runs this front end above VGA — you are at 1920x1440. That convergence across four independent hardware and software sources is the strongest single statement this angle can make about P2. (Header is proprietary: cite it, never copy it. It is also not available on iOS, so it is evidence, not a port target.)

leads.title: Energy characterization and optimization of image sensing toward continuous mobile vision (LiKamWa et al., MobiSys 2013)
leads.claim: Five commercial CMOS image sensors instrumented directly. Active/idle power at default configuration: A1 2592x1944 163.5/161.9 mW; A2 768x506 189.5/141.8 mW; B1 3264x2448 338.6/225.4 mW; B2 2592x1944 225.1/218.6 mW; B3 752x480 137.1/105.9 mW. Central negative result: "image sensors are not energy-proportional: energy per pixel is in fact inversely proportional to frame rate and resolution of image capture" — energy per megapixel is roughly 6-8 mJ/MP for most sensors (3 mJ/MP for the low-analog-power B3), and "energy per megapixel increases by an order of magnitude as the resolution is dropped from 3 MP to 0.3 MP". Two hardware levers measured: optimal external clock frequency "reduces the power up to 50% or 30%", and aggressive standby between frames. For 1 MP at 5 FPS the three sensors go 185/112/114 mW at default, to 106/95/55 mW with optimal clock, to 9.9/5.1/5.2 mW with aggressive standby ("5% of the original"). Standby mode itself is 0.5-1.5 mW versus ">100 mW in idle state".
leads.why: P2 says the extra energy is 'going somewhere else' beyond CPU. This quantifies one of the somewheres that has nothing to do with your GPU code: the sensor. At 1920x1440 (2.76 MP) and 30 fps, 6-8 mJ/MP puts the sensor alone in the hundreds of milliwatts, before the ISP, before Dawn, before any of your kernels. Crucially it is NOT free to just halve the frame rate — energy per pixel goes UP as you slow down, because idle power dominates. The lever that actually pays is dropping capture resolution (which XRSLAM's own iPhone config already does to 640x480) or getting the sensor into standby between frames, not merely lowering fps.

leads.title: Draining our Glass: an energy and heat characterization of Google Glass (LiKamWa et al., APSys 2014)
leads.claim: Measured system power on Glass XE12 (OMAP4430, Cortex-A9): idle 22 mW; static application 1023 mW at ~18% CPU; "Camera preview callback" 2366 mW for 53 min of battery, where "the act of running the camera service and previewing a frame uses 85% CPU utilization at 600 MHz. Furthermore, the IVA and GPU are activated"; "Running a Face Detection app" with OpenCV "brings the device to a full 100% CPU Utilization at 600 MHz. This draws a large 3318 mW, for only 38 minutes of battery life"; video capture 2963 mW; video chat 2960 mW. Thermal: video chat reaches "a stable 51.9 C (124 F)", static idle app "a stable 35.2 C". Fitted Newton's-cooling model: for 3 W of SoC draw delta-T = 28.9 C, for 1 W delta-T = 11.2 C, C/hA = 0.0040 per second, giving the two stated rules "For every watt drawn by the OMAP, the steady-state surface temperature will rise by delta-T approximately 10 C higher than its environment" and "The Glass surface temperature will rise by 90% of delta-T in 10 minutes". Throttling behaviour: "At high temperatures, Glass firmware limits the frequency to 600 MHz or 300 MHz to cool down by reducing power."
leads.why: This turns P2's thermalState timeline into physics you can predict rather than observe. Two facts matter for you: (1) the camera preview path alone, before any of your vision code, cost 1343 mW over the static-app baseline on a device whose ISP and GPU were also engaged — the same class of hidden cost you are looking for; (2) the 10-minute time constant means your 300 s run captured only about 40% of the eventual steady-state temperature rise, so the 173 s in 'serious' is a lower bound and a longer run will be worse. It also gives you a cheap predictor: measure average SoC watts, multiply by ~10 C, compare to ARKit.

leads.title: Efficient and Accurate Downfacing Visual Inertial Odometry on GAP9 (2025) — per-stage cycle counts and mW for a full VIO front end
leads.license: n/a (paper; authors state they open-source the GAP9 implementation)
