leads.claim: 10-core GAP9 RISC-V SoC at 370 MHz, QQVGA imaging, VD56G3 sensor over MIPI CSI-2, MPU-9250 IMU. "Studies have shown that GAP9 uses between 64 mW and 68 mW at 370 MHz when utilizing the nine-core compute cluster", and a two-core configuration "will strike a better power-to-latency trade-off at a power draw of 35 mW to 45 mW". Table II cycle counts, single-core vs 8-core cluster: ORB Feature Detection 7,718.8 kCycles -> 1,143.6 kCycles (6.75x); ORB Blurring 1,785.5 -> 245.8 (7.26x); ORB Feature Extraction 7,050.6 -> 908.1 (7.76x); ORB Matching 4,688.2 -> 601.8 (7.79x); ORB Total 21,243.1 -> 2,899.3 (7.33x); optimized PX4FLOW 593.1 -> 81.3 (7.30x); SuperPoint feature extraction 30,036.3 kCycles multi-core; rigid-body estimation 66.9 kCycles; Kalman filtering 156.0 kCycles. "The maximum achievable frame rate of 118.5 FPS of ORB renders GAP9 an ideal platform". Reducing the clock to 95 MHz gives 312 FPS aggregate at higher latency. The paper cites Navion as "24 mW to process frames at 171 FPS".
leads.why: A 2025 data point that the whole VIO front end fits in tens of milliwatts when the resolution is small and the parallelism is right — and it separates detection from tracking cleanly (ORB detection is 1,143.6 of 2,899.3 kCycles, i.e. 39% of the ORB pipeline, while the sparse-flow alternative PX4FLOW is 81.3 kCycles, 14x cheaper than ORB detection alone). That ratio is the same shape as your P1 problem: detection is the expensive half and it is the half that does not need to run every frame. The near-linear 7.3x parallel speed-up across all stages is also a useful sanity bound for what your GPU should be extracting.

leads.title: NanoSLAM: Enabling Fully Onboard SLAM for Tiny Robots (2023)
leads.claim: Full onboard SLAM on a 44 g nano-drone using the GAP9 commercial RISC-V low-power parallel processor, within "a power budget of only 87.9 mW", achieving "accuracy of 4.5 cm and an end-to-end execution time of less than 250 ms".
leads.why: A modern upper bound for what complete onboard SLAM costs in energy when it is designed for it: under 90 mW. Your iPhone 14 Pro is spending enough to sit in thermalState 'serious' for 58% of a 300 s run. The gap is not a factor of two, it is orders of magnitude, and the explanation across every source in this angle is the same three things: resolution, detection duty cycle, and how much of the pipeline runs on every frame rather than every keyframe.

leads.title: KAIST AR/pose-estimation ASIC line — 27 mW camera pose engine and 0.89 uW/fps pose engine (cited inside Navion JSSC)
leads.venue: IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, vol. 50, no. 11, pp. 2513-2523 (Hong, Kim, Kim, Kim, Nam, Yoo)
leads.claim: Titled "A 27 mW Reconfigurable Marker-Less Logarithmic Camera Pose Estimation Engine for Mobile Augmented Reality Processor" (DOI confirmed via Crossref; also A-SSCC 2014, DOI 10.1109/asscc.2014.7008897). Navion's reference list additionally cites, verbatim: [17] J. S. Yoon et al., "A unified graphics and vision processor with a 0.89 uW/fps pose estimation engine for augmented reality," IEEE TVLSI, vol. 21, no. 2, pp. 206-216, 2013; [19] Z. Li et al., "A 1920x1080 30-frames/s 2.3 TOPS/W stereo-depth processor for energy-efficient autonomous navigation of micro aerial vehicles," IEEE JSSC, vol. 53, no. 1, pp. 76-90, 2018.
leads.why: Three more independent silicon data points bracketing the same conclusion as Navion: marker-less AR camera pose in tens of milliwatts. Note especially Li et al. — that is the one design in this whole survey that runs at 1920x1080, and it needed a dedicated 2.3 TOPS/W ASIC to do 30 fps of stereo depth at that resolution. That is the cost of the resolution you have chosen. I could not open these three (paywalled, no OA copy found); the titles, venues and page numbers above are transcribed from the Navion JSSC reference list and Crossref, not invented.

leads.title: OpenVINS is GPL-3.0 — its KLT/keyframe front end cannot be copied
leads.claim: The LICENSE file at master begins "GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE / Version 3, 29 June 2007". By contrast Kimera-VIO's LICENSE.BSD is BSD-2-Clause ("Copyright 2019 Massachusetts Institute of Technology") and openxrlab/xrslam is Apache-2.0 (confirmed via the GitHub API license field).
leads.why: Saves you from the obvious next stop. OpenVINS is the filter-based VIO everyone reaches for when they want a KLT front end with a redetection policy, and it is off-limits under your rule alongside ORB-SLAM2/3, VINS-Mono/Fusion, DSO and SVO. The clean set for this problem is exactly three: XRSLAM (Apache-2.0, already yours), Kimera-VIO (BSD-2), maplab (Apache-2.0), plus stella_vslam (BSD-2) which you already use for keyframe insertion.

leads.title: Apple AMX is undocumented and unsupported — dead end for CV offload
leads.license: repo is a reverse-engineering reference; the ISA itself is undocumented by Apple
leads.claim: Describes "Apple's undocumented AMX instructions, issued from CPU, executed on a special accelerator execution unit", explicitly "neither documented nor supported by Apple", with a header "for accessing AMX instructions" carrying "use at your own risk". Operations are a 32x32 matrix compute grid with f16/f32/f64 FMA, bf16 from M2, and 8/16-bit integer multiplicands. Documented chips are M1 Max, M2, M3, M4 Max; the repo makes no statement about A16 or any A-series part.
leads.why: Closes the 'Apple AMX for CV' branch of this assignment. It is matrix-multiply silicon, not image silicon; there is no public A16 documentation; using it would be an undocumented private instruction path on one of your three platforms only, which fails your tri-platform rule before it fails anything else. Same verdict for the Neural Engine: the community reference (github.com/hollance/neural-engine) documents it purely as a Core ML layer accelerator with an unsupported-layer list, i.e. convolution graphs, not Shi-Tomasi and not sparse LK.

leads.title: Apple VNGenerateOpticalFlowRequest — the only Apple-blessed hardware flow path, and Apple calls it resource-intensive
leads.claim: Generates directional change vectors for each pixel between two same-size images; result type `[VNPixelBufferObservation]?`; results reported at full resolution even when a region of interest limits the analysed area; configurable `computationAccuracy` (ComputationAccuracy enum) and `outputPixelFormat`, plus `keepNetworkOutput`; revisions 1 and 2; available iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+. Apple's own performance note: "Optical flow requests are resource-intensive, so create only one request at a time, and release it immediately after generating optical flows."
leads.why: Worth knowing so you can stop looking. It is DENSE per-pixel flow, not the sparse pyramidal LK on ~200-300 tracked points that your front end needs; the `keepNetworkOutput` property implies a neural implementation, so it would not be bit-exact with OpenCV under any circumstances; Apple itself flags it as expensive; and it exists only on Apple platforms, which fails the Mali/Adreno requirement outright. Combined with AMX and ANE both being dead, the conclusion for this angle is that iOS exposes no usable fixed-function path for your front end — the GPU really is the right target on iPhone, and the savings have to come from doing less work, not from different silicon.

leads.title: Nobody has published a WebGPU computer-vision front end — the full arXiv WebGPU corpus is 27 papers, none on CV, SLAM or phones
leads.venue: arXiv API, full-text search on "WebGPU", all years
leads.claim: The complete arXiv result set for "WebGPU" is 27 entries. They are LLM inference in the browser (WebLLM 2412.15803, Llamas on the Web 2605.20706, dispatch-overhead studies 2608.08730 and 2604.02344), Gaussian splatting and rendering (WebSplatter 2602.03207, Visionary 2512.08478, 2608.17390, 2407.19977), volume and geospatial visualization (2309.04393, 2605.19737, 2602.23660, 2506.23364), security and fuzzing (DarthShader 2409.01824, WebGPU-SPY 2401.04349, 2606.26412), numerics and tooling (WgPy 2503.00279, 2206.06428, 2312.11729), and cloth simulation (2507.11794). Not one paper covers feature detection, optical flow, SLAM, visual-inertial odometry, or a WebGPU compute pipeline running on a phone GPU.
leads.why: Your cross-cutting question was whether anyone else has taken this approach. On the published record, no. A bit-exact WGSL/Dawn replica of an OpenCV front end driving a real VIO on a phone has no precedent in the literature — which means two things: there is no prior art to borrow tuning from, and there is nobody who has already measured and published the failure modes you are hitting. Every performance lever this angle found comes from the algorithm side (resolution, detection duty cycle, keyframe gating), not from the WebGPU side, and that is consistent with there being no WebGPU CV community to learn from yet.

leads.title: 功耗优化 · 方案篇 · Android功耗优化指导规范 (掘金)
leads.claim: Whole-device power accounting on Android phones: "Camera功耗 200mA+，占整机的25%以上" (camera alone is 200mA+, >25% of total device current). Dropping capture frame rate from 30fps to 15fps measured "CPU下降13%，整机功耗下降120mA". Thermal limiting engages at ~43°C shell temperature and is released at ~39°C; shell temp runs ~2°C above battery temp. Baseline test hygiene stated as battery >=30%, battery temp <=37°C.
leads.why: This is the single most directly actionable P2 evidence I found. It says the camera subsystem by itself is a quarter of device power at full rate - which is exactly the 'extra energy going somewhere else' bucket in our 173s-in-serious measurement, and it is NOT CPU (our CPU load already matches ARKit). It also quantifies the lever: halving capture rate bought 120mA and 13% CPU on a phone. For us that reframes P1: pushing the camera channel from 30 to 60 fps is not free headroom, it is a direct power increase on the subsystem that already dominates. And the 43°C-on / 39°C-off hysteresis gives a concrete thermal model for why our session sits in 'serious' for 173/300s once it enters.

leads.title: 抖音 Android 性能优化系列：抖音功耗优化实践 (ByteDance engineering, 掘金)
leads.venue: 掘金 (juejin.cn) - 字节跳动终端技术团队
leads.claim: Douyin feed scenario measured at ~440mA average current (≈11%/hour on a 4000mAh device). Power is attributed to four blocks: "抖音的 feed 功耗主要集中在 SOC(CPU，GPU，DDR)，Display，Audio，WIFI". Camera recording measured at "200mA+，占整机的 25%以上". Reducing frame rate to 30Hz gave "功耗显著降低了120ma". SurfaceView vs TextureView for video: "平均功耗低 20mA左右". Low Power Mode gains "稳定在 20mA 以上".
leads.why: First-party engineering measurement (not SEO filler) from a team shipping a camera-heavy app at scale, corroborating the 200mA/25% camera figure independently. Important nuance for P2: they bucket SoC as CPU+GPU+DDR together - DDR traffic is a named consumer. Our full-resolution (1920x1440) GPU pass every frame moves a lot of bytes through DRAM, so 'CPU load equals ARKit but energy does not' is consistent with a DDR-bandwidth story rather than an ALU story. Suggests instrumenting bytes/frame, not just GPU ms/frame.

leads.title: 原创轻量VIO算法、简单易上手——XRSLAM帮你快速搭建移动平台AR应用 (OpenXRLab 官方中文发布，腾讯云开发者社区转载)
leads.venue: 腾讯云开发者社区 (OpenXRLab official Chinese announcement)
leads.claim: Upstream's own Chinese announcement of the exact library we forked states the mobile design point is "30fps以上的数据处理帧率" (30+ fps processing rate), that "特征匹配采用了OpenCV的光流来实现" (feature matching implemented with OpenCV optical flow), and that recent iOS devices ship pre-calibrated so demos run directly. Platforms: Linux/Mac/Android/iOS. Accuracy claimed SOTA on EuRoC with "显著的领先性" over VINS-Mono. No iPhone model, no ms breakdown, no power/thermal, no initialization time given.
leads.why: Directly bounds P1: our 28.4 poses/s is not a regression, it is upstream's stated design point. Upstream never targeted a 60 Hz camera channel, so 'detection runs on EVERY frame because that is what the upstream tracker does' is a design assumption inherited from a 30 fps target, not a requirement. If we want 59.9 poses/s we are outside the source we replicated and need a different authoritative source for the detection cadence - which means the 60 fps push is a product decision, not a lossless port. Also confirms the front end is plain OpenCV optical flow (what we bit-exactly ported).

leads.title: RD-VIO: 动态环境下移动增强现实的稳健视觉惯性里程计 (中文解读)
leads.claim: Chinese walkthrough of the paper behind XRSLAM (Jinyu Li, Xiaokun Pan, Gan Huang, Ziyang Zhang, Nan Wang, Hujun Bao, Guofeng Zhang; code = github.com/openxrlab/xrslam). Initialization is explicitly three-stage: "(1) visual-only SfM on initial frames, (2) aligning IMU measurements with SfM results to resolve gravity and scale, (3) full bundle adjustment". Introduces a sub-frame mechanism ("one keyframe carries a set of sub-frames") to survive pure-rotation/stationary segments without filling the sliding window, plus IMU-PARSAC two-stage outlier rejection. Mobile AR evaluation was run on an iPhone X against ARKit and ARCore with APE reported in millimetres; "in fast-paced scenarios (A1, A2), comparable performance to ARKit and ARCore". EuRoC MH_01_easy RMSE 0.0659 m. Sliding window = 8 frames.
leads.why: This is the authoritative source for the tracker we shipped, in Chinese, and it confirms two things we need for P4. First, the 3.6 s to first pose is structural: the source's own bootstrap is visual-only SfM then IMU alignment then full BA, so translation is required by construction - no parameter tweak fixes it, only a different initializer (see the CVPR-2023 decoupled-initialization lead). Second, the authors already benchmarked against ARKit/ARCore on an iPhone X, so there is a published same-device comparison protocol we can reuse rather than invent, and the sub-frame mechanism is the upstream-sanctioned answer to the pure-rotation case that also degrades our bootstrap.

leads.title: 稳定性性能系列之十——卡顿问题分析：从掉帧到流畅体验 (掘金)
leads.claim: Quantifies Android thermal throttling on phones: "正常: CPU 2.0GHz, GPU 600MHz / 发热后: CPU 1.2GHz (降低40%), GPU 400MHz (降低33%)", with overall "性能下降: 30-50%". Frame budget stated as 16.6ms for 60fps; jank perception thresholds 32ms (1 dropped frame, subtle) / 48ms (2, noticeable) / 64ms+ (severe). Recommends Systrace/Perfetto offline, FrameMetrics API and Choreographer online.
leads.why: Independent Chinese measurement of the exact mechanism behind P1: sustained load downclocks the GPU by about a third and costs 30-50% overall. Our observed 5ms -> 19-22ms is roughly 4x, i.e. considerably worse than a pure clock story - which is itself informative: a 33% clock drop cannot explain 4x, so something else (contention with the camera ISP for memory bandwidth, or a queue/back-pressure effect) is likely dominating and worth isolating before we optimize kernels further. Also gives the standard instrumentation stack Chinese teams use to prove it.

leads.title: 研究团队提出嵌入式GPU定向FAST特征检测加速方法 (网易，论文 "Faster than Fast: Accelerating Oriented FAST Feature Detection on Low-end Embedded GPUs" 中文解读)
leads.venue: 网易 (NetEase) digest of a paper by Tokyo Univ. of Science / Dalian Univ. of Technology / Nanjing Univ.
leads.claim: Accelerates oriented-FAST (the FAST + Harris half of ORB, stated to be ~50% of ORB compute) on low-end embedded GPUs using CUDA. Reported: "平均加速比超过7.3倍" vs OpenCV GPU; FAST detection 2.2-4.5x and Harris detection 1.1-13x on Jetson TX2; 6.21x on AGX Xavier vs the GPU baseline. Frame rates: ~144 FPS at 768x432 and ~55 FPS at 1280x720 on TX2; >270 FPS and >80 FPS respectively on AGX Xavier. Baselines were OpenCV CPU ORB, OpenCV GPU ORB and CUDA_ORB. Single-layer and four-layer pyramid configurations tested.
leads.why: The closest Chinese-language evidence that corner detection on a small GPU is worth doing, with a per-stage breakdown (FAST vs Harris scale very differently: 2.2-4.5x vs 1.1-13x). Two caveats that matter to us: it is CUDA on Jetson, not a phone GPU under a camera load, and crucially there is NO ARM NEON baseline - the comparison is against OpenCV's own GPU path. So it does not answer whether mobile-GPU detection beats NEON, and its 55 FPS at 1280x720 on TX2 is in the same ballpark as our own downclocked numbers at 1920x1440.

leads.title: FPGA和GPU加速的视觉SLAM系统中特征检测器研究 (电子发烧友)
leads.claim: Search snippet (page itself returns HTTP 468 to my fetcher): "本文首次针对视觉SLAM流程开展硬件加速特征检测器的对比研究，通过对比现代SoC平台（Nvidia Jetson Orin与AMD Versal）上最佳GPU加速方案" - described as the first comparative study of hardware-accelerated feature detectors for a visual-SLAM pipeline, comparing the best GPU-accelerated solutions for FAST, Harris and SuperPoint on Nvidia Jetson Orin and AMD Versal SoCs.
leads.why: If the underlying paper exists it is the only head-to-head GPU-vs-FPGA-vs-CPU feature-detector comparison I found in Chinese sources, and it covers exactly the three detectors that bracket our front end (FAST, Harris - we ported Harris/goodFeaturesToTrack - and a learned alternative). Worth chasing the original English paper: a per-detector energy-per-frame table is precisely what P1+P2 need to decide whether GPU detection is the right place to spend the thermal budget. I could not open the page, so treat the claim as snippet-only.

leads.title: VIO 初始化探究：旋转平移解耦的高效鲁棒初始化 (深蓝学院公开课，贺一家)
leads.venue: 深蓝学院 open course, 2023-03-09, 101 min
leads.license: n/a (talk); underlying CVPR-2023 work not license-verified
leads.claim: A 101-minute Chinese talk by 贺一家 (PhD) presenting CVPR 2023 work on rotation-translation-decoupled VIO initialization, framed around the engineering problem that initialization must be "fast, accurate, high success rate" and that "a good initial value is the system's foundation for stable operation". The landing page carries no numeric results (no seconds-to-init, no success-rate table); slides are behind registration.
leads.why: This is the only Chinese-language pointer I found aimed squarely at P4. XRSLAM/RD-VIO's bootstrap is visual SfM -> IMU alignment -> full BA, which is exactly the coupled formulation this line of work replaces; decoupling rotation from translation is the published route to converging with less translation, i.e. shorter time-to-first-pose. Next step is to identify the corresponding CVPR 2023 paper and check its license and code before we could replicate it - the talk alone is not implementable.

leads.title: 安装一个为RK3588S优化的、启用了OpenCL (GPU加速) 和 NEON (CPU加速) 的OpenCV 4.10版本 (博客园)
leads.claim: Build recipe for OpenCV 4.10 on RK3588S with Mali Valhall G610 (libmali-valhall-g610-g13p0-x11-gbm), enabling both paths: -D WITH_OPENCL=ON and -D ENABLE_NEON=ON, disabling wechat_qrcode/face/sfm/xfeatures2d, and pinning the Mali driver against apt upgrade. Contains NO measured numbers - no ms, no fps, no GPU-vs-NEON comparison at all.
leads.why: Useful as a negative datapoint on the cross-cutting question. The state of the Chinese-language art for 'OpenCV on a Mali GPU' is a build recipe that turns both OpenCL and NEON on and never measures which one wins, let alone whether outputs match. Nobody in this community appears to be doing what we are doing (bit-exact GPU replicas of specific OpenCV 4.0.1 kernels), which means we should not expect to find a shortcut here - and it also means our bit-exactness harness is genuinely novel prior art rather than a reinvention.

leads.title: opencv使用opencl加速不明显 / opencv opencl arm加速 (51CTO博客)
leads.claim: Title and search snippet only (the article body returns empty to my fetcher, twice): "opencv使用opencl加速不明显 opencv opencl arm加速" - i.e. OpenCV's OpenCL (T-API) acceleration on ARM was found to be insignificant, referencing OpenCV v4.5.5 source. Dated 2024-05-10. No numbers recoverable.
leads.why: This is the shape of the negative result the brief asked me to hunt for - a Chinese practitioner reporting that OpenCV's own GPU path on ARM did not pay off. I could not open it so I cannot cite a number, but the title alone is worth someone re-fetching from a different network. Caveat: OpenCV T-API's OpenCL path is not the same thing as our hand-written WGSL kernels, so even if confirmed it indicts the library's generic GPU path, not GPU compute per se.

leads.title: Android性能测试踩坑：降频后 CPU 使用率还能信吗？(CSDN)
leads.claim: Search snippet only (blog.csdn.net article pages return HTTP 521 to my fetcher): a 2-hour stress test held CPU usage at a healthy-looking 45%, but the device had already thermally throttled to 408 MHz, so users reported degradation while the metric looked stable.
leads.why: A methodology warning that lands directly on our P2 framing. We report '0.80 core-equivalents, same as ARKit' as evidence that the extra energy is not CPU - but core-equivalents computed against a throttled clock is a different quantity than against a nominal clock, and if our run spends 173/300s in 'serious' while ARKit spends 0s, the two 0.80 figures are not measured at the same clock and are not comparable. Worth re-deriving CPU work as cycles (or normalizing by the sampled frequency) before concluding the CPU is exonerated.

leads.title: 详解iOS之ARkit为何碾压对手（一）(掘金)
leads.claim: Explains ARKit's monocular 3D + metric scale as two frames plus IMU dead reckoning ("IMU航位推算法来获得计量尺度"), and asserts "苹果 ARKit 已经把误差下降到 10% 以下". No initialization-time measurement, no device model, no comparison table.
leads.why: Weak, and included mainly as a boundary marker for P4: the popular Chinese account of why ARKit yields a usable pose almost immediately is 'IMU dead reckoning gives scale', with no measurement behind it. I found no Chinese source that actually measures ARKit's time-to-first-pose or explains its bootstrap, so our 1.5 s vs 3.6 s gap has no Chinese-language prior art to lean on - the RD-VIO paper's own iPhone X ARKit comparison remains the better anchor.

leads.title: VSLAM前端：金字塔光流跟踪算法 (腾讯云开发者社区)
leads.claim: Chinese derivation of pyramidal Lucas-Kanade for a VSLAM front end, quoting the production OpenCV parameter set verbatim: "winSize=Size(21,21), int maxLevel=3, TermCriteria(COUNT+EPS, 30, 0.01)". Explicitly does NOT discuss re-detection cadence (tracking only) and gives no timing in ms.
leads.why: Marginal, but it pins the de-facto Chinese-community pyrLK configuration (21x21 window, 3 pyramid levels, 30 iterations, eps 0.01) that we can cross-check our bit-exact replica's parameters against. More telling by omission: a canonical Chinese VSLAM-frontend article on optical flow says nothing at all about how often features are re-detected, which is precisely the knob P1 hangs on - reinforcing that 'detect every frame' is an unexamined default in this community too.

leads.title: CUDAによる局所特徴量計算の高速化とソースコード公開 (Fixstars /proc/cpuinfo)
leads.claim: Multi-scale FAST keypoint detection (the cv::ORB::detect pipeline) at FHD 1920x1080: OpenCV CPU on Core i9-10900 (10c/20t) = 2.5 ms, CUDA on RTX 3060 Ti = 1.6 ms — only 1.56x. At 4K 5.4 -> 2.9 ms (1.86x), 8K 17.5 -> 5.5 ms (3.18x). Descriptors are the opposite story: BAD256 for 10k keypoints CPU-MT 5.9 ms vs CUDA 0.66 ms (~9x), HashSIFT256 174.6 ms vs 0.89 ms (~200x). Dataset SceauxCastle (11 images, openMVG).
leads.why: This is the single most decision-relevant number I found for P1. A full desktop discrete GPU beats a desktop CPU at multi-scale FAST detection by only 1.56x at FHD. Corner detection is bandwidth/serial-NMS bound, not arithmetic bound — so the fact that your CLAHE+detection costs ~5 ms nominal and 19-22 ms downclocked on an A16 is not a porting bug, it is the shape of the problem. The corollary is directional: the GPU pays off on the descriptor half, not the detection half. If XRSLAM's front end is detection+LK (no descriptors), the GPU has almost nothing to win and a lot of thermal budget to lose — which is exactly the P1/P2 pattern you measured. It also argues that the fix for P1 is not making the kernel faster but running detection less often (see VITAMIN-E lead).
leads.license: Apache-2.0 (the code); blog post itself is Fixstars corporate
leads.venue: Fixstars tech blog (now hosted on Zenn)

leads.title: fixstars/cuda-efficient-features (GitHub)
leads.claim: Apache-2.0. Implements multi-scale FAST corner detection 'based on OpenCV's cv::ORB::detect' plus BAD and HashSIFT descriptors on CUDA. Embedded-GPU numbers (Jetson Xavier, i.e. an ARM+integrated-GPU class part): detection FHD 5.6 ms / 4K 12.1 ms / 8K 27.5 ms; descriptors for 40k keypoints BAD256 19.1 ms, HashSIFT512 24.8 ms. Desktop RTX 3060 Ti detection FHD 1.6 / 4K 2.9 / 8K 5.5 ms. README does NOT claim numerical identity to OpenCV — it explicitly claims *different* (better-distributed) keypoints via a configurable nonmaxRadius NMS.
leads.why: Two things you can use directly. (1) The Jetson Xavier column is the closest public embedded-GPU datapoint to your A16: 5.6 ms for FHD multi-scale FAST detection at nominal clocks — the same order as your ~5 ms, which independently says your kernel is not slow, your thermal headroom is. (2) It is Apache-2.0 and structured as a full replica of cv::ORB::detect's multi-scale FAST, so it is a legitimate 'one authoritative source, copied whole' candidate if you ever need a CUDA/compute reference for the detection stage. Note the license-clean caveat that matters for your no-self-research rule: they deliberately deviated from OpenCV on NMS, so copying it is a product decision (different keypoints), not a lossless speed-up.

leads.title: iPhoneのローカルLLM：GPUは短距離、Neural Engineは長距離
leads.claim: iPhone 17 Pro (A19 Pro), 10-minute sustained decode: GPU-backed runtimes lose 25% of throughput within 13-40 seconds of continuous load; the Neural Engine holds full speed for 90+ seconds before meaningful degradation. Sustained/burst retention: CoreML-ANE 33 -> 22 tok/s (67%), MLX-GPU 48 -> 18 tok/s (38%), LiteRT-LM-GPU 56 -> 27 tok/s (48%). Wall power measured with powermetrics on M4 Max: CoreML/ANE 12.7 W vs MLX/GPU 24.7 W vs llama.cpp/GPU 24.5 W — ANE is roughly half the power for the same work.
leads.why: Direct evidence for P2 and for why P1's '5 ms nominal -> 19-22 ms downclocked' happens on a 13-40 second timescale. The measured 2x power ratio between GPU and ANE on Apple silicon is the quantitative version of your 'the extra energy is going somewhere else'. Practical read: a continuous full-res GPU compute load is the single most power-expensive way to do per-frame work on an iPhone, and the platform demotes it within tens of seconds. It also suggests a concrete (product-decision) escape hatch you may not have costed: moving CLAHE / detection to the ANE via a CoreML-expressible formulation, or at minimum accepting that GPU-every-frame at 60 Hz is thermally out of reach on this class of device.

leads.title: 【スマホの熱中症対策】ThermalState API 実践活用ガイド (iOSDC Japan 2025)
leads.claim: Atsushi Otsubo (Luup), iOSDC Japan 2025, 2025-09-19. Measured ProcessInfo.ThermalState transition times on iPhone 12 Pro. High CPU/GPU load, indoors 27C: Nominal->Fair 70 s, Fair->Serious 40 s (i.e. 'serious' at ~110 s). Direct sunlight 30C, no extra load: Nominal->Fair 40 s, Fair->Serious 85 s, Serious->Critical 115 s, then high-temp warning at 236 s with display surface at 52.8C. Sunlight + high load: 35 s / 30 s / 30 s. Per-state mitigation playbook: Fair = defer background work and prefetch; Serious = cut network/BT I/O, lower location accuracy, reduce frame rate and simplify animation; Critical = minimum interactive functionality only.
leads.why: Gives you the Japanese-community baseline your P2 number needs context against: a heavy GPU app on an iPhone 12 Pro reaches 'serious' in about 110 seconds at room temperature. Your run spent 173 of 300 s in serious, i.e. you entered serious at roughly the same point — you are behaving like a generic heavy GPU app, and ARKit's 0 s is the anomaly to explain, not your 173 s. Also the only structured, source-cited statement I found in Japanese of what iOS actually does at each state (charging slowdown, display dimming, camera flash and camera functions disabled, frame-rate drops), which matters because your camera channel is downstream of thermal state.

leads.title: ARKit におけるカメラの解像度とフレームレート (堤修一 / shu223)
leads.claim: Enumerates ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportedVideoFormats per device. iPhone X / iOS 12: rear camera 1920x1440@60, 1920x1080@60, 1280x720@60. iPhone 7 Plus: 1920x1080@60 and 1280x720@60 only (no 1920x1440). iPhone 12 Pro / iOS 14.3: same rear set. iPhone 15 Pro / iOS 17.1: adds 3240x2160@30 and 30 fps variants of most formats. Default videoFormat = first element of supportedVideoFormats, and Apple orders that array highest-quality first, so ARKit defaults to 1920x1440@60 on modern iPhones.
leads.why: Pins down the comparison you are making in P1/P2. ARKit itself runs a 1920x1440@60 camera channel and still spends 0 s in 'serious' over 300 s on the same device — so full-resolution camera capture is NOT the thermal culprit; your full-resolution GPU work every frame is. It also names the exact escape hatch that exists on the platform: 1280x720@60 is a supported ARVideoFormat on every device back to the 7 Plus, which is a 4.5x pixel reduction on the CLAHE+detection kernels while keeping the 60 Hz pose rate P1 needs. Worth flagging as a product decision (it changes results, so not lossless).
leads.venue: Qiita (author is the 'Practical ARKit' book author)

leads.title: ARKit ReplayDataの中身を覗いてみる (Koki Ibukuro / asus4)
leads.claim: Reverse-engineers ARKit's own ReplayData .mov: an 18-stream muxed container. Stream 0:0 = RGB video 1920x1440 (stored RGB, converted to YCbCr on replay); 0:2 = depth video 640x480 at 10 fps; 0:6/0:8/0:10 = accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer time series; 0:12 = CMDeviceMotion (quaternion + rotation rate); 0:13 = CLLocation incl. GPS and accuracy; 0:14 = camera intrinsics, extrinsics and lens distortion coefficients; 0:15 = ~24 MB of what he reads as per-frame feature-point data. Streams 0:1/0:3/0:5 carry per-frame camera metadata including exposure time, intrinsic matrix, and sensor SNR. Example 300 MB file: ~40 MB RGB, ~24 MB depth, ~24 MB feature buffer, rest metadata. Streams 0:7/0:9/0:11 empty on his device.
leads.why: The only Japanese-community look inside ARKit's actual data contract I could find, and it is unusually informative for P4 and P1. It shows ARKit's replay input includes CMDeviceMotion (a fully-fused device attitude) and per-frame lens distortion + SNR alongside the raw IMU — i.e. ARKit is fed a pre-fused orientation, which is the most plausible mechanism for 'usable pose almost immediately' (3-DoF attitude first, 6-DoF once SfM converges) versus your 3.6 s. It also confirms feature points are a first-class per-frame stream, and that ARKit's depth is only 640x480@10fps — a reminder that ARKit does not do full-res work on every channel every frame. Actionable next step: this file format is your route to a bit-comparable ARKit-vs-XRSLAM replay harness on identical input.

leads.title: 【CVPR2019論文解説】VITAMIN-E: 密な特徴点追跡によるMonocular Visual SLAM (産総研 SMRG)
leads.claim: Japanese explainer by AIST's Smart Mobility Research Group of Yokozuka et al., CVPR 2019. VITAMIN-E replaces detect+descriptor-match entirely: it tracks the positions of image-intensity curvature extrema, using a low-resolution coarse pass to estimate the scene-wide 'dominant flow' as an affine transform, which then predicts where each extremum lands at full precision. BA uses subspace Gauss-Newton — one variable updated at a time with others fixed, so only 6x6 inverses appear, no Schur complement on a large matrix — cheap enough to run per-frame rather than per-keyframe. Reported: 36 ms/frame tracking, CPU only, no GPU; 100% success on all 11 EuRoC sequences; V102 trajectory error 9.3 cm vs DSO 53.0 cm; output far denser than ORB-SLAM/DSO.
leads.why: This is the most direct attack on P1's root cause I found: your detection runs on EVERY frame 'because that is what the upstream tracker does'. VITAMIN-E is an authoritative, published alternative where per-frame detection does not exist at all — the dominant-flow prediction replaces it — and it hits 36 ms/frame on CPU alone with better accuracy than DSO. Two caveats to check before it is usable to you: (a) the article does not state code availability or license, and the well-known implementations are third-party reimplementations, so this may fail your 'one authoritative source we can copy' bar; (b) it is a different tracker, not a lossless speed-up of your ported path, so adopting it is a product decision. Even if unusable as code, it is strong evidence that 'detect every frame' is a choice, not a requirement, and the AIST authors are Japanese and reachable.
leads.license: unknown — article states nothing; verify before any use

leads.title: iPhoneでリアルタイム顔モザイク：YOLOv8 + Metalで30fps安定を実現した話 (Studist)
leads.claim: iPhone 16e, 1920x1080 camera at 30 fps (33.3 ms budget). Measured per-frame Metal pipeline: letterbox preprocessing 1.3 ms + YOLO inference 8-11 ms + mosaic kernel 4-5 ms = 15-17 ms total. Detection runs on every frame ('毎フレーム顔検出を行っていますが、30fpsで十分余裕があるので問題ありません'). Author states the choice of 30 fps over 60 fps was deliberate for heat: '発熱も抑えられる（iPhone 16eは放熱が弱い）'. Uses CVMetalTextureCache for zero-copy CVPixelBuffer -> MTLTexture on unified memory.
leads.why: A Japanese production engineer independently arrived at the exact trade you are fighting in P1: at 30 fps, per-frame full-res GPU work is comfortable; at 60 fps it is not, and the stated reason is heat, not compute. Their 15-17 ms of GPU work per frame at 1080p on an A18-class part is the same order as your 19-22 ms downclocked figure, which is a useful third-party sanity check that your kernels are in the normal range. Also worth checking against your own pipeline: they get to zero-copy via CVMetalTextureCache; a Dawn/WebGPU path that copies the camera buffer into a GPU buffer each frame would pay a cost they do not, and that copy is pure thermal waste at 60 Hz.

leads.title: CoLi-BA: 高速なバンドル調整アルゴリズムの解説 (Fixstars) + zju3dv/CoLi-BA
leads.claim: Japanese walkthrough of CoLi-BA (Ye et al. 2022). Three levers: (1) linearize reprojection error on the unit sphere instead of the z=1 plane, which improves the conditioning of the resulting matrices; (2) a skew-symmetric reformulation that collapses the Hessian blocks to cross products and normalized vectors, cutting operation count; (3) reorder camera computations by a greedy approximation to the minimum Hamiltonian path so hot matrix blocks stay in CPU cache. Fixstars' own measurement on a 12-core 2.2 GHz CPU over 10 KITTI-derived cases: 0.3x the runtime of g2o (3.3x faster) and 0.15x the runtime of Ceres (6.7x faster). Reference implementation github.com/zju3dv/CoLi-BA is MIT-licensed (verified on the repo), depends on Eigen and vendors Ceres as a submodule for comparison.
leads.why: Aimed squarely at the wall recorded in your local-BA line: 77.5% of local BA sits inside Ceres' minimizer where you concluded you cannot move. CoLi-BA is an authoritative, MIT-licensed, single-source implementation that reports 6.7x over Ceres on the same problem class, measured independently by a Japanese HPC firm rather than only self-reported by the authors. MIT clears your license bar outright, and it is plain C++/Eigen so it ports to iOS/Android without a GPU. Caveat to flag before adopting: the unit-sphere linearization changes the objective, so this is a results-altering product decision, not a lossless swap — you would need your ply-sha / points3D gate to be re-baselined.

leads.title: CUDAによるバンドル調整の高速化とソースコード公開 (Fixstars)
leads.claim: Full BA (Levenberg-Marquardt + Schur complement + Cholesky) for ORB-SLAM2 on KITTI seq 00. Problem size 1,332 cameras / 133,383 points / 561,116 observations. Core i7-6700K with g2o took ~12 s; their CUDA implementation on a GTX 1080 took 1.2 s (10x). Critically, the breakdown shows Cholesky decomposition alone is 908.3 ms of the 1,232 ms total — i.e. after GPU-parallelizing residuals, Hessian assembly and the Schur complement, ~74% of what remains is the sparse factorization. Built on cuSPARSE/cuSOLVER. Repo: github.com/fixstars/cuda-bundle-adjustment.
leads.why: Useful as a stage-account rather than as code (CUDA, and it is full BA not local BA). The 908/1232 ms split is the transferable finding: once you parallelize everything around it, the linear solve dominates and it is the part that does not parallelize well. That is a strong prior for why your local-BA GPU ambitions would stall, and it independently supports the CoLi-BA direction (attack the linear algebra's structure on CPU) over a GPU port of Ceres. Same author group as the cuda-efficient-features lead, so the measurement discipline is consistent.
leads.license: repo license not stated in the article — verify (Fixstars' sibling repo is Apache-2.0)

leads.title: 【Unity】Unity上からiOS端末の発熱状態を取得する
leads.claim: Bridges ProcessInfo.thermalState into Unity via an Objective-C++ shim (ProcessInfoBridge.mm) + P/Invoke. Documents the four states and Apple's per-state guidance. Concrete observation: on an iPhone X running a GPU-heavy scene (many overlapping translucent planes), the state walked from Nominal at launch to Serious while the scene merely sat idle rendering. Recommends thermal-state-driven graceful degradation: drop frame rate, lower visual quality, disable non-essential features including camera access.
leads.why: Second independent Japanese datapoint (after the iOSDC talk, different device and different workload) that a purely GPU-bound iOS workload reaches 'serious' on its own with no user interaction — reinforcing that P2's 173 s is a GPU-residency problem, not a CPU-load problem (your CPU is already at ARKit parity, 0.80 cores). The 'disable camera access' line is notable: it is the same lever the platform pulls on itself at serious, which is consistent with your back-pressure/latency collapse in P1. Low technical depth, but it is clean corroborating evidence and it names the exact API surface for instrumenting your own 300 s runs per state.

leads.title: 特徴記述アルゴリズムHashSIFTのCUDA高速化 (Fixstars)
leads.claim: Companion post to cuda-efficient-features, dedicated to the HashSIFT descriptor on CUDA. From the sibling article's shared benchmark table (Core i9-10900 / RTX 3060 Ti, 10k keypoints): HashSIFT256 604.9 ms single-thread CPU, 174.6 ms multi-thread CPU, 0.89 ms CUDA; HashSIFT512 740.1 / 315.6 / 0.99 ms. Published 2023-12-21.
leads.why: Did not open this one directly, but it is the other half of the Fixstars local-feature work and the descriptor side is where the 200-300x GPU wins live. Relevant only if your pipeline ever needs a descriptor stage (relocalization, loop closure, cross-session matching against your archived-photo rebuild) — that is the stage where a GPU port actually pays for its thermal cost, unlike detection. Flagged mainly so you do not spend GPU budget on the wrong half of the front end.

leads.title: stella_vslam チュートリアル (@ymd-stella)
leads.claim: Japanese-language tutorial for stella_vslam written by ymd-stella, who is the project's active maintainer (the same handle appears as the maintainer on the stella_vslam org). Two posts: a general tutorial (2022-10-13) and a ROS 2 tutorial (2022-10-15). Confirms the project has a Japanese-speaking maintainer publishing Japanese docs on Qiita.
leads.why: Directly relevant to your standing decision to replicate stella_vslam's keyframe_inserter as the authoritative source for trigger rules: the maintainer is Japanese and publicly answerable in Japanese. That matters because your keyframe work already turned on subtle criteria semantics (almost_all_lms_are_tracked=0.9 turning out to be the thing that sets spacing, not SVO's min_distance). A short question in Japanese to this maintainer is a cheaper way to resolve 'what does this criterion mean' than another round of instrumentation. Not a technical lead in itself — a channel.

leads.title: IROS2022まとめ - SLAM編 - (@np_hsgw)
leads.claim: Japanese survey post covering eight IROS 2022 SLAM sessions, listing papers, proposed methods and — per the Hatena Bookmark summary — which of them have code available. 3 Hatena bookmarks, published 2022-12-07.
leads.why: Not opened, and it is an aggregator rather than a primary source, so low confidence. Included only because it is the one Japanese-language index I found that explicitly tracks code availability per SLAM paper, which is the axis your license rule turns on (method described in a paper is worthless to you unless there is a copyable permissive implementation). Potentially a cheap way to enumerate non-GPL front-end candidates you have not yet considered. Skip if time-constrained.

leads.title: ARCore issue #667 "Impact of CameraConfig on performance?" — Google engineer states ARCore's motion tracker is fed 640x480
leads.claim: Google ARCore engineer (@inio, 2018-12-07): "By default we attach two consumers to the camera: a 640x480 (or 640x360 on some devices) ImageReader to supply our motion tracking engine, and a nominally 1920x1080 SurfaceTexture to provide the background image for rendering. If you request a CPU image resolution other than the smallest (default), this will mean attaching a second ImageReader (third surface) to the capture session, increasing memory bandwidth used by the ISP or hardware scaler. Mostly this just means additional power usage with the extra DRAM writes..." Same engineer in issue #568 (2018-09-24): "enabling a higher-resolution CPU image will increase power usage and device heating." Measured on Pixel 2 (reporter: "The default on my Pixel 2 seems to be VGA").
leads.why: This is the single clearest statement of what a shipping AR system actually feeds its tracker: VGA to the tracker, 1080p only to the display. You are feeding 1920x1440 to the tracker — 9.0x the pixel count ARCore's tracker sees (2.76 Mpx vs 0.307 Mpx). It also names the exact cost mechanism you are paying in P2: extra ISP/hardware-scaler work and extra DRAM writes, i.e. energy that does not show up as CPU core-equivalents (your 0.80 matches ARKit, so the delta is exactly the kind of bandwidth/GPU energy described here). Cutting tracker input to 640x480 attacks P1 (5 ms nominal GPU work becomes ~0.6 ms of pixels), P2 (less ISP/DRAM traffic, less GPU), and P3 (each 1920x1440 NV12 buffer is ~4.15 MB; VGA is ~0.46 MB) simultaneously. See also https://developers.google.com/ar/develop/java/camera-configs, which adds that a lower-resolution GPU texture "may help improve app performance by reducing GPU load and lowering memory bandwidth requirements" and that "Fixed focus is generally better for tracking (and is the ARCore default on most devices)".

leads.title: AVCaptureVisionDataOutput — Apple does keypoint detection, orientation, descriptors and Hamming matching inside the iOS capture pipeline, and ARKit uses it
leads.claim: AVCaptureVisionDataOutput (a private AVCaptureOutput subclass in AVFCapture.framework) exposes: gaussianPyramidBaseOctaveDownscalingFactor, gaussianPyramidOctavesCount, maxKeypointsCount, keypointDetectionFlowType, subPixelThreshold, featureOrientationAssignmentEnabled, featureBinningEnabled, dynamicThresholdingEnabled, featureMatchingEnabled, featureMatchingDescriptorSize, hammingDistanceThreshold, orientationDistanceThreshold, sigmaDistanceThreshold, squareDistanceDisparityFraction, laccConfigAndMetadata, plus its own minFrameDuration / minBurstFrameDuration / maxBurstDuration. Corroborated independently in three places: (a) nst/iOS-Runtime-Headers Frameworks/ARKit.framework/ARImageSensor.h declares an ivar `AVCaptureVisionDataOutput * _visionDataOutput`, a method `_configureVisionDataOutputForSession:` and `triggerVisionDataBurst`; (b) the same properties appear at the capture-graph layer as Celestial.framework's FigCaptureVisionDataSinkConfiguration (_gaussianPyramidOctavesCount, _keypointDetectionThreshold, _maxKeypointsCount, _maxFrameRate, sinkType); (c) the symbol appears in macOS 11.x SDK CMCapture/CMImaging .tbd stubs, so it is a long-standing capture-pipeline sink, not an app-level GPU pass.
leads.why: This is the most likely answer to your P2 question 'the extra energy is going somewhere else... whatever ARKit does that we do not'. On iPhone, the Gaussian pyramid, corner detection, orientation assignment and binary-descriptor matching that you implemented in WGSL/Dawn are done by a fixed-function block in the camera/ISP path and delivered as a separate capture sink with its own frame-rate cap. ARKit therefore pays near-zero GPU energy for its front end while you pay full GPU energy every frame. Consequence: parity with same-device ARKit on power (P2) and on the 16.7 ms GPU budget (P1) is structurally out of reach as long as you run the front end on the GPU at full resolution — the honest levers are fewer pixels, fewer detect-frames, and IMU forward-integration, not a faster kernel. Practical caveat: this is a private API you cannot ship against, and it is reverse-engineering evidence, not something to copy. Treat it as the reason your target is unfair, and use it to set the bar with the user.
leads.license: NOT USABLE — Apple private API / reverse-engineered headers; evidence only, do not implement against

leads.title: XRSLAM upstream's own iOS app runs the camera at AVCaptureSession.Preset.vga640x480 @ 30 fps with IMU at 100 Hz
leads.claim: xrslam-ios/visualizer/src/Camera.swift line 28: `init?(position: AVCaptureDevice.Position = .back, preset: AVCaptureSession.Preset = .vga640x480, queue: DispatchQueue? = nil)`; output pixel format kCVPixelFormatType_32BGRA (line 46). ViewController.swift line 255: `camera.setFps(30)`; line 235 `sceneView.preferredFramesPerSecond = 30`. Motion.swift line 27: `init?(updateInterval: TimeInterval = 0.01 ...)` i.e. IMU at 100 Hz. The shipped per-device calibration xrslam-ios/visualizer/configs/'iPhone 14 Pro.yaml' declares `resolution: [640, 480]` with intrinsics for that size. slam_params.yaml: max_keypoint_detection: 300, min_keypoint_distance: 25.0, sliding_window size 5, tracker_frequent: 3. Camera.swift also already defines a `cameraDidDrop()` delegate hook.
leads.why: Your own authoritative source — the exact repo and the exact iPhone 14 Pro config file — is calibrated and configured for 640x480 @ 30 fps, not 1920x1440. Under your own rule ('replicate ONE authoritative source in full'), running the ported front end at 1920x1440 is already a deviation from upstream, and it is a 9.0x deviation in pixel count. This is the cheapest possible experiment for P1/P2/P3: set the input to the resolution upstream calibrated for, and the 19-22 ms downclocked GPU cost should drop roughly with pixel count while the intrinsics in the shipped yaml become correct rather than rescaled. Note also `max_keypoint_detection: 300` — upstream expects a few hundred keypoints from a VGA frame, so a 1920x1440 input is not buying you the point count the config assumes.

leads.title: ARKitCore (iOS 18.2) — ARKit's auxiliary vision sensor defaults to 640x480 @ 10.0 fps, and every ARVideoFormat carries a 3-entry frameRatesByPowerUsage table
leads.venue: decompiled ARKitCore.framework from an iPhone 17,1 iOS 18.2 (22C152) restore image
leads.claim: In ARWorldTrackingConfiguration, the ultrawide vision sensor path defaults to width=640, height=480 (overridable by the user default read at `com.apple.arkit.imagesensor.back.ultrawide.*` for width/height), and its default frame rate is 10.0 fps (`com.apple.arkit.imagesensor.back.ultrawide.frameRate`, else `double v19 = 10.0`); it then builds `[ARVideoFormat initWithImageResolution:... 640.0, 480.0]` and calls `setFrameRatesByPowerUsage:` with a 3-element array. ARVideoFormat.m: `- (NSInteger)framesPerSecond { return [frameRatesByPowerUsage firstObject]; }` and a method `- (ARVideoFormat *)videoFormatWithUnthrottledLowPowerUsageFramerate`; also `+ bestVideoFormatForDevicePosition:deviceType:resolution:frameRate:videoBinned:`. ARImageSensor.m line ~1754 selects the live rate as `[[format frameRatesByPowerUsage] objectAtIndexedSubscript:[self powerUsage]]`, with `setPowerUsage:` / `forceUpdatePowerUsage:`. Separately, ARFrameRateLimitingStrategy.m implements `-initWithFrameRate:` + `-shouldProcessData:` which drops work whenever `timestamp - lastTimestamp <= 1.0/frameRate` (keeping the last 5 timestamps in an ARCircularArray), and ARImageScalingTechnique.m offers `-initWithDownscaleFactor:` / `-initWithScaledSize:` with GPU scaling passes. ARWorldTrackingTechnique.m accepts video resolutions 640x480, 1280x720, 1440x1080, 1920x1080, 1920x1440 and has a `_shouldUseFullResolutionVisionDataIntrinsics` flag that rescales intrinsics by a factor from visionDataOutputParameters.
leads.why: Three mechanisms you do not have, all aimed at exactly P1 and P2. (1) ARKit runs a *separate, small, slow* vision stream (640x480 @ 10 fps default) alongside the 1920x1440 @ 60 fps display stream — the tracker and the backdrop are decoupled, which is the same architecture as ARCore's 640x480 ImageReader + 1080p SurfaceTexture. (2) Every video format has three frame rates indexed by a power-usage level, and the live rate is `frameRatesByPowerUsage[powerUsage]` — i.e. ARKit throttles capture rate as a function of a power/thermal state. That is why ARKit spends 0 s in 'serious' where you spend 173 s: it gives up frame rate first. (3) ARFrameRateLimitingStrategy is a per-technique rate gate — the answer to 'detection currently runs on EVERY frame because that is what the upstream tracker does' is that the system you are benchmarked against explicitly does not. Caveat: decompiled private framework — use as evidence and as a design template only; do not copy any of it.
leads.license: NOT USABLE — decompiled Apple private framework; evidence only

leads.title: Apple ARPositionalTrackingConfiguration — the documented low-power 6DoF mode "runs the camera at lowest possible resolution and frame rate"
leads.claim: Apple, verbatim: "A configuration that tracks only the device's position in 3D space. Enables 6 degrees of freedom tracking of the iOS device by running the camera at lowest possible resolution and frame rate. Use this configuration when you don't need to parse the camera feed, such as for example, virtual reality scenarios." Related docs read the same day: ARConfiguration.supportedVideoFormats — "the order of this array always puts higher-quality formats before lower-quality formats"; AVCaptureDevice.Format.isVideoBinned — "Binning is a pixel-combining process which can result in greater low light sensitivity at the cost of reduced resolution"; AVCaptureVideoDataOutput.alwaysDiscardsLateVideoFrames — default true, and "When set to false, the output gives delegates more time to process old frames before it discards new frames, but application memory usage may increase significantly as a result."
leads.why: Apple's own public API concedes the central point of your P1/P2: full-rate 6DoF pose does not need a high-resolution, high-rate camera feed, and the sanctioned way to get cheap poses is to lower both. If ARPositionalTrackingConfiguration.supportedVideoFormats on an iPhone 14 Pro is enumerable on-device, it directly tells you the resolution/rate Apple itself considers 'lowest possible' for 6DoF — a one-line experiment that gives you the target to aim your XRSLAM front end at, from a first-party source. The alwaysDiscardsLateVideoFrames note is also your P3 warning: a deep late-frame queue is exactly how 276 MB grows.

leads.title: ARCore CameraConfig.TargetFps reference — "TARGET_FPS_60: Increases power consumption and may increase app memory usage"
leads.claim: Google, verbatim: "TARGET_FPS_60 — Target 60fps camera capture frame rate. Increases power consumption and may increase app memory usage. See the ARCore Supported Devices page for a list of devices that currently support 60fps." versus "TARGET_FPS_30 — ... Available on all ARCore supported devices." Also: "Actual camera capture frame rates can be lower than the target frame rate under low light conditions, in order to accommodate longer exposure times."
leads.why: A first-party vendor statement that ties a 60 fps camera channel to all three of your remaining gaps at once: power (P2), memory (P3), and — via the low-light exposure caveat — the fact that a 60 fps channel is not even reliably 60 fps indoors, which undermines the premise of P1. Combined with the ARCore engineer's experiment report in issue #604, you have two independent Google sources saying the 60 fps camera channel is a bad trade for handheld AR. Useful when you have to justify to the user why you are not chasing 59.9 poses/s via a 60 fps camera.

leads.title: AndroidX CameraX ImageAnalysis.java — Android's official CV input defaults to 640x480, KEEP_ONLY_LATEST, queue depth 6, and warns that blocking the producer stalls other streams
leads.claim: Source lines (androidx-main, file read 2026-09-08): line 1256 `private static final Size DEFAULT_TARGET_RESOLUTION = new Size(640, 480);`; line 263 `static final int DEFAULT_BACKPRESSURE_STRATEGY = STRATEGY_KEEP_ONLY_LATEST;`; line 264 `static final int DEFAULT_IMAGE_QUEUE_DEPTH = 6;`; line 266 `DEFAULT_OUTPUT_IMAGE_FORMAT = OUTPUT_IMAGE_FORMAT_YUV_420_888`; line 1258 `DEFAULT_ASPECT_RATIO = AspectRatio.RATIO_4_3`. Javadoc for STRATEGY_KEEP_ONLY_LATEST (lines ~127-145): "Only deliver the latest image to the analyzer, dropping images as they arrive... This strategy ignores the value set by setImageQueueDepth(int). Only one image will be delivered for analysis at a time. If more images are produced while that image is being analyzed, they will be dropped and not queued for delivery." Javadoc for STRATEGY_BLOCK_PRODUCER (lines ~147-165): "Once the producer has produced the number of images equal to the image queue depth, and none have been closed, the producer will stop producing images... When the producer stops producing images, it may also stop producing images for other use cases, such as Preview, so it is important for the analyzer to keep up with frame rate, on average."
leads.why: Direct answer to the Android half of your assignment and to your P1 back-pressure collapse. Google's own image-analysis use case defaults to VGA and to DROP-LATEST rather than block; the javadoc explicitly documents the failure mode you hit — blocking the producer to apply back-pressure does not just slow the analyzer, it stalls the whole camera session including the preview, which is exactly 'back-pressure kicks in and latency collapses'. Actionable: make the tracker path drop-latest (never block the capture session) and forward-integrate IMU across the dropped frames, rather than letting queue depth control the shutter. Apache-2.0, so unlike the ARKit evidence this is code you may actually copy, and it is available on Mali and Adreno by construction.

leads.title: Apple CoreMedia dropped-frame reason taxonomy — OutOfBuffers / FrameWasLate / Discontinuity, with Apple's stated cause for each
leads.claim: kCMSampleBufferAttachmentKey_DroppedFrameReason: "Sample buffers with this attachment contain no image or data buffer. They mark a dropped video frame. This attachment identifies the reason the frame was dropped." The three values, verbatim: OutOfBuffers — "The module providing sample buffers has run out of source buffers. This condition is typically caused by the client holding onto buffers for too long and can be alleviated by returning buffers to the provider." FrameWasLate — "A video capture client has indicated that late video frames should be dropped and the current frame is late. This condition is typically caused by the client's processing taking too long." Discontinuity — "The module providing sample buffers has experienced a discontinuity, and an unknown number of frames have been lost. This condition is typically caused by the system being too busy."
leads.why: This is the instrument you need to tell apart the three competing explanations for P1's 28.4 vs 59.9 poses/s, which currently all look the same from the outside. FrameWasLate means your GPU pass missed the deadline; OutOfBuffers means you are holding CVPixelBuffers too long (which is also a direct P3 lead — every retained 1920x1440 NV12 buffer is ~4.15 MB, so a handful explains a good chunk of the 276-266 MB delta); Discontinuity means the SoC is thermally saturated and it is not your code's fault. Read the attachment in captureOutput(_:didDrop:from:) and log the histogram over a 300 s run before optimising anything. Note XRSLAM's own Camera.swift already has an (empty) cameraDidDrop() hook to hang this on.

leads.title: RD-VIO (the algorithm inside XRSLAM) — the authors' own iPhone deployment is 640x480 @ 30 Hz with 100 Hz IMU, benchmarked against ARKit
leads.claim: Section 4.4.4 'Mobile AR Application', verbatim: "We deploy RD-VIO to iOS platform and develop a simple AR demo to show its accuracy and robustness. We use 30 Hz images data with resolution 640 x 480 and IMU data which consists of angular velocity and acceleration with 100Hz captured by the iPhone X. RD-VIO can run in real-time on mobile devices." Section 4.4.3 'Online Comparison': ARKit vs ARCore vs RD-VIO run simultaneously on three phones strapped together (two iPhone X + one Xiaomi Mi 8) with VICON ground truth over five cases A0-A4; the authors explicitly concede "both ARKit and ARCore are comprehensive VI-SLAM systems. They've benefited from extensive engineering optimizations, spanning hardware, software, and chip-level enhancements. In contrast, our research centers on crafting a compact visual-inertial odometry system that strikes a balance between being lightweight and robustness." Module timings in Table 2 are reported on an Intel i7-7700 @3.6 GHz desktop, not on phone.
leads.why: The paper behind the code you ported states its intended operating point as 640x480 @ 30 Hz — same as the shipped iOS config. It also gives you a ready-made, published comparison protocol against same-device ARKit (rigidly co-mounted phones + VICON, five motion cases) if you need to defend a resolution/rate change as not hurting accuracy. And the authors' own framing — that ARKit/ARCore win partly through 'chip-level enhancements' — is independent corroboration of the AVCaptureVisionDataOutput finding: the people who wrote your tracker did not expect to match ARKit on cost.

leads.title: HoloLens 2 Research Mode paper — a shipping AR headset feeds its visual-inertial SLAM four 640x480 grayscale cameras at 30 fps, on a dedicated low-power HPU
leads.claim: Table 1 'Research Mode camera frames': VLC = 640 x 480, 8-bit. Body text: "Four visible-light tracking cameras (VLC): Grayscale cameras (30 fps) used by the system for real-time visual-inertial SLAM." Depth: AHAT 512x512 @ 45 fps near-depth ("the HoloLens 2 saves power by calculating only 'aliased depth'"), Long Throw 320x288 @ 1-5 fps far-depth. Architecture: "The device features a second-generation custom-built Holographic Processing Unit (HPU 2.0), which enables low-power, real-time computer vision. The HPU runs all the computer vision algorithms on device (head tracking, hand tracking, eye gaze tracking, spatial mapping etc.)... The CPU on the SoC (a Qualcomm SnapDragon 850) remains fully available for applications." Microsoft's own docs also warn: "Enabling Research Mode uses more battery power than using the HoloLens 2 under normal conditions" (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/mixed-reality/develop/advanced-concepts/research-mode).
leads.why: Third independent shipping AR system, third confirmation of the same answer to your assigned question: production trackers eat 640x480 grayscale at 30 fps. Note the additional pattern — the cameras that feed SLAM are GRAYSCALE, i.e. no chroma plane at all, whereas you are pulling full YUV/BGRA at 1920x1440. If your WGSL front end only consumes luma, taking the Y plane of a 420f buffer (or a smaller binned format) removes chroma bandwidth for free and is bit-exact. Also note the low-rate/low-res tiering: even inside one device, different perception tasks get different rates (45 / 30 / 1-5 fps) rather than everything running at display rate — the same lesson as ARKit's frameRatesByPowerUsage and ARCore's ~10 Hz VIO.
leads.license: MIT (microsoft/HoloLens2ForCV samples); paper is arXiv preprint

leads.title: ARCore "Buffering camera frames" — frame-delay queue of up to 6 frames, ~6 MB per 1080p buffer, and the caveat that buffering is not guaranteed to help
leads.claim: Google, verbatim: "Each additional camera frame buffered increases memory utilization. For example, a 1080p texture consumes approximately 6 MB of memory (obtained by multiplying a resolution of 1920 x 1080 by three bytes RGB data per pixel)." Observed frame-delay values in ARCore's own logcat are non-trivial: "Update Frame Delay to 6 frames", "to 4 frames", "to 2 frames", "to 0 frames" ("Note: The size of the buffer can vary over time"). And the negative result: "Using multiple camera frames is not guaranteed to decrease variability of frame rates, and using a multithreaded rendering pipeline is not guaranteed to provide better performance in all circumstances" — dependent on app rendering pipeline, threading model, device CPU architecture and OS scheduling. Buffering is force-enabled when Augmented Images or Augmented Faces are on, or on certain devices.
leads.why: A concrete, vendor-published memory accounting rule for P3: buffer count x bytes-per-frame is a first-class term, and a 1920x1440 NV12 frame is ~4.15 MB, so a 2-3 frame queue is 8-12 MB — the same order as your entire 276 vs 266 MB gap. Before hunting allocations elsewhere, count in-flight CVPixelBuffers and IOSurfaces. It is also a documented negative result relevant to P1: Google says deeper camera buffering is NOT reliably a latency or frame-rate win, so adding queue depth is not the fix for your back-pressure collapse — dropping is.

leads.title: ARCore "Configuring the camera" — CameraConfig separates CPU image size from GPU texture size, and lower GPU texture resolution is the documented way to cut GPU load and memory bandwidth
leads.claim: Google, verbatim: "CameraConfig describes the properties of the underlying camera sensor, including: the camera ID; ... FPS (frames per second) range; CPU image dimensions; GPU texture dimension..." The API splits these explicitly: getImageSize() "Gets the dimensions of the image frames for processing that are sent on CPU stream" vs getTextureSize() "Gets the dimensions of the image frames for texture that are sent on GPU stream" (https://developers.google.com/ar/reference/java/com/google/ar/core/CameraConfig). Guidance: "Selecting an alternate GPU texture resolution. On supported devices, ARCore may provide additional GPU texture resolutions. Selecting a lower resolution GPU texture may help improve app performance by reducing GPU load and lowering memory bandwidth requirements, although is not guaranteed to improve performance in all cases." Also: "Fixed focus is generally better for tracking (and is the ARCore default on most devices)."
leads.why: The API shape itself is the design lesson for your architecture: an AR system exposes two independent resolutions, one for the tracker and one for the display, and never conflates them. Your pipeline currently has one 1920x1440 stream doing both jobs, which forces the tracker to pay display-grade pixel costs (P1, P2, P3). On iOS the equivalent split is an AVCaptureSession with a full-res video connection for the backdrop plus a separate lower-res connection/downscale for the tracker — which is exactly what ARKitCore does (ARImageScalingTechnique + a separate vision stream). The fixed-focus note is a free bonus: continuous autofocus both burns power and silently changes the intrinsics your bit-exact front end assumes are constant.

leads.title: Euphrates (ISCA 2018) — published mobile power budget: image sensor ~150 mW, ISP ~150 mW, CNN accelerator ~700 mW, vs CPU cluster >3 W
leads.claim: Figure 1 caption and Sec. 2: the continuous-vision pipeline is annotated Camera Sensor (~150 mW) -> ISP (~150 mW) -> CNN Accelerator (~700 mW). Sec. 2.1: "the typical power consumption of an image sensor, an ISP, and a CNN accelerator combined is about 1 W... whereas the CPU cluster alone can easily consume over 3 W". The paper's baseline resolution assumption: "TOPS is based on the 480p (640x480) resolution common in smartphone cameras." Sec. 2.2 notes commercial motion-enabled camera ISPs (ARM Mali C-71, Qualcomm Spectra) that already produce motion vectors inside the ISP, which Euphrates exploits to skip per-frame CV work.
leads.why: Gives you an order-of-magnitude budget for P2 that reframes the problem: the camera sensor plus ISP is roughly 300 mW, i.e. a minority of a 3-5 W thermally-limited phone. So the camera pipeline per se is probably NOT why you sit 173 s in 'serious' while ARKit sits 0 s — the full-resolution per-frame GPU pass is. That is a useful negative result: do not spend a week on capture-format micro-optimisation expecting to fix P2; spend it on pixels-per-frame and frames-per-detection. Secondary: the ISP-motion-vector angle (ARM Mali C-71, Qualcomm Spectra) is the Android-side analogue of Apple's AVCaptureVisionDataOutput, and confirms this is an industry-wide 'move the front end off the general-purpose engines' trend rather than an Apple quirk. Caveat: these are 2018 estimates for a generic mobile SoC, not measurements on an iPhone 14 Pro.

leads.title: Qualcomm FastCV 1.8.0 headers + prebuilt library (fastcv.h / fastcvDsp.h / LICENSE), shipped 2025-07-09 via opencv_3rdparty
leads.claim: I downloaded and read this package. LICENSE = SPDX BSD-3-Clause-Clear, (c) 2024-2025 Qualcomm Innovation Center (NOTICE also carries Edward Rosten's FAST BSD notice). fastcv.h (v1.8.0) exposes the whole of our front end on the ARM CPU: fcvCornerHarrisu8 / fcvCornerHarrisScoreu8 / fcvCornerHarrisAdaptiveu8, fcvGoodFeatureToTracku8, fcvCornerFast9u8 / fcvCornerFast10u8 (+InMaskScore variants), fcvCornerRefineSubPixu8, fcvPyramidCreateu8_v1..v4, fcvPyramidSobelGradientCreatef32/i16, fcvFilterSobel3x3/5x5/7x7, fcvImageHistogramEqualizeu8, and fcvTrackLKOpticalFlowu8 / _v2 / _v3 / f32. The DSP-offload header fastcvDsp.h (Q6/Hexagon, 'Q'-suffixed entry points, dated 2025-07-09) contains ONLY: fcvQ6Init/fcvQ6DeInit, fcvHwMemAlloc/Free, fcvFFTu8Q, fcvIFFTf32Q, fcvFilterCannyu8Q, fcvFilterCorr3x3s8_v2Q, fcvFilterCorrNxNu8Q/u8f32Q/u8s16Q, fcvFilterThresholdOtsuu8Q, fcvSumOfAbsoluteDiffs8x8u8_v2Q. There is NO corner detector, NO Harris, NO goodFeaturesToTrack, NO pyramid build and NO LK optical flow on the DSP surface. fastcv.h's own overview says the unified binary contains 'FastCV for ARM' (any ARM CPU) and 'FastCV for Snapdragon' (QTI chipsets only); the only occurrence of the word GPU in the entire 1.4 MB header is an error code, 'Hardware GPU failed to respond'.
leads.why: This is the sharpest possible vendor answer to our assigned question. Qualcomm, which owns both the DSP and the GPU, ships corner detection and pyramidal LK on the CPU and offloads to the Hexagon DSP only FFT, Canny, correlation, Otsu and SAD. So 'put feature detection on the DSP' is not a path Qualcomm itself supports as of July 2025 — the DSP entry points do not exist. Combined with the license (BSD-3-Clause-Clear, permissive) this is copyable in principle, but see the iOS blocker in the fastcv.cmake lead.
leads.venue: Qualcomm Innovation Center / distributed by OpenCV 3rdparty

leads.title: Arm Compute Library release notes: 'Remove computer vision support from CL backend' (v21.05)
leads.claim: Read in full. Under 'v21.05 Public major release' the changelog lists 'Remove computer vision support from Arm Neon backend' and 'Remove computer vision support from CL backend', then enumerates the deleted functions. Deleted from the OpenCL (GPU) backend: CLHarrisCorners, CLOpticalFlow, CLGaussianPyramid, CLLaplacianPyramid, CLFastCorners, CLScharr3x3, CLSobel3x3/5x5/7x7, CLDerivative, CLCannyEdge, CLEqualizeHistogram, CLHistogram, CLMeanStdDev, CLWarpAffine/Perspective, CLMagnitude, CLPhase, CLNonLinearFilter, CLMinMaxLocation (39 functions). The identical list was deleted from the NEON backend (NEHarrisCorners, NEOpticalFlow, NEGaussianPyramid, NEScharr3x3, ...). The same release also removed all GLES kernels. These functions had been marked deprecated one release earlier, in 'v20.11 Public major release' (kernels named explicitly: CLHarrisScoreKernel, CLHarrisScoreFP16Kernel, CLScharr3x3Kernel, ...).
leads.why: Arm built, shipped and maintained GPU (OpenCL) implementations of EXACTLY our front end — Harris corners, pyramidal LK optical flow, Gaussian pyramid, Scharr/Sobel, histogram equalisation — and then deleted the whole GPU CV backend in v21.05 (2021). That is the strongest available vendor signal that a mobile-GPU port of classic OpenCV-style feature detection was not judged worth maintaining. It is a negative result on our exact approach, from the GPU vendor, and it saves us from assuming nobody tried.

leads.title: Arm GPU Best Practices Developer Guide 101897 — Compute shading / Image processing
leads.claim: Read via the r.jina.ai text proxy of this exact page (developer.arm.com/support.arm.com serve the body from JS, so the raw URL returns only a shell). Arm's own Do/Don't/Impact block says: Do 'Use fragment shaders for simple image processing.' and 'For more complicated scenarios try using and monitoring the performance of compute shaders.' Don't 'use imageLoad() in compute unless you must use coherent read and writes within the dispatch' and don't 'use compute to process images generated by fragment shading' (backwards dependencies cause pipeline bubbles). Impact: 'Compute shaders can be slower and less energy-efficient than fragment shaders for simple post-processing workloads.'
leads.why: Arm explicitly states that compute shaders can be BOTH slower and less energy-efficient than fragment shaders for simple image processing. Our CLAHE / pyramid / Scharr stages are simple image processing, and we run them as compute dispatches. On Mali this is the wrong shader stage by the vendor's own guidance, and it bears directly on P2 (thermal) as well as P1. It also gives us a cheap, lossless experiment: re-express the pure-map stages (CLAHE LUT apply, pyramid downsample, Scharr) as fragment shaders and measure — output can stay bit-identical.

leads.title: Hot Chips 27: 'Architecture of the Hexagon 680 DSP for Mobile Imaging and Computer Vision' (Lucian Codrescu, Qualcomm)
leads.claim: Downloaded the PDF and extracted the text. Slide 20, 'Imaging & Vision Kernel Benchmarks': DSP with HVX vs quad Krait CPU with full NEON optimisation, quad Krait at 2.65 GHz, single DSP/HVX at 725 MHz, 'core power only excluding SoC infrastructure, DDR, etc.' — result annotated '1-3x faster' and '4-18x lower energy' per pixel. Slide 21, full application (low-light video enhancement): '3x faster' and '10x lower energy' vs quad Krait. Slide 22 gives the mechanism: 'Unlike CPUs, the bulk of the power is spent in compute datapath'; CPU is OOO/superscalar with short vectors and high-MHz design (clock power + leakage overheads), DSP is in-order VLIW with long vectors, only L2 used for image data, designed for low power. Slide 7: HVX has 1024-bit SIMD, 8/16/32-bit fixed point, and 'NO floating-point — Smaller & Lower Energy Design — Algorithmically not needed for majority of CV/Imaging Apps'.
leads.why: This is the canonical vendor power argument for DSP over CPU for imaging/CV, with numbers and units, and it never compares against the GPU — the GPU is simply not in the frame for this workload. Two consequences for us: (a) the 4-18x energy/pixel figure is a ceiling on what any DSP move could buy on P2, and it is measured against NEON not against a GPU; (b) HVX is fixed-point only, so a DSP port could never be bit-exact with our float OpenCV replica — it would be a product decision, not a lossless speed-up.

leads.title: Arm KleidiCV — Arm's official OpenCV acceleration library, CPU only
leads.claim: Read the announcement blog and the repo README (https://gitlab.arm.com/kleidi/kleidicv, SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0, AArch64). KleidiCV is 'an open-source library of optimized routines for accelerating Computer Vision (CV) workloads on Arm CPUs', integrating into OpenCV with no application changes. Covered ops include colour conversions (RGB/BGR/grey/YUV), Gaussian blur, dilate/erode, Sobel and resize. Three code paths — Neon, SVE2, Streaming SVE/SME2 — chosen by runtime hardware detection. Measured on a Samsung Galaxy S22 Cortex-X2 core: 'mean uplift across the different operations is over 75%'. The blog contains no GPU path and no GPU-vs-CPU comparison at all.
leads.why: Read next to the ACL v21.05 deletion, this is Arm's revealed position across a decade: in 2021 they removed GPU CV, and in 2024 they launched a CPU-only, Apache-2.0 accelerator for the very same OpenCV primitives we ported to WGSL (Gaussian blur, Sobel, resize, cvtColor). If we ever need an Android CPU fallback or a cross-check oracle for P1 back-pressure, this is a permissive, vendor-authored, OpenCV-compatible implementation we are allowed to copy. It does not currently cover Scharr, pyrDown, goodFeaturesToTrack or LK.

leads.title: Qualcomm's FastCV module in opencv_contrib — trackOpticalFlowLK, FAST10, buildPyramid, sobelPyramid (Apache-2.0 wrappers), explicitly NOT OpenCV-compatible
leads.claim: Read the README and the headers under modules/fastcv/include/opencv2/fastcv/. README: 'This module provides wrappers for several FastCV functions not covered by the corresponding HAL in OpenCV or have implementation incompatible with OpenCV' and 'This module supports ARM architecture only.' Headers (Copyright (c) 2024-2025 Qualcomm Innovation Center, SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0) declare cv::fastcv::trackOpticalFlowLK(...) with defaults winSize 7x7 and TermCriteria(MAX_ITER|EPS, maxIterations 7, maxEpsilon 0.03f*0.03f); cv::fastcv::FAST10(src, mask, coords, scores, barrier, border, nmsEnabled) documented against fcvCornerFast9InMaskScoreu8; cv::fastcv::buildPyramid(src, pyr, nLevels, scaleBy2, borderType, borderValue) with ORB 0.8408964 scaling; cv::fastcv::sobelPyramid(pyr, dx, dy, outType). There is also a DSP sub-namespace cv::fastcv::dsp with fcvdspinit()/fcvdspdeinit() and only filter2D, SAD, threshold, FFT, Canny.
leads.why: Direct confirmation from the vendor's own OpenCV integration that their accelerated LK/FAST/pyramid are NOT drop-in bit-exact replacements for OpenCV ('implementation incompatible with OpenCV') — they had to be exposed as a separate namespace rather than as a HAL override. For us that is the key line: any vendor-accelerated route to feature detection on Qualcomm silicon is a product decision that changes results, not a lossless speed-up. The default parameters (7x7 window, 7 iterations, eps 0.03^2) are also a useful reference point against our XRSLAM/OpenCV LK settings.

leads.title: OpenCV's FastCV HAL wiring (3rdparty/fastcv/fastcv.cmake and hal/fastcv/include/fastcv_hal_imgproc.hpp)
leads.claim: Read both files. fastcv.cmake downloads a prebuilt FastCV only for ANDROID (aarch64 / armv7) or 'UNIX AND NOT APPLE AND NOT IOS AND NOT XROS' with AARCH64 — i.e. there is no iOS, no macOS, no visionOS binary at all, and 32-bit Linux is explicitly 'not supported for now'. fastcv_hal_imgproc.hpp (Copyright (c) 2024 Qualcomm Innovation Center, Apache-2.0) overrides exactly these OpenCV HAL hooks: cv_hal_medianBlur, cv_hal_sobel, cv_hal_boxFilter, cv_hal_adaptiveThreshold, cv_hal_gaussianBlurBinomial, cv_hal_warpPerspective, cv_hal_pyrdown, cv_hal_cvtBGRtoHSV, cv_hal_cvtBGRtoYUVApprox, cv_hal_canny. fastcv_hal_core.hpp adds lut, normHammingDiff8u, mul/sub/addWeighted, transpose2d, meanStdDev, flip, rotate90, SVD32f, gemm32f. Notably absent from the HAL: cornerHarris, goodFeaturesToTrack, calcOpticalFlowPyrLK, CLAHE, Scharr.
leads.why: Two hard constraints for us in one file. (1) FastCV has no iOS build, so the DSP/NEON route fails our tri-platform rule at the first hurdle — the iPhone 14 Pro is our primary target. (2) Even where FastCV IS available, Qualcomm chose to HAL-override only the pointwise/filter layer (pyrDown, Sobel, Gaussian, Canny) and deliberately left corner detection and LK outside the transparent-acceleration path — the same split we see in fastcvDsp.h. That is a consistent vendor verdict about which parts of a front end are worth hardware-specialising.

leads.title: Arm GPU Best Practices 101897 — Compute shading / Shared memory and Workgroup sizes
leads.claim: Read both pages via the r.jina.ai text proxy. Shared memory page: 'Arm GPUs do not implement dedicated on-chip shared memory for compute shaders' — the shared memory available is system RAM backed by the load-store cache. Do: 'Use shared memory to share significant computation between threads in a workgroup', 'Keep your shared memory as small as possible, as it reduces the chance of thrashing the data cache'. Don't: 'Do not copy data from global memory to shared memory on Arm GPUs. Doing so pollutes the caches.' Workgroup sizes page: 'Use 64 as a baseline workgroup size', 'Use a multiple of 4 as a workgroup size', 'Try smaller workgroup sizes before larger ones, especially if using barriers or shared memory', 'When working with images or textures, use a square execution dimension, for example 8x8'; Don't: 'Do not use more than 64 threads per workgroup', 'Do not assume that barriers with small workgroups are free from performance costs'. Impact: shaders that spill to stack raise load/store utilisation and external bandwidth.
leads.why: Our WGSL kernels are written against a desktop/Metal mental model where workgroup shared memory is fast scratchpad. On Mali it is cache-backed system RAM, and the staging pattern (load a tile into shared, barrier, compute) is the pattern Arm explicitly tells you not to use. This is the concrete, vendor-sourced checklist to run our CLAHE / pyramid / Scharr / Harris kernels against before we blame the hardware — and every item on it is a lossless, bit-exact change.

leads.title: Arm forum: Peter Harris (Arm) on GPU front-end scheduling overhead from many small compute dispatches
leads.claim: Read the thread. Peter Harris (Arm employee) attributes the gap between 'compute queue active' and 'GPU active' cycles to front-end scheduling overhead, with three named causes: 'High density of small workloads (e.g. many small compute kernels)', 'High densities of pipeline barriers (e.g. many separate pipeline barriers between workloads)', and 'High numbers of workloads that trigger L2 cache flushes'. He also notes the offline compiler only analyses the shader itself and cannot see API-level inefficiency around it. In the reported case roughly 113 kilo-cycles out of 181 total (181 - 40 compute - 28 load/store) were front-end scheduling rather than shader execution — i.e. about 62% of GPU cycles were overhead, not work.
leads.why: Our per-frame front end is a chain of many small dispatches with barriers between them (CLAHE stages, per-pyramid-level blur+downsample, Scharr, Harris, NMS). Arm's own GPU architect says that shape of workload burns most of its cycles in the front end and in L2 flushes, which the shader compiler cannot show you. That is a plausible mechanism for the 5 ms -> 19-22 ms collapse in P1 that has nothing to do with clock speed, and the fix (fuse dispatches, remove barriers, avoid L2 flushes) is lossless.
leads.venue: Arm Community, Mobile Graphics and Gaming forum

leads.title: Arm Compute Library v21.02 — CLHarrisCorners.cpp and CLOpticalFlow.cpp (last release containing Arm's OpenCL GPU CV)
leads.claim: Fetched both files at tag v21.02. Headers read 'Copyright (c) 2016-2020 Arm Limited. SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT' (CLHarrisCorners) and 'Copyright (c) 2017-2020 Arm Limited. SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT' (CLOpticalFlow).
