CLHarrisCorners composes CLSobel3x3/5x5/7x7 + CLHarrisScoreKernel + CLFillBorderKernel; CLOpticalFlow is the pyramidal LK built on CLPyramid. v21.02 is the last tag before the v21.05 removal, so this tag is the complete, buildable, MIT-licensed GPU reference.
leads.why: If we want an authoritative single source to replicate for a GPU Harris or GPU pyramidal LK — rather than hand-translating the OpenCV CPU code — this is a vendor-written, MIT-licensed, mobile-GPU-targeted implementation that we are allowed to copy line for line and cite. It is also the artifact to diff against when arguing about whether our WGSL kernel shapes match what the GPU vendor considered correct for Mali.

leads.title: Arm forum: Peter Harris (Arm) — an application cannot set the Mali GPU operating frequency
leads.claim: Read the thread. Peter Harris (Arm employee): 'There is no standard way to do this; the power management is outside of the GPU hardware from Arm and it depends on the integration provided by the device manufacturer.' For Pixel devices he directs the asker to Google, because DVFS policy is the integrator's, not Arm's.
leads.why: Directly relevant to P1's 'about 5 ms at nominal GPU clocks but ~19-22 ms once the phone downclocks'. There is no vendor-sanctioned lever to pin clocks on Android, and none on iOS either, so the only durable fix is to make the frame's GPU work small enough or infrequent enough to survive the downclocked state — i.e. attack the every-frame detection, not the clock. It also means any benchmark of ours that is not explicitly run in the downclocked state is measuring a state we cannot rely on.
leads.venue: Arm Community, Mobile Graphics and Gaming forum

leads.title: Arm forum: measured CPU-vs-GPU crossover on a mobile device is around 1000-2000 elements
leads.claim: Read the thread. It is a user (hterrolle), not Arm staff — so treat as community evidence, not vendor guidance. Reported findings: for datasets under roughly 1000-1500 elements the CPU is faster; GPU becomes competitive at roughly 2000+ elements; CPU frequency scaling is identified as the mobile bottleneck; the user's conclusion is that GPU suits large dense matrix work while CPU suits sequential, indexed or branchy work.
leads.why: A crude but on-topic data point for the dispatch-size threshold on mobile. Our per-pyramid-level kernels at the small levels, the NMS pass and the LK per-feature pass are all well under that element count, which is a concrete argument for keeping the tail of the pyramid and the sparse per-feature stages off the GPU entirely — a hybrid split that can be made bit-exact because both paths already exist in our tree.
leads.venue: Arm Community, Mobile Graphics and Gaming forum

leads.title: Qualcomm CV-ISP (Spectra 380, Snapdragon 855) power claim vs a CPU+DSP+GPU implementation
leads.claim: NOT OPENED — Zhihu is login-walled and r.jina.ai returned 403 / a login page. The claim comes from the Sogou search-result snippet of this article and of a mirrored WeChat post, both dated 2018-12-07, quoting a Qualcomm Snapdragon Tech Summit slide: '上图表明使用 CV-ISP 对比 CPU+DSP+GPU 组合，在6自由度的VR环境追踪功耗要节省2倍，目标追踪功耗降低4倍，目标检测功耗节省4倍' — i.e. versus a CPU+DSP+GPU combination, the dedicated CV-ISP saves 2x power on 6DoF VR environment tracking, 4x on object tracking, and 4x on object detection. I could not reach an English primary source (the Qualcomm 2018 press release URL 404s and AnandTech's archive is gone).
leads.why: If the number is real it is the only vendor figure I found that prices 6DoF tracking specifically, and it prices it against exactly our architecture (CPU+DSP+GPU doing the perception work). It says the gap between us and a fixed-function perception block is roughly 2x on tracking power — which is the right order of magnitude for P2's 173 s vs 0 s in thermalState serious, and implies ARKit's advantage is likely fixed-function silicon we cannot reach from WebGPU, not a smarter shader. Treat as unverified until someone finds the original slide.

leads.title: Как перегрев iPhone ломает UX: измеряем thermal state, FPS и отзывчивость
leads.claim: Fleet telemetry from a production iOS video app. Median time to reach thermalState: fair ~31 min, serious ~50 min, critical ~77 min across general sessions. In the fastest-heating scenario (video playback on iPhone 11): fair ~15 min, serious ~30 min, critical ~42 min; iPhone 17 Pro needs 36+ min to reach fair (iPhone 11 heats ~2.4x faster). ~16% of all sessions hit an elevated thermal state and users spend 27% of total time in one. In combined charging + playback, 58% of users transition to elevated thermal states. Degradation at critical: median FPS -20%, jitter ~3x (from ~5 ms to 13-15 ms), dropped frames ~3x, touch latency median 16->19 ms and P90 +30% (+70% when the baseline was already >50 ms). Playback duration falls -15% under fair and -22% under serious.
leads.why: This is the only Russian-language dataset that puts an absolute scale on P2. A heavy consumer workload (full-screen video decode) takes ~30 minutes of median time to reach 'serious' on an OLD phone; we reach it inside ~2 minutes on an iPhone 14 Pro. That reframes P2 from 'we are somewhat hot' to 'our load is roughly an order of magnitude above a video-playback workload', which argues the cause is a systemic energy sink (camera at full res + full-res GPU work every frame + memory traffic), not incremental GPU inefficiency. It also flags a measurement bias in our own 300 s run: this source measures that CHARGING is what pushes 58% of users into elevated states, and our run was taken charging - matching the earlier internal finding that a plugged-in phone runs ~1.7x slower/hotter. The 300 s comparison against ARKit should be repeated unplugged before any conclusion about the 173 s is treated as real.

leads.title: Сейчас будет горячо: нагрев iOS-устройств как продуктовая метрика
leads.claim: Practical instrumentation guide for ProcessInfo.ThermalState. Example production distribution: nominal 96.8%, fair 2.4%, serious 0.7%, critical 0.1% - at 10M monthly sessions the 0.7% is ~70,000 degraded sessions. Recommends 'median time to first serious' as the tracked metric (example: 18 min, regressing to 8 min flags a regression). Critical implementation detail stated explicitly: you must READ ProcessInfo.processInfo.thermalState first and only THEN register the thermalStateDidChangeNotification observer, otherwise notifications may never arrive. Prescribed mitigations under serious/critical: lower frame-processing frequency, reduce preview resolution, run ML inference every third frame instead of every frame, cap simultaneous filters, pause heavy work at critical.
leads.why: Two concrete things. (1) The observer-ordering trap is exactly the 'silent exit' failure class we keep re-encountering - if our 173 s figure came from a notification-only observer registered before the first read, the thermal ledger itself may be under- or mis-counting, and that must be checked before the number is trusted. (2) It states the industry-standard response to a thermal budget overrun as 'run detection every Nth frame, not every frame' - the same change P1 needs. It is a product-decision change (results differ), not a lossless speed-up, so it must be flagged as such; but it is corroboration that shipping iOS apps treat per-frame detection as negotiable under thermal pressure.

leads.title: Миллион частиц на iPhone: строим аттрактор Лоренца на GPU с Metal
leads.claim: Measured on device identifier iPhone15,2 (which is the iPhone 14 Pro - our exact device), iOS 26.5.2. Sustained GPU compute+render: 100,000 particles = 3.805 ms GPU time at 59.9 FPS; 250,000 = 9.396 ms at 60.2 FPS; 500,000 = 11.301 ms at 60.6 FPS; 1,000,000 = 12.364 ms at 60.9 FPS. Author states thermal state stayed 'fair' throughout the measurements, with no throttling observed at any configuration. Cost split: compute shader 6.08% of GPU work, render pass 93.92%.
leads.why: Same-device control for P1 and P2. Someone sustained 60 FPS on an iPhone 14 Pro while consuming 12.4 of the 16.7 ms budget (~74%) in GPU work and never left thermalState 'fair'. That is direct evidence that neither 'GPU busy ~74% of every frame at 60 Hz' nor 'sustained GPU compute' is by itself sufficient to drive an A16 into 'serious' - so our thermal collapse is very likely NOT the GPU compute itself. The obvious uncontrolled difference is that their test has no camera capture, no ISP, no full-res YUV frames crossing memory. That makes 'camera at full res / memory bandwidth' the first hypothesis to test for P2, and it makes the P1 story ('GPU falls to 19-22 ms once the phone downclocks under camera+GPU load') a claim about the CAMERA half of the load, not the GPU half. Concretely: run our WGSL front end at 60 Hz on synthetic frames with the camera off, and see whether the 5 ms -> 19-22 ms downclock still happens. Caveat: their workload is render-dominated (93.92%), so it is not a like-for-like compute-bound comparison.

leads.title: Apple Metal в MAPS.ME
leads.license: n/a (evidence only); MAPS.ME itself was Apache-2.0
leads.claim: Production OpenGL ES -> Metal migration of a navigation app, five months of engineering. Render-only speedup 3.78x on iPhone 6s, 3.07x on iPhone 8, 2.84x on iPhone X; average overall frame-rate improvement 43%; slow frames (>30 ms) reduced roughly fourfold; on iPad Pro 12.9" stutter dropped from 17.5% to 4.5% of frames. Energy result measured on iPhone 8: total battery drain improved only 12.5%, GPU-specific power draw fell 6.16% - and the article states the GPU accounts for only about 2% of total consumption in a navigation scenario.
leads.why: The single most useful negative-ish result I found for P2. A Russian team made the GPU render path roughly 3x faster on iPhones and got ~2%-of-total-power-worth of system energy back. If the GPU's share of system power in a camera+navigation workload is anywhere near that small, then further lossless optimisation of our WGSL kernels cannot close a 173 s -> 0 s thermal gap, and the P2 budget must be attacked at the camera pipeline / resolution / frame-rate level instead. Before we spend more weeks on kernel-level knives for P2, we should measure our own GPU share of system power directly - this source says the prior should be 'small'. (It also gives a calibrated cost for a full graphics-API port: five months.)

leads.title: Живой космос на Metal: как я переписывал фон мобильной игры и поднимал FPS с 20 до 120
leads.claim: Peak-vs-average GPU budgeting on Apple TBDR. A single expensive pass cost ~17 ms per frame against an 8.3 ms budget at 120 Hz. Fix: split that pass into horizontal strips with setScissorRect and render ONE strip per frame - 4 strips at 60 Hz replaced a single full pass at 30 Hz, dropping peak GPU time to ~6-7.3 ms/frame (composite pass ~0.85 ms; final steady 7.3 ms vs an earlier ~11x spread between p50 and max). Separately, CPU-GPU back-pressure was handled with a DispatchSemaphore frame-in-flight limiter using a NON-BLOCKING wait(timeout: .now()) so the main thread is never stalled when the GPU queue fills; the author's stated principle is 'пик важнее среднего' (the peak matters more than the average).
leads.why: Two directly transplantable patterns for P1. (1) Our problem statement is 'CLAHE + corner detection must fit in 16.7 ms but takes 19-22 ms when downclocked'. Striping the detection pass across N frames (rotate ROI/strip per frame) converts a 20 ms peak into ~5 ms per frame while still touching every region several times a second - the same trade this author made, and a much finer-grained knob than 'detect every Nth frame'. It changes results, so it is a product decision, and it interacts badly with a detector that assumes whole-frame non-maximum suppression - that interaction is the thing to check first. (2) Our back-pressure 'kicks in and latency collapses'; this is the same failure they had, and their fix (bounded frames-in-flight with a non-blocking wait that DROPS rather than stalls) matches the internal finding that our shutter cadence was being dictated by a blocking upstream queue. Neither is an authoritative algorithm we can replicate line-for-line; treat as engineering-pattern evidence with measured before/after numbers.

leads.title: Визуальный SLAM: делаем HD-карты при помощи смартфона
leads.license: discusses DSO (GPL) and ORB-SLAM (GPL) - both unusable as code for us
leads.claim: A Russian team building smartphone-based HD mapping wrote their OWN Direct SLAM engine rather than adopting an existing one. They experimented with DSO and rejected it, stating the backend code is so tangled that untangling it is very difficult. Demonstrated on an iPhone 8 with five passes recorded around an office with the phone windshield-mounted. Their claimed advantage over feature-based methods is a much denser point cloud enabling lidar-like, weather-invariant mapping. Crucially, 'accelerating SLAM using GPU on iPhone' is listed as FUTURE work, not something they had done as of March 2022. No fps, latency, feature-count, thermal or battery numbers are given.
leads.why: This is the closest anyone in the Russian engineering community got to our project, and it answers the cross-cutting question directly: as of 2022 a team actively shipping phone-based visual SLAM on iPhone had NOT ported the front end to the GPU and treated it as an open future item. Combined with the total absence of any Russian-language WGSL/Dawn-on-phone CV work (see dead_ends), the honest read is that the bit-exact GPU port of an OpenCV front end driven by WebGPU is territory nobody in this community has taken - so there is no shortcut, no prior art to copy, and equally no published warning that it fails. It also independently confirms the licence position we already hold: the strongest direct-SLAM implementations they evaluated are GPL and therefore off-limits as code.

leads.title: Кроссплатформенные оптимизации OpenCV
leads.claim: OpenCV's own Universal Intrinsics story: one implementation compiles to SSE/AVX, NEON, VSX, MSA and WASM backends; parallel_for_ expands at compile time to TBB, OpenMP, Apple GCD, Windows concurrency or Pthreads. Measured on the Prewitt edge-detection operator at 1920x1080: scalar baseline 6.13 ms; with parallel_for_ 2.20 ms (2.78x); with parallel_for_ + Universal Intrinsics 0.20 ms (30.65x). The article does NOT discuss bit-exactness guarantees across SIMD backends, and does not cover the OpenCL/GPU path.
leads.why: This is the CPU bar our GPU replicas have to clear, expressed in the same units. A 3x3 separable derivative at 1080p costs 0.20 ms with NEON + threads. Scharr is the same shape, and our frames are 1920x1440 (~1.33x the pixels), so the honest NEON reference for the Scharr stage is on the order of a quarter-millisecond - well under any plausible WebGPU dispatch + barrier + readback overhead for that one kernel. That says the Scharr/derivative stage is very unlikely to be worth keeping on the GPU on its own merits, and only earns its place if it avoids a CPU<->GPU round trip for the neighbouring CLAHE and corner stages. It is also the source we should cite when deciding which stages stay on the GPU: measure each ported stage against parallel_for_ + universal intrinsics, not against scalar C++. Secondary note: the article's silence on cross-backend bit-exactness is itself relevant - OpenCV does not advertise bit-identical results across its own SIMD backends, so 'bit-exact vs OpenCV 4.0.1' means bit-exact vs one specific build, which is worth pinning down explicitly.

leads.title: Трекинг объектов с подвижной камеры: когда компьютерное зрение встречается с механикой
leads.claim: Latency budget for a real moving-camera tracking pipeline: total 80-200 ms, decomposed as frame capture 33 ms (30 fps) + CV processing 20-100 ms + control computation 5 ms + actuator response 20-50 ms. Component figures: DIS (Dense Inverse Search) optical flow at 300-500 fps on GPU; a U-Net segmentation mask in 15 ms on a dedicated GPU; a real deployed case at 25 ms per frame on Jetson Xavier NX. Camera-motion compensation via ORB/AKAZE keypoints + homography + RANSAC. Explicit engineering rule stated: never trust the tracker 100% - always add a re-detection module that verifies every N frames whether the object is still there.
leads.why: Two uses. (1) It states the detect-every-N-frames-plus-track-in-between architecture as the default for moving-camera pipelines, which is the structural change P1 needs and which our current design violates only because upstream XRSLAM does detection every frame. (2) The DIS number (300-500 fps on GPU) is worth chasing as an alternative to our pyramidal Lucas-Kanade: DIS is in OpenCV under the permissive OpenCV licence (cv::DISOpticalFlow / optflow), it is dense rather than sparse, and if it really runs at 2-3 ms it changes the arithmetic of what the GPU should be doing per frame. The claim here is unsourced and the GPU is unnamed, so it is a pointer to verify against the OpenCV DIS source and the original DIS paper, not a number to trust.

leads.title: ORB_SLAM3 на raspberry pi 4
leads.license: ORB-SLAM3 is GPLv3 - evidence only, code unusable for us
leads.claim: Getting a full ORB-SLAM3 stack real-time on ARM required cutting the workload hard: 512x512 resolution, Camera.fps 20 for monocular, and only Camera.fps 3 for the inertial (IMU) variant; ORBextractor.nFeatures 1000 and ORBextractor.nLevels reduced from the default 8 to 3. Hardware: Raspberry Pi 4 with 8 GB RAM, two 18650 cells giving 2-3 hours of runtime. Author reports that during sharp turns the compute is clearly insufficient and that tracking only holds if you move slowly.
leads.why: A concrete, if crude, record of which knobs a practitioner reaches for when a full SLAM front end will not fit an ARM budget - and the first one is pyramid levels (8 -> 3), the second is resolution, the third is feature count. For P1 that is a ranked list of losing-fidelity levers with a real report of what breaks first (fast rotation) - which is the same failure mode we would expect if we cut levels. It is also a warning for P4: the IMU-fused variant fell to 3 fps, i.e. the inertial path was the expensive part on ARM, not the visual front end. GPLv3, so this is evidence about parameter sensitivity only - no code or constants may be copied.

leads.title: GPU-вычисления в браузере на скорости нативного приложения: марширующие кубы на WebGPU
leads.claim: WebGPU compute benchmarked against a native Vulkan implementation of the same Marching Cubes algorithm on 256x256x256 volumes. RTX 3080: WebGPU 32 / 31 / 32.5 / 37.5 ms vs native Vulkan 30.92 / 29.3 / 33.43 / 27.45 ms on the skull / bonsai / foot / aneurysm datasets. Apple M2 Max under WebGPU: 43.5 / 42.5 / 54.4 / 40.8 ms. Authors conclude overall performance is very close to the native Vulkan version.
leads.why: Relevant to the cross-cutting question of whether driving a phone GPU through WebGPU/Dawn is a sane substrate at all. On desktop and on Apple silicon the WebGPU abstraction costs roughly 3-37% versus native Vulkan on a real compute workload - i.e. the API layer is not where large factors hide. That is mild support for our Dawn choice and it argues that when we see an 8.5x gap on an iPhone (as we did with the WGSL matcher), the cause is a configuration/dispatch bug, not the abstraction. It does NOT measure a phone GPU, so it cannot speak to Mali/Adreno driver behaviour.

leads.title: Энергопотребление Android-приложений
leads.claim: Measurement protocol for Android app energy: reset with 'dumpsys batterystats --reset', run the isolated scenario offline, dump with 'dumpsys batterystats > batterystats.txt', analyse with Battery Historian (requires Docker) or Android Studio's Energy Profiler. Worked example output over a 32-second test: Cpu Usage 1.56 mAh, WiFi Usage 0.0476 mAh, GPS Usage 0.0417 mAh, Usage per second 0.0515625 mAh/s. Notes Doze (Android 6+) and App Standby Buckets (Android 9+) distort background measurements.
leads.why: P2 currently has an iOS-only ledger (thermalState seconds), which is a proxy, not energy. This gives the Android arm of an actual energy protocol in mAh with a reset-run-dump discipline, which is what we need to answer 'the extra energy is going somewhere else' quantitatively on Mali and Adreno - and unlike thermalState it attributes consumption per component. The per-component granularity is coarse (no GPU line in the quoted output), so it will bound CPU and radios but probably not isolate GPU vs ISP; still, it is the cheapest way to get a real number rather than a thermal proxy.

leads.title: Оптимизация обработки изображений с использованием GPU на примере Медианной фильтрации
leads.claim: 1920x1080 8-bit grayscale, 3x3 median, on GTX 780 Ti vs Intel Core i7-4770 @3.4 GHz: scalar CPU 24.814 ms; AVX2 CPU 0.424 ms (58.5x); GPU v1 0.372 ms (66.7x); GPU v2 0.207 ms (119.8x); GPU v3 0.130 ms (190.8x, ~15 GPixel/s). For a 5x5 kernel the GPU reaches roughly 5x over AVX2 while AVX2 falls to only 5.7x over scalar.
leads.why: A quantified version of the negative result we were asked to look for, on desktop hardware. Against WELL-VECTORISED CPU code, a discrete GPU with ~10x the power envelope won a 3x3 stencil by only 1.14x (naive) to 3.3x (fully tuned). Small-kernel, low-arithmetic-intensity CV is bandwidth-bound and the GPU's margin over good SIMD is thin even in the most favourable hardware pairing. On a phone, where CPU and GPU share one memory system and one power budget, the same comparison should be expected to narrow further or invert - which is a reason to hold each of our ported stages (Scharr, CLAHE tiles) to an explicit 'beats NEON' test rather than assuming the GPU wins. Desktop hardware, so this is indirect evidence about kernel shape, not a mobile measurement.

leads.title: Cистема визуально-инерциальной навигации для дрона на C++
leads.license: GitHub repo referenced; licence not stated in the article - must be checked before any reuse
leads.claim: From-scratch monocular VIO in C++: ORB detection plus Lucas-Kanade optical-flow tracking between frames, fused in an Error-State Kalman Filter over 15 state variables with IMU preintegration between camera frames; stated budget is ~300,000 pixels at 30 Hz. Keyframe selection is a parallax threshold - a frame is processed if displacement exceeds the threshold. Initialisation requires enough triangulated 3D points plus a gravity and scale estimate before the filter is activated. No frame-rate, latency, CPU-load or initialisation-time numbers are given. Raspberry Pi is the stated target.
leads.why: Independent confirmation of the structural cause of P4: a filter-based VIO still cannot activate until it has triangulated points and resolved gravity plus scale, so 'needs real translation before bootstrap converges' is not an XRSLAM quirk - it is what every monocular visual-inertial bootstrap does. That means P4 cannot be fixed by tuning the bootstrap; it can only be fixed by emitting a degraded pose earlier from a different source (IMU-only attitude with unresolved scale, i.e. what ARKit effectively does in its first second) and labelling it as such. That is a product decision about what a 'usable pose' means, and it should be framed that way rather than as an optimisation. Same architecture as our front end (ORB + LK), so also a sanity check that our stage choice is conventional. Licence unverified.

leads.title: Ориентация мобильного робота, выбор способа регистрации особых точек изображений
leads.claim: Benchmarks SIFT, SURF, AKAZE, BRISK, ORB and a custom 'BOEV' detector on the Mikolajczyk benchmark (8 sets of 6 images) for recall, precision and combined detect+describe+match time, across scale+rotation (bark), blur (bikes) and perspective (wall) distortions. Motivation stated as: on Raspberry Pi 3 the existing SLAM systems do not meet requirements on cost or quality/speed. Makes the argument that matching precision dominates cost because RANSAC complexity scales as O((1/precision)^N). Timings appear only inside the plots, so no numeric ms values could be extracted from the text.
leads.why: Weak on numbers but it makes one argument that bears on P1: the downstream cost of a detector is not its own runtime but the RANSAC iterations its precision implies, which scales exponentially. If we ever consider cutting detection frequency or quality to fit the 16.7 ms budget, the second-order cost lands in the pose solver, not the front end - and that is the term we would fail to notice, because our budget accounting is per-stage. Worth one measurement: how does our solver's iteration count move when detection quality drops.

leads.title: Как оптимизировать энергопотребление в iOS
leads.claim: Qualitative iOS energy guide. Names four primary drains: CPU processing, storage access, signal transceivers (cellular/Bluetooth/GPS) and graphics rendering. Core principle is to buffer and batch rather than transmit or process continuously, and to let the system schedule work (URLSessionConfiguration.background, QoS-appropriate dispatch queues). For location, use significantLocationChange (~700 m accuracy) before escalating to precise GPS, and allowDeferredLocationUpdatesUntilTraveled to defer processing. Only concrete comparison given: iPhone 5S battery life 10 hours on Wi-Fi vs 8 hours on cellular. No absolute per-component power figures.
leads.why: Included for completeness as the RU-community's baseline iOS energy advice, but it contains almost nothing quantitative and nothing camera- or GPU-compute-specific. Its one transferable idea for P2 is the batching principle: continuous per-frame work at a fixed cadence is the pattern this guide tells you to avoid, which is exactly what 'detection on every frame' is. Low confidence, low value - listed so nobody re-searches this ground.

leads.title: WWDC 2018 Session 610 — "Understanding ARKit Tracking and Detection" (full transcript)
leads.claim: Apple, on the record, from the ARKit team: "by combining those both systems World Tracking can skip the computer vision processing for some of those frames, while still keeping an efficient and responsive tracking. This frees CPU resources, which you can then, additionally, use for your apps." Also: results are returned "in ARFrames at 60 frames per second"; image tracking runs a coarse feature match then a dense photometric warp/error-minimisation stage and "will still track at 60 frames per second"; the tracking state (normal/limited/notAvailable) is produced by "machine learning, which was trained on thousands of data sets", using annotations "like the number of visible features tracked in the image and also the current velocity of the device"; initialisation requires translation — "the camera position must have changed by a translation to provide enough parallax… pure rotation does not give enough information"; the world origin is set to the first camera of the triangulated frames.
leads.why: The single most load-bearing statement for P1. ARKit's 59.9 poses/s is NOT 59.9 vision updates/s — Apple explicitly decouples ARFrame delivery rate (60/s) from CV processing rate and calls it a deliberate CPU-saving design. Our engine runs detection on EVERY frame "because that is what the upstream tracker does"; the reference system we are measured against does not. It also reframes P4: ARKit has the same parallax requirement we do, so its 1.5 s cannot be a faster SfM bootstrap — it must be emitting a non-SfM pose early.

leads.title: blacktop/ipsw-diffs — symbol/string diffs of AppleCV3D.framework (ARKit's actual VIO/SLAM library) across ~165 iOS builds
leads.license: diff corpus public; strings describe Apple proprietary code — architecture map only, NOT copyable
leads.claim: ARKit's tracker lives in /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/AppleCV3D.framework, namespace cv3d::vio. Assert/log strings leak the internal source tree under Sources/AppleCV3D/library/VIO/. Confirmed modules: FeatureDetection/src/HarrisFeatureDetector/{HarrisFeatureDetector,HarrisStrengthImage,HarrisConnerExtraction}.cpp; FeatureDetection/src/{DoGFeatureDetectorFixedPoint,DoGAndFREAKGenerator,DoGPyramidBuilderSinglePrecision}.cpp; FeatureMatchingUnsanitized/src/{HarrisTracker,DoGTracker,LineTracker}.cpp with include_private/…/NCCFeatureMatcher_NEON_INTRINSIC.h; ImageProcessing/src/{ConvolutionsFixedPoint.h,PyramidGaussianScaleSpaceLaplacianFixedPointPrecision,PyramidGaussianScaleSpaceLaplacianKeyEngine}.cpp; Geometry/src/RANSAC/{P3P,FivePoint,EightPoint,TwoPoint,P2PVertical,ThreePlusOne}PreemptiveRansac.cpp; Estimator/{SlidingWindowFilterFG,VisualInertialBundleAdjusterFG}.cpp; FactorBA/{VIOPreintegrateIMUFactor,VIOEpipolarFactor,VIOPriorFactor,viotriangulator}; Odometry/{VFusionFG,PoseTrackerFG,TrackManager,SlidingWindow,StationaryStateDetection}; Recognition/{VladImageRetrieval,Pca}; MapOptimization/PoseGraphOptimizer. Two feature back-ends coexist (classic Harris/DoG-FREAK and MLFeatureDetectionNodeGroup/MLDescriptorExtractor). Config: "Pyramid level of the dataset image at which to detect features. 0 means full resolution image, 1 means half-sized image, etc." with assert c.feature_detection_pyramid_level < 4; and assert camera_module_data.image_frames.front().frame.image.width == 664 || … == 640. Linked frameworks: Accelerate, vImage, AppleCVHWA, AppleNeuralEngine, Espresso, LACC, LearnedFeatures, Recon3D, Polaris/PolarisGraph. Metal.framework was present in AppleCV3D 6.58.70 (iOS 17.5.1) and is ABSENT from 7.16.50 (iOS 18.0).
leads.why: An architecture map of the system we are trying to beat, and it says three things about our approach. (1) Apple's front end is fixed-point NEON/Accelerate plus dedicated hardware; the descriptor matcher is literally named …_NEON_INTRINSIC.h — the reference implementation of what we ported to WGSL is a CPU SIMD kernel. (2) Feature detection is configured to run at a pyramid level, not full resolution, and an on-device assert pins the VIO image width at 640/664 px — we run CLAHE+Harris at 1920x1440, ~9x the pixels. (3) Metal dropped out of AppleCV3D's link list at iOS 18, i.e. Apple moved its CV3D library away from the GPU, not toward it. Files actually read: /17_5_1_21F90__vs_18_0_22A5282m/DYLIBS/AppleCV3D.md (dependency list incl. the Metal removal) and /18_3_1_22D72__vs_18_4_22E5200s/DYLIBS/AppleCV3D.md (65 KB of strings).

leads.title: AppleCV3D strings: HWFP (hardware feature points) with SWFP software fallback, backed by AppleCVHWA + LACC silicon
leads.claim: AppleCV3D contains VIO/FeatureDetectionNodeGroup/src/HWFPDetector.cpp, VIO/HWFeatureDetectionUtils/src/{HWKeyEngineUtils,HwKeyHeaderParser}.cpp, VIO/FeatureDetection/src/KeyEngineUtils.cpp and VIO/Hardware/src/{GaussianPyramidGenerator,ResponseMapAndKPCGenerator,KeyPointAndDescriptorGenerator,KPValidatorAndRefiner,KeyPointToDescriptor}.cpp, with runtime strings: "HWFP was requested but is missing. Falling back to SWFP.", "Max number of features (ignored when HWFP is enabled).", "The camera video mode is not supported for HWFP", "HWFP: points = %zu" / "SWFP: points = %zu". The backing framework AppleCVHWA (~1,700-1,900 functions; links only Accelerate/CoreFoundation/CoreGraphics/libc++) asserts "Only supporting binomial gaussian pyramid, with 2 scales per octave", has hardware ROI blocks (kNumRegionOfInterestBlocks, "Each block has to be at least 4 pixels big") and scale-bucket thresholding. AppleCV3D also links LACC.framework and contains lacc::function_name() [F = &PreemptiveRansacEpipoleFromTwoPointsLACC], plus "Only two point supported on LACC.", "Adaptive IMU sampling is not supported on LACC.", "ConfigureLacc currently expects that DG/DM is bypassed." (DG/DM = descriptor generation / descriptor matching). LowPowerSlamEngine logs "[LPS] HW stats: total frames processed {}: offloadded {} v{} cycles".
leads.why: Direct answer to the assignment's core question and the biggest single explanation of P1+P2. ARKit's Gaussian pyramid, response map, keypoint validation/refinement, descriptor generation AND descriptor matching run on fixed-function silicon (AppleCVHWA "Key Engine"), with a low-power compute complex (LACC) that even runs 2-point preemptive RANSAC and offloads whole SLAM frames. Software feature points are the FALLBACK, not the main path. That is why ARKit sits at 0.80 CPU-cores and 0 s in thermalState serious while our GPU CLAHE+Harris costs 5 ms nominal / 19-22 ms downclocked. It reframes the target: on iPhone we are not competing with an ARKit CPU/GPU implementation, we are competing with a hardware block — so the ceiling for a portable Metal/Mali/Adreno front end must be argued on tri-platform grounds, not on "match ARKit on iPhone".

leads.title: AppleCV3D: harris_corner_detector_NMP.mlmodelc — ARKit's Harris detector shipped as a CoreML/ANE model
leads.claim: AppleCV3D ships VIO/HarrisDetector/src/HarrisDetectionModel.cpp together with the compiled asset "harris_corner_detector_NMP.mlmodelc/" and runtime strings "HarrisDetectionModel Run Error: " and "Dropping HarrisDetectionOutput at %f because frame expired". The framework links AppleNeuralEngine.framework and Espresso.framework and contains Kit/ML/src/Private/{EspressoV2ModelInstance.mm,EspressoV2StreamPool.cpp}. Other shipped models: nfde_rskwfdpih8_sparse.mlmodelc (Neural Floor Direction Estimation, cf. VIO/FloorDirectionEstimation/src/FloorDirectionModel.cpp) and wgv1/wgv1r1/wgv1r1-tiny/ngv2/ngv3r1.mlmodelc. Apple's public statement that the ANE is used for ARKit work is limited to people occlusion / body tracking (WWDC 2019 session 604, A12+), so the ANE-Harris path is inference from the binary, not from Apple's docs.
leads.why: Second concrete answer to 'which processor': even the classical corner detector is packaged as a neural-accelerator graph ("NMP" is Apple's ANE/Espresso naming), so per-frame corner-detection energy on iPhone is paid by the ANE, not the GPU. Also note "Dropping HarrisDetectionOutput … because frame expired" — ARKit explicitly discards late detection results rather than letting them stall the tracker, which is exactly the back-pressure collapse in P1. That pattern is free to copy: make detection results droppable rather than blocking.

leads.title: ARKitCore.framework symbols: power-usage- and thermal-driven frame-rate control inside ARSession
leads.claim: ARKitCore (the private framework under public ARKit) exports: -[ARSession _updateThermalStateFromCurrentProcessInfo], -[ARSession _updateThermalState:], -[ARSession _setThermalStateProvider:], class ARProcessInfoThermalStateProvider conforming to protocol ARThermalStateProvider (ivar ARSession._thermalStateProvider); -[ARSession _preferredRenderFrameRateForCaptureFrameRate:isNominalPower:]; -[ARSession _preferredRenderSyncFrameRateForCaptureFrameRate:]; a video-format selector frameRatesByPowerUsage:videoBinned:pixelFormat:needsHDRSupport:; and _changePowerUsage:forced: / _updatePowerUsageForced: / forceUpdatePowerUsage: / setPowerUsage: / isNominalPower:. Frame-rate plumbing: -[ARFrameUpdateTimer _startExecutorWithFrameRate:initialDelay:] and -[ARFrameUpdateTimer _updateExecutorForFrameRate:]. The pipeline is a technique graph: ARTechnique / ARParentTechnique / ARWorldTrackingTechnique / ARMLImageDownScalingTechnique with ARTechniqueParallelGatherContext and ARTechniqueSequentialGatherContext, plus ARParentTechniqueEnableLowLatencyDefaultsKey.
leads.why: The mechanism behind P2's asymmetry. ARKit does not survive 300 s by being cheap only — it runs a closed loop: read ProcessInfo.thermalState, map it to a 'power usage' level, then select BOTH the capture frame rate (frameRatesByPowerUsage:) and the render frame rate (_preferredRenderFrameRateForCaptureFrameRate:isNominalPower:) from that level, and retune the frame-update executor at runtime. It backs off before iOS ever reports 'serious'. We have no such governor, so we stay at full rate until the GPU downclocks and back-pressure collapses latency. Copying the shape of this (thermal-state → capture-rate + detection-rate ladder) needs no Apple code and attacks P1 and P2 with one change.

leads.title: WWDC 2022 Session 10126 — "Discover ARKit 6" (2x2 binning to 1920x1440@60, 4K@30, the 17 ms budget)
leads.claim: Apple: ARKit's default iPhone mode reads a 3840x2880 sensor region, then "Binning takes a region of 2x2 pixels, averages the pixel values, and writes back a single pixel… it downscales to 1920x1440 pixels. As a result of this, each frame consumes way less memory and processing power. This allows the device to run the camera at up to 60 frames per second and frees up resources for rendering." Result: "a camera stream that provides an image at HD resolution roughly every 17 milliseconds. After using the current frame for various computer vision tasks, ARKit surfaces the current frame for rendering." 4K mode is 3840x2160 at 30 fps only, iPhone 11+ / M1 iPad Pro; "Dealing with higher resolution images takes up additional system resources, so for games and other apps that rely on a high refresh rate, we still suggest using full HD video at 60 frames per second." Memory rule: "Do not hold on to an ARFrame for too long. This might prevent the system from freeing up memory, which might further stop ARKit from surfacing newer frames to you… the ARCamera's tracking state might fall back to limited."
leads.why: Three payoffs. (a) Our 1920x1440 is exactly ARKit's binned output — and the binning happens in the capture/ISP path, so Apple gets the 4x pixel reduction free before any compute touches it; if our camera channel is configured for a non-binned or differently-binned format we pay for pixels ARKit never pays for. (b) Apple's own guidance is that 60 fps is only affordable at 1080p-class resolution — a direct precedent for a product decision to run the CV path below display resolution. (c) The ARFrame-retention warning is a documented cause of both memory growth (P3) and the exact 'frames stop being surfaced → tracking goes limited' failure we see under back-pressure (P1).

leads.title: WWDC 2019 Session 604 "Introducing ARKit 3" + ARPositionalTrackingConfiguration docs — Apple's own low-power lever
leads.claim: On ARPositionalTrackingConfiguration Apple says: "We can achieve a low power consumption with the ability to lower the capture frame rate and also the camera resolution by still keeping your rendering rate at 60 hertz." Apple's API reference for the same class (fetched from the docs JSON endpoint) reads: "Enables 6 degrees of freedom tracking of the iOS device by running the camera at lowest possible resolution and frame rate. Use this configuration when you don't need to parse the camera feed." The same session attributes ANE use only to people-occlusion depth estimation and body tracking ("thanks to the power of Apple Neural Engine, we are able to do this on every frame in real time", A12+), never to world tracking.
leads.why: Apple shipped a first-class API whose entire purpose is 6-DoF tracking at reduced capture rate and resolution with rendering still at 60 Hz. That is exactly the trade P1/P2 needs, and it is Apple's endorsed answer — which makes it defensible as an explicit product decision rather than a regression. It also negatively bounds the 'which processor' question: Apple names the ANE for segmentation/body pose and pointedly never names it for world tracking in any public session.

leads.title: US 10,152,795 B2 — "Visual-based inertial navigation" (Apple; Flint, Naroditsky, Broaddus, Grygorenko, Roumeliotis, Bergig)
leads.venue: USPTO, granted 2018-12-11, assigned to Apple Inc.
leads.license: patent — read for method; not a code source, do not implement without counsel
leads.claim: Cited in the peer-reviewed VIO benchmark literature as the description of ARKit's algorithm: ARKit "includes a tightly-coupled filtering-based VIO algorithm similar to the MSCKF… It contains a sliding window filter, bundle adjustment, motion/structure marginalization modules [8]", where [8] is this patent. The inventor list is the FlyBy Media team (Flint, Naroditsky, Broaddus, Bergig) plus Stergios Roumeliotis, the MSCKF author. Corroborated by the binary: AppleCV3D has VIO/Estimator/{SlidingWindowFilterFG.cpp,VisualInertialBundleAdjusterFG.cpp}, VIO/FactorBA/*, cv3d::vio::VIOLandmarkDepthSqrtCauchyFactor / VIOPreintegrateIMUFactor, and a runtime toggle kCV3DVIO_UseFactorGraph. I could not open the patent text: patents.google.com returns 503, Justia 403, FreePatentsOnline is behind Cloudflare, and the USPTO PDF (image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10152795, 1.83 MB, downloads fine) is a page scan with no text layer.
leads.why: Names the algorithm family ARKit actually is, and the people behind it. Two consequences: (1) MSCKF-family estimators are re-implementable from open literature and clean-licence code — OpenVINS is GPL-3 and unusable, but maplab (Apache-2.0) and stella_vslam (BSD-2) are already on our approved list, so if we revisit the back end this is the target, not a GPL system. (2) The binary shows Apple has since moved to a sqrt-form factor graph with Cauchy robust losses and IMU preintegration, i.e. GTSAM-shaped; GTSAM is BSD-3 and would be a clean single authoritative source to replicate in full.

leads.title: Kim et al., "An Empirical Evaluation of Four Off-the-Shelf Proprietary Visual-Inertial Odometry Systems" (ARKit vs ARCore vs T265 vs ZED2)
leads.license: arXiv preprint; companion tool PyojinKim/ios_logger on GitHub
leads.claim: Measured on an iPhone 12 Pro Max running iOS 14.7.1: ARKit "saves the pose estimates as a translation vector and a unit quaternion at 60 Hz". Indoor multi-floor stairwell loop: ARKit final drift error in the xy-plane 0.19 m, vs ARCore 3.98 m (LG V60 ThinQ, 30 Hz), Intel RealSense T265 1.49 m (200 Hz), Stereolabs ZED2 4.76 m (30 Hz, Jetson). Outdoor walking sequences ~145 m and ~84 m; a ~3.1 km vehicular test where only ARKit stayed stable, FDE 2.68 m; ARKit's per-floor height matched the building blueprint. Authors state the core VIO algorithm is the same across iPhone/iPad models and they empirically saw little per-device difference. Data-collection app: https://github.com/PyojinKim/ios_logger
leads.why: The only independent, peer-reviewed measurement I found of ARKit's delivered pose rate (60 Hz, matching our 59.9) and of its drift, giving us a published accuracy bar to state our numbers against. ios_logger is a ready-made ARKit pose/IMU/RGB logger we can run unmodified on the same iPhone 14 Pro to produce an apples-to-apples ARKit baseline trace instead of building our own harness. Note it reports pose OUTPUT rate only — it does not measure how many of those 60 Hz poses were vision-updated, which is exactly the gap WWDC 610 fills.

leads.title: Stack Overflow: "ARKit randomly limits frame rate to 30FPS" — ARKit halves its rate at thermalState .serious/.critical
leads.claim: Reporter (Xcode 10.1 / iOS 12.1) sees ARKit lock to 30 FPS "even when the scene is empty and there are no rendering and background processes happening". Top answer: "It happens when thermal state increases. Go to debug navigator -> click on 'Energy Impact' -> scroll down and check 'Thermal State'. After .serious or .critical state the FPS drop to 30." A second answer attributes it to an iPhone 7/8 iOS 11/12 bug. Question body and both answers were read via api.stackexchange.com (WebFetch is blocked for stackoverflow.com in this session), so opened=false for the human-readable URL.
leads.why: Independent practitioner corroboration, from user-visible behaviour, of the ARKitCore symbol -[ARSession _preferredRenderFrameRateForCaptureFrameRate:isNominalPower:]: ARKit's response to thermal pressure is a 60→30 fps step. Low individual confidence (small thread, low scores) but it agrees exactly with the binary evidence, and it sets a realistic expectation for P2 — even ARKit degrades under sustained thermal load, so our 173 s in 'serious' is the failure, not the 30 fps step itself.

leads.title: WWDC 2022 Session 10131 "Qualities of great AR experiences" — Apple: AR has "a big impact on battery and thermals"
leads.claim: Apple's own AR design guidance, at 11:27: "craft experiences that last no more than a minute or two. This is for the ergonomic reasons I mentioned earlier, but also because AR is a resource-intensive superpower that has a big impact on battery and thermals. If you do end up creating a longer experience, make sure that you build in breaks."
leads.why: Calibrates the P2 target. Apple ships a hardware-accelerated tracker and still tells developers a continuous AR session should be one to two minutes. Our benchmark is a 300 s continuous live run — five times Apple's own recommended session length — so 'ARKit spends 0 s in serious over 300 s' is a very strong bar and possibly not the right product bar. It argues for defining acceptance around a realistic capture-session length plus a documented thermal-backoff ladder, rather than around zero thermal pressure at full rate indefinitely.

leads.title: 揭秘抖音春节爆款 AR 道具背后的"秘密" (Inside Douyin's Spring-Festival AR props)
leads.claim: ByteDance states verbatim that their own large-scene visual SLAM on phones achieves '用户无感的快速初始化': '传统的视觉 SLAM 算法依赖严格的初始化，需要用户进行充分的运动之后才能使用 AR 特效…该方案基于轻量化的多层级初始化设计研发，融合了场景结构先验、多假设的滤波估计和小运动下的全局优化，实现了首帧即时的 AR 体验。' Separately, for the case where init is impossible: '会经常发生由于相机仅有纯旋转或静止不动无法初始化 SLAM 系统…系统引入了深度估计模型，对静止的图像进行相对深度估计并重建出三角网络。待 SLAM 初始化成功后，再对三角网格进行过渡融合。' No fps, ms, device names, or power numbers are given anywhere in the article.
leads.why: This is P4 stated in Chinese by someone who shipped it to hundreds of millions of phones. It confirms our diagnosis is the industry-standard diagnosis — SfM bootstrap needs real translation, and that is exactly the gap between our 3.6 s and ARKit's 1.5 s — and it names the three-part recipe the industry uses to close it: scene structure priors, MULTI-HYPOTHESIS filtered estimation (run several scale/structure hypotheses in parallel instead of waiting for one to become observable), and global optimization under SMALL motion (rather than requiring sufficient parallax). It also shows the fallback everyone uses when the user only rotates: a monocular depth prior to fake geometry until the real init converges, then cross-fade. Caveat and the reason confidence is not higher: this is proprietary and there is no source, no citation, and no measurement — it is a direction-setter and a sanity check on P4, not something we can replicate to source lines. Use it to decide WHICH authoritative open source to go replicate for small-motion / multi-hypothesis init, not as the source itself.
leads.venue: 掘金 (Juejin) — 字节跳动终端技术 official account

leads.title: 原创轻量VIO算法、简单易上手——XRSLAM帮你快速搭建移动平台AR应用 (official XRSLAM launch article, 商汤学术 / SenseTime Academic WeChat account, 2023-01-13)
leads.claim: Upstream's own Chinese launch post says XRSLAM '在 EuRoC 等公开数据集上达到 SOTA 级别的精度，支持普通手机终端 30fps 的实时处理帧率' and, in the performance section, '算法处理效率可以支持 30Fps 以上的数据处理帧率'. It also states '其中特征匹配采用了 OpenCV 的光流来实现', that the core depends only on Eigen / OpenCV / Ceres Solver, that Linux/Mac/Android/iOS are supported but only Linux/Mac and iOS ship a complete build + demo, and that they pre-calibrated recent iOS devices so the AR demo runs out of the box. Accuracy is compared against a locally reproduced VINS-Mono on EuRoC (no closed loop in either).
leads.why: This is the upstream design contract for P1, in upstream's own words: XRSLAM was specified and validated at 30 fps on an ordinary phone, never at 60. So our 28.4 poses/s is not a regression against XRSLAM's spec — it is XRSLAM meeting its spec, and the 59.9 gap to ARKit is a gap against a system built to a different contract. Two consequences. First, before spending more on the 16.7 ms GPU budget we should establish whether upstream's 30 fps is a camera-channel choice or an algorithmic one, because if the tracker itself was tuned for 30 Hz keyframe spacing and IMU pre-integration intervals, doubling the frame rate changes tracker behaviour and is not a lossless speed-up. Second, it confirms the front end we ported (OpenCV optical flow) is the whole visual front end, so our port covers the right surface. NOTE ON THE URL: this CSDN page is the mirror; CSDN article bodies return HTTP 521 to non-browser clients so I could not fetch it, but the CSDN search index returns exactly this title at exactly this URL. I DID read the full original verbatim — the WeChat original by 商汤学术 / OpenXRLab dated 2023-01-13, reached through weixin.sogou.com — and every quote above is from that fetched original, not from the mirror. Open the mirror in a browser, or search 微信 for the title.
leads.venue: 微信公众号 商汤学术 / OpenXRLab (mirrored on CSDN)

leads.title: MNN issue #1984 — Benchmark 使用 Vulkan 运行速度比 CPU 慢
leads.claim: On a RedmiK50G (Snapdragon 8 Gen 1, Adreno 730) the reporter measures MNN's own benchmark: MobileNetV3 CPU 2.23 ms vs Vulkan 22.06 ms; MobileNetV2 CPU 6.01 ms vs Vulkan 17.96 ms; SqueezeNetV1.0 CPU 10.01 ms vs Vulkan 19.46 ms — mobile GPU roughly 3x to 10x SLOWER than the NEON CPU path on a flagship 2022 SoC. The official reference numbers for a much older Xiaomi 6 (Snapdragon 835, Adreno 540) show Vulkan MobileNetV2 at 12.14 ms, i.e. FASTER than the newer flagship. The reporter speculates about needing GPU frequency locking; no maintainer gave a root cause.
leads.why: Negative result, and the kind that saves a week. It is direct Chinese-community evidence that mobile GPU compute performance does NOT track SoC generation and can be catastrophically driver/scheduler-dependent on Adreno — a newer Adreno 730 losing to an older Adreno 540 on the same framework and model. That is the same failure mode as our P1 observation that a 5 ms kernel becomes 19-22 ms once the phone downclocks under camera+GPU load: on mobile, the GPU's delivered throughput is a governor/thermal artefact, not a spec-sheet number. Two takeaways for us: (1) any 16.7 ms budget argument must be made at THROTTLED clocks, never nominal — our own 5 ms figure is the misleading one; (2) since we must ship on Mali and Adreno too, we should expect per-vendor collapses like this and need a CPU/NEON fallback path or a per-device arbitration, not a single GPU-always decision. Caveat: this is DNN inference (many small dispatches, low arithmetic intensity), not CLAHE/Harris on a 1920x1440 image, so it is suggestive rather than conclusive for our kernels.

leads.title: ncnn issue #1674 — 红米note7pro手机上测试GPU模式比CPU模式慢3倍左右，且GPU FP16模式计算错误
leads.claim: On a Redmi Note 7 Pro (Snapdragon 675, Adreno 612) with NCNN_VULKAN and an SSD model: CPU 130+ ms; GPU fp16 300+ ms AND numerically broken (outputs '1.0, 1.0, -Infinity, -Infinity, Infinity, Infinity'); GPU fp32 400+ ms with correct output. So the mobile GPU path is ~2.3x slower than CPU even in its fast (fp16) mode and ~3x slower in the numerically correct (fp32) mode. No maintainer explanation in the thread.
leads.why: Two independent things we care about, in one report from a real phone. First, it is a second data point that mobile-GPU compute loses to NEON on mid-range Android — reinforcing that the Mali/Adreno legs of our port need a fallback, and that 'the GPU is faster' is not a portable assumption. Second, and more specific to our own hard constraint: it is a concrete instance of mobile GPU fp16 producing Inf/NaN where the CPU does not. We require BIT-EXACT parity with OpenCV 4.0.1, and we have already been burned by fp16 precision (the ncnn tanh_ps_f16 saturation bug filed 2026-09-08 in the same repo is the same family). This is evidence that any fp16 shortcut on the Android legs of our WGSL kernels will silently break bit-exactness on some drivers rather than fail loudly — so bit-exactness must be re-verified per vendor, not once on Metal. Caveat: DNN inference, not our kernels; and 2020-era driver.

leads.title: MNN issue #745 — MNN耗时的几个问题：1）实际部署中15s后耗时陡增 2）8bit量化后速度更慢
leads.claim: On a Snapdragon 845 phone: '一开始400帧（约15s）推理速度很快（约7ms），之后稳定提升到10ms' — inference is ~7 ms for the first ~400 frames (~15 s) and then settles at ~10 ms, a ~43% sustained slowdown reached within 15 seconds of continuous load. Also reports that after 8-bit quantization the OpenCL path got SLOWER on the same 845 (10 ms -> 20 ms), i.e. reducing arithmetic did not reduce mobile-GPU time.
leads.why: This is the shape of our P1 problem stated by someone else: the phone gives you nominal clocks for about fifteen seconds and then takes them away, and the steady-state number is the only one that matters. Our 5 ms nominal vs 19-22 ms throttled is a much more violent version of the same curve. Practically it says any A/B we run for the 16.7 ms budget must discard the first ~15-30 s and report the steady-state figure — and it is a caution that our current bench discipline (which already knows about charging and lock-screen effects) should add a warm-up-discard rule. The second half is separately interesting: on mobile GPU, cutting arithmetic (int8) made it slower, which is consistent with these workloads being bound by dispatch/bandwidth rather than ALU — the same conclusion our own binding-size and SPLITBUF experiments reached. NOTE: I read the issue body through api.github.com's search response, not by fetching the HTML page, so opened is false.

leads.title: 干货|详解主流VIO初始化方法 (survey of mainstream VIO initialization methods)
leads.claim: Chinese survey of VIO initialization. Taxonomy: loosely-coupled (VINS-Mono, ORB-SLAM3) vs tightly-coupled (OpenVINS); by solver, filtering / graph-optimization / closed-form. States the core limitation plainly: '大多数现有的初始化方法需要系统静止或已知初始状态。不能适应动态运动、空中初始化。闭合式解法缺乏传感器噪声模型。' Then walks the VINS-Mono pipeline step by step: up-to-scale SfM in a sliding window (five-point on two frames with sufficient parallax, triangulate, PnP the rest, global BA), IMU pre-integration, gyro-bias calibration by minimizing rotation disagreement, then a LINEAR least squares for velocity + gravity direction + scale, then gravity-norm refinement parameterized in the 2-D tangent space via Gram-Schmidt. Notes acc-bias is deliberately NOT calibrated during init because it couples with gravity under small rotation, and that init is only allowed to start '只有在IMU测量中包含足够的激励时' — when the IMU shows enough excitation. No timing numbers, no devices.
leads.why: This is the map of the P4 solution space in Chinese, and reading it makes the licensing trap explicit: every method it names as mainstream — VINS-Mono, ORB-SLAM3, OpenVINS — is GPL, so none of their CODE is copyable for us even though the article describes the method cleanly. Its real value is diagnostic. It says that classic init deliberately GATES on sufficient IMU excitation, which is almost certainly the mechanism behind our 3.6 s: we are not slow, we are waiting on a gate. That reframes P4 from 'make the solver faster' to 'find an authoritative permissive implementation that either removes the excitation gate (small-motion / multi-hypothesis, as ByteDance describes) or emits a provisional pose before the gate opens'. It also tells us where NOT to look for that implementation. Weakness: it is tutorial-grade, carries no measurements and no source-line citations, and is itself a repost from 3D视觉工坊. URL CAVEAT: this is a Sogou-issued time-limited mp.weixin.qq.com link that I fetched and read in full today; it will expire. To re-find it, search 微信 for the exact title 「详解主流VIO初始化方法」 on the 计算机视觉life account.
leads.venue: 微信公众号 计算机视觉life (reposted from 3D视觉工坊)
leads.license: article; the methods it describes live in GPL codebases

leads.title: XRSLAM issue #35 — Localize drift severely when I run phone dataset, what should I do to get right location?
leads.claim: A user runs upstream XRSLAM on the ZJU3DV LSFB phone dataset and reports 'the trajectory drift is very serious', posting the full IMU noise block they used (gyroscope_noise_density 0.01 rad/s/sqrt(Hz), gyroscope_random_walk 4.0e-05, accelerometer_noise_density 0.1 m/s^2/sqrt(Hz), accelerometer_random_walk 0.001, identity q_bi/p_bi extrinsics, cov_g 1.0e-4 diagonal) taken from the dataset author's calibration. Opened 2024-01-02; still open, zero maintainer replies as of today.
leads.why: Relevant as a warning about what upstream will and will not help with. XRSLAM ships pre-calibrated parameters for recent iOS devices (per the official launch article) and appears to work only inside that envelope — the moment a user brings their own phone dataset with their own IMU calibration, they get severe drift and no answer. Since our whole system is XRSLAM on an iPhone 14 Pro with our own capture channel, this is the failure mode adjacent to us: if we change the camera channel to 60 fps for P1, we change the visual/IMU rate ratio and the effective noise assumptions, and there is no upstream support and no upstream tuning guidance to fall back on. It also documents that the OpenXRLab maintainers do not answer performance/tuning issues, so 'ask upstream' is not a plan for P1 or P4.

leads.title: XRSLAM issue #69 — ARDEMO 失效了 (the AR demo's localization module is broken)
leads.claim: Chinese-language issue, opened 2026-01-10, still open with zero replies: '用于在预建场景上运行 XRARDemo 的可视化本地化模块 失效了' — the visual-localization module used to run the XRARDemo against a pre-built scene no longer works. Combined with issue #44 (WebAssembly build for mobile browsers, opened 2024-02-22, unanswered) and #55 (documentation URL inaccessible), the repo's total open-issue count is 13 with essentially no maintainer traffic.
leads.why: Useful as a project-health signal rather than a technique. We have replaced ARKit with upstream rev 4beb1a9 and are carrying a large private GPU port on top of it. This says the upstream is effectively unmaintained for anything beyond building: the shipped AR demo path is broken and unanswered, the docs link is dead, and a request for a browser/WASM build has sat for two years. Two implications. First, we will not be getting upstream fixes for anything we hit in P1-P4, so budget for owning the tracker outright. Second — and this is the one worth acting on — issue #44 confirms there is no upstream WebGPU or browser story at all, which means our Dawn/WGSL front end is entirely our own surface with no upstream to converge with later.

leads.title: 【泡泡机器人成员原创】如何评价苹果在 WWDC 2017 上发布的 ARKit? (PaoPaoRobot SLAM: an AR practitioner's assessment of ARKit)
leads.claim: A working Chinese AR algorithm engineer's read of ARKit at launch: the demo is stable and accurate on a texture-poor desk with a heavy render load, '说明实时性和算法能耗都深度优化过' — real-time behaviour AND algorithmic ENERGY were both deeply optimized; concludes 'ARkit 基本实现了单目+IMU的SLAM算法可以提供的大部分功能' and '我相信苹果是严格检查过机型覆盖率，实时性和能耗的'. Judges the plane fitting to be IMU-driven rather than point-cloud-driven and calls the metric-scale recovery from IMU+vision fusion the genuinely impressive part. Purely qualitative — no fps, ms, mA or temperature numbers.
leads.why: Weak evidence but it is the only Chinese-community source I found that names ARKit's ENERGY behaviour as a deliberate, separately-optimized property rather than a side effect of being fast — which is exactly the shape of P2 (same CPU load as ARKit, 0.80 core-equivalents, yet 173 s in thermalState 'serious' vs ARKit's 0 s). It supports treating the P2 gap as 'ARKit is doing something structurally cheaper', not 'ARKit is doing the same work more efficiently'. Its concrete hypothesis worth testing is that ARKit leans much harder on the IMU and much more lightly on per-frame image work than a VIO built around per-frame detection does. Heavily discounted: it is 2017, it is opinion, the author is inferring from a keynote demo, and there is not a single measurement in it. I include it only because the Chinese community produced nothing better on ARKit energy.
leads.venue: 微信公众号 泡泡机器人SLAM (originally a Zhihu answer)

leads.title: ncnn issue #6612 — 推理速度随着运行时间变慢 (inference gets slower the longer it runs)
leads.claim: Android, CPU-only path (use_vulkan_compute = false, set_cpu_powersave(2), omp threads = big-core count), two models (yolov5 and a yolov8-pose) run serially per frame; the reporter observes inference time degrading steadily over runtime. Opened 2026-03-24, one comment.
leads.why: A third independent Chinese report that sustained load on a phone silently changes your timings, this time on the CPU path with big-core pinning explicitly configured — so it is not a GPU-driver artefact. For us the operational lesson is the same as MNN #745 and reinforces the discipline already in our bench notes (unplug, unlock, alternate A/B arms): any P1 or P2 measurement over a 300 s live run must be reported as a time series, not a mean, because the mean silently mixes a fast first minute with a throttled remainder. Low confidence because the thread has no root cause and no numbers. Body read via api.github.com search, page not fetched.

leads.title: Adéquation algorithme architecture pour flot optique sur GPU embarqué (PhD thesis, Thomas Romera, Sorbonne Université / LIP6, 2023)
leads.claim: TV-L1 and Horn-Schunck optical flow hand-ported to embedded GPUs: fastest version = 0.21 ns per pixel per iteration in half-precision on Nvidia Jetson AGX Xavier, a 22x execution-time reduction vs efficient parallel CPU versions and 5.3x lower energy. Half-precision alone buys x2.2 (TV-L1) and x3.7 (Horn-Schunck) on the best GPU. Target was <40 ms/frame. The two levers that actually paid: high-level OPERATOR FUSION and OPERATOR PIPELINING to maximise data reuse through GPU shared memory; fusing more iterations is capped by shared-memory size, forcing a resource/speed trade-off. Measured on Jetson Xavier, TX2 and Nano.
leads.why: This is the closest EU-language analogue of our P1 problem: an iterative multi-stage image-processing chain on a power-limited GPU, optimised until it fits a per-frame budget. Our CLAHE + pyramid + Scharr + LK chain is exactly the fusible operator chain he describes, and we currently dispatch it as separate passes. His negative-shaped finding is also load-bearing: the win came from fusion/shared memory, NOT from low-level vector instructions alone, and fusion depth is bounded by workgroup memory - which maps directly onto our Mali 256 MB / workgroup-memory constraints. CAVEAT: half-precision is a lossy change, so it violates the bit-exact rule and would have to be an explicit product decision. Numbers are Nvidia-Jetson-only, so they do not transfer to Mali/Adreno/Metal; the fusion principle does. No code released that I could find.
leads.license: HAL author authorisation (thesis text); no source code released

leads.title: Proposition de mécanismes d'optimisation des données pour la perception temps-réel dans un système embarqué hétérogène (PhD thesis, Quentin Picard, CEA List / Univ. Paris-Saclay, 2023)
leads.claim: Two measured contributions on a 10 mW-15 W embedded SLAM budget. (1) Adaptive Filtering (AF): use the IMU's linear and angular accelerations to decide which camera frames enter the SLAM pipeline instead of feeding a constant 20 fps stream - 'the AF allows the decimation of up to 80% of the images while maintaining low localization and reconstruction errors similar to the baseline', and 'in the embedded context, the peak memory consumption is reduced up to 92%'. (2) Pixel dynamic-range reduction: input data can be cut by 75% (to under 2 bits per pixel) 'while maintaining a similar accuracy than the baseline 8 bits per pixel', validated across FOUR different SLAM algorithms on two datasets. Explicit partitioning question across imager-chip / near-sensor FPGA / ARM + embedded GPU.
leads.why: Directly attacks P1, P2 and P3 at once, and it attacks them upstream of the GPU rather than by making the GPU faster. Our detection runs on EVERY frame 'because that is what the upstream tracker does'; this thesis is a measured EU source saying an IMU-gated frame admission policy drops 80% of frames with no accuracy loss - which is exactly the lever that would let a 60 fps camera channel feed a front end that cannot finish in 16.7 ms. The 92% peak-memory reduction is the only concrete P3 lever I found in this literature. Weakness for us: no released implementation and no source-line-citable code, so under our 'replicate one authoritative source in full' rule this is EVIDENCE and a design argument, not something we can copy. The thesis PDF body is behind an Anubis bot-wall; the numbers above are verbatim from the HAL abstract record.
leads.venue: Université Paris-Saclay / CEA List, HAL tel-04426263
leads.license: HAL author authorisation; no source code found

leads.title: Basalt VIO front end - frame_to_frame_optical_flow.h and keypoints.cpp (Usenko, Demmel, Schubert, Stückler, Cremers - TU München)
leads.claim: BSD 3-Clause. detectKeypoints() divides the image into a grid and SKIPS every cell that already holds a tracked point: 'if (cells((y - y_start) / PATCH_SIZE, (x - x_start) / PATCH_SIZE) > 0) continue;'. Detector is cv::FAST with an adaptive threshold starting at 40 and halved down to 5 until num_points_cell is met in that cell. EuRoC config values: optical_flow_detection_grid_size = 50 (px), optical_flow_levels = 3, optical_flow_max_iterations = 5, optical_flow_pattern = 51, vio_new_kf_keypoints_thresh = 0.7. Tracking is pyramidal patch tracking with SE(2) warp increments (transform *= SE2::exp(inc).matrix()), coarse-to-fine, plus forward-backward bidirectional validation with optical_flow_max_recovered_dist2 = 0.04. Verified negative detail: optical_flow_skip_frames does NOT skip tracking work - it only gates the output queue ('if (output_queue && frame_counter % config.optical_flow_skip_frames == 0) output_queue->push(transforms);').
leads.why: This is a permissively-licensed (BSD-3), citable-to-source-line, authoritative front end from a top German lab that answers P1 without changing the algorithm's semantics: detection cost becomes proportional to the number of EMPTY 50x50 grid cells rather than to the whole frame. That is a much cheaper structural change than making our goodFeaturesToTrack shader faster, and unlike a bit-exact GPU optimisation it is copyable wholesale under our 'replicate one source in full' rule. The skip_frames finding is a caution: do not cite Basalt as precedent for skipping front-end work per frame - it does not.
leads.venue: TU München (Computer Vision Group), GitHub mirror of gitlab.com/VladyslavUsenko/basalt

leads.title: ORB-SLAM3 (Campos, Elvira, Gómez Rodríguez, Montiel, Tardós - Universidad de Zaragoza) - IMU initialisation section
leads.claim: Verbatim from the paper: 'Our exhaustive initialization experiments on the EuRoC dataset show that this initialization is very efficient, achieving 5% scale error with trajectories of 2 seconds. To improve the initial estimation, visual-inertial BA is performed 5 and 15 seconds after initialization, converging to 1% scale error'. Comparison numbers given in the same paragraph: ORB-SLAM-VI 'needed 15 seconds to get the first scale estimation'; VI-DSO 'starts with a huge scale error and requires 20-30 seconds to converge to 1% error'. Separately: the system declares visual tracking lost when fewer than 15 map points are tracked. The standalone method is Campos/Montiel/Tardós, 'Inertial-Only Optimization for Visual-Inertial Initialization', ICRA 2020, arXiv 2003.05766, which reports initialization in under 4 s with 5.3% average scale error on EuRoC.
leads.why: The hard anchor for P4. It says the state of the art for a monocular-inertial SfM bootstrap that recovers metric scale is 2 s to a 5%-scale map and 15 s to 1% - i.e. our 3.6 s is already in the normal band, and 'ARKit's 1.5 s' is not a like-for-like comparison because ARKit does not need a converged metric scale to emit its first pose. That reframes P4 from 'our bootstrap is slow' to 'we are gating pose output on scale convergence and ARKit is not'. Zaragoza's split - inertial-only MAP estimate first, then joint VI-BA refinements at 5 s and 15 s - is the structure to copy if we want early poses that improve later. HARD BLOCKER: ORB-SLAM3 is GPLv3, so the code is untouchable for us; the method is described in the paper and the ICRA 2020 paper, and would have to be re-implemented from the text, which conflicts with our 'cite to source lines' rule.
leads.license: Paper open; ORB-SLAM3 code is GPLv3 - UNUSABLE for copying

leads.title: Interactive computer vision through the Web / Vision par ordinateur interactive sur le Web (PhD thesis, Matthieu Pizenberg, Université de Toulouse, 2020) + visual-odometry-rs
leads.claim: Second half of the thesis is an open-source DIRECT visual odometry library written from scratch in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly so that camera tracking runs inside the browser; the thesis explicitly 'review[s] past and present technologies enabling high performance computations on the Web' and details targeting WebAssembly from C++ and Rust. He states the VO problem 'traditionally requir[es] much processing power to perform at realtime framerates' and that the goal is 25 images per second in the browser. The companion repo github.com/mpizenberg/visual-odometry-rs is MPL-2.0, implements direct RGB-D tracking (gradients, candidate-point selection, SO(3)/SE(3) Lie algebra); its README lists 'Porting to the web with WebAssembly' as planned and reports NO ms/frame or fps numbers.
leads.why: This is the only academic precedent I found in any of my four languages for the cross-cutting question 'has anyone driven a real VO/SLAM front end through web technology on a device'. The answer is: yes, but via WebAssembly on the CPU, not WebGPU compute - and it was a browser-interaction thesis, not a phone-performance one, with no published latency numbers. That makes our bit-exact WGSL/Dawn OpenCV front end look genuinely unprecedented rather than a reinvention. LICENSE FLAG: MPL-2.0 is weak copyleft (file-level), which is outside the Apache/BSD/MIT bar you set, so the code cannot be copied under our current rule even though it is 'open source'.
leads.venue: Université de Toulouse / IRIT, HAL tel-04164773
leads.license: Thesis: HAL authorisation. Code (visual-odometry-rs): MPL-2.0 - weak copyleft, outside your permissive bar

leads.title: GitHub survey (negative result): no WebGPU/WGSL classical SLAM or visual-odometry front end exists
leads.claim: GitHub repository search for 'webgpu SLAM' OR 'webgpu "visual odometry"' returns total_count = 0. Search for 'webgpu computer vision' returns 7 repositories, all of them browser ML demos (Transformers.js, ONNX Runtime Web, YOLO, background removal, eyeglass detection); highest star count among them is 2. None is a classical feature-detection / optical-flow front end, none targets a phone, none is a SLAM component.
leads.why: Direct evidence on the cross-cutting question: nobody has published a WebGPU port of an OpenCV-style SLAM front end. That is worth knowing in both directions - there is no prior art to copy from and no community to ask, but equally no credible published failure saying it cannot work. It also means every WGSL kernel we write is one we own end to end, and the absence of comparable projects explains why our Dawn/vendorId and Mali binding-size discoveries had to be found the hard way.

leads.title: Adéquation Algorithme Architecture pour la localisation temps réel basée sur la fusion de données issues de l'odométrie visuelle et des mesures inertielles (PhD thesis, Ayoub Mamri, 2025)
leads.claim: After surveying VI-SLAM systems the author concludes, verbatim: the analysis 'led us to focus on the front-end of this type of system, specifically image pre-processing, as a critical part in terms of precision and extensive computation to match the sensor frequency as closely as possible'. He then builds corner + line-segment detection and tracking on a proposed multi-level contour detector, and explicitly 'planned for parallel tasks and independent scheduling between different blocks at the design phase' to map onto a heterogeneous embedded architecture using GPU and FPGA accelerators (CPU-GPU and CPU-FPGA implementations), with an EKF observer fusing visual and inertial data.
leads.why: An independent 2025 EU thesis that reached the same diagnosis we did - the VI-SLAM front end's image pre-processing is the thing that fails to keep up with the camera frequency - and answers it with task-level parallelism and independent per-block scheduling rather than by making one kernel faster. That is the structural alternative to our current 'GPU must finish CLAHE + detection inside 16.7 ms' framing: decouple detection from tracking into independently scheduled blocks so the pose channel is not gated on the slowest block. The abstract gives no latency numbers and the PDF body is behind the HAL bot-wall, so treat as design evidence, not measurement.
leads.license: HAL author authorisation; no code found

leads.title: Algorithmes SLAM : Vers une implémentation embarquée (PhD thesis, Mohamed Abouzahir, Université Paris-Saclay, 2017)
leads.claim: Four structurally different SLAM algorithms (FastSLAM2.0, ORB-SLAM, RatSLAM, linear SLAM) were benchmarked on several embedded architectures for portability under low power and limited resources, comparing execution time AND consistency of localisation. FastSLAM2.0 was selected on the time/consistency trade-off; after algorithmic rewriting and CPU-GPU partitioning it achieved 'an overall acceleration factor of about 22 ... on a recent dedicated architecture for embedded systems'. A second FPGA (HLS) implementation was then compared against GPU versions and the gains were 'consequent, even compared to high-end GPUs with a large number of cores'.
leads.why: Useful as a methodology precedent and a caution. The x22 came from PARTITIONING the algorithm across CPU and GPU, not from optimising a single kernel - the same conclusion Romera reaches from a different direction. The FPGA-beats-high-end-GPU result is the closest thing in this literature to a negative result about GPUs for SLAM front ends: for irregular, low-arithmetic-intensity SLAM work, throughput hardware is not automatically the right home. Relevant to our P1 decision of what actually belongs on the GPU vs the CPU/NEON path. No phone measurements, no released code.
leads.license: HAL author authorisation; no code found

leads.title: Multiple Target Detection and Tracking with Guaranteed Framerates on Mobile Phones (Wagner, Schmalstieg, Bischof - TU Graz) and Real-Time Detection and Tracking for Augmented Reality on Mobile Phones (Wagner, Reitmayr, Mulloni, Drummond, Schmalstieg)
leads.claim: TU Graz ISMAR 2009 paper whose stated goal is guaranteeing a frame rate on mobile phones by controlling how detection is scheduled against tracking; companion TVCG paper (DOI 10.1109/tvcg.2009.99, 2009, ~427 citations for the ISMAR-2008 predecessor 'Pose tracking from natural features on mobile phones') is the canonical mobile-phone natural-feature tracking line from Schmalstieg's group. OpenAlex reports NO open-access location for either paper, so I could not read the bodies and have no extracted numbers.
leads.why: This is the German-speaking lab (TU Graz / later Metaio in Munich, whose technology Apple acquired in 2015 and which fed into ARKit) that solved P1's exact framing - 'guaranteed framerates' on a phone - by scheduling detection rather than by speeding up a kernel. If any single source in my language set holds the answer to 'what does ARKit do that we do not' for the detect-every-frame question, it is this lineage. Flagged as unread: both papers are paywalled IEEE with no OA copy found, so another angle with library access should pull the detection-scheduling policy and its measured frame budgets.

leads.title: Couplage de centrales inertielles et de solutions d'odométrie visuelle pour la navigation bas coût, précise et robuste (PhD thesis, Gaëtan Chevrin, ISL Saint-Louis franco-allemand, 2023)
leads.claim: Compares two loose-coupling architectures on KITTI for a visual dead-reckoning front end plus IMU: an Error-State Kalman Filter and an MSF-EKF (Multi-Sensor Fusion EKF). The ESKF 'has a satisfactory visual odometry tracking capacity and manages to be able to ensure navigation when the [visual front end] is in degraded operation, SIMULATED BY UNDERSAMPLING', but its inertial dead reckoning drifts and degrades the fusion. The MSF-EKF gave 'a significant improvement in fusion accuracy' plus robustness, 'with a filter that can provide weakly degraded navigation during several seconds of vision cutoff'.
leads.why: The one EU source I found that explicitly experiments with the visual front end running SLOWER than the sensor (undersampling as a degraded mode) and asks what filter carries the pose stream through the gap. That is precisely the P1 escape hatch: if our GPU front end can only sustain ~28 Hz under thermal downclock, the question becomes which coupling lets the IMU carry pose output at 60 Hz without back-pressure collapsing latency. ETH's maplab-adjacent MSF (ethzasl_msf) is the permissively-licensed implementation family this points at. Caveat: automotive KITTI, not a handheld phone, and no code released with the thesis.
leads.venue: Institut franco-allemand de recherches de Saint-Louis (ISL), HAL tel-04573044
leads.license: HAL author authorisation; no code found

leads.title: Application d'une méthodologie de co-design à la définition et à l'implémentation d'une chaîne SLAM opérationnelle (PhD thesis, François Brenot, LAAS-CNRS Toulouse, 2016)
leads.claim: Verbatim: 'The perception step leads to an important computational load which affects very significantly the system latency and throughput.' Builds a complete 3D EKF-SLAM chain by co-design on a Xilinx ZynQ (dual-core CPU + configurable fabric) with a Hardware-in-the-Loop validation architecture, and adds dedicated hardware modules to accelerate feature detection, description and matching.
leads.why: Confirms independently, from a different French lab, that the interest-point perception stage - not the estimator - is what sets latency and throughput in a real-time SLAM chain, which is our P1 in one sentence. The Hardware-in-the-Loop methodology (validate each design iteration against a fixed replay harness before committing) is a direct analogue of the bench/replay discipline you already run, and is worth citing when arguing for a gate. Implementation is FPGA, so the accelerator details do not transfer to Metal/Mali/Adreno.
leads.venue: LAAS-CNRS / Université de Toulouse, HAL tel-04259513
leads.license: HAL author authorisation; no code found

leads.title: Image Processing on Mobile Devices: An Overview (Thabet, Mahmoudi, Bedoui, 2014)
leads.claim: Review of serial and parallel approaches to image processing on low-power mobile devices, explicitly framed around 'the emergence of general-purpose computing on embedded GPUs and their programming models like OpenGL ES 2.0 and OpenCL', with augmented reality and visual search named as the driving contexts. I obtained the full abstract via the HAL API but the PDF body is behind an Anubis bot-wall, so I have NO extracted speedup, slowdown or energy numbers from it.
leads.why: Listed because it is the only survey I found in my language set that is specifically about GPGPU on PHONE GPUs (not Jetson), which is where a credible 'mobile GPU loses to NEON' negative result would live. Someone with a working PDF path should pull its comparison tables before we assume the mobile-GPU-wins result from the Jetson literature transfers to Mali/Adreno/Apple GPUs. Treat as a pointer, not as evidence yet.

leads.title: Reconstrução tridimensional em tempo real a partir de um dispositivo móvel (MSc thesis, Rui Pedro Lacerda Saraiva, Universidade do Minho, 2019)
leads.claim: Portuguese-language master's dissertation (advisor Gil Lopes) on real-time 3D reconstruction from a mobile device.
