I opened the repository landing page successfully; it exposes only title/author/advisor and a 15.46 MB PDF link - no abstract, no fps/ms figures, no device model and no GPU API were visible without downloading the full PDF.
leads.why: Included only to record that it exists and is the single Portuguese-language hit in the whole search that is on-topic for on-device real-time 3D from a phone. Low expected value - a 2019 MSc thesis is unlikely to beat what you already have - but it is the one PT lead worth a PDF download if someone wants completeness on the Lusophone literature.

leads.title: open_vins issue #137 — "Running OpenVINS GPU-accelerated?"
leads.license: GPL-3.0 (repo) — evidence only, do not copy code
leads.claim: OpenVINS maintainer Patrick Geneva (goldbattle), 2021-01-31: "I looked at using the OpenCV GPU accelerated *descriptor* matching but only saw a very marginal speed up x1.5 on a Jetson Nano. Additionally this was only the case when the amount of features were in the 2 thousands and I saw that actually on the resource constrained systems the OpenCV GPU accelerated descriptor extraction and matching HURT frontend performance. On a 1080ti, there was usually greater then x2 speedup even for 100s of features." He also states the front-end feature tracking is where the majority of time goes on resource-constrained systems, and points to uzh-rpg/vilib as the thing that actually works ("< 3ms on average for both extraction and tracking every frame").
leads.why: This is the single clearest NEGATIVE result from an authoritative VIO maintainer on exactly our thesis: GPU-offloading an OpenCV front end wins on a discrete GPU and LOSES on a constrained mobile-class device. It matches our P1/P2 symptom shape (5 ms nominal, 19-22 ms downclocked). It also names the one project that beat CPU on embedded hardware (vilib, CUDA-only) and confirms the estimator side is NOT where the time is — so our decision to port the front end was right, but the device-class caveat was published five years ago and we should have priced it.

leads.title: vilib issue #6 — "OpenCV parameter compatibility" (author states they never conformity-tested against calcOpticalFlowPyrLK)
leads.venue: uzh-rpg/vilib (UZH Robotics & Perception Group, "Faster than FAST")
leads.license: BSD-3-Clause (verified: LICENSE.txt, Copyright 2019-2020 Balazs Nagy, RPG UZH) — PERMISSIVE, copyable
leads.claim: Author Balazs Nagy, 2020-05-21, answering whether their GPU KLT tracker matches OpenCV: "for the feature tracker, we did not perform conformity tests, apart from the tests we performed to measure its runtime." He enumerates exactly why GPU LK diverges from OpenCV: "employed pyramid levels, termination criteria, window size, interpolation/no interpolation of the template patch, non-associativity of floating point operations, floating-point precision." He contrasts this with FAST, which he calls "a really well-defined algorithm (bonus, it is based on integer operations), for which we could easily come up with a comparison framework."
leads.why: This is the closest prior art to what we built and it is a direct statement that the state of the art did NOT attempt what we did. The best-known GPU VIO front end in the field shipped without bit-exact parity and said so. Two consequences: (1) our bit-exactness is genuinely novel in this community, not a re-tread; (2) his integer-vs-float observation is the mechanism — FAST is bit-exactable because it is integer, LK is not, which is why our pyrLK replica is the expensive part. vilib is BSD-3-Clause so its CUDA kernels ARE legally copyable as an algorithm reference for the GPU decomposition (not the API).

leads.title: vilib issue #16 — "test_vilib results - Jetson Nano vs TX2" (GPU-vs-CPU per-stage microbenchmarks)
leads.claim: Jetson TX2, MaxN power mode, EuRoC MH1, posted by RPG coauthor foehnx 2021-06-25: Harris detector CPU avg 16018 us vs GPU avg 1732.39 us (9.2x); FAST CPU 9736.55 us vs GPU 1220.09 us (8.0x); image pyramid CPU 190.65 us vs GPU-device 79.33 us; feature tracker GPU 878.54 us avg. On the WEAKER Jetson Nano (same test, brendanlb 2020-10-13): image pyramid CPU 265.69 us vs GPU-device 290.04 us — the GPU is SLOWER than the CPU for the pyramid stage; FAST CPU 13537.4 us vs GPU 8008.92 us (only 1.7x, versus 8.0x on TX2). Also note the CPU detector found 4671 features vs the GPU's 316 — not the same output.
leads.why: Per-stage numbers on two device classes, which is exactly the axis P1/P2 live on. The pyramid — cheap, memory-bound, exactly like our CLAHE+pyramid stage — is the stage that flips to a LOSS first when the device gets weaker. That is the same failure mode as our 5 ms -> 19-22 ms downclock collapse. It argues for keeping the pyramid on CPU/NEON and putting only the arithmetic-dense corner response on GPU, rather than moving the whole chain. Also a caution: their GPU/CPU feature counts differ by 15x, so their 'speedups' are not like-for-like.

leads.title: opencv PR #29450 — "Feat: add OpenCL SIFT detector and descriptor" (merged 2026-07-06), integrated-GPU perf table
leads.claim: OpenCV maintainer asmorkalov's own CI numbers, 2026-07-15. Discrete GPU (GeForce 2080 Ti vs Ryzen 2700x): Compute::OCL_SIFTOclFixture 640x480 = 19.992 ms CPU vs 8.805 ms GPU (2.27x); 1280x720 = 63.616 vs 16.817 (3.78x); 1920x1080 = 127.852 vs 31.402 (4.07x). INTEGRATED GPU (Intel Core i5-1135G7 igfx): 640x480 = 32.683 CPU vs 27.151 GPU (1.20x); 1280x720 = 108.696 vs 110.451 (0.98x); 1920x1080 = 256.809 vs 258.808 (0.99x). The FIRST version of the kernel measured 0.16-0.17x (6x SLOWER than CPU); the author diagnosed it as one work-item per keypoint with hist[360] in private memory = 1440 bytes of registers per work-item, capping occupancy at ~12%, leaving most SMs idle.
leads.why: The most recent (two months ago) authoritative measurement of GPU-vs-CPU feature detection, from the OpenCV maintainers, with an integrated-GPU column. On an integrated GPU the fully-optimised GPU detector is a WASH at 720p and 1080p — which is the device class our iPhone GPU behaves like once it downclocks. It is a strong prior that P1 cannot be solved by making our detector kernel faster, and points at frame-rate decoupling (detect every Nth frame) instead. Second, the register-pressure/occupancy diagnosis is a concrete, transferable audit item for our own WGSL kernels — we should check private-array sizes per invocation before assuming the kernel is bandwidth-bound.

leads.title: opencv issue #11408 — "Arm: fix the test failure of OCL_Imgproc/CLAHETest.Accuracy on ODROID-XU4" (race condition in clahe.cl)
leads.claim: Reporter tomoaki0705 on Ubuntu 16.04 ARM ODROID-XU4 + Mali-T628, OpenCV 3.4.1-dev: OCL_Imgproc/CLAHETest.Accuracy/18 and /19 (params 8x64, clipLimit 10) fail NON-DETERMINISTICALLY — the same binary passed on a rerun. "I could figure out that the result from GPU was varying, when the CPU version kept still." Root cause: a race condition in the reduction in modules/imgproc/src/opencl/clahe.cl (lines 134-137), where the barrier was inside a WAVE_SIZE-conditional #if. The failure did NOT reproduce on other Mali parts (Tinker Board, Firefly RK3399 / Mali-T860). Fixed by commit 87a4f4ab3afc1eaed05480f16bbae570a3d33254 (PR #11409).
leads.why: This is our exact algorithm (CLAHE), our exact claim (bit-exact GPU vs CPU), on our exact hardware class (ARM mobile GPU), and it failed — silently, intermittently, and only on one vendor part. Two actions: (1) audit our WGSL CLAHE histogram reduction for the same implicit-wave-width assumption (WGSL has no wave-size guarantee at all, so a subgroup-width assumption there is worse than in OpenCL); (2) treat 'passes on Apple, therefore bit-exact' as unproven for Mali/Adreno — the OpenCV precedent is that one Mali part fails while another passes. Note OpenCV 4.0.1 (our reference) already contains this fix, so the CPU/OCL reference we replicated is the post-fix one.

leads.title: opencv issue #15932 (Mali-T860 T-API slower than CPU) and #25871 (Mali-G310, maintainer: OpenCL was built for desktop GPUs)
leads.claim: #25871 (2024-07, Mali-G310 r0p0, OpenCV 4.10.0, 32 kB local memory, max work group 512): user reports cvtColor and friends under OpenCL are slower than CPU; OpenCV maintainer asmorkalov replies "OpenCL code was mostly developed for desktop GPUs (Intel, AMD, NVIDIA). It may be less efficient with mobile chips." #15932 (2019-11, Firefly RK3399 / Mali-T860, OpenCV 3.3.1, cvtColor+GaussianBlur+Canny on lena.jpg through UMat): "Using the cv::UMat data structure I cant have faster result in any program that I write" — confirmed still reproducing on OpenCV 4.5.5 by a second user in 2022. Related: #20696 measures UMat->Mat readback at ~7 ms for 720p vs ~1.5 ms for Mat->UMat, and 5 ms (Intel) / 14 ms (NVIDIA) in other reports.
leads.why: Two independent Mali parts, five years apart, with an OpenCV maintainer confirming the general finding: the standard OpenCV GPU path loses to the CPU on ARM mobile GPUs for cheap per-pixel filters. Our WGSL port is not OpenCV's OCL code, but the underlying constraint (small mobile GPU, dispatch and readback overheads dominating cheap kernels) is the same, and it is a direct warning for the Mali/Adreno half of our cross-platform requirement — where we have not yet measured. The readback asymmetry in #20696 is worth an explicit measurement in our pipeline: if our keypoint readback is the hidden cost, that is a different fix than making the kernel faster.

leads.title: xrslam XRSLAMManager::PushImage does two full-resolution cv::Mat clones per frame (found via issue #63)
leads.license: Apache-2.0 — copyable, and it is our own dependency
leads.claim: I read xrslam-interface/src/XRSLAMManager.cpp at rev 4beb1a9 (current main). PushImage() at line 104: for channel==1 it does `opencv_image->image = img.clone()` (line 116) AND THEN `opencv_image->raw = img.clone()` (line 131) — two full-resolution copies of every frame. For channel==3/4 it does a cvtColor into ->image and still clones the full colour source into ->raw. At our 1920x1440 that is ~2.76 MB (gray) or ~11.1 MB (BGRA) of allocate+memcpy per frame, ~83-332 MB/s of heap churn at 30 fps, before any tracking work happens. Separately, in issue #63 a user reports that the iOS path delivers channel = 3 by default ("未修改前控制台输出 image-->channel = 3") and had to force image.channel = 1, and independently fingered this same `opencv_image->raw = img.clone()` line as the locus of an iOS bug.
leads.why: A concrete, unexplored candidate for BOTH P2 (173 s in thermalState serious with CPU load equal to ARKit's — 'the extra energy is going somewhere else') and P3 (276 MB vs 266 MB). Two per-frame full-res clones are pure DRAM traffic, which is exactly the kind of load that costs power without showing up as core-equivalents. `raw` is only needed for visualisation; if our build does not consume it, the second clone is free to delete, and the first can become a no-copy cv::Mat wrapper over the pixel buffer. This is inside our own dependency at our own pinned rev, Apache-2.0, and verifiable on the host without a device.

leads.title: xrslam PR #70 / issue #63 — iOS pose-convention regression, and maintainer's warning that post-632b72d commits skipped iOS adaptation
leads.claim: Our pinned rev 4beb1a9 IS the merge commit of PR #70 (dated 2026-02-10, and it is currently main HEAD) — I confirmed via the commits API. PR #70's diagnosis: between 632b72d and main, XRSLAM_RESULT_CAMERA_POSE changed meaning and started composing camera_to_body_rotation/translation (XRSLAMManager.cpp:168), while xrslam-ios/visualizer/configs/slam_params.yaml still had output.q_bo/p_bo set to the camera extrinsic — so the camera extrinsic was applied TWICE, making placed AR objects slide opposite to device motion. Fixed by setting output.q_bo to identity and p_bo to zero. Separately, in issue #63 (2025-09-06) maintainer panxkun writes: "因为后续的代码更新忽略了 ios 上的同步适配，可能引入了一些未知的 bug" (later code updates neglected the iOS synchronisation adaptation and may have introduced unknown bugs) and recommends falling back to 632b72d as the last known-good iOS commit. PR #70 also added an iPhone 16e sensor config.
leads.why: Directly load-bearing for us because 4beb1a9 is precisely our rev. Good news: we already have the double-extrinsic fix. Bad news: the maintainer's statement is that iOS-side synchronisation adaptation was skipped across the whole post-632b72d range and PR #70 only fixed the one bug its author tripped over — so other iOS-only defects in that range are unaudited by upstream, which is a live hypothesis for P4 (3.6 s to first pose) and for any pose-quality anomaly we see. Concretely worth diffing 632b72d..4beb1a9 for anything touching the iOS feed ordering and timestamping.

leads.title: gpuweb issue #1202 — "Out-of-bounds clamping brings big perf regression" (robust buffer access, and Dawn's toggle to disable it)
leads.claim: TFJS team measured a 1024x1024 matmul in WebGPU with robust buffer access (RBA) on vs off via Chrome's `--disable-dawn-robustness`: macOS Radeon Pro 555X 6.594 -> 5.454 ms; macOS Intel Iris Plus (ICL) 8.022 -> 5.137 ms (36% faster); Windows UHD630 (CFL) 36.98 -> 21.807 ms (41% faster); NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti 0.626 -> 0.468 ms. Summary in the issue: "17%~40% perf regressions on different GPUs ... specially on integrated GPUs." RBA is implemented by inserting clamp() around every array index, including storage-buffer, workgroup-shared and local-array accesses. Dawn maintainer Kangz: "a 20-40% perf regression for sandboxing is quite big."
leads.why: We embed Dawn natively rather than running in a browser sandbox, so the RBA toggle is ours to set — and unlike almost every other speed-up available to us, disabling it is BIT-IDENTICAL for any shader that never indexes out of bounds (clamping only changes behaviour on accesses that are already bugs). The measured win is largest exactly on integrated GPUs, which is our device class. If our WGSL kernels are index-heavy (pyramid taps, LK window gathers, histogram bins all are), this is a plausible double-digit percent on P1 for a one-line Dawn instance change, and it is testable on the Mac bench first. Caveat: must be paired with a positive control proving the toggle actually took effect, and an out-of-bounds audit of every kernel before shipping.

leads.title: gpuweb issue #4995 — "Create timestamp-query2 for tiled architectures" (GPU timing is unreliable on Apple TBDR and ARM)
leads.claim: greggman posted 9 render passes with monotonically varying instance counts. On Windows/NVIDIA the per-pass timestamps track the work (66 us for 2 instances, 3867 us for 2973). On an M1 Mac the LAST pass reports the most time regardless of its work (11010 us for 1 instance), i.e. passes are being merged and the timings are meaningless. Apple's WebGPU engineer mwyrzykowski: "There is no guarantee on TBDR at least Apple's GPUs that the pass 1 completes before pass N, pass N may complete first." From the GPU Web WG minutes 2024-12-04 quoted in-thread: "To make timestamps make sense on ARM, only way to do it is with full pipeline barriers between every pass" and the suggested workaround is "wait for GPU idle, then submit only that work, and time it. Slow but gives results." IMPORTANT CAVEAT IN OUR FAVOUR: the reporter states that with COMPUTE passes, timestamp-query behaves as expected on the same devices.
leads.why: Methodological, and it bites us specifically because our whole optimisation practice is per-stage GPU segment accounting on Apple and Mali. This is the authoritative statement of when those numbers are lies. The useful part is the compute-pass carve-out: our pipeline is all compute, so our per-dispatch timings are probably sound — but that is now something to positively verify (a known-heavier dispatch must report a larger number) rather than assume, and the WG's serialise-and-time recipe is the fallback when a segment account looks impossible.

leads.title: VINS-Mobile issue #93 — HKUST author states 30 Hz is the ceiling for both the iPhone camera and VINS itself
leads.claim: PeiliangLi (VINS-Mobile author), 2017-10-26: "It's determined by Apple API. According to my test, the max frequency of raw image is 30 HZ. And the max frequency which vins can process in real-time is also 30 HZ." Related in the same repo: #85, marginalization takes >500 ms on Snapdragon 820 versus the 60 ms on iPhone 7 Plus claimed in the paper; #98/#136 confirm the shipped pipeline runs 640x480 (portrait 480x640) and that users feeding 1920x1080 must resize AND recalibrate intrinsics; #100 shows FAIL_SFM/FAIL_COST/FAIL_ALIGN at bootstrap disappearing when the build switches from Debug to Release/-O2.
leads.why: Reframes P1. The reference monocular VIO systems on iPhone are all 30 Hz visual-update systems, and ARKit's 59.9 poses/s is almost certainly not 60 visual updates/s — it is IMU propagation to display rate on top of a lower-rate visual update. If so, the right target is not 'run CLAHE+detection in 16.7 ms' but 'propagate poses at 60 Hz from a 30 Hz visual backbone', which makes P1 an output-path problem rather than a GPU-throughput problem and sidesteps the thermal wall in P2 entirely. Also #100 is a warning shot for our bit-exactness: on this codebase the compiler optimisation level alone decided whether the SfM bootstrap converged.

leads.title: open_vins issue #164 — "Decrease time delay/computation time of outputs" (embedded VIO latency budget, and downsampling made it WORSE)
leads.claim: User on Jetson Xavier NX, T265 stereo at 848x800/30 fps, reports ~270 ms end-to-end pose latency at only ~40% CPU. Maintainer WoosikLee2510: at 30 fps you must process under 33 ms, "Even if you drop 2/3 of the measurements, you still have 100 ms which seems not feasible in your current setup." goldbattle: "We have been able to out of the box run on the Jetson Nano ... at 28-30fps." Crucially, when the user enabled OpenVINS's `downsample_cameras` option the result was NEGATIVE: "I noticed when using the downsampling that the execution time is significantly higher (about 100ms higher)." Recompiling OpenCV and OpenVINS with -O3 and -march for the target arch gave only a small improvement. Also relevant: goldbattle notes the odometry topic IMU-propagates from the latest state to the most recent IMU sample specifically "to facilitate low latency estimation", separate from the (more accurate) pose topic.
leads.why: Two things. First, the IMU-propagated low-latency output topic is the same architectural answer to P1 that VINS-Mobile #93 implies: decouple pose OUTPUT rate from visual UPDATE rate. That is the cheapest possible fix for 28.4 -> 60 poses/s and it costs no GPU work at all. Second, the downsampling result is a documented negative: reducing input resolution to save front-end time made the total 100 ms WORSE in a real deployment, which is a caution against the obvious 'just drop to 960x720' response to P1/P2 before we measure where the time actually goes.

leads.title: opencv PR #29273 — "Extended spatialGradient API and applied to different detector algorithms" (fused Sobel2D inside goodFeaturesToTrack/cornerHarris), merged 2026-06
leads.license: Apache-2.0 — copyable, contributor explicitly affirms not GPL-derived
leads.claim: Merged upstream 2026-06-09: "Add a public Sobel2D API computing dx/dy in a single fused pass with 3x3 and 5x5 kernels (SIMD-dispatched). The float (CV_32F) path folds the output scale and float store into the kernel, avoiding a separate convertTo pass." Integrated into cornerEigenValsVecs — which backs cornerHarris, cornerMinEigenVal, cornerEigenValsAndVecs AND goodFeaturesToTrack — plus Canny, HoughCircles, GeneralizedHough, IntelligentScissors. Perf and accuracy tests added; maintainer asmorkalov reviewed and asked for it to be folded into the existing spatialGradient rather than a new API. Related follow-up PR #29801 "fused spatialGradient + dispatched SIMD Canny" (merged 2026-08).
leads.why: An authoritative, permissively licensed, upstream-MERGED restructuring of exactly the stage we ported: the dx/dy derivative pass feeding Harris/goodFeaturesToTrack, fused into one pass with the scale and the float store folded in. That is a directly transferable shape for our WGSL — one dispatch instead of separate Scharr-dx, Scharr-dy and convert passes, which cuts both dispatch count and the intermediate buffer traffic that #4995-style tiled GPUs are most sensitive to. It satisfies our replicate-one-source rule (cite to OpenCV source lines) rather than being an invented fusion. Two caveats to check before adopting: whether the fused path is bit-identical to the two-pass path we replicated, and that it postdates our 4.0.1 reference so it is a deliberate reference bump, not a silent one.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums – "Slow performance on iPhone 12/Pro/Max when copying pixel data from metal texture"
leads.claim: MTLTexture.getBytes() on a 1920x1440 texture takes 40-50 ms on iPhone 12 Pro Max, vs ~5 ms for a 1242x2688 texture on iPhone Xs Max and 3 ms for 2388x1668 on iPad Pro (8-20x regression). An Apple Graphics & Games engineer states the cause is lossless GPU texture compression on newer Apple silicon: the CPU must decompress on read-back. Three fixes given: (1) blit the texture into an MTLBuffer with an MTLBlitCommandEncoder and read buffer.contents (recommended, pool the buffers), (2) blitEncoder.optimizeContentsForCPUAccess(texture) before getBytes, (3) set MTLTextureDescriptor.allowGPUOptimizedContents = false at creation. Drawable textures are worse still (50 ms vs 5 ms on 12 Pro Max). Reference implementation: github.com/noah-z/SolvingSlowPerformanceOfGetBytes
leads.why: This is your exact resolution (1920x1440) on an Apple GPU one generation before your iPhone 14 Pro, and your front end must return corner lists / CLAHE output to the CPU every frame. If any part of your read-back path touches a compressed MTLTexture rather than an MTLBuffer, tens of milliseconds per frame are being spent in CPU decompression that no WGSL kernel optimisation will ever remove - and it would be misattributed to 'GPU downclocking'. Dawn's WGSL storage-texture vs storage-buffer choice decides which path you are on. Cheap to test: measure with allowGPUOptimizedContents=false as a positive control.
leads.venue: Apple Developer Forums (Graphics & Games, DTS answer)

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums – "iPhone X overheating with AVCaptureVideoDataOutput"
leads.claim: iPhone X with AVCaptureSession at AVCaptureSessionPreset3840x2160 (4K) @ 60 fps, doing NO processing beyond displaying frames through a pass-through GLSL shader (RosyWriter-style), overheats within 30 seconds, heat concentrated on the back near the camera. Reproduced across iOS 11.1.2, 11.2 beta 3 and 11.3 beta 3 (slightly less in 11.3b3). No Apple engineer reply.
leads.why: Negative-control evidence for P2: at high resolution and 60 fps the camera channel plus a trivial shader is on its own enough to overheat an iPhone, with zero CV work. Before attributing your extra energy to 'full-resolution GPU work every frame', run this control - camera at 1920x1440 @60 with the engine detached - and see how much of the 173 s in .serious is the channel itself. If most of it is, the productive lever is capture format, not kernel optimisation, and P1's premise ('go to a 60 fps channel') is what is buying the thermal problem.

leads.title: Stack Overflow – "Metal Compute versus ARM Neon" (answer)
leads.claim: Answer, verbatim: "GPGPU only makes sense when dealing with a huge amount of computations, because the data transfer/ HW initialization time spoils the fun in addition to the horrible APIs such as OpenCL. NEON on the other hand is tightly integrated into the main pipeline and thus, is way more responsive while packing more than adequate punch. AI and crypto coin mining have been pretty much the only areas I've seen so far where GPGPU makes sense. For anything lighter, SIMD is the way to go."
leads.why: A practitioner statement of the exact counter-thesis to your whole port: for per-frame, latency-sensitive, modest-arithmetic image kernels on an ARM SoC, NEON's zero dispatch latency can beat a GPU whose win is eaten by submission and transfer overhead. It is opinion, not measurement, so it is not a verdict - but combined with your own P1 number (5 ms nominal vs 19-22 ms downclocked) it says the honest A/B you still owe yourself is GPU-WGSL vs a NEON CPU arm of the SAME front end on the SAME device at the SAME thermal state, not GPU vs scalar C++.

leads.title: Stack Overflow – "Why does those Google image processing sample Renderscript runs slower on GPU in Nexus 5" (+ accepted answer)
leads.claim: On a Nexus 5 (Adreno 330), 6 of 13 of Google's own RenderScript image-processing sample algorithms run SLOWER on the GPU than on the CPU; convolution and other memory-bound kernels underperform while pure-math kernels win. Accepted answer from the RenderScript side: "Don't believe the hype regarding GPUs. For some workloads they are faster. However, for many workloads, the difference is small or negative. You have at least 2 different processor types, don't worry about which one get used, only worry if the performance is what you want." Concrete tuning guidance follows: prefer float over double, RS_FP_RELAXED where IEEE-754 is not needed, multiplication over division, native_* (e.g. native_powr) over full-precision routines, typed rsGetElementAt_* over rsSample/generic get, script globals over rs_allocation loads for kernel constants; and it notes known global-load performance problems on the Nexus 4/5/7v2 GPU path. Companion report: a trivial pass-through RenderScript kernel runs ~3x slower on the Adreno 330 GPU than on the CPU (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/20381691).
leads.why: The single best negative result found for your cross-cutting question: a vendor's own optimised mobile-GPU image-processing samples lose to the CPU on half of the kernel set, and the failing half is the memory-bound convolution family - which is exactly what CLAHE, the Gaussian pyramid and Scharr derivatives are. It predicts that your pyramid/derivative stages will be the ones that do not pay, and matches your own segment accounting from the extractor work. Note also the precision caveat: several of the listed speed levers (native_*, relaxed FP) are exactly the ones your bit-exactness rule forbids - so on a phone the lossless GPU port is competing with one hand tied.

leads.title: OpenCV issue #15932 – "Transparent Api on RK3399-Mali T860 producing running slower than cpu"
leads.claim: OpenCV 3.3.1, Firefly RK3399 with Mali-T860, Ubuntu 18.04.3: no cv::UMat (T-API/OpenCL) program tested was faster than the plain CPU Mat equivalent. Reported pipeline: imread -> cvtColor(COLOR_BGR2GRAY) -> GaussianBlur(3x3, sigma 1.5) -> Canny(0,50), timed with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock in microseconds. clinfo output attached; issue still open.
leads.why: Second independent Mali data point, on the same kernel family as your front end (grayscale + Gaussian + gradient/edge). Two open OpenCV issues on two different Mali generations both reporting no GPU win reinforces that your Android-Mali arm needs its own defended measurement rather than an assumption that the iOS result carries over - which matches your 'no platform-specific knives' rule but cuts the other way: a knife that is neutral on Mali is not automatically neutral once thermals are included.

leads.title: Chips and Cheese – "Snapdragon 8 Gen 1's iGPU: Adreno Gets Big" + its Hacker News thread
leads.claim: Microbenchmarked Adreno 730 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 1): 900 MHz max clock (per Snapdragon Profiler); LPDDR5 51.2 GB/s theoretical, just under 50 GB/s measured; system-level cache ~73.56 GB/s at just above 243 ns load-to-use latency; local memory 59.68 bytes per SP cycle (~430 GB/s aggregate) at 62.33 ns; L1 texture cache 64 B/cycle/SP; shared 256 KB L2; DRAM-access regression vs the older Adreno 530. In the HN thread (id 39628015), MindSpunk: "The second you go off the happy path of a tiler the performance drops like a rock, like in the compute example in the linked article... bandwidth to main memory is very power hungry so eating the cost of binning is worth it when your power envelope is 5W"; kllrnohj: tile-based rendering "has more performance cliffs and requires more game developer care to avoid hitting issues."
leads.why: Hard numbers for the Android half of P1/P2. At ~50 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth in a 5 W envelope, a full-resolution CLAHE + pyramid + Scharr + Harris pass at 1920x1440x60 fps is bandwidth-bound long before it is ALU-bound - which is the same conclusion your own Mali W256/binding work reached from the other direction. The 243 ns SLC latency also explains why more, smaller dispatches hurt: every extra pass re-reads the image from a cache tier that is ~4x further away than local memory. Use it to argue the fix is fewer, fused, lower-resolution passes rather than faster kernels.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums – "Core ML Model Prediction in 120 FPS faster than 60 FPS"
leads.claim: Same model, same machine (MacBook Pro M2, ProMotion): average prediction time 7.46 ms when driven at 120 fps / 120 Hz, but 10.91 ms when driven at 60 fps / 60 Hz - i.e. the LIGHTER duty cycle is SLOWER per inference. The reporter further observed that raising P-CPU utilisation raised Neural Engine utilisation and lowered prediction time. Apple DTS noted 10.91 ms still fits a 60 fps budget and recommended Instruments (Metal, System Trace) to correlate frequency states with latency.
leads.why: A counter-intuitive DVFS result that bears directly on how you interpret P1. If a heavier, steadier submission cadence keeps clocks ramped, then your '~5 ms nominal vs ~19-22 ms downclocked' may not be a pure thermal story - an intermittent, bursty 30 fps GPU duty cycle can itself keep the GPU in a low performance state, and going to 60 fps could partly pay for itself. Caveat to state loudly: this is an M2 Mac, not an iPhone 14 Pro, so it is a hypothesis to test with performance-state locking (lead #2), not a result to adopt.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums – "What are the gaps between individual computer shader invocations in metal GPU trace?"
leads.claim: iPhone 11 / iOS 15.6: a chain of dependent compute shaders, all encoded, dispatched and committed together in one batch, shows gaps between consecutive dispatches that consume significant GPU time, with no CPU-GPU synchronisation involved and bandwidth / read-write buffer limiters not notably high. Apple Graphics & Games engineer: the gaps are likely other GPU workload from different shaders running in between; advice is to disclose the Compute Shader track in the trace and file a Feedback Assistant report with the .gputrace.
leads.why: Speaks to the part of P1 you have already localised - your own accounting put 6.7 s in per-dispatch binding/pyramid overhead rather than in the keypoint kernel. This says an Apple engineer's first explanation for such gaps is contention with OTHER GPU work on the device, which on your setup means the camera preview / display compositing path competing with your compute queue. Test: run the same kernel chain with the preview surface detached, and compare the gaps. If they collapse, the fix is scheduling and pass fusion, not the kernels.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums – "How to avoid device heating problem while using AR Kit & Scene Kit in application"
leads.claim: Apple DTS engineer states that ARKit has high energy impact, especially on older devices, and that the OFFICIAL ARKit Xcode template project can cross the thermal limit on an iPhone 6s within a minute. The reporting developer's ARKit+SceneKit app drives Xcode's energy gauge to dark red quickly when the AR scene is on screen.
leads.why: Calibrates the P2 baseline. Your comparison is 'ARKit spends 0 s in serious on iPhone 14 Pro over 300 s'; Apple's own position is that ARKit is a high-energy API whose stock template can go thermal in 60 s on a 6s. So ARKit's 0 s on a 14 Pro is not evidence that a VIO front end is cheap - it is evidence that Apple's tracker is doing much less full-resolution work per frame than yours. That reframes P2 from 'find our energy leak' to 'find out what ARKit is NOT doing' - most likely running its tracker on a heavily downsampled image and not detecting on every frame.

leads.title: Apple Developer Forums – "Metal & Compute shaders: performance issue"
leads.claim: A7 iPad, iOS 9 beta 4, MetalImageProcessing sample doing colour-to-grayscale on an 800x533 image: 40 FPS, CPU 24.6 ms / GPU 18 ms. The reporter benchmarked four paths and ranked them: Metal graphics (vertex/fragment) fastest, GLES a very close second, Metal COMPUTE ~5x slower than Metal graphics on A7 (only ~1.5x slower on A8), Core Image comparable to Metal compute. Discussion attributes it to an immature compute path, different data-feeding bottlenecks vs the heavily optimised render path, and an iOS 9 regression vs iOS 8.
leads.why: Suggests a concrete, testable alternative shape for the ported stages: on Apple GPUs a per-pixel image operation expressed as a fragment shader over a full-screen quad has historically beaten the same work as a compute kernel. Your CLAHE / pyramid / Scharr stages are pure per-pixel maps and would port to a render pass with bit-identical arithmetic; only the Harris/goodFeaturesToTrack reduction genuinely needs compute. Caveat: this is A7/A8 on an iOS 9 beta and the compute path has matured a great deal since - treat it as a hypothesis worth one A/B arm, not a finding.

leads.title: Stack Overflow – "SceneKit AR game fps getting low and the device getting hot with use" (answer)
leads.claim: Answer identifies the core issue as running ARKit's 6-DoF tracking at 60 fps alongside SceneKit/RealityKit rendering, which strains CPU and GPU and causes rapid battery drain and heat. Concrete budgets given: keep any single model under 10K polygons and the whole scene under 50K polygons; avoid ray-traced shadows (use baked or simulated); minimise PBR/metallic-reflective shaders; avoid high-resolution textures; reduce physics load; and explicitly - lower the TRACKING and rendering frame rates below the standard 60 fps where feasible.
leads.why: Independent practitioner confirmation that 60 fps tracking is itself treated as the thermal cost driver on iOS, and that the community's standard remedy is to lower the tracking rate rather than optimise the tracker. Relevant to P1 as a product decision to flag: if 28.4 poses/s at a stable thermal state beats 60 poses/s that collapses under back-pressure, the honest comparison against ARKit may need to be per-pose latency and drift at a matched thermal state, not pose rate.

leads.title: 8th Wall / Niantic Spatial WebAR engine — gr8gl.h: GPU (GLSL) feature detector forked from OpenCV ORB, shipped alongside a CPU OpenCV implementation
leads.claim: File header states verbatim: "Gr8 features were originally forked from OpenCV's orb features", followed by the full OpenCV BSD license text. The repo ships BOTH implementations of the same detector: `Gr8Cpu` (CPU, built on a vendored cut-down OpenCV at third_party/cvlite — calib3d/core/features2d/flann/imgproc) and `Gr8Gl` (GPU). reality/engine/features/feature-detector.h holds both as members (`Gr8Cpu feat_; Gr8Gl glFeat_;`) with parallel entry points commented "// CPU features." and "// GL features.". The GPU side is reality/engine/features/gr8-feature-shader.h: separate GLSL programs shaderInput_, shaderPyramidBlur_, shaderPyramidDecimate_, shader1_/2_/3_, with constants scoreThresh_ = 4.0f and nmsTolerance_ = 1.0f ("0 is NMS, 1 is NMES, 255 is no NMS"). Repo license MIT, 467 stars, last push 2026-09-07.
leads.why: This is the closest prior art to our entire project that exists in public: a shipping mobile AR company took OpenCV's feature front end, forked it, and built a GPU shader replica of it, keeping the CPU version as the twin — and since January 2026 the source is MIT. It is an authoritative implementation we are allowed to copy verbatim under our replication rule, and it settles the cross-cutting question (yes, someone else took this approach; they used WebGL/GLSL rather than WebGPU). It also gives us a second reference to check our OpenCV-parity choices against.
leads.license: MIT (engine framework); individual files carry the OpenCV BSD header

leads.title: 8th Wall tracking-controller.cc — the whole CV pipeline runs every frame but is deliberately 2 frames behind so GPU readback never blocks
leads.claim: Production comment above processPipeline(): "Runs the entire pipeline on each frame but lags 2 frames behind. This allows us to have deferred reads of the camera frame from the gpu to the cpu." — implemented as `if (data()->pipeline.size() < 2) { return false; }`. Frame staging ends with `data()->gl->draw(p.realityTextureId, GlRealityFrame::Options::DEFER_READ);`. The DEFER_READ contract is documented in reality/engine/features/gl-reality-frame.h: "If DEFER_READ is set, this does not block on the GPU unless a previously requested call to draw is still pending", plus `enableWebGl2PixelBuffer()` ("Enables the use of the WebGL 2 features such as pixel pack buffer"). camera-loop.ts also puts the CV on a separate offscreen WebGL context: "computeCanvas is an offscreen canvas that runs our Emscripten computer vision algorithms. It is not added to the dom."
leads.why: This is a direct, copyable answer to P1. Our failure mode is exactly theirs: GPU work that sometimes exceeds the frame budget causes the engine to fall behind, back-pressure kicks in, latency collapses. Their fix is not to make the GPU faster — it is to buy two frames of pipeline latency plus an asynchronous pixel-pack readback, so a 19–22 ms GPU pass at downclocked rates still never stalls a 16.7 ms channel. Also note the CV runs on its own GL context, separate from the render context.

leads.title: 8th Wall constraints-helper.ts — production camera resolutions for WebAR SLAM, with measured per-resolution texture-upload cost on a Pixel 2
leads.claim: iOS list is only two entries: `{width:{min:960},height:{min:720}}` then `{width:{min:640},height:{min:480}}`. Android comment "// Preferred android resolution for performance:" precedes `{width:{exact:960},height:{exact:720}}`. Each higher Android fallback carries a measured upload cost annotation: 1920x1440 "texSubImage: pixel2 ~20ms"; 1600x1200 and 1440x1080 "~13ms"; 1280x960 "~10ms"; 960x720 "~6ms"; 640x480 "~3ms"; 320x240 "~3ms". Also documents native camera frame rates found via chrome://media-internals: "Pixel 6: 30 to 35 fps, Pixel 5a: 30 to 35 fps, Pixel 4: 35 to 45 fps".
leads.why: Hard evidence against our 1920x1440 tracking channel, from a shipping product. On iOS they never request more than 960x720 for SLAM. And the ~20 ms number is not the CV cost — it is *just the CPU→GPU texture upload* of one 1920x1440 frame, i.e. more than a whole 16.7 ms budget before any CLAHE or corner detection runs. If our 5 ms nominal / 19–22 ms throttled GPU figure is measured at 1920x1440, dropping the tracking channel to 960x720 is a ~4x pixel reduction and is the single cheapest lever for both P1 and P2. Note this is a product decision (results change), so it needs flagging as such.

leads.title: 8th Wall production detector parameters: 500 features/frame, 4 pyramid levels, scale 1.44, benchmarked at 480x640
leads.claim: detection-config.h: `static constexpr int FEATURES_PER_FRAME_GL = 500;` used as the DetectionConfig default. gr8-benchmark-test.cc (author Erik Murphy-Chutorian, 8th Wall CEO/founder) says "These mirrors the parameters that are in 8th Wall XR" for `Gr8Cpu::create(500, 1.44f, 4, 31, 0, 2, Gr8CpuInterface::FAST_SCORE, 5)` — 500 keypoints, scale factor 1.44, 4 pyramid levels, patch size 31, FAST_SCORE — and the benchmark fixture is named Benchmark480x640 over the SIMPLE10_480x640 dataset. The GL benchmark is a stub: "// TODO(christoph): Make the following benchmark use the future OpenGL version." (it still calls Gr8Cpu).
leads.why: Gives us an outside calibration point for how much per-frame feature work a shipping mobile AR front end actually does: 500 keypoints, 4 levels, at VGA. If our XRSLAM/goodFeaturesToTrack budget is materially larger than this at 1920x1440, the P1/P2 gap is a budget problem, not a kernel-efficiency problem. The stubbed GL benchmark is also a mild negative signal: even they never published a CPU-vs-GL timing comparison.

leads.title: Unity Apple ARKit XR Plugin changelog — ARKit itself falls back to a 30 fps update mode under thermal throttling
leads.claim: Entry under [3.0.0-preview.3] - 2019-09-26: "The 'match frame rate' option did not account for thermal throttling, which can put ARKit into a 30 frames per second update mode while Unity would keep trying to update at 60 frames per second." Same entry also: the option "could incorrectly cause execution to be blocked while waiting for a new frame, leading to long frame times."
leads.why: Reframes P1 and P2 together. ARKit's 59.9 poses/s is not unconditional — under thermal pressure Apple's own tracker halves its update rate rather than falling behind, and the documented failure mode of a consumer that insists on the higher rate is blocking and long frame times, which is precisely our back-pressure collapse. This is a licence to make pose rate thermally adaptive (30 Hz when hot) instead of treating 60 Hz as the target, and it means our 300 s ARKit baseline may itself contain 30 fps stretches we should check for before assuming a 2.1x gap.

leads.title: Qualcomm Hexagon DSP (Hot Chips 2013) — AR feature detection moved off ARM/NEON: 52% less CPU, 7% less time, 32% less total device power
leads.claim: Slide 18, "Computer vision offload – ARM/neon to Hexagon DSP": "Augmented Reality Java App finding objects in image using FastCV Feature Detect. Comparison of Feature Detect run on: App CPU (ARM/Neon), App DSP (Hexagon)". Results bars: "52% Less CPU", "7% Less Time", "32% Less Power*", with footnote "* Power measured at the device battery". Source line: "Qualcomm internal measurements".
leads.why: The best quantified prior measurement I found for P2. It says the payoff for moving AR feature detection off the CPU is almost entirely *energy* (32% at the battery), not latency (7%) — which matches our situation where CPU load is already at ARKit parity (0.80 cores) but thermal state is not. It also names the offload target the silicon vendor endorses for this exact workload: the DSP, not the GPU. That is a negative datapoint for the assumption that GPU is the right engine for corner detection on a phone, and it argues our energy accounting should be per-frame joules at the battery, not milliseconds.

leads.title: Snap Spectacles — Lens Performance Overlay: explicit CPU/GPU power-budget zones and the thermal-standby threshold
leads.claim: Three documented zones: under 100% CPU/GPU — "Lens is battery runtime constrained and running efficiently within budget. This is the target zone."; 100–125% — "Lens is thermally runtime constrained; performance may throttle or runtime may shorten."; over 125% — "Lens is significantly thermally constrained and will very likely trigger thermal standby or shutdowns", especially combined with capture. Render guidance: "Keep render time under ~16ms to maintain 60 FPS", target "close to 60 FPS". Monitored metrics are Lens CPU %, Lens GPU %, battery level, FPS and render time (ms). Companion page (developers.snap.com/spectacles/best-practices/performance-optimization/environment-setup-guidance) gives "100 LUX is recommended (some tracking possible below this)" but no numeric temperature thresholds.
leads.why: A shipping AR vendor publishing a normalised power budget rather than an fps target — 100% is the battery-life line, 125% is the thermal-shutdown line — is exactly the instrument we lack for P2. We currently measure thermalState occupancy after the fact (173 s of 300 s in 'serious'); this gives us a per-frame leading indicator to instrument instead, and a defensible definition of 'over budget' that is independent of whether the frame happened to land in 16.7 ms.

leads.title: Niantic Spatial SDK depth docs — heavy per-frame inference runs at reduced resolution and is reused across frames via a temporal warp matrix
leads.claim: "Depth images are delivered as CPU-accessible buffers, typically at a lower resolution than the camera images to balance performance and memory usage." And: "NSDK provides a temporal warping feature to enhance temporal consistency between frames. Each inferred depth image is associated with the world-space camera pose corresponding to the AR image used during inference. NSDK includes utility functions that compute an interpolation matrix, which transforms normalized image coordinates to make the depth image appear as if it were captured from the current camera pose. For efficiency, the display matrix and the interpolation (warp) matrix can be combined, allowing the depth image to be sampled only once." Release 4.1.0.
leads.why: Niantic's shipping pattern for expensive per-frame vision on a phone is: run it at lower resolution, tag the result with the pose it was computed from, and reproject it into the current pose rather than recomputing. That is the structural argument for P1 — 'detection currently runs on EVERY frame because that is what the upstream tracker does' is not what shippers do — and it shows the bookkeeping (pose-tagged result + warp matrix) that makes decoupling the detection rate from the camera rate safe.

leads.title: 8th Wall Open Source page — SLAM is deliberately excluded from the MIT release and stays binary-only
leads.claim: "Released in January 2026, the Distributed Engine Binary includes SLAM and is available under a binary-only license". The MIT "Open Source Engine Framework" includes "Core engine architecture, Face Effects, Image Targets, Sky Effects" and states "SLAM is not included in the open source release and remains available only through the Distributed Engine Binary." packages/engine/README.md: "an open source version of the 8th Wall engine with SLAM, VPS, and Hand Tracking removed. The SLAM, VPS, and Hand Tracking algorithms remain proprietary to Niantic Spatial". Build config is `bazel build --config=wasmreleasesimd` (WASM + SIMD).
leads.why: Two things we need to know. (1) Negative result: there is no permissively-licensed shipping browser/mobile SLAM back end to copy — the one company that had one carved it out precisely when open-sourcing everything else, so our XRSLAM choice stands. (2) The build target is WASM+SIMD, i.e. the leading WebAR company drives its non-SLAM CV on the CPU through WASM SIMD and uses GL only for the pyramid/feature stage. That bounds how much of the front end anyone else has actually pushed to the GPU.
leads.license: MIT for framework; binary-only proprietary for SLAM

leads.title: 8th Wall gr8gl-slow + gr8gl regression tests — the reference-vs-fast bit-exactness harness for a GPU feature detector
leads.claim: reality/engine/features/ contains gr8gl.h/.cc (fast GL path), gr8gl-slow.h/.cc (a separate deliberately-slow implementation exposing the same constants: kBytes = 32, HARRIS_SCORE = 0, FAST_SCORE = 1, PATCH_SIZE = 31, plus `retainBest(keypoints, nPoints, cols)` which "Retain[s] the best nPoints from the set of keypoints, taking into account both response and geometry"), and three test files: gr8gl-test.cc, gr8gl-retain-best-regression-test.cc, gr8gl-retain-best-benchmark-test.cc. There is also gr8cpu-nop.cc (a no-op CPU build) and fake-feature-detector.cc.
leads.why: This is somebody else's answer to our lossless-gate problem, and it is testable code we can copy the shape of: keep a slow reference implementation of the GPU kernel in-tree, pin it with a *regression* test rather than only a unit test, and provide a nop/fake detector so the surrounding pipeline can be timed with the detector removed. Given our repeated pain with silent exits and probes that fail without evidence, an in-tree slow reference plus a nop arm is directly usable.

leads.title: Designium XR (JP) — hands-on device verification of the 8th Wall engine binary, and the platform shutdown timeline
leads.claim: Published 2026-02-12. Method: two builds of the same AR app differing only in which engine is loaded (CDN-hosted vs bundled binary), tested by three AR-experienced engineers across multiple Android and iOS devices, on World Tracking (SLAM), Absolute Scale, Image Targets (flat/curved/conical), Face Effects, Sky Effects, and World Tracking x Image Targets; two measures per feature — qualitative stability/tracking/recognition, and "1分間プレイし続けた際のfpsレンジ比較" (fps range compared over one minute of continuous play). Result: "パフォーマンスの差異は認められませんでした" (no performance difference observed). Also records that the 8th Wall platform shut down 2026-02-28, that the engine binary is obfuscated/minified JS ("内部ロジックや最適化の仕組みはブラックボックス"), and that exported flat Image Targets ship flat.json + flat_original.jpg + flat_target.jpg + flat_geometry.jpg + flat_thumbnail.png.
leads.why: Useful as a methodology datapoint rather than a number: the industry's own acceptance test for a tracking-engine swap is an fps *range* over a one-minute continuous run on real devices plus a blind qualitative panel — i.e. a sustained-load test, not a cold-start benchmark. That matches the thermal reality behind our P1/P2 and is the shape our own 300 s comparison already has. Also confirms nobody outside Niantic can inspect the shipping SLAM binary.

leads.title: 8th Wall forum — WebAR frame rate decays over ~1 minute on a recent iPhone (user report)
leads.claim: Google result (2025-08-20), thread titled "Frame rate drops when overlay UI is used", snippet: "I've also tested on my Wife's iPhone 13 Pro Max and the frame rate drops to 40+ at around 1+ mins. So it could all be just phone's CPU...". A second thread (2023-08-14) titled "What should the FPS of my 8th Wall experience be?" contains "Performance on Android devices can also vary greatly between models."
leads.why: An ordinary developer independently observing the same shape as our P1/P2: a WebAR session that holds frame rate for about a minute on a flagship iPhone and then decays, with the decay attributed to the phone rather than the content. Corroborates that sustained-run degradation (not cold-start cost) is the real constraint, and that the industry sees it too. Weak evidence — I could not open the thread, so the exact thread URL and full text are unverified.

leads.title: SVO의 동적 주파수 할당을 이용한 저전력 구현 (Low power implementation of semi-direct visual odometry using dynamic frequency scaling) — 장민수, 아주대학교 석사학위논문
leads.claim: Ajou Univ. MSc thesis (2017, RISS id T14553399). Treats a visual-odometry front end (SVO) as a periodic real-time task on a heterogeneous multicore embedded system and scales CPU operating frequency per period so that each frame just meets its deadline instead of always running at max clock. Measured result: 소모 전력 효율 55.4% 향상 — 55.4% improvement in power-consumption efficiency versus a fixed CPU frequency, while still satisfying the real-time requirement (thesis compares execution time, number of real-time violations, and consumed power for fixed-frequency vs the proposed scheme).
leads.why: P2 says our CPU load is the same as ARKit's (0.80 core-equivalents) yet we burn 173 s of 300 s in thermalState 'serious'. This is the only Korean source I found that measures the exact lever we are not pulling: run the pipeline at the lowest clock that still meets the per-frame deadline rather than racing to idle. 55.4% is a large number for a change that is behaviour-preserving (bit-identical output, only timing changes) — it would be a lossless P2 fix under our own rules. The thesis also confirms SVO-class front ends are periodic-deadline workloads, which is the framing our back-pressure collapse in P1 needs.
leads.license: thesis, full text access-gated on RISS; method described in abstract/TOC

leads.title: QoS를 고려한 스마트폰 GPU의 에너지 최적화 기법 (A QoS-Aware Energy Optimization Technique for Smartphone GPUs) — 김도한, 서울대학교 석사학위논문
leads.claim: SNU MSc thesis (2015, advisor 김지홍, RISS id T13743553). Analysed the ARM Mali-400MP device driver and found the stock utilization-based GPU DVFS governor drives the GPU at a HIGHER frequency than the workload actually needs, causing inefficient energy burn. Their replacement observes achieved FPS per available GPU frequency per application and picks the lowest frequency that holds the target FPS, factoring in remaining battery: average 9.9% and maximum 23% GPU energy-efficiency improvement over utilization-based DVFS, with an average FPS difference of only ~0.4 (essentially no performance loss); allowing a deliberate FPS drop extended battery life by an average of 8.5 minutes.
leads.why: This is a mechanism claim, not a correlation, and it points straight at P2 and at P1's '~19-22 ms once the phone downclocks'. It says the mobile GPU governor mis-estimates demand from utilization alone — which is exactly what a bursty 5 ms compute job at 30-60 Hz looks like (high instantaneous utilization, low average work). If the same overshoot is happening on our device, our GPU is being clocked up and heated more than our workload requires, and the fix is an FPS-target-driven frequency choice rather than more kernel micro-optimization. Measured on Mali-400MP (Android), so it needs re-validation on A16/Adreno/newer Mali, but it is a Korean primary source with numbers.
leads.venue: 서울대학교 대학원 전기·컴퓨터공학부 (Seoul National University), 석사

leads.title: OS-level energy/temperature management for mobile processing units — 김영근, 고려대학교 박사학위논문
leads.claim: Korea Univ. PhD thesis (2018, RISS id T14924360), real-measurement based on Android development boards. Three results: (1) a multimedia-aware task scheduler that pins media threads to little cores saves 8.9% system-wide energy on average and improves non-multimedia app performance by 13.7%; (2) signal-strength-aware selective offloading: +30.1% performance, -25.0% system-wide energy vs offloading that ignores signal strength; (3) M-DTM — on a thermal emergency of the big cores, MIGRATE the application to the little cores instead of lowering big-core voltage/frequency; this cools the big cores faster and therefore buys more time at max big-core frequency: +10.6% performance and -3.6% system-wide energy vs conventional DTM, while still satisfying thermal constraints.
leads.why: P2's core symptom is thermal state, not average CPU load — 0.80 core-equivalents identical to ARKit yet 173 s in 'serious'. This thesis is the Korean primary source on why heterogeneous mobile SoCs handle thermal emergencies badly with DVFS alone, and quantifies migration-to-little-cores as the better answer. On iOS we cannot schedule cores directly, but the same insight maps to QoS class / thread affinity choices for our front-end threads, and it gives us a vocabulary and a measured baseline for arguing about where the extra energy in P2 is actually going.

leads.title: 임베디드 GPU에서의 글로벌 워크 크기 최적화 (Global work size optimization for embedded GPU) — 신익희, 충남대학교 석사학위논문
leads.claim: Chungnam National Univ. MSc thesis (2018, advisor 김형신, RISS id T14771340). Explicit negative result: 'various OpenCL optimization studies were conducted, but the effect was not seen in embedded GPU' — the standard desktop-GPU OpenCL optimization playbook does not transfer to embedded GPUs. Measured: when the kernel execution time is shorter than the input data transfer time (SpMV benchmark), the OpenCL version has LOWER throughput than the sequential CPU code; only when kernel time and transfer time are both long enough (Mandelbrot) does parallelization win. Proposes a way to compute the optimal global work size analytically, without a tuning sweep. Thesis TOC includes a dedicated section 'ARM Mali GPU에서의 OpenCL 최적화에 관한 연구'.
leads.why: This is the negative result the brief asks for, from a Korean lab, and it matches our own accumulated Mali/Adreno experience (binding-size and workgroup knobs mostly noise; the win came from device-reported limits, not from generic advice). Two directly usable things: (a) it names the exact regime where mobile GPU LOSES — kernel time < transfer time, which is precisely where a 5 ms CLAHE+corner kernel at 60 Hz sits once camera-frame upload is counted; (b) an analytic global-work-size rule would replace our per-device sweeps and is consistent with our 'pick layout from device self-reported limits' finding. Worth reading before spending another week on WGSL dispatch shape tuning.
leads.venue: 충남대학교 대학원 컴퓨터공학과 (Chungnam National University), 석사

leads.title: 모바일 GPU를 이용한 실시간 병렬영상처리 라이브러리 (Real-Time Parallel Image Processing Library using Mobile GPU) — 이종환·강승헌·이만희·이성철·김학일·박인규, 정보과학회논문지
leads.claim: Inha Univ. (박인규 group), Journal of KIISE: Computing Practices and Letters 20(2), 2014, pp.96-100, KCI-listed. Built a real-time image-processing library for commercial Android smartphones on BOTH OpenGL ES 2.0 GLSL and OpenCL 1.1, and benchmarked it function-by-function against OpenCV for Android (the CPU library). Result: 모바일 CPU 대비 모바일 GPU를 이용한 영상처리 속도가 평균 3배 이상 가속 — mobile GPU averaged more than 3x faster than the mobile CPU across the compared OpenCV functions. The paper also contrasts GLSL vs OpenCL as the parallelization vehicle and recommends an effective method.
leads.why: This is the closest Korean prior art to what we actually built: a GPU reimplementation of OpenCV image-processing functions on a phone, validated against OpenCV itself as the reference. It gives a Korean-community magnitude for the payoff (>3x over CPU OpenCV, averaged, on 2014-era mobile GPUs) which is a sanity check on our own numbers, and it is the same lab that later published the OpenCL multiview-stereo and on-device AR work. Useful mainly as EVIDENCE that the shape of our approach has been taken before in Korea and that it wins — but note it was OpenGL ES/OpenCL, not WebGPU, and it does not claim bit-exactness.
leads.venue: 정보과학회논문지: 컴퓨팅의 실제 및 레터 (Journal of KIISE), 한국정보과학회
leads.license: KCI journal, paywalled full text; abstract public

leads.title: 온디바이스 AI 얼굴 식별 파이프라인 최적화 — 하이퍼커넥트 (Hyperconnect) 기술 블로그
leads.claim: Hyperconnect (Azar, Korean video-chat company) engineering blog, 2026-01-23. Galaxy S24 / Android 14, TFLite CPU, 500 repetitions per scenario, measured fully charged AND on external power, with 5-10 minutes of device cooling between measurement runs. Baseline pipeline 138.2 ms/image, 7.2 photos/s. After optimization: 86.8 ms (-37.2%) and 45.9 photos/s (+530%). Stage table: predicate-pushdown before decode cut decoding 8.9 ms -> 1.9 ms (-79%); heap-based top-K cut that stage 78%; replacing TFLite TensorBuffer.getFloatValue() with bulk floatArray removed accumulated JNI call overhead. Critically: raising TFLite interpreter count 1->2->4 raised throughput 16.6 -> 37.9 photos/s (2.28x) but PUSHED per-image latency 60.3 -> 105.3 ms; adding a recognition-model thread pool brought it back to 86.8 ms at 45.9 photos/s. They also report increasing the TFLite thread-pool size made some ops 7-8x SLOWER because those ops were not compute-intensive and communication overhead dominated.
leads.why: Two things we can use. (1) P1 is a throughput-vs-latency problem stated as a rate problem: this is a Korean industrial measurement showing that instancing the model/pipeline raises throughput ~6.4x while making single-item latency worse — the same trade we would face if we ran two detector instances to hit 60 fps, and it tells us to expect latency regression, which is exactly what 'back-pressure kicks in and latency collapses' describes. (2) Their measurement protocol is a direct counterweight to our own recorded rule that plugging in makes the phone thermally limited: they deliberately measure on external power AND force 5-10 min cooling between arms. Their negative result on thread-pool size (7-8x slowdown on non-compute-bound ops) is the same class of finding as our own barrier/scan-strip dead ends.

leads.title: ETRI, 온디바이스용 고성능 비전SW 개발 — OpenVX 국제표준 적합성 인증 (ZDNet Korea)
leads.claim: ETRI (Korea's national ICT research institute) announced 2020-08-26 that its 'high-performance low-power vision processing software for on-device devices' passed Khronos OpenVX conformance — 6,162 separate function tests — the first Korean organization and one of only 13 organizations worldwide certified (alongside NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Intel, TI). ETRI additionally developed an 'OpenVX 응용 실행을 위한 런타임 환경 경량화 기술' — a lightweight OpenVX runtime that applies mobile GPU parallel compute, selecting vision modules to match the product's hardware and auto-optimizing. ETRI states measured confirmation that mixing GPU with CPU rather than using CPU only both improves performance and reduces required power. Named researcher: 김정시 책임연구원, ETRI 고성능디바이스SW연구실. Motivation given: SoC fragmentation forces vendors to rewrite and re-optimize vision SW for every chip.
leads.why: This is the Korean answer to our cross-cutting question, and it is a different answer than ours: instead of hand-porting each OpenCV kernel to a bit-exact WGSL replica per platform, encode the front end as an OpenVX graph and let a conformant runtime pick CPU/GPU per SoC. OpenVX is a Khronos standard with a published conformance suite (6,162 tests) — i.e. an off-the-shelf bit-level parity oracle of the kind we currently have to build ourselves. Worth a serious look before we port more kernels: OpenVX covers pyramids, Harris/FAST corners, optical flow (vxOpticalFlowPyrLKNode) and histogram equalization, which is most of our front end. Also directly supports P2 with a vendor-neutral claim that CPU+GPU mixing lowers power vs CPU-only.
leads.venue: ZDNet Korea (press coverage of ETRI announcement)
leads.license: news article; OpenVX itself is a Khronos royalty-free standard

leads.title: 특징점 추출의 병렬구현과 반복패턴의 효율적 매치 방법 — 김재영, 울산대학교 석사학위논문
leads.claim: Univ. of Ulsan MSc thesis (2015, advisor 전희성, RISS id T13376136). Parallelized SIFT (Gaussian kernel, scale-space pyramid, keypoint extraction, local-memory usage optimization) on a SIMD many-core processor and validated it as follows: '매니코어를 이용한 SIFT 알고리즘 구현 결과는 기존의 OpenCV 구현 결과와 정확도면에서 동일하였고' — the many-core SIFT results were IDENTICAL in accuracy to the existing OpenCV implementation — and the many-core implementation beat both a high-performance CPU and a GPU implementation on execution time. The thesis separately analyses execution time, system utilization, energy efficiency and area efficiency PER SIFT OCTAVE and derives an optimal model from that.
leads.why: Two uses. First, it is Korean precedent for our exact validation discipline: port the detector, then prove parity against OpenCV rather than against a self-invented reference — which is the discipline our own install-gate feedback says we keep needing. Second, the per-octave energy-efficiency breakdown is the shape of analysis P2 needs: our pyramid is the part of the GPU front end whose cost scales with resolution, and knowing which octaves pay for themselves in energy (not just in milliseconds) is a cheaper lever than shaving kernels. Caveat: hardware is a SIMD many-core, not a mobile GPU, so the timing numbers do not transfer — the methodology and the parity claim do.
leads.venue: 울산대학교 대학원 전기전자·컴퓨터공학과 (University of Ulsan), 석사

leads.title: MAXST / BITMAX AR SDK — Visual SLAM and AR Fusion Tracker developer documentation (Korean AR SDK vendor)
leads.claim: MAXST/BITMAX (Seoul) ships a commercial smartphone AR SDK whose own tracker is documented as 'Visual SLAM = VIO + Loop Closing', monocular RGB camera only, and explicitly 'optimized for the smartphone environment, unlike the existing other SLAMs, which requires separate hardware equipped with sensors'. They also document a Sensor-fusion SLAM (RGB camera tightly coupled with IMU) intended to replace their Instant Tracker. Separately, their 'AR Fusion Tracker' (https://developer.maxst.com/MD/doc/6_2_x/features/fusion) is defined as their own tracker PLUS 'the powerful tracking functions of the ARKit and ARCore' — their own tracker establishes the target coordinate system, ARKit/ARCore carries the pose when the target leaves view. iOS documentation includes a full Metal rendering path for every tracker variant.
leads.why: Relevant to P4 and to the whole-approach question. A Korean vendor that DID build its own smartphone VSLAM still shipped a hybrid product where ARKit/ARCore supplies continuous tracking and their own component supplies the map/anchor semantics. That is an existence proof for the architecture that would fix P4's 3.6 s vs 1.5 s directly — take the platform pose immediately, hand over to (or fuse with) our own map once XRSLAM's SfM bootstrap converges. It conflicts with our stated 'no vendor AR SDK' rule if we consumed their SDK, but the architectural split does not require their SDK, and ARKit-as-pose-source is a different dependency than ARCore-as-world-map (which we already ruled out for having no local map).
leads.venue: BITMAX Co., Ltd. (formerly MAXST), Seoul — developer.maxst.com

leads.title: Visual-SLAM Roadmap (Korean edition) — Level 06 VIO/VINS and Resources, by Hyunggi Chang (changh95)
leads.claim: MIT-licensed, Korean-language curated Visual-SLAM roadmap maintained by a Korean CV/SLAM engineer (1.8k stars on github.com/changh95/visual-slam-roadmap). The VIO level enumerates the field by system with one-line 핵심 개념: filter-based (MSCKF Mourikis 2007, ROVIO Bloesch 2015, OpenVINS Geneva 2020) and optimization-based (OKVIS Leutenegger 2015, VINS-Mono Qin 2018, VI-DSO, VINS-Fusion, maplab Schneider 2018, Kimera-VIO Rosinol 2020, Basalt Usenko 2020, ORB-SLAM3, DM-VIO von Stumberg 2022, OKVIS2 2022, AirVO 2023, OKVIS2-X 2025). It states explicitly that '상용 XR 스택(Meta Quest, ARKit/ARCore)은 가장 널리 배포된 VIO 시스템으로, 사례 연구로서 살펴볼 가치가 있음' — the commercial XR stacks are the most widely deployed VIO systems and are worth studying as case studies. Foundational reading listed: Woodman 2007 inertial navigation, Forster 2015 IMU preintegration on manifold, Solà 2017 quaternion error-state KF.
leads.why: Our binding constraint is licence-clean replication targets: ORB-SLAM2/3, VINS-Mono/Fusion, DSO and SVO are all GPL and therefore dead to us, and we already know maplab is Apache-2.0 and stella_vslam is BSD-2. This Korean-community index is the fastest way to enumerate the remaining permissively-licensed VIO systems we have NOT yet checked — OKVIS/OKVIS2, Basalt, Kimera-VIO, DM-VIO, AirVO — each of which has a published implementation and a keyframe/marginalization policy we could replicate whole rather than assembling our own. It also names the exact three foundational sources for IMU-side work, which is what P4's bootstrap needs.

leads.title: 고속 주행 차량에서의 시각 오도메트리 향상을 위한 적응형 키프레임 생성 기법 (Adaptive Keyframe Generation Method for Improving Visual Odometry in High Speed Motion) — 이동현, 광운대학교 석사학위논문
leads.claim: Kwangwoon Univ. MSc thesis (2025, 로봇학과, RISS id T17297133). Frames keyframe selection as THE critical determinant of VO system performance, and attacks the opposite failure mode from ours: when the platform moves fast or sensor data is briefly unavailable, the inter-frame gap grows and there are too FEW keyframes. Method: estimate the sufficient number of images and adaptively GENERATE extra keyframes by video frame interpolation, with an added loss term that minimizes motion blur so the synthesized keyframes are actually suitable for VO. Reports superior performance across multiple trajectory evaluations.
leads.why: Useful as the mirror image of P1. Our pose rate is 28.4/s against ARKit's 59.9 and our camera channel is 30 fps — so we are in exactly the 'too few frames per unit of motion' regime this thesis is about, just caused by channel rate rather than vehicle speed. It supports decoupling keyframe/pose cadence from camera cadence as a legitimate axis, and it is a 2025 Korean source, i.e. current. The interpolation half is a product decision (it synthesizes images that the camera never saw, so it is explicitly not lossless) and should be flagged as such if pursued; the 'estimate the sufficient number of images' half is the part that is safe.

leads.title: 단안영상-관성 SLAM의 깊이 추정 방법 및 IMU초기화 연구 — 김효중, 중앙대학교 석사학위논문
leads.claim: Chung-Ang Univ. MSc thesis (2020, 전자전기공학과 제어및시스템, RISS id T15509819). Uses a SMARTPHONE IMU specifically and studies precise initial-alignment for monocular visual-inertial SLAM: an accurate magnetometer (지자기 센서) calibration algorithm, plus Kalman-filter estimation of gyroscope and accelerometer error components, so that inertial navigation supplies absolute scale and attitude at high rate without diverging. Motivation stated: visual SLAM alone is sensitive to fast motion and lighting change; inertial gives high-frequency attitude and absolute scale but diverges with sensor error.
leads.why: P4 is 3.6 s vs ARKit's 1.5 s and the stated cause is that XRSLAM needs real translation before its SfM bootstrap converges. This is the Korean source on the other half of that bootstrap — getting the IMU aligned and de-biased fast enough that scale and attitude are usable early. It is smartphone-IMU specific (not a MEMS-lab bench IMU), which matters because our device is an iPhone 14 Pro. Lower confidence than the other P4 leads because the abstract reports no time-to-convergence number, so it would have to be read in full before we could tell whether it actually shortens initialization or just improves its accuracy.

leads.title: Multiview Stereo Matching on Mobile Devices Using Parallel Processing on Embedded GPU (Jeon & Park, Inha Univ.) and companion on-device AR work
leads.claim: Inha Univ. (박인규 group), Journal of Broadcast Engineering 24(6) 2019, pp.1064-1071: parallelizes a full multiview stereo matching algorithm with OpenCL on mobile GPUs and 'provide[s] various optimization techniques on the embedded hardware with limited resource', demonstrating that complex CV algorithms previously requiring high-performance hardware now run on a smartphone and an embedded board. Same group, JAKO202218262149224 (2022, Jeong & Park): a deep-learning on-device AR system on Android splitting camera pose estimation / depth estimation / object augmentation across OpenCL for GPU parallelization, TensorFlow Lite, and OpenGL ES, evaluated on augmentation accuracy and processing time in both mobile and PC environments. Neither public abstract carries the runtime numbers.
leads.why: Establishes that the Inha VCL lab is the one Korean academic group with a decade-long continuous line on exactly our problem — porting heavyweight vision pipelines to mobile GPUs and measuring them (2012 GLSL framework, 2014 OpenCL SIFT/SURF, 2014 library vs OpenCV, 2019 multiview stereo, 2022 on-device AR). If we want a Korean counterpart to compare notes with on mobile-GPU CV optimization technique lists, this is the group. Low standalone value because the abstracts withhold the numbers; listed so the next pass knows where to dig (the Journal of Broadcast Engineering is open access, so the full PDFs should be reachable).

leads.title: Image Feature-Based Real-Time RGB-D 3D SLAM with GPU Acceleration (Lee, Kim, Myung — KAIST)
leads.claim: KAIST (Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Hyun Myung's group), Journal of Institute of Control, Robotics and Systems 19(5), 2013, pp.457-461, DOI 10.5302/J.ICROS.2013.13.8002. A real-time RGB-D 3D SLAM system in which GPU acceleration is applied specifically to the FEATURE EXTRACTION stage via parallel computation, with 6-DOF visual odometry from 3D-RANSAC over 2D image features plus depth, a feature manager for loop closure, and graph-based back-end optimization. No fps/ms/GPU-model figures appear in the public abstract.
leads.why: The earliest Korean-lab instance I could find of the specific architectural choice we made — GPU-accelerate the detector inside a SLAM front end while leaving the rest on CPU — from a well-known KAIST robotics group. Value is as provenance and as a contact point, not as a measurement: the abstract carries no numbers, and the platform is desktop-class RGB-D, not a phone. Listed last because it is the weakest of the leads; open the full ICROS PDF only if we want the Korean-lab lineage documented.

leads.title: cuVSLAM: CUDA accelerated visual odometry and mapping (NVIDIA, arXiv 2506.04359v3)
leads.license: paper CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; the cuVSLAM library itself is NVIDIA proprietary (github.com/nvidia-isaac/cuVSLAM shows no OSI license)
leads.claim: NVIDIA's shipping GPU visual-odometry front end on Jetson does NOT detect every frame and does NOT run at your resolution. §2.1: keypoint selection = Shi-Tomasi 'Good Features to Track' on an N×M grid, top-k per patch with k > floor(K_I/(N*M)) (eq. 1); then 'On regular frames, we perform tracking only for the left camera for the tracks that are still active... When the number of successfully tracked keypoints falls below a threshold, a keyframe is created' — feature *selection* runs only at keyframe creation. Table 1, Jetson AGX Orin 64GB MAXN, 768×480 color: track-call time Mono 2.7 ms, Stereo 1.8 ms, Stereo-Inertial 3.8 ms, Multicam 2-stereo 2.0 ms, 3-stereo 2.3 ms, Mono-Depth (640×480) 15.1 ms. Live via Isaac ROS 3.2 with RealSense at 640×480 @60 FPS: Stereo CPU 5.5% / GPU 1.7%; Stereo-Inertial (30 FPS, IMU 200 Hz) CPU 1.3% / GPU 2.2%; Mono-Depth CPU 2.6% / GPU 55.0%. §A.2: 'For Mono-Depth mode, the average callback time for 720p resolution reached 37.7ms, which exceeds the 33.3ms frame interval required for 30 FPS operation. This timing constraint indicates GPU overload on the Orin AGX platform... resulted in the system skipping approximately half of the incoming frames.' Their fix: 'we recommend either reducing the frame rate to 15 FPS or decreasing the resolution to VGA, as our experiments revealed no significant difference in cuVSLAM visual tracking quality between VGA and HD resolutions.' On Jetson Orin Nano Super in 25W mode, mono-depth was stable only at 424×240; at 31 ms average call vs the 33 ms interval, ~30% of frames were dropped even though 'the average GPU load remained below 40%'. And: 'for systems involving freely moving cameras with rapid scene changes, such as handheld cameras or unmanned aerial vehicles, we recommend increasing frame rates to 60 FPS'.
leads.why: This is the single closest external analogue to your system — a production, GPU-accelerated, Shi-Tomasi+pyramidal-LK front end on an embedded SoC — and it contradicts three of your design choices at once. (a) P1: it decouples detection from frames; detection fires on keyframe creation, triggered by tracked-count falling below a threshold. Your 'detection on EVERY frame because upstream does it' is not what the state-of-the-art embedded system does. (b) P1/P2: it runs at 768×480 or 640×480, i.e. 0.31–0.37 Mpix vs your 1920×1440 = 2.76 Mpix (7.5–9×), and NVIDIA explicitly measured no tracking-quality difference between VGA and HD. Your 5 ms nominal / 19–22 ms throttled CLAHE+detection budget is almost certainly a resolution problem before it is a GPU problem. (c) P1: it independently reproduces your exact failure mode with numbers — when per-frame cost crosses the frame interval, the system silently drops ~half the frames; NVIDIA's remedy is lower rate or lower resolution, never back-pressure. Also note the reference point for how cheap this can be: 1.8 ms/frame and 1.7% GPU on an AGX Orin for the whole stereo visual-tracking call. The library is proprietary so you cannot copy the code, but the paper is citable evidence and the policy is described precisely enough to source a replication decision to a permissive implementation (see Kimera-VIO and Basalt leads).

leads.title: NVIDIA Developer Forums — 'OpenCV-Cuda functions running far slower than expected on Jetson Xavier NX' (t/223548)
leads.claim: Measured on a Jetson Xavier NX devkit in 20W/6-core mode vs a laptop dGPU, same code: cv::cuda::remap 1.14 ms -> 6.39 ms (5.6x), optical flow (no up/downloads) 0.66 ms -> 6.72 ms (10.2x), small uploads/downloads 0.03 ms -> 0.42 ms (14.0x), cv::cuda::goodFeaturesToTrack 2.23 ms -> 11.03 ms (4.9x). The user then diagnosed the cause with Jetson Power GUI: 'the GPU is far from running at 1.1 GHz as announced, but running between 300 and 600 MHz instead (the maximum I observed for short duration was 800MHz)' and explicitly ruled out throttling — 'GPU temperature 41°C, total power 8W, GPU load <60%'. Setting GPU MIN_FREQ=MAX_FREQ=1.1 GHz in a custom nvpmodel profile did NOT work; only `sudo nvpmodel -m 6 && sudo jetson_clocks` did, after which optical flow went 6.72 -> 3.52 ms (1.91x) and remap 6.39 -> 4.22 ms. NVIDIA's engineer confirmed: 'By default, Jetson uses the dynamic frequency. So you will need to run the jetson_clocks to fix the frequency to the maximum.' Even after pinning, optical flow remained 66% slower than a pure core-count/clock scaling model predicted.
leads.why: This is the closest published diagnosis of your P1 root cause and it reframes it. Your 5 ms nominal vs 19-22 ms 'once the phone downclocks under a camera+GPU load' is a ~4x factor — the same 4.9x this user measured on cv::cuda::goodFeaturesToTrack, on a board where the GPU was NOT thermally throttled (41 °C, 8 W) but simply never ramped past 300-600 MHz because the workload was short and bursty. On iOS you have no jetson_clocks equivalent, so the actionable reading is: (a) do not assume 'thermal' — a DVFS governor that fails to ramp on short bursts produces the identical signature, and merging your per-frame GPU work into fewer, longer dispatches can change the governor's decision; (b) the 14x blow-up on 0.03 ms uploads/downloads says fixed per-dispatch cost dominates small kernels on embedded GPUs, which is a direct argument for fewer/larger dispatches in your CLAHE+detect chain; (c) budget at the low clock, not the nominal one.

leads.title: NVIDIA Developer Forums — 'Real-time fleet camera analytics on Jetson Orin' (t/375850): design for the throttled clocks
leads.claim: Practitioner (CEO of Au-Zone Technologies, production fleet perception on embedded) states the embedded-vision budgeting rule verbatim: 'Thermal is your real constraint, not peak FPS. A sealed enclosure under sustained inference means you should design for the throttled clocks, not the datasheet. Lock a power mode up front (15W or 25W), then run a multi-hour tegrastats soak at worst-case ambient with all streams live before you finalize model sizes. If the pipeline only hits its FPS target at boost clocks, it doesn't hit it.' Concrete mitigations he lists: 'Don't run full-frame models for both scene and driver. Keep the DMS model on a cropped cabin ROI at reduced resolution and rate'; gate expensive work off a cheaper non-visual signal (IMU/CAN) rather than inferring at full rate; 'consider pushing one of the models to DLA to preserve GPU headroom'; and 'Measure latency end-to-end (sensor -> detection -> MQTT out), not just inference time'. The original poster's symptom: 'Orin NX in a sealed enclosure without active cooling starts throttling under sustained inference load in hot climates, which shows up as dropped frames rather than a clean error.'
leads.why: It is the community's explicit answer to the exact framing in P1 ('it takes about 5 ms at nominal GPU clocks but ~19-22 ms once the phone downclocks'). The rule is that the 19-22 ms number IS your budget and the 5 ms number is meaningless — an iPhone in a user's hand at 173/300 s in thermalState 'serious' is a sealed enclosure under sustained load.
