It also supplies a measurement protocol you can adopt directly for P2 (lock/record the power state, multi-hour soak at worst-case ambient with the camera live, end-to-end latency not kernel time) and two P2 levers you have analogues for on iPhone: reduced-resolution/ROI work, and offloading to a fixed-function engine instead of the GPU. Practitioner claim, not a measured paper — treat as design guidance, not evidence.

leads.title: NVIDIA Developer Forums — ArgusMonoNode NV12→RGB8 at 4000×3000 on Orin Nano: GPU 2.4 ms vs fixed-function VIC 14.8 ms, and they chose VIC (t/363316)
leads.claim: Jetson Orin Nano Super, MAXN_SUPER, jetson_clocks, 4000×3000 (12 MP) @72 fps, standalone measurements (not through the GXF pipeline): NPP on GPU (nppiNV12ToRGB_8u_P2C3R_Ctx) 2.4 ms average, 72 fps; VPI on the VIC fixed-function engine 14.8 ms average, ~60 fps. Through the Isaac ROS/GXF pipeline the same conversions cost 21.4 ms (GPU) and 37.4 ms (VIC), i.e. GXF added ~19 ms and ~23 ms of pure framework overhead. NV12 passthrough with no conversion at all: 0.05 ms, full 72 fps. VIC time was 37.4 ms at 435 MHz vs 37.6 ms at 115 MHz — clock-independent, so not compute-bound. NVIDIA's own VPI reference number for NV12_ER→RGBA8 at 1080p on VIC is 'around 0.82 ms (±0.0007 ms)'. The deployment decision: 'NPP gives full 72fps but uses GPU cycles. VPI VIC gives ~60fps but leaves the GPU completely free for inference. We'll likely go with VIC since freeing the GPU is more valuable than the extra 12fps.'
leads.why: Three things you can act on for P2. (1) The most expensive thing in a full-resolution embedded camera pipeline is often the format conversion, not the algorithm — 21 ms/frame at 12 MP just to turn NV12 into RGB. Your 1920×1440 CLAHE+detect sits on top of whatever your capture path is doing; measure that separately before blaming the detector. (2) NV12 passthrough is 0.05 ms — i.e. the right move is to never materialise a full-res RGB/gray copy at all, and to consume the camera's native plane. On iOS the analogue is consuming the Y plane of the CVPixelBuffer directly as a Metal texture rather than converting. (3) A team deliberately picked a 6x SLOWER fixed-function engine to keep the GPU free — that is the CPU-vs-GPU-placement principle you asked about, stated as a deployment decision, and it argues for pushing CLAHE/pyramid onto the iPhone ISP/VideoToolbox/vImage path where a fixed-function or NEON route exists, rather than assuming GPU is the right home for every stage.

leads.title: PX4 Discuss — 'cuVSLAM as a medium for Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO)' (t/49220)
leads.claim: A lab team flying PX4 with an OAK-D stereo pair + cuVSLAM reports the robotics answer to 'we cannot sustain the camera rate': over-provision the camera and let frames drop, then compensate the resulting latency downstream. Verbatim: 'we upped the frame rate of the stereo pair in the OAK-D up to 45 Hz, so that if we dropped frames, we could meet the alleged minimum 30 Hz that PX4 has recommended. Then we made sure to update EKF2_EV_DELAY accordingly (ours was 50ms, but probably could be tuned better).' Result was stable position-hold flights, autonomous takeoff/hover/land, 'absolutely no toilet bowling'. Earlier in the thread, bench tests showed 'a couple centimeters of odometry drift and a couple degrees rotational drift' over non-flying movement tests.
leads.why: Relevant to P1 in a way that reframes the metric. In robotics, nobody tries to make the vision front end produce a pose per display frame; the vision system feeds an estimator (EKF2) that runs at IMU rate and outputs pose continuously, and the vision channel only has to clear a MINIMUM rate (~30 Hz here) with an explicitly declared measurement latency (EKF2_EV_DELAY = 50 ms). Your '28.4 poses/s vs ARKit 59.9' may be comparing your vision-update rate against ARKit's IMU-propagated output rate. If XRSLAM has (or you add) an IMU propagator that emits poses between camera updates, you can hit 60 poses/s without touching the 16.7 ms GPU budget — and that changes P1 from a throughput problem into a state-propagation problem. Worth checking exactly what your 28.4/s counts before optimising the detector.

leads.title: isaac_ros_visual_slam issue #126 — odometry rate collapses to 5-20 Hz vs 90 Hz expected; fixed by intra-process comms
leads.claim: Jetson Orin Nano 8GB + RealSense D455 (640x360x30 depth, 848x480x15 RGB, gyro/accel 200 Hz). The image topic measured a steady 90 Hz ± 1 Hz, but '/visual_slam/tracking/odometry ... starts with a diminished frame rate of 5-20 Hz where we would expect 90 Hz', recovering to 90 Hz after several seconds; merely running `ros2 topic hz` on a camera topic in another terminal was enough to re-trigger the drop. Reporter's resolution: 'Running with intra-process communication instead of separate nodes seems to fix the issue, and generally things seem to run smoother and more reliably with this setup', though it does not fully eliminate the warnings. Related NVIDIA thread t/328244 shows the same system emitting 'Delta between current and previous frame [34.164736 ms] is above threshold [34.000000 ms]' at 640x480@30, with NVIDIA's answer being that the threshold is the tunable `image_jitter_threshold_ms` parameter ('Acceptable time delta between consecutive synced image messages. If the messages exceed the threshold, it might be an indication of message drop from the source').
leads.why: Two cautions for P1. First, the visible symptom ('we deliver 28.4 poses/s while the camera runs at 30') was, in the closest comparable production system, NOT the tracker's compute at all — it was transport/copy overhead between the camera producer and the SLAM consumer, cured by zero-copy intra-process delivery. Before you re-architect detection, isolate how much of your 28.4/s deficit is buffer handoff between the camera channel, the Metal/Dawn queue and the engine thread. Second, NVIDIA's production handling of late frames is a tunable jitter threshold plus a warning, not back-pressure that collapses latency — your 'back-pressure kicks in and latency collapses' behaviour is a design choice you can replace with drop-oldest plus a declared timestamp, which is what every robotics stack does.

leads.title: SLAMBench2: Multi-Objective Head-to-Head Benchmarking for Visual SLAM (ICRA 2018)
leads.venue: ICRA 2018 (Bodin, Wagstaff, Saeedi, Nardi, Vespa, Mawer, Nisbet, Lujan, Furber, Davison, Kelly, O'Boyle)
leads.license: repo pamela-project/slambench reports NOASSERTION — verify before reuse
leads.claim: An academic harness that treats SLAM as an explicitly multi-objective problem: it reports frame rate (FPS), absolute trajectory error, memory consumption, and power consumption in Watts as co-equal metrics, with per-stage fine-grained timing, over 8 integrated algorithms (KinectFusion, ElasticFusion, LSD-SLAM, ORB-SLAM2, OKVIS, etc.) and 3 platforms named ODROID (Hardkernel ODROID-XU3), TK1 (Jetson TK1) and GTX1080. Important caveat stated in the paper: the power metric 'was relatively ad-hoc, and only supported a specific embedded system (ODROID-XU3)' which exposes on-board power sensors, and 'fine-grained power sensors are still uncommon in embedded development'. The paper demonstrates an accuracy/speed Pareto exploration for KinectFusion (OpenCL) on the ODROID board to find Pareto-optimal parameter settings.
leads.why: Directly on your P2/P3 methodology gap. The framing you need for 'ARKit spends 0 s in thermalState serious and we spend 173 s' is a Pareto front over (pose rate, ATE, memory, Watts), tuned per platform — not a single-number comparison. SLAMBench2's KinectFusion-on-ODROID study is the template: sweep the front-end parameters (resolution, detection interval, feature budget) and pick the Pareto point, rather than assuming full-res-every-frame and then optimising the kernel. Also a useful negative note: even a dedicated academic benchmark could only measure real power on one board with on-die sensors — iOS thermalState occupancy may be the only power proxy you can get, so treat it as your primary P2 metric rather than looking for a Watts number.

leads.title: eLinux — Jetson/Computer Vision Performance: measured board power for CPU vs GPU computer-vision workloads (2016 snapshot)
leads.claim: Whole-board power at 12V with the default fan (0.4W), Jetson TK1 idle ~1.6 W: OpenCV bgfg_segm on CPU = 2.8 W at ~7 FPS (MOG2); the SAME sample on GPU = 2.4 W at ~34 FPS — the GPU version was both ~5x faster and lower total board power. Other GPU workloads on the same board were far hungrier: CUDA bilateralFilter 11.4 W at ~34 FPS @640x480, CUDA boxFilter 7.0 W at ~23 FPS @1024x1024, OpenCV brox_optical_flow 11.5 W, VisionWorks car detector 10 W at ~5 FPS @720p. The page also documents the CPU-side alternative: OpenCV4Tegra (NEON SIMD + multi-core + some GLSL) 'typically provides between 2x - 5x speedup on Tegra 3, Tegra 4 or Tegra K1 compared to regular OpenCV', while the CUDA 'gpu' module gives '5x - 20x speedups on Tegra K1' only for functions suited to GPUs, with 'Some functions (such as Haar Cascade Classifiers) ... not as suited to GPUs so only get minor speedups or don't exist'.
leads.why: The nearest thing I found to a direct energy answer for P2's 'the extra energy is going somewhere else'. It shows the answer is workload-specific rather than categorical: on the same board, one CV workload got faster AND cheaper on the GPU, while other GPU kernels pulled 7-11.5 W against a 1.6 W idle — i.e. a fully-occupied embedded GPU is a 5-10x power multiplier over idle, which is exactly the shape of your thermalState result. It also documents the vendor's own position that NEON+multicore is a 2-5x lever on ARM and that GPU only wins 5-20x for suitable functions — a caution against assuming your bit-exact WGSL port beats a NEON path at 16.7 ms budget. Caveat: Tegra K1 / OpenCV 2.4.9 era, so treat as directional, not as numbers to quote for A16.

leads.title: No prior art: WebGPU/WGSL SLAM or visual-odometry front ends do not exist on GitHub
leads.claim: Authenticated GitHub search API repository queries run 2026-09-08: 'webgpu slam' -> total_count 0; 'webgpu visual odometry' -> 0; 'webgpu computer vision opencv' -> 0; 'wgsl optical flow' -> 0; 'vulkan ORB feature extraction' -> 0; 'opencl ORB SLAM GPU' -> 0. 'wgpu slam' -> 2, both irrelevant (ognis1205/slam-at-home, 21 stars, no license; podo-os/slam-viewer, 10 stars, BSD-3-Clause, a map VIEWER not a front end). Code search for 'wgsl goodFeaturesToTrack' -> 3 hits, all unrelated (a gpu.js learning page, a WebGPU panorama stitcher, a notes file).
leads.why: Direct answer to your cross-cutting question: in the open-source robotics/embedded world nobody has taken your approach — bit-exact GPU replication of an OpenCV front end driven by WebGPU. Every embedded practitioner who GPU-accelerates a VIO front end does it in CUDA (cuVSLAM, OpenCV cuda module), in a vendor fixed-function block (VPI/PVA/VIC, Movidius), or not at all. Two implications: (a) you will find no reference implementation, no known-good constants and no prior negative results to inherit — everything you learn about Dawn/WGSL corner detection on a phone you will learn first; (b) it also means the cross-platform portability argument (iOS Metal + Mali + Adreno from one WGSL source) is genuinely the only thing your approach buys over CUDA-on-Jetson, so it should be weighed explicitly against the option of a NEON/Accelerate CPU path plus a per-platform fixed-function stage.

leads.title: ArduPilot Discuss — Integration of ArduPilot and VIO tracking camera, Parts 1 & 2 (Intel RealSense T265)
leads.venue: ArduPilot Discuss (GSoC 2019 blog series, Thien Nguyen)
leads.claim: The canonical drone-community solution to a power/compute-constrained VIO: move the whole V-SLAM off the application processor. 'The T265's selling point is that all of the complicated V-SLAM algorithms and software run directly on the device itself, thus the computational resources required for the companion computer to run VIO/V-SLAM algorithms, much like these projects on ROVIO ... would be greatly reduced.' System requirements are stated by data type: 'For pose (x y z position and orientation) data: Any board with USB2 should be sufficient. For fisheye image streams: USB3 is required' — i.e. the pose stream costs almost nothing to consume, and a Raspberry Pi 3B with no USB3 runs the full localization use case.
leads.why: Included as the P2 boundary condition rather than as something you can copy (the T265 is a proprietary Movidius VPU and is discontinued). The robotics community's actual verdict on 'our VIO burns too much power on the application processor' was to buy dedicated silicon, and the industry consensus you are up against on iPhone is the same: ARKit is running significant parts of its tracker on Apple's ISP/ANE/dedicated blocks that you cannot reach from Dawn. It is worth stating explicitly in your P2 write-up that a CPU-load-equal comparison against ARKit (0.80 core-equivalents each) does not imply equal silicon usage, and that closing the 173 s vs 0 s gap purely inside a WGSL compute pipeline may not be reachable. No LiDAR/no-cloud constraints are respected here but the vendor-SDK exclusion applies.

leads.title: isaac_ros_visual_slam issue #165 — 'Low frame rate': 3-4 FPS output while the camera streams at ~90 FPS
leads.claim: On an RTX 2060 (not even embedded), with a RealSense streaming images and other topics at ~90 FPS, the visual_slam node output '3-4 FPS' most of the time, but 'sometimes it just runs smoothly on ~90fps' from the identical launch command, 'with no obvious difference in htop or nvidia-smi'. The reporter also noted that merely subscribing to /camera/infra1/image_rect_raw from another machine on the LAN raised the rate to about 60. NVIDIA's responses were about camera firmware/auto-exposure and library versions, not about tracker compute.
leads.why: Corroborates issue #126 from a second reporter and adds the key diagnostic signature for P1: when a VO pipeline collapses from 90 to 3-4 Hz with NO change in CPU or GPU utilisation, the bottleneck is a scheduling/handoff/synchronisation stall, not arithmetic. If your 28.4 poses/s is accompanied by a GPU that is not saturated, look at where the frame waits — queue submission, buffer acquisition, thread handoff — before optimising CLAHE. Weak as evidence (unresolved, desktop GPU), included because the failure signature is distinctive and cheap to check against your own traces.

leads.title: Visual-Inertial SLAM for Unstructured Outdoor Environments: Benchmarking the Benefits and Computational Costs of Loop Closing
leads.claim: Seven VI-SLAM systems (ORB-SLAM3 M-I/S-I, VINS-Fusion, OpenVINS(+VINS-Fusion LC/+HLoc/+Maplab), Kimera, SVO Pro, HFNet-SLAM, AirSLAM) run at 30 / 15 / 5 FPS on the SAME data, host = Intel Core i9-13900HX, 64 GB, Ubuntu 20.04 in Docker. Table 4: ORB-SLAM3 stereo-inertial mean RMSE ATE (Perimeter) = 0.51 m at 30 FPS AND 0.51 m at 15 FPS (LC on), rising to 1.23 m only at 5 FPS. Table 3: HFNet-SLAM mono-inertial mean ATE actually IMPROVES 1.57 m (30 FPS) -> 1.28 m (15 FPS) -> 1.29 m (5 FPS). Table 7 (CPU % of one core / memory GB, Garden Medium Perimeter, LC on): ORB-SLAM3 M-I mean CPU 419.50% @30 FPS -> 325.35% @15 FPS (memory 1.57 -> 1.48 GB); ORB-SLAM3 S-I 403.02% -> 315.23%; VINS-Fusion 266.84% -> 138.73% (-48%); Kimera 638.89% -> 443.41%; SVO Pro 289.07% -> 162.30%. ORB-SLAM3 M-I fails completely at 5 FPS.
leads.why: This is the single most directly usable measurement for P1. It says: going 30 -> 15 FPS costs ~0 accuracy across seven independent systems while cutting front-end CPU by 22-48%; the cliff is at 5 FPS, not 15. Inverted for us: you do NOT need a 60 fps channel, and if you do go to 60 fps you can run detection at 30 Hz and lose nothing measurable. It also gives you a published, citable reason to make 'detection every frame' a product decision rather than a fidelity requirement. Caveat to flag: measured on a desktop CPU with a ground robot at walking speed, not a handheld phone.

leads.title: Kimera: an Open-Source Library for Real-Time Metric-Semantic Localization and Mapping (Kimera-VIO)
leads.claim: Section II-A, verbatim design rule: 'Feature detection, stereo matching, and geometric verification are executed at each keyframe, while we only track features at intermediate frames.' Section III-D timing: 'The vision front-end module shows a bi-modal distribution since, for every frame, we just perform feature tracking (which takes an average of 4.5 ms), while, at keyframe rate, we perform feature detection, stereo matching, and geometric verification, which, combined, take an average of 45 ms.' Front end is Shi-Tomasi corners + Lucas-Kanade tracking (i.e. the same goodFeaturesToTrack + pyramidal LK pair we ported). Repo MIT-SPARK/Kimera-VIO, 1912 stars, license BSD-2-Clause (verified via GitHub API).
leads.why: You said detection runs on every frame 'because that is what the upstream tracker does'. Kimera-VIO is an authoritative, BSD-2-Clause, actively used VIO whose front end is the SAME OpenCV pair as ours and which detects ONLY at keyframes. It is copyable in full under your replication rule, and its own numbers show the detect path is 10x the tracking path (45 ms vs 4.5 ms). This is the cleanest single source to replicate for P1 without inventing a keyframe policy.

leads.title: ILLIXR: Enabling End-to-End Extended Reality Research (arXiv version: Exploring Extended Reality with ILLIXR)
leads.claim: Full XR pipeline (OpenVINS or Kimera-VIO for head tracking + IMU integrator + reprojection + display) measured on desktop (RTX 2080) vs NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier in 10 W mode, high-power and low-power configs. Table 1 targets: AR power today HoloLens 2 > 7 W vs ideal AR 0.1-0.2 W; 'the AR power gap alone is two orders of magnitude'. Power breakdown (Fig. 7b): 'SoC and Sys consume more than 50% of total power on Jetson-LP' — CPU+GPU+DDR are less than half the energy. Quality table: pose ATE = 0.33 +/- 0.15 m (desktop), 0.70 +/- 0.33 m (Jetson-hp), 13 +/- 10 m (Jetson-lp); ATE/degree 8.6 -> 18 -> 138. Text: 'the average VIO frame rate for Jetson-LP stayed high, but the variability in the per-frame execution time resulted in many missed deadlines, which could not be fully compensated by the IMU or reprojection.' Motion-to-photon (AR Demo): 3.0 +/- 0.9 ms desktop, 5.6 +/- 1.4 ms Jetson-hp, 12.0 +/- 3.4 ms Jetson-lp.
leads.why: Two P1/P2 findings that match our symptoms exactly. (1) 'CPU load is 0.80 core-equivalents, same as ARKit, so the extra energy is going somewhere else' — ILLIXR measured that on a mobile-class SoC more than half of XR power is SoC + system (memory controllers, display, camera path, interconnect), not CPU/GPU. That is where to look, and it argues the full-res camera feed itself is a prime suspect. (2) They show that mean frame rate staying high while per-frame VARIANCE grows is exactly what destroys pose quality (ATE 0.33 m -> 13 m for the identical algorithm), which is our 'back-pressure kicks in and latency collapses' failure written up as a measured phenomenon.
leads.license: ILLIXR testbed is open source (check per-component licenses; OpenVINS component is GPL-3.0)

leads.title: RD-VIO: Robust Visual-Inertial Odometry for Mobile Augmented Reality in Dynamic Environments (the algorithm inside OpenXRLab XRSLAM)
leads.claim: Section 4.4.4 Mobile AR Application: 'We use 30 Hz images data with resolution 640 x 480 and IMU data ... with 100 Hz captured by the iPhone X. RD-VIO can run in real-time on mobile devices.' Table 2 module running time (Intel i7-7700 @3.6 GHz, VINS-Mono front-end vs RD-VIO): Keypoint Tracking 8.34 / 7.47 ms; Pre-Integration 0.44 / 0.04; Non-Keyframe PnP 17.78 / 1.27; IMU-PARSAC - / 1.07; Keyframe BA 19.18 / 30.9; Keyframe Marg 32.91 / 3.99; Keyframe Average 60.87 / 42.4; All-frame Average 44.72 / 18.38 ms. Head-to-head vs ARKit on VICON ground truth with two iPhone X + one Xiaomi Mi 8 rigidly tied together: RD-VIO has slightly larger APE than ARKit in a slow static scene (A0), 'on par with ARKit and ARCore in fast-paced scenes (e.g. cases A1 & A2)', and substantially lower APE than both in a scene with moving people (A3). On initialization: 'due to their poor initialization performance, a longer time was required for system initialization ... For example, OpenVINS requires 40 seconds for initialization on MH_01_easy and 35 seconds on MH_02_easy.'
leads.why: This is the upstream authors' own deployment of the exact code we shipped, and they run it at 30 Hz / 640x480 on an iPhone X — not 60 fps at 1920x1440. That is a strong argument that our P1/P2 targets are self-imposed: the authoritative source's own mobile configuration is a quarter-VGA-class 30 Hz pipeline. It also gives the only published XRSLAM-vs-ARKit accuracy comparison against VICON, and their per-module timing shows the front end (7.47 ms keypoint tracking) is not the expensive part on a CPU — keyframe BA is. Finally the OpenVINS 40 s initialization number sets context for P4: 3.6 s is already good for this family of algorithms; 1.5 s is an ARKit-class number, not a research-VIO number.

leads.title: Viability of Feature Detection on Sony Xperia Z3 using OpenCL (MSc thesis)
leads.claim: Max Danielsson and Thomas Sievert, Blekinge Institute of Technology, 2015, with Sony Mobile. Harris-Hessian detector + FREAK descriptor written in OpenCL, run on the GPU of a Sony Xperia Z3 (Snapdragon 800, Adreno 330, 128 ALUs, 4 shader processors). Measured: 'time spent inside of kernels for Harris-Hessian is measured to 5477 ms in a given run and 5705 ms is reportedly spent from the start of the first kernel to the end of the last. Execution of FREAK takes roughly 228 ms.' Same code on desktop i5 + GTX660: 252 ms total application, 161 ms Harris-Hessian of which 150 ms in kernels, FREAK 60 ms — i.e. the phone GPU is ~36x slower than a 2012 desktop GPU on the identical kernels. Thermal experiment: kernel run in a loop for 3500 s while logging on-chip temperature and unit clock frequency; from ~20 C ambient the GPU 'appears to have found a resting temperature variation zone around 50 degrees' after roughly 60 minutes, with visible GPU frequency drops; abstract concludes 'Execution times on Xperia Z3 is deemed insufficient for real-time applications while desktop execution shows that there is future potential. Heat generation is not a problem for the implementation.'
leads.why: The closest published thing to what we did: someone else took an OpenCV-style corner detector, wrote it as GPU kernels, and ran it on a phone GPU, then measured BOTH real-time viability and sustained thermal behaviour over an hour. It is a hard negative on 2014-era Adreno (so it dates, but it is the reference point people cite), and its thermal methodology — log SoC temperature and per-unit clock frequency while looping the kernel, look for the resting temperature and the frequency drops — is directly reusable for our P2 investigation of why we sit 173/300 s in thermalState 'serious'.

leads.title: A Benchmark Comparison of Monocular Visual-Inertial Odometry Algorithms for Flying Robots
leads.claim: MSCKF, OKVIS, ROVIO, VINS-Mono (+/- loop closure), SVO+MSF, SVO+GTSAM on EuRoC (20 Hz WVGA mono + 200 Hz IMU), each run on four platforms with CPU%, memory% and per-frame processing time sampled at 1 Hz: ThinkPad W540 (i7-4810MQ 2.8 GHz, 32 GB, 47 W), Intel NUC (i7-5557U 3.1 GHz, 16 GB, 28 W), UP Board (Atom x5-Z8350 1.44 GHz, 4 GB, 12 W), ODROID XU4 (Exynos 5422 A7@1.5 GHz + A15@2.0 GHz, 2 GB, 10 W, 32-bit, NEON). Negative results: ROVIO on the UP Board — 'no combination of parameters was found such that the filter converged successfully', and the authors attribute it to update rate: 'suggesting that the update rate was too slow with the low clock rate of the Up Board's CPU, despite its otherwise sufficient computing resources'. VINS-Mono could not run with loop closure at all on the ODROID and had to drop from 150 to 100 tracked features on both embedded boards; OKVIS had to drop 400 -> 200 features, keyframe window 5 -> 3, IMU-linked frames 3 -> 2; ROVIO 25 -> 10 features on ODROID. On low frame rate they warn: OKVIS tolerated 'low update rates there due to long per-frame processing times ... but the tolerance of low frame rate may be due in part to the low-speed trajectories in the EuRoC dataset.'
leads.why: The canonical VIO-on-embedded benchmark and the counterweight to lead #1. It is the documented case where dropping the effective update rate did NOT degrade gracefully — a filter-based VIO diverged outright. If we cut the pose/detection rate we should expect the risk to sit in the estimator, not the front end, and the paper names the tell (filter divergence, not gradual ATE growth). It also warns that EuRoC's slow motion flatters low-frame-rate results, which is exactly the caveat to apply to lead #1's 15 FPS finding before we trust it on a handheld phone.

leads.title: ADVIO: An Authentic Dataset for Visual-Inertial Odometry
leads.claim: Back-to-back capture rig: iPhone 6s + Google Pixel + Google Tango tablet rigidly mounted, ~4.5 km of handheld pedestrian motion, ground truth from INS + manual floor-plan fixes. Table 2 records exactly what ARKit runs on: 'iPhone | ARKit pose | 60 Hz' and 'Video | RGB video | Resolution 1280x720 | 60 Hz'; ARCore on the Pixel emits pose at only 30 Hz; Tango 60 Hz. The camera during capture 'is controlled by the ARKit service ... the focal length is kept fixed'. Comparison outcome: Tango best, 'ARKit performs well', ARCore occasionally fails on false visual loop closures, and the two open-source research systems evaluated on the same smartphone data — ROVIO (via maplab) and PIVO — 'diverge and are not shown' in the trajectory figures. ARKit's only catastrophic case was one hard outdoor sequence with 'the classic inertial dead-reckoning failure'.
leads.why: Hard evidence about the baseline we are being measured against: ARKit's 60 Hz pose stream on an iPhone 6s is fed by a 1280x720 camera, not a 1920x1440 one. That reframes P1 and P2 together — we are paying full-resolution camera + full-resolution GPU work per frame to chase a pose rate that Apple achieves at 720p. Also a sobering prior for the whole project: two published open-source VIOs diverged on ordinary handheld phone data where ARKit did not.

leads.title: Visual-Inertial Odometry on Resource-Constrained Systems (PhD thesis, Mingyang Li, UC Riverside)
leads.claim: VIO ported to Android via the NDK and run on a Samsung Galaxy S2 (1.2 GHz Exynos 4210). Simulation on-phone: hybrid MSCKF/SLAM filter averages 33.78 ms per update, 'corresponding to a rate of approximately 30 images per second' with images recorded at 20 Hz — runtime 45.8% smaller than MSCKF 2.0 and 55.6% smaller than m-SLAM. Real-world 5.5 km / 7922-image driving dataset at 10 Hz images, on the same phone processor: 139 ms per update for MSCKF 2.0, 774 ms for m-SLAM, 77 ms for the hybrid filter. Explicit low-frame-rate compensation: 'In this dataset, to compensate for the low frame rate of the images, we use lower feature-detection thresholds, which leads to a larger number of features. Specifically, 540 features are tracked in each image on average, and the average track length is 5.06 frames.'
leads.why: A thesis that quantifies the exact tradeoff we face and states the standard mitigation in one line: when you lower the frame rate, lower the detection threshold and carry MORE features per image. That is a concrete, citable recipe for a 30 Hz (or every-other-frame detection) configuration that does not just throw information away. It is also the earliest careful accounting of VIO cost on a phone SoC.

leads.title: Feature Detection and Description using a Harris-Hessian/FREAK Combination on an Embedded GPU
leads.claim: Peer-reviewed version of the BTH work above (Danielsson, Sievert, Grahn, Rasmusson). OpenCL Harris-Hessian + FREAK evaluated on a Sony Xperia Z3 phone and an Nvidia GTX 660 desktop, compared against FAST/BRISK and ORB on both execution time and matching quality. Conclusion as recorded on the publisher page: 'execution times on the Xperia Z3 are insufficient for real-time applications while desktop execution shows future potential'; the Harris-Hessian/FREAK combination was found sensitive to rotation but good on scale-variant images.
leads.why: The citable, peer-reviewed form of the strongest published negative result on mobile-GPU corner detection. If anyone asks 'has this been tried', this plus the thesis is the answer for the OpenCL/Adreno era. Note the hardware is 2014-class; a 2026 A16/Adreno 660/Mali-G76 result is not covered by it, so it bounds the claim rather than settling it.

leads.title: A Benchmark Comparison of Four Off-the-Shelf Proprietary Visual-Inertial Odometry Systems
leads.claim: Sensors 22(24):9873, 2022, open access. Benchmarks four commercial/proprietary VIO systems against ground truth. Indexed in OpenAlex with 'ARKit' in title/abstract, so ARKit is one of the systems compared. NOT OPENED — MDPI returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl with a browser user agent, so the exact device list and per-system ATE numbers are unverified here.
leads.why: If it can be opened from a browser it is the most likely source of a same-device, ground-truthed ARKit accuracy baseline to sit beside our own 300 s run — i.e. the number that tells us whether matching ARKit's pose rate is even the right target, or whether ARKit's advantage is accuracy rather than rate. Flagged as unverified: open it before citing any number from it.

leads.title: Understanding the Characteristics of Mobile Augmented Reality Applications
leads.claim: ISPASS 2018. Authors Huixiang Chen, Yuting Dai, Hao Meng, Yilun Chen, Tao Li (University of Florida), published April 2018 — author list and date verified against the Crossref API. The paper characterizes mobile AR applications' system behaviour (the ISPASS venue is a performance-analysis conference, so the content is CPU/GPU/memory/power characterization). NOT OPENED — no open-access copy found in OpenAlex, IEEE Xplore returns 403, and general web search was unavailable this session, so no numbers are quoted here.
leads.why: This is the most likely published source of a component-level power/energy breakdown of a mobile AR pipeline on a phone — the missing measurement for P2, where our CPU load matches ARKit's but 173/300 s still go to thermalState 'serious'. Worth one manual lookup through an institutional IEEE subscription. Listed with no claimed numbers precisely because I could not read it.

leads.title: Selective image pyramid computation for motion blur mitigation in visual-inertial tracking (US 12,148,128 B2 / WO 2022/245821 A1)
leads.claim: Snap Inc. Mechanism (abstract, read via PATENTSCOPE record for WO/2022/245821): access a frame; read the optical sensor's CAMERA OPERATING PARAMETERS at capture time (exposure etc.); determine the sensor's MOTION during that exposure (IMU); compute a MOTION BLUR LEVEL from those two; then 'determine whether to downscale the first image using a pyramid computation algorithm based on the motion blur level.' No measured ms/mW figures are given in the abstract; no device named.
leads.why: This is the closest published mechanism to P1. Our GPU spends ~5 ms nominal / 19-22 ms downclocked on CLAHE + corner detection at 1920x1440 EVERY frame because upstream XRSLAM builds the full pyramid every frame. Snap's criterion says the pyramid is conditional, and the condition is computable from data we already have on the iPhone 14 Pro at zero cost: AVCaptureDevice exposureDuration + the IMU angular/linear rate we already feed XRSLAM. It gives us a principled, citable gate ('blur level') instead of a self-invented threshold, and it changes results (fewer levels on some frames), so it must be flagged as a product decision, not a lossless speed-up. Note the licensing trap: this is a mechanism to understand, not code to copy - there is no permissive implementation here, so if we adopt it we still need one authoritative OSS source to replicate.
leads.license: Patent (Snap Inc.) - mechanism and vocabulary only, do not copy

leads.title: Direct scale level selection for multilevel feature tracking under motion blur (US 12,192,625 B2 / WO 2022/246383 A1 / EP 4341902)
leads.claim: Snap Inc. Mechanism (abstract read via PATENTSCOPE, WO/2022/246383): for two consecutive images, determine a motion blur level for each, identify the SCALE CHANGE between them, then 'determine a first optimal scale level for the first image based on the first motion blur level and the scale change' and likewise for the second. i.e. pick ONE pyramid level per frame directly rather than searching all levels. No numbers in the abstract.
leads.why: Companion to the selective-pyramid patent and the sharper form of it for P1: instead of asking 'build the pyramid or not', it asks 'which single level is the right one for THIS frame'. Our pyramidal Lucas-Kanade and goodFeaturesToTrack currently run over the whole pyramid every frame; a per-frame single-level decision is the largest structural cut available on the already-ported path at a 60 fps channel. It is lossy relative to our bit-exact OpenCV 4.0.1 replica, so it lands in the 'explicit product decision' bucket. The pairing of blur level + inter-frame scale change is the vocabulary to carry into a search for a permissively licensed implementation.

leads.title: Keypoint detection and feature descriptor computation (US 2023/0095621 A1 / WO 2023/049590 A1 / EP 4405895)
leads.claim: Qualcomm Incorporated, filed for XR systems. Mechanism (abstract, read in full): obtain feature information for a feature in the CURRENT frame where 'the feature information is based on one or more PREVIOUS frames'; determine an estimated pose for the current frame; obtain a DISTANCE associated with the feature; then 'determin[e] an estimated scale of the feature in the current frame based on the feature information..., the estimated pose, and the distance'. No measured numbers in the abstract.
leads.why: This is the same P1 cut as Snap's, derived from geometry instead of blur: if you already know a landmark's depth and you have a predicted pose, its scale in the next frame is computable, so you never need to search the scale space (i.e. never need the full pyramid) for already-tracked features. XRSLAM already has both inputs - IMU-propagated pose and triangulated landmark depth - so this is implementable inside our existing state, and it only affects re-detection of NEW features. Two independent large filers (Qualcomm + Snap) converging on 'predict the scale, skip the pyramid' is strong evidence that per-frame full-pyramid detection is the recognised waste in mobile VIO front ends, which is exactly our P1 diagnosis.

leads.title: Aggregating features from multiple images to generate historical data for a camera (US 2024/0144526 A1 / WO 2024/096973 A1)
leads.claim: Microsoft Technology Licensing, LLC. Mechanism (abstract, read in full): identify a first feature set in an image at time t1 and a second set at t2; obtain MOVEMENT DATA describing the camera's motion between t1 and t2; 'use[] the movement data to REPROJECT a pose embodied in the first image to correspond to a pose embodied in the second image'; aggregate the two feature sets into an aggregated set; 'the aggregated set of features for the camera are then CACHED'. No measured numbers in the abstract.
leads.why: Directly attacks the sentence in our own problem statement - 'Detection currently runs on EVERY frame because that is what the upstream tracker does.' Microsoft's answer is a persistent, IMU-reprojected, cached feature store: the features from earlier frames are warped forward into the current pose and reused, so a full detection pass is not needed per frame. For us this is a scheduling change on top of an unchanged bit-exact detector (the detector output is identical when it runs; we just run it less often), which makes it the cheapest P1 lever to prototype and the one least likely to disturb the CLAHE/Scharr/Harris/pyrLK equivalence we already proved. It also touches P3: a cached aggregated feature set is a memory cost, so measure footprint when trying it.

leads.title: Fast initialization for monocular visual SLAM (US 2014/0126769 A1 / WO 2014/070483 A1 / EP 2915140)
leads.claim: Qualcomm Incorporated, published 08.05.2014. Mechanism (abstract, read in full): 'a three-dimensional (3D) target is initialized IMMEDIATELY from a first reference image and PRIOR TO PROCESSING A SUBSEQUENT IMAGE'; subsequent reference images are then processed and 'the 3D target is tracked in six degrees of freedom'; 'the 3D target is REFINED based on the processed one or more subsequent images'. No latency numbers in the abstract.
leads.why: This is the published form of exactly what ARKit appears to do and what XRSLAM refuses to do, and it is the single most direct answer to P4 (3.6 s vs 1.5 s). Our bootstrap waits for real translation because it insists on a correct two-view SfM solution before emitting anything; Qualcomm's claim is to emit a usable 6DoF pose from ONE image by assuming an initial 3D target (effectively a planar/assumed-depth hypothesis) and then correcting it as parallax arrives. It reframes P4 from 'make SfM converge faster' to 'ship a provisional structure at frame 1 and refine' - a product decision (early poses are wrong in scale/shape until refined), and one worth costing before we touch the estimator. Filed 2012-2014, so this family is at or near expiry, which also makes it a good pointer to now-unencumbered prior art.

leads.title: Fast and robust initialization method for feature-based monocular visual SLAM using inertial odometry assistance (US 12,115,685 B2)
leads.claim: Assignee MIDEA GROUP CO., LTD., Foshan CN. Appl. 17/305,655, filed 12 Jul 2021, granted 15 Oct 2024, pre-grant pub US 2023/0010105 A1; 16 claims, 12 drawing sheets; inventors Thanh Huy Ha, Yi Chen, Zhicai Ou. Mechanism (abstract read directly off page 1 of the granted PDF): store in a QUEUE, per frame, a data record holding both frame-derived information and IMU information; 'in accordance with a determination that the sequence of inertial odometry data satisfies a first criterion: calculating a first relative pose between the first frame and the second frame'; and 'in accordance with a determination that a difference between the first relative pose and the information extracted from processing the respective frame satisfy a first threshold: generating an initial map of the portion of the environment based on the first data record and the second data record.'
leads.why: The concrete P4 recipe: the IMU, not the vision front end, decides WHICH frame pair to bootstrap from. XRSLAM's 3.6 s is spent feeding candidate pairs into SfM until one converges; here inertial odometry gates the pair (enough baseline) and then a consistency check between the IMU relative pose and the visual measurement gates acceptance. That is a scheduling/selection change outside the estimator, so it does not disturb our bit-exact front end at all. Caveat before anyone gets excited: Midea is an active assignee (granted 2024) and this is a patent, not code - we can use the mechanism to structure the search for a permissively licensed initializer, not to copy. Cross-check against our existing memory note that stella_vslam (BSD-2) is the clean source for keyframe/insertion criteria.

leads.title: Periodic parameter estimation for visual-inertial tracking systems (US 11,662,805 / US 12,210,672 / US 12,704,900; WO 2022/146786)
leads.claim: Snap Inc. Mechanism (abstract, read in full): 'A device OPERATES the visual-inertial tracking system WITHOUT RECEIVING A TRACKING REQUEST from a virtual object display application.' While doing so it accesses sensor data, identifies a first calibration parameter value and STORES it. Later it 'detect[s] a tracking request from the virtual object display application' and, in response, accesses the stored first value and derives a second calibration parameter value from it. Family also covers a sibling filing 'Long term in-field IMU temperature calibration' (US 2024/0192024).
leads.why: A P4 lever nobody on our team has costed: part of ARKit's 1.5 s advantage is almost certainly that iOS has been running and calibrating the sensor stack before the app asked. This claims the warm-start explicitly - run the VI tracker off-request, cache calibration, and start the on-request session from cached values instead of from cold. Concretely for us: if XRSLAM's bootstrap time includes converging IMU bias/extrinsic/temperature terms, caching them across sessions removes that from the 3.6 s. It also matters for P2: 'operate the tracker when nobody asked' is an energy cost, so the same patent family is a warning that the warm-start is not free.

leads.title: Thermal management for extended reality ecosystem (US 12,248,346 B2 / US 2023/0112115 A1 / WO 2023/064227)
leads.claim: Meta Platforms Technologies, LLC. Mechanism (abstract, read in full): receive a request to perform a task; from sensor data across a set of disjoint devices including a wearable, determine a 'THERMAL-CONSTRAINT DIFFERENTIAL' for EACH device; determine the plurality of 'WORKLOAD ASSIGNMENTS' needed to accomplish the task; distribute those assignments across devices 'to satisfy one or more power or thermal constraints associated with each device'. Sibling: 'Rendering workload management for extended reality' (US 2023/0215074 / WO 2023/129552) - decide whether to REDUCE a rendering workload based on a characteristic of the content. No degrees-C or watt figures in the abstracts.
leads.why: This is the vocabulary we are missing for P2. We currently observe an outcome (173 s of 300 s in iOS thermalState 'serious' vs ARKit's 0 s) with no control loop at all - our pipeline does the same full-resolution GPU work regardless of thermal state. Meta's framing gives the two nouns to design around: a per-subsystem thermal-constraint differential (headroom) and decomposition of the perception task into workload assignments that can individually be shed or downgraded. On a single phone there is no second device to offload to, so the transferable half is the second sibling: a policy that explicitly decides to REDUCE the workload when headroom is negative, rather than letting back-pressure and latency collapse do it implicitly as they do now.
leads.license: Patent (Meta Platforms Technologies) - mechanism and vocabulary only

leads.title: Lightweight and low power cross reality device with high temporal resolution (US 2022/0129066 A1 / US 2025/0321633 A1 / CN 113678435)
leads.claim: Magic Leap, Inc. Mechanism (abstract, read in full): 'The wearable display system may DYNAMICALLY RESTRICT PROCESSING of image data from either or both cameras based on detected conditions and XR function being performed. For tracking an object, image information may be processed for PATCHES of a field of view of either or both cameras corresponding to the object.' Full stereo/other image information is used only 'when event-based object tracking yields an INADEQUATE QUALITY METRIC'. The tracked object may be a stationary object in the physical world, 'enabling calculation of the pose of the wearable display system and of the wearer's head'.
leads.why: Two mechanisms for P1/P2 that do not need Magic Leap's DVS hardware. (1) Processing patches of the FOV around known landmarks instead of the whole 1920x1440 frame - our Harris/goodFeaturesToTrack and pyrLK are the exact stages that would benefit, and we already know where the tracked landmarks project. (2) The escalation rule: run the cheap path by default, and fall back to full-frame processing only when a quality metric says the cheap path failed. That is a closed-loop version of the fixed 'detect every frame' policy we inherited, and it gives us a defensible criterion rather than a self-chosen threshold. The DVS/plenoptic parts of the disclosure are not portable to an iPhone 14 Pro - ignore those.

leads.title: Sony Interactive Entertainment - moving crop region per frame for HMD stereo perception (JP 2024-024367 A)
leads.claim: Sony Interactive Entertainment LLC, JP publication 22.02.2024. Mechanism (English abstract, read in full): 'A crop unit 274 of an image generation device sequentially acquires frames of moving images taken by a stereo camera of a head-mount display. A region control unit 300 DETERMINES A REGION TO CROP from each frame WHILE MOVING THE REGION WITH RESPECT TO THE TIME AXIS according to a predetermined rule. A crop processing unit 302 crops some regions from each frame according to the determination. A correction unit 304 corrects an image formed by cropping by using a correction parameter prepared in relation to a plurality of regions set as regions to crop.' Stated problem: 'to efficiently acquire information of an actual world by using a taken image.'
leads.why: The cheapest possible P1/P2 idea and the one that maps most directly onto a GPU budget: don't process every pixel every frame, process a sub-window that ROTATES over the frame across time, so the whole field is covered over N frames at 1/N the per-frame cost. At a 60 fps channel with a 16.7 ms budget and a downclocked GPU costing 19-22 ms for full-res CLAHE + detection, an N=2 or N=4 rotating crop is arithmetically sufficient on its own. It is also compatible with keeping our detector bit-exact on the pixels it does see. Found only via a Japanese-language query; it does not surface in English searches.

leads.title: Dynamic camera selection and switching for multi-camera pose estimation (WO 2024/118233 / US 2026/0099943 / CN 120344998)
leads.claim: Qualcomm Incorporated (inventor Kuchibhotla, Phalguni). Mechanism (abstract, read in full): 'a process can include PREDICTING A FUTURE POSE of the apparatus; identifying a set of TRACKED FEATURES; and SELECTING A SUBSET of cameras from a plurality of cameras for feature tracking based on the identified set of tracked features and the future pose of the apparatus.' Related Apple filing found in the same query: 'Dynamic camera selection' (US 2023/0401732 A1 / CN 119343930), switching between cameras for determining information about a physical environment.
leads.why: Generalises to P1 even though we are monocular: the claimed decision procedure is 'predict where you will be, work out which features will still be visible, and only run the expensive vision on the sensor/region that will actually contribute'. Substitute 'pyramid level' or 'image region' for 'camera' and it is the same scheduling primitive as leads 1-4. It is included mainly as corroboration that predicted-pose-driven gating of the front end is the industry-standard lever, and as the source of the phrase 'select a subset ... based on the identified set of tracked features and the future pose', which is a good query string for finding a permissively licensed implementation.

leads.title: Electronic Device with Centralized User Experience Manager (US 2024/0201776 A1)
leads.claim: Apple Inc., published 20.06.2024, IPC G06F 1/3287. Mechanism (abstract, read in full): 'An electronic device may include software and hardware subsystems that are CENTRALLY CONTROLLED by a user experience manager. The user experience manager can IDENTIFY A CURRENT USER CONTEXT and ENFORCE A CORRESPONDING POWER AND PERFORMANCE POLICY for the various subsystems that is optimized for [that context].' Surfaced repeatedly at the top of thermal + visual-inertial + power queries.
leads.why: The nearest thing found to a description of the machinery on the other side of our P2 comparison - why the SAME iPhone spends 0 s in thermalState 'serious' running ARKit and 173 s of 300 s running ours. The claimed structure is a single arbiter that knows the user context and pushes one coherent power/performance policy down into every subsystem, including the camera and the compute blocks. Our stack has no such arbiter: camera resolution, GPU work per frame and engine rate are all fixed constants chosen at build time. Treat this as evidence for a design requirement (one policy owner that can lower camera resolution, detection cadence and pyramid depth together as one decision) rather than as an algorithm to copy. It is a pre-grant publication with no measurements.
leads.license: Patent (Apple) - vocabulary and design requirement only

leads.title: CMOS-assisted inside-out dynamic vision sensor tracking for low power mobile platforms (US 2019/0356849 / US 2021/0075964 / WO 2019/221580)
leads.claim: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd., Appl. No. 16/415,813, inventors Michael Sapienza / Ankur Gupta. Mechanism (abstract, read in full): a dynamic vision sensor (DVS) emitting an asynchronous event stream plus a CMOS image sensor emitting frames; a 'HYBRID FEATURE HANDLER' takes either input and supplies tracked features to a visual-inertial SLAM pipeline doing inside-out tracking; and a 'SENSOR SCHEDULER configured to SWITCH OFF THE CMOS IMAGE SENSOR based on a current value of one or more CMOS control factors'.
leads.why: Include this as a NEGATIVE result that saves time. It is the top hit for 'visual inertial' + 'power consumption' across every database queried, so anyone repeating this search will land on it - but its whole saving comes from having an event sensor to fall back to while the frame camera is powered down, and the iPhone 14 Pro has none. It is not implementable for us and there is no permissive code. The one portable idea is the noun 'sensor scheduler': an explicit component whose job is deciding when the frame camera runs, separate from the tracker. Our camera runs continuously at full resolution at 30 fps regardless of what the tracker needs, and P2 says that is part of the energy bill.
leads.license: Patent (Samsung) - not implementable without a DVS

leads.title: Efficient multi-scale ORB without image resizing (US 2023/0410461 A1 / WO 2023/245133 / EP 4540793 / CN 119365904)
leads.claim: Snap Inc. (US pre-grant lists inventor Nithin Gollahalli Ananda; EP/WO list SNAP INC as applicant). Mechanism (abstract, read in full): 'accessing a camera image generated by an optical sensor of an augmented reality (AR) device, accessing a query image from a storage of the AR device, and identifying, using a feature detector program, the query image in the camera image WITHOUT SCALING THE CAMERA IMAGE.' i.e. multi-scale robustness is obtained by varying the detector's own sampling pattern rather than by resizing the image into a pyramid.
leads.why: Third member of the Snap 'stop paying for the pyramid' cluster, and the most radical: it removes image resizing from the multi-scale path entirely. For us the resize/blur passes are a measured cost on the GPU (our own bench history shows two-pass blur and pyramid construction are a large share of the extract budget on both Mali and A16), so a detector that gets scale invariance without building the pyramid attacks the same P1 bytes from a third direction. Caveats: the claim is scoped to marker/query-image detection rather than general VIO corner tracking, and ORB is not our detector - we replicate OpenCV goodFeaturesToTrack/Harris. Lowest applicability of the three Snap filings; listed for completeness of the mechanism space.
